OP001 Effects of oxytocin receptor antagonization in migraine: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human provocation study

M. P. Fitzek1,2, P. Kleist1, C. Handtmann1, L. H. Overeem1, K. S. Lange1,2, C. L. Höhne1, C. Angerhöfer1, U. Reuter1,3, B. Raffaelli1,2

1Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Department of Neurology, Berlin, Germany; 2(Junior) Clinician Scientist Program, Berlin Institute of Health (BIH), Berlin, Germany; 3University Hospital Greifswald, Greifswald, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP001

Objective Hormonal phases with a decline in oxytocin (OT) levels are associated with an increased incidence of migraine attacks. Beyond temporal correlations, OT multifaced functions, including analgesic effects, interactions with the CGRP pathway and modulation of the trigeminovascular system further support a potential role in migraine pathophysiology. The aim of this study was to investigate whether inhibition of OT signaling through receptor blockade induces migraine attacks in humans.

Methods In this randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, cross-over study, women with episodic migraine (18-45 years, 1-5 monthly migraine days) and healthy female controls were randomized to receive an infusion of the OT-receptor antagonist atosiban (6.75 mg bolus over 1 min + 30.75 mg over 1.5 h) or placebo on two experimental days separated by at least one week. All participants were required to undergo continuous hormonal contraception in order to ensure stable estrogen and progesterone levels. The primary endpoint was the difference in the incidence of migraine attacks between atosiban and placebo during the 12-hour post-infusion period.

Results Twenty women with migraine (27.1 +/- 5.6 years) and 20 healthy controls (25.7 +/- 6.8 years) completed the study. During the 12-hour observation period, 30% of migraine patients experienced migraine attacks after atosiban vs. 20% after placebo (p = 0.51). Headache of any kind was reported by 75% after atosiban vs. 55% after placebo (p = 0.34), with no significant difference in headache intensity over 12 h. Healthy controls did not develop migraine but reported headaches in 45% after atosiban vs. 30% after placebo (p = 0.25).

Conclusion Short-lasting oxytocin inhibition through the OT-receptor antagonist atosiban did not significantly increase the incidence of migraine attacks in women with episodic migraine, although a numerical trend was observed.

OP002 Biochemical profiling and symptomatology of androgen deficiency in males with cluster headache – A prospective case-controlled study

W. Naber1, R. Brandt1, M. Leon Morales - Grooters2, R. van der Wal2, S. van den Berg2, J. Goeman1, A. Maassen van den Brink2, R. Fronczek1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Rotterdam, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP002

Objective Cluster headache (CH) is considered a male-dominated disorder, suggesting a role for androgens in its pathophysiology. We aimed to evaluate hormone profiles in CH.

Methods In this prospective case-controlled study, fasted morning blood samples were collected in 30 males with chronic CH (CCH) and 33 males with episodic CH (ECH, in episode and remission) and in 30 healthy age-matched males(HC). Androgen dysfunction surveys (QADAM, AMS) were collected simultaneously. Steroid hormone profiles were compared between groups: total testosterone(tT) including biochemical hypogonadism(tT≤10.5); hormonal pathways and individual hormones. Regression models were applied with BMI, age and smoking as covariates.

Results Biochemical hypogonadism was observed in 20% of participants with CCH(n=6), 6% with ECH(n=3) and 7% with HC(n=2). AMS and QADAM scores were worse in participants with hypogonadism, in ECH (AMS:β=9.59, p<0.001,QADAM:β=-5.25, p<0.001), and CCH(AMS:β=8.78, p<0.001,QADAM:β=-4.59, p<0.001) compared to HC. Apart from one case, gonadotrophin concentrations were not increased, suggesting a central origin. In the unadjusted model, we observed a trend towards a lower, albeit non statistically significant, mean tT in participants with CCH versus HC (CCH:β=-2.35 nmol/L, p=0.059). In the adjusted model, the differences attenuated, suggesting a strong effect of BMI and age on the mean tT(CCH:β=-0.93 nmol/L, p=0.524;ECH:β=0.55 nmol/L, p=0.674). Measures of hormonal pathways and individual hormones did not differ between groups.

Conclusion Biochemical hypogonadism was observed in 1 out of 5 males with CCH. tT trended to be lower in CCH, but this appeared driven by BMI and age since it attenuated after correction. Androgen deficiency symptoms were more prevalent in CH compared to healthy controls, independent of hypogonadism. Physicians should be aware of potential increased risk and symptoms of (central) hypogonadism in CCH. Further investigation should explore shared underlying mechanisms and tT suppletion in CH.Fig. 1 (abstract OP002).Fig. 2 (abstract OP002).Fig. 3 (abstract OP002).

OP003 Non-paralytic botulinum toxin A in trigeminal neuralgia

A. David Pereira1, B. Davletov2, A. Andreou1

1King’s College London, London, UK; 2University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP003

Objective Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is the most common craniofacial chronic neuropathic pain type and is among the most severe pain types. It manifests as short, electric shock-like pain paroxysms in areas enervated by the trigeminal nerve. Acute treatments are ineffective, and current preventative pharmacotherapies are often limited by poor specificity, inadequate efficacy, and severe side effects. To address these limitations, recombinant botulinum toxin A (BoNT/A) molecules (el-Bitox/A) retaining analgesic but minimal paralytic activity have been developed. This study evaluated el-Bitox/A analgesic efficacy and safety versus native BoNT/A and carbamazepine (CBZ), to the gold-standard treatment, in a TN rat model.

Methods TN was induced by chronic constriction injury of the infraorbital nerve (IoN-CCI) in male and female rats, and mechanical allodynia was monitored over two weeks using von Frey monofilaments. el-Bitox/A (20 ng) and BoNT/A (5 U) were injected subcutaneously into the ipsilateral cheek one week post-surgery. CBZ (30 mg/kg) was given intraperitonially for 7 days and effects assessed after the first dose (acute) and 7 days (chronic). Body weight was monitored as an indirect measure of facial paralysis due reduced jaw strength and impaired food intake.

Results Mechanical allodynia was reversed by el-Bitox/A and BoNT/A. Acute CBZ had no effect on mechanical allodynia, and only partial reversal was seen after 7 days (n=5–7 per group; P<0.05). BoNT/A, but not el-Bitox/A or CBZ, caused significant weight loss (P<0.05), confirming the non-paralytic profile of el-Bitox/A. Vehicle had no effect in both parameters (n=6 per group).

Conclusion Both BoNT/A and el-Bitox/more effectively reversed TN-associated hypersensitivity than the gold-standard CBZ. However, BoNT/A had significant side effects that can be avoided by using the non-paralytic el-Bitox/A. These findings highlight el-Bitox/A as a promising, effective treatment option for neuropathic pain.

OP004 Interictal subcortical and cortical anomalies in the sensorimotor pathway of subjects with migraine: A resting state high-density EEG analysis

G. Sebastianelli1, C. Porcaro2, S. Gilli1, C. Abagnale1, F. Casillo1, G. di Lorenzo3, G. Coppola1

1Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Medico Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies, Latina, Italy; 2University of Padua, Department of Neuroscience (DNS) and Padova Neuroscience Center (PNC), Padua, Italy; 3University of Rome Tor Vergata, Department of Systems Medicine, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP004

Objective To determine whether the interictal electroencephalographic (EEG) changes observed in subjects with migraine result from aberrant rhythmic pacemaker activity of subcortical or cortical structures within the sensorimotor pathway.

Methods A resting state 64-channel EEG was recorded in 42 subjects with migraine without aura (MO) during their interictal phase and for comparison in 42 healthy volunteers (HV). The brain activity of four nodes in the sensorimotor pathway (brainstem, thalamus, S1, and M1) was extracted using a functional source separation approach (FSS) with ad-hoc spatial functional constraints. Spectral characteristics and Higuchi’s fractal dimension (FD) were examined for each node to estimate the linear and non-linear brain activity and its complexity.

Results Compared to HVs, subjects with MO had significantly elevated FD values in the brainstem and thalamus in both the left and right hemispheres. No significant differences in FD values were observed between the two cortical nodes (S1 and M1). Additionally, MO showed an increase in delta and a decrease in alpha power spectral density in all four nodes of the sensorimotor system.

Conclusion Subjects with MO during the interictal phase have alterations in the linear and non-linear functioning of the brainstem and thalamic subcortical nodes in the sensorimotor system. These alterations may be pivotal in the migraine pathophysiology, causing changes in the rhythmic patterns of the cortex.

OP005 Neurofilament light chain and glial fibrillary acidic protein as serum biomarkers of treatment response to CGRP monoclonal antibodies in migraine

K. Berati1,2, K. A. Ebner1,2, N. Rommers2, S. Sellathurai1,2,3,4, A. Gugleta2, K. Schoenholzer1,2,3,4, A. Gantenbein1,5, T. Sprenger6, S. Schaedelin2,3,7, A. Maleska Maceski2,3,7, P. Benkert2,3,7, C. Granziera1,2,3,4, J. Kuhle1,2,3,7, A. Papadopoulou1,2,3,4

1University Hospital Basel, Clinic of Neurology, Basel, Switzerland; 2University Hospital of Basel, Department of Clinical Research, Basel, Switzerland; 3Research Center for Clinical Neuroimmunology and Neuroscience Basel (RC2NB), University Hospital Basel and University of Basel, Basel, Switzerland; 4Translational Imaging in Neurology (ThiNK) Basel, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Faculty of Medicine, University Hospital and University of Basel, Basel, Switzerland; 5ZURZACH Care, Department of Neurology and Neurorehabilitation, Bad Zurzach, Switzerland; 6University Hospital of Zuerich, Zurich, Switzerland; 7University Hospital of Basel, Neuroimmunology Unit and Multiple Sclerosis Centre, Basel, Switzerland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP005

Objective There is urgent need for biomarkers in migraine. We aimed at investigating the associations of serum -neurofilament light chain (sNfL) and -glial fibrillary acidic protein (sGFAP) with treatment response to Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide monoclonal antibodies (CGRP mAbs).

Methods In this prospective observational study, patients with chronic or high-frequency episodic migraine were recruited, before treatment start with CGRP mAbs. sNfL and sGFAP levels were measured at baseline (BL) and month 6 (M6) and were converted to percentiles as previously described. Treatment response was defined as ≥50% reduction in monthly headache days (MHD) at M6 vs. BL. The trajectories of biomarker percentiles were investigated using linear mixed models. The associations of BL-biomarkers with treatment response were analyzed using univariable- and stepwise multivariable logistic regression.

Results 68 patients (median age:40 years(y), disease duration:17 y, 84% female, 60% chronic, median MHD at BL:18) were included. sNfL and sGFAP levels at BL were not elevated (median percentile of sNfL:39, IQR [19, 61], sGFAP:30, IQR [13, 54]). At M6, 33/68 (49%) of the patients were responders. Biomarker percentiles did not change over six months (median sNfL at M6:32, sGFAP:33; both p>0.465). Univariable analysis showed no significant associations between BL sNfL or sGFAP, and treatment response at M6 (p=0.523 and p=0.082, respectively). In the multivariate analysis, higher sGFAP percentile at BL (OR=0.958, 95% CI [0.922, 0.994], p=0.023) and more BL-MHDs (OR=0.839, 95% CI [0.723, 0.972], p=0.020) were associated with lower probability of being a responder.

Conclusion Higher sGFAP percentiles at baseline were associated with worse response to CGRP-mAbs in the multivariable analysis. While the role of this biomarker in migraine is still under investigation, a potential value in disease phenotyping and prediction of treatment responses seems promising and should be validated in larger cohorts.

OP006 Corneal confocal microscopy reveals nerve fiber laterations in migraine irrespective of subtype or visual hypersensitivity

G. M. Terwindt1, R. van Welie1, F. van Welie1, A. Dahan1, M. Tavakoli1, M. van Velzen1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP006

Objective Corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) is a noninvasive ophthalmic imaging technique for evaluating the corneal microstructure, particularly the subepithelial nerve plexus. This dense, dynamic plexus contains small nerve fibers from the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. This study aimed to evaluate corneal nerve alterations in individuals with migraine, including its subtypes and visual hypersensitivity (measured with L-VISS).

Methods Participants were individuals with episodic (EM) or chronic (CM) migraine, and controls. All subjects underwent CCM, and automated corneal nerve fiber density (ACNFD), length (ACNFL), and branch density (ACNBD) were assessed using the Rostock Cornea Module (Heidelberg Retina Tomograph III). Data were compared with age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers.

Results Reduced ACNFD, ACNFL, and ACNBD were found in migraine participants compared to controls (all p <0.001). No difference was found between EM and CM, and regression analysis showed no significant effect for (inter)ictal visual hypersensitivity.

Conclusion These findings support the utility of CCM as a sensitive tool for detecting nerve fiber pathology in migraine and highlight its potential in further understanding migraine pathophysiology. The observed nerve changes, present irrespective of migraine frequency status or visual hypersensitivity, suggest a broader role for peripheral nerve dysfunction in migraine beyond sensory hypersensitivity symptoms.

OP007 Breaking the chronic migraine cycle: Semaglutide modulates pain, well-being, and cannabinoid signaling in a preclinical study

A. Micov1, K. Sićović1, K. Nastić1, M. Dinić2, U. Pecikoza1

1Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Belgrade, Department of Pharmacology, Belgrade, Serbia; 2University of Belgrade, Institute of Molecular Genetics and Genetic Engineering (IMGGE), Belgrade, Serbia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP007

Objective Chronic migraine (CM) is a disabling neurological disorder that profoundly impairs quality of life. Up to 70% of patients are dissatisfied with current prophylactic therapies. GLP-1 receptor agonists, particularly liraglutide, have shown potential in reducing pain hypersensitivity in preclinical and clinical settings. Chronic migraine has been associated with dysregulation of the endocannabinoid system (ECS), including altered CB1 receptor (Cnr1) and endocannabinoid-degrading enzyme (Faah, Mgll) expression. We aimed to assess semaglutide’s effects on pain-like behaviour, well-being, and cannabinoid signaling in a mouse model of CM.

Methods Male and female mice developed a CM-like state through repeated intraperitoneal (i.p.) nitroglycerin injections. Semaglutide (subcutaneous) or propranolol (i.p., reference drug) was administered daily over nine days. The orofacial glutamate test (chemical-stimulus evoked facial pain) and the burrowing test (indicative of spontaneous pain and well-being) were used for behavioural evaluation. Brainstem and trigeminal ganglia (TG) samples were collected post-mortem for qPCR analysis of Cnr1, Faah, and Mgll mRNA expression to assess ECS involvement.

Results Semaglutide significantly reduced glutamate-evoked nociceptive behavior in both sexes, with efficacy comparable to propranolol. However, only semaglutide restored burrowing behaviour in males and females. Molecular analysis revealed sex- and region-specific ESC modulation: in males, semaglutide upregulated Cnr1 and Faah in the brainstem and downregulated Cnr1 and Mgll in the TG; in females, brainstem Faah and Mgll expression was decreased.

Conclusion Semaglutide reduced pain-like behaviour comparably to propranolol while also enhancing motivational behavior, suggesting broader benefits for overall well-being. Semaglutide modulated ECS in a sex-specific manner, indicating distinct neurobiological responses in males and females. These results support semaglutide as a promising candidate for CM therapy.Fig. 1 (abstract OP007).Fig. 2 (abstract OP007).Fig. 3 (abstract OP007).

OP008 Cannabidiol in chronic migraine prevention: Results of a pilot randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

C. Laino1, A. J. Arroyo2, S. Amaya3, N. Maresca4, A. L. Bazan5, E. Musella5, E. Spitzer6, M. Tinelli6, D. di Leo6, M. Deprati6

1National University of La Rioja, Institute of Biotechnology-Pharmacology, La Rioja, Argentina; 2Hospital Provincial Dr Vera Barros, Neurology, La Rioja, Argentina; 3Hospital de la Madre y el Niño, Nursing, La Rioja, Argentina; 4Hospital Provincial Dr Vera Barros, Pharmacy, La Rioja, Argentina; 5Hospital Provincial Dr Vera Barros, Biochemistry, La Rioja, Argentina; 6Laboratorio ELEA, Investigacion y Desarrollo, Buenos Aires, Argentina

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP008

Objective To evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of escalating doses of Cannabidiol (CBD) for the prevention of chronic migraine.

Primary objective

To evaluate the change in the average number of migraine days per month with increasing doses of CBD over the 3-month treatment period compared to the placebo group.

Secundary obtective

To assess the evolution of migraine intensity in relation to treatment from baseline and explore the relationship between CBD dose escalation and migraine-free days.

Methods This study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial for CBD dose escalation, involving 30 patients with chronic migraines, selected according to specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. Elea Laboratory (Argentina) provided the investigational product (CBD) along with a corresponding placebo. All participants were divided into three groups: placebo, CBD at 10 mg/ml, or 20 mg/ml, for a duration of three months.

Results After three months, CBD 10 mg/ml and CBD 20 mg/ml demonstrated a 68% and 79% reduction in monthly migraine days compared to the placebo group (Fig. 1).

After three months, the CBD 10 and 20 mg/ml groups reported that 64% of patients experienced migraine-free days, with the CBD 20 mg/ml treatment showing an increase to 79%. In contrast, the percentage of patients treated with a placebo decreased by 15%, indicating that migraine-free days diminished rather than increased, which is a negative outcome (Fig. 2).

Somnolence was the most commonly observed side effect during the three treatments.

Conclusion The results of this study demonstrate that CBD at 10 or 20 mg/ml appears to be effective and well-tolerated for the preventive treatment of chronic migraine, justifying further studies with a larger population.Fig. 1 (abstract OP008).Migraine days (mean ± 95% CI) during each 1-month interval. ** P < 0. 05Fig. 2 (abstract OP008).Relationship between CBD dose escalation and migraine-free days Safety

OP009 Exploring the central effect of anti CGRP-monoclonal antibodies in migraine patients: A resting-state functional MRIstudy

I. Cetta1,2,3, F. Genovese1,2,3, A. Visentini1,2,3, L. Zanandrea2,3, B. Colombo2, M. Filippi1,2,3, R. Messina1,2,3

1Neuroimaging Research Unit, IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy; 2IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Neurology Unit, Milan, Italy; 3Vita-Salute San Raffaele University, Milan, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP009

Objective While MRI studies have explored brain changes in migraine patients treated with anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), direct comparisons with untreated patients over time are lacking. We used resting-state functional MRI (RS-fMRI) to compare patients treated with mAbs (mAbs group) to untreated (non-mAbs group), aiming to isolate treatment-specific central effects.

Methods Forty-eight migraine patients were enrolled: 37 received mAbs and 15 were untreated. Thirty-three matched healthy controls (HC) were assessed at baseline. Clinical and MRI evaluations were performed at baseline and after 3 months (3 M). Resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) was analyzed using a seed-to-voxel approach based on 11 regions of interest, including cerebellum, periaqueductal gray (PAG), pons, thalamus, hypothalamus, and spinal trigeminal nucleus (STN). Clinical outcomes included monthly migraine days (MMD), acute medication day (AMD) and pills (AMP), pain intensity, disability, headache impact, and cutaneous allodynia.

Results At baseline, migraine patients showed increased RS FC between the left (L) pons and L frontal gyrus and reduced FC between the cerebellum and right (R) insula compared to HC. Moreover, the mAbs group, characterized by higher MHD, MMD, and AMP, showed reduced RS FC between the L STN and the L cerebellum compared to the non-mAbs group. After 3 M, compared to non-mAbs patients, the mAbs group demonstrated greater overall clinical improvement and a significant increase in RS FC between the L STN and L cerebellum, which correlated with decreased migraine frequency.

Conclusion Patients eligible for mAbs showed altered pain network connectivity, indicating a more severe phenotype. Compared to untreated, mAbs patients had greater clinical improvement and STN network reorganization, supporting central effects beyond the natural disease course. Rs-FC may serve as a biomarker of migraine severity and treatment response.

OP010 Selective reduction of circulating β-CGRP in patients developing de-novo constipation during anti-CGRP antibody therapy

L. de La Guerra-Sasián1,2, G. Gárate1,2, V. González Quintanilla1,2, M. Muñóz1,2, M. Polanco1,2,3, M. Pascual-Mato1,2, J. Pascual Gómez1,2,3

1Marqués de Valdecilla Health Research Institute (IDIVAL), Santander, Spain; 2Marqués de Valdecilla University Hospital, Santander, Spain; 3Universidad de Cantabria, Santander, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP010

Objective To investigate the role of CGRP isoforms in the development of de-novo constipation in migraine patients treated with monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP (mAb-CGRP).

Methods We conducted a prospective study in 133 patients diagnosed with high-frequency episodic or chronic migraine. Plasma concentrations of α-CGRP and β-CGRP were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) at baseline (M0) and three months (M3) after initiating mAb-CGRP therapy. Clinical data, including onset of constipation, comorbidities, and therapeutic response, were collected and analyzed.

Results De-novo constipation was reported in 12 patients (9.0%) following initiation of mAb-CGRP treatment. Baseline demographics, efficacy parameters, use of concomitant preventive therapies, and most comorbidities did not differ between groups, except for a higher prevalence of anxiety/depression in those with constipation. A significant reduction in α-CGRP levels was observed at three months (M0: 49.5 [IQR 29.2–73.8] pg/mL; M3: 40.5 [20.4–61.0] pg/mL; p < 0.0001), occurring similarly in both groups. While overall β-CGRP levels remained unchanged over the course of treatment (M0: 4.0 [2.1–6.2]pg/mL; M3: 4.3 [2.5–6.0]pg/mL; p=0.574), a selective reduction was observed only in patients who developed constipation (M0: 6.1 [4.7–8.4] pg/mL; M3: 5.0 [3.6–5.7] pg/mL; p=0.034).

Conclusion This is the first study to demonstrate a selective decrease in β-CGRP in patients with de-novo constipation during mAb-CGRP therapy. The findings support a mechanistic role of β-CGRP antagonism, particularly relevant to gastrointestinal function regulation, in this adverse event, while α-CGRP antagonism appears more closely tied to therapeutic migraine benefit.

This research was supported by grant PMP22/00183.

OP011 Unraveling the spectrum of migraine resistant to Anti-CGRP treatments: Is there a role for the endocannabidiome system?

G. Vaghi1,2, R. Greco1, A. Zanaboni2, C. Demartini1,2, M. Francavilla1,2, S. Facchetti1,2, M. Corrado1, F. Bighiani1,2, A. Antoniazzi1,2, F. Cammarota1,2, V. Grillo1,2, G. Sances1, M. Allena1, N. Ghiotto1, E. Guaschino1, R. Ornello3, S. Sacco3, C. Tassorelli1,2, R. de Icco1,2

1IRCCS Mondino Foundation, Headache Science & Neurorehabilitation Unit, Pavia, Italy; 2University of Pavia, Department of Brain and Behavioral Sciences, Pavia, Italy; 3University of L’Aquila, Department of Biotechnological and Applied Clinical Sciences, L’Aquila, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP011

Objective Monoclonal antibodies targeting the CGRP pathway (mAbs) fail in nearly 40% of migraine individuals that may bear a non CGRP-dependent phenotype, potentially attributable to endocannabinoid system (eCBome) dysfunction. Primary aim is to compare eCBome catabolizing enzymes expression of Fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and Monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) between mAbs Responders (RES) and Non-responders (NON-RES). Secondary aims assess differences in other eCBome enzymes (DAGL, NAPE, NAAA), plasma levels of endocannabinoid-associated lipids (AEA, 2-AG, PEA, OEA) and neuropeptides (CGRP, PACAP and VIP).

Methods We enrolled 59 individuals treated with mAbs (age 43.2 ± 13.2 years), 83.1% females, 34 with high frequency episodic migraine, 25 with chronic migraine, who failed 3.4±1.1 preventive medication classes. NON-RES presented <50% reduction in monthly migraine days in the third month of mAbs compared to baseline. At baseline, we assessed mRNA gene expression (Relative Quantification-RQ) of FAAH and MAGL and eCBOMe enzymes in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and performed plasma quantifications of endocannabinoid-associated lipids and neuropeptides.

Results Out of the 59 subjects, 45 completed the 3-month follow-up, with 57.8% (n=26) qualifying as RES. MAGL expression was higher in NON-RES (1.97±0.61 RQ) vs. RES (1.58±0.63 RQ, p=0.018). No differences were observed for FAAH (NON-RES 0.75±0.22 RQ vs. RES 0.74±0.25 RQ, p=0.868) and the other eCBome components analyzed. Among neuropeptides, only VIP presented higher plasma levels in NON-RES (151.80±73.33 RQ) vs. RES (91.84±54.89, p=0.031).

Conclusion NON-RES presented an elevated 2-arachidonoyl glycerol turnover, a key component of the eCBome. This is consistent with previous evidence of an increased MAGL expression in migraine individuals with a severe disease phenotype. Our preliminary findings suggest that a eCBome dysfunction may be pronounced in mAbs NON-RES.

OP012 Alpha-synuclein deficiency attenuates nociceptive signaling in mouse trigeminal afferents relevant to migraine

G. Krivoshein1, R. Giniatullin2, A. M. J. van den Maagdenberg1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, Netherlands; 2University of Eastern Finland, Kuopio, Finland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP012

Objective Migraine has been linked to an elevated risk of neurodegenerative disorders, yet the biological mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. One potential link involves α-synuclein, a neuronal protein encoded by the Snca gene, which is essential for synaptic plasticity and neurotransmitter release. While abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein, is a hallmark of Parkinson Disease (PD), its role in pain signalling is poorly understood. Notably, in PD, a very common accompanying symptom is pain, the mechanisms of which are little understood. Interestingly, α-synuclein is a part of neuronal secretory machinery, which is relevant to migraine-related mechanisms of pain, associated with transmitter/neuropeptide release. In this study, we investigated the impact of α-synuclein deficiency on nociceptive signaling in trigeminal meningeal afferents, a key pathway implicated in migraine pathophysiology.

Methods Adult C57BL/6JOlaHsd mice (Harlan strain) of both sexes, which carry a chromosomal deletion of the Snca gene, served as the experimental group. Age- and sex-matched C57BL/6J mice were used as controls. Electrophysiological recordings of nociceptive spiking activity were obtained from trigeminal meningeal afferents under baseline conditions and following stimulation with 50 mM KCl to assess generalized excitability.

Results Baseline nociceptive spiking activity was reduced in meningeal afferents of C57BL/6JOlaHsd mice (31 ± 23 spikes/10 min) compared to C57BL/6J controls (997 ± 382 spikes/10 min). Similarly, KCl-induced neuronal excitability of primary afferents was dramatically lower in C57BL/6JOlaHsd mice (64 ± 27 spikes/30 s), representing a 4.7-fold reduction relative to controls (305 ± 63 spikes/30 s).

Conclusion These findings indicate that α-synuclein deficiency attenuates nociceptive signaling in the trigeminal system, suggesting a previously unrecognized role for α-synuclein in modulating pain pathways associated with migraine.

OP013 Semaglutide mitigates pain hypersensitivity and cognitive dysfunction in a murine model of chronic migraine: Possible role of opioidergic signaling pathways

K. Sićović1, K. Nastić1, M. Dinić2, U. Pecikoza1, A. Micov1

1University of Belgrade, Department of Pharmacology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Belgrade, Serbia; 2University of Belgrade, Institute of Molecular Genetics and Genetic Engineering (IMGGE), Belgrade, Serbia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP013

Objective Chronic migraine (CM) is a debilitating headache characterized by persistent pain hypersensitivity and cognitive deficits. Therapeutic strategies targeting both domains remain limited. Preclinical data suggest that GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), particularly liraglutide, may alleviate pain in CM. While their procognitive effects are established in other neurological conditions, it is unclear if these benefits extend to CM. We aimed to assess whether semaglutide (a GLP-1 RA) improves pain sensitivity and cognition in a mouse model of CM, focusing on opioidergic signaling and sex differences.

Methods A CM-like state was induced in C57BL/6 mice of both sexes by repeated intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections of nitroglycerin. Semaglutide (subcutaneous) and propranolol (i.p.; positive control) were administered daily for nine days. Pain hypersensitivity was evaluated using the von Frey test (VFT), and cognitive performance by the novel object recognition test (NORT). Opioidergic involvement was assessed by (1) naloxone (non-selective opioid receptor antagonist) and (2) qPCR analysis of Glp1r and Pomc1 mRNA expression in brainstem and trigeminal ganglia.

Results Semaglutide dose-dependently reduced both basal and acute mechanical hypersensitivity, with efficacy comparable to propranolol in both sexes. Unlike the reference drug, semaglutide significantly improved cognitive performance regardless of sex. Naloxone reduced its antinociceptive effect in the VFT and tended to diminish cognitive benefits in the NORT, indicating opioidergic mediation. In brainstem, both Glp1r and Pomc1 were upregulated in males, while only Glp1r was increased in females. No significant changes were detected in trigeminal ganglia.

Conclusion Semaglutide mitigated pain hypersensitivity via opioidergic pathways and, in contrast to the reference drug, improved cognitive performance in CM mice. These findings support its potential to address both nociceptive and cognitive domains of CM.

OP014 Implementation of an occupational health programme for migraine management: Lessons from the workplace MiGRA-Care study

M. Plácido1,2, R. Gil-Gouveia3,4, L. Ferreira5,6, R. Paizinho2, B. Santos2, P. A. Laires1

1NOVA National School of Public Health, Public Health Research Centre, Comprehensive Health Research Center, Lisbon, Portugal; 2MiGRA Portugal - Portuguese Migraine and Headache Patients’ Association, Lisbon, Portugal; 3Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 4Universidade Católica Portuguesa, Center for Interdisciplinary Research in Health, Lisbon, Portugal; 5Universidade do Algarve - ESGHT, Research Centre for Tourism, Sustainability and Well-Being (CinTurs), Faro, Portugal; 6Centre for Innovative Biomedicine and Biotechnology, Coimbra, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP014

Objective Migraine is a leading contributor to productivity loss. Despite international recommendations, occupational health interventions for migraine remain scarce. This study aimed to evaluate preliminary implementation outcomes of Workplace MiGRA-Care, a migraine management programme at work.

Methods A Type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation randomized study was conducted in Portuguese companies with ≥250 employees. The intervention comprised 4 components: (1) training sessions for health professionals, (2) workplace migraine management checklist, (3) digital self-management toolkit, and (4) migraine-specific medical consultation. Participants with self-reported migraine were randomized (1:1) to intervention or control.

Results Recruitment began in Nov 2023 and lasted 11 months. Of 155 companies identified, 139 were contacted and 56 responded. Following screening, 35 companies attended a project presentation and 11 (8%) adopted the programme. Main reasons for non-participation were insufficient occupational health capacity (n=12; 34%), internal bureaucratic hurdles (n=4; 11%), and cost concerns (n=1; 3%). One company was national, 7 in northern Portugal and 3 in Lisbon district. Sectors included electric equipment, public administration, communications, transport, social services, food, retail, health, and insurance. 539 workers consented; 371 met eligibility and were randomized. Around 80% were female, 70% had higher education, 80% reported prolonged computer use, over half lacked medical follow-up, and <25% used preventive treatment. In 9 companies, most workers had office roles; 1 company had >70% workers in physical roles, and another >70% workers in customer service. By June 2025, the intervention was completed in 7 companies with 80 consultations over 8 months, 11 participants dropped out and 16 missed appointments.

Conclusion It is viable to implement a migraine programme at work, despite logistical challenges. The sector diversity and worker profiles support the programme’s scalability.

OP016 Overlap between perceived triggers, premonitory symptoms, and symptom persistence across migraine phases: A REFORM study

J. Thuraiaiyah1, R. H. Christensen1,2,3, H. M. Al-Khazali1,2,3, A. Wiggers1, M. Ashina1,2,4, H. Ashina1,2,3

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Faculty of Health and Medical Sciences, Copenhagen, Denmark; 3Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Translational Research Center, Copenhagen, Denmark; 4Danish National Knowledge Center on Headache Disorders, Copenhagen University Hospital – Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP016

Objective To evaluate the overlap between common trigger factors and corresponding premonitory symptoms in persons with migraine, and to assess the presence of non-headache symptoms across migraine phases.

Methods Individuals with migraine were enrolled in this cross-sectional study during September 2020 to June 2022 as part of the prospective, single-center Registry for Migraine (REFORM) study. Data was based on participant recall. The presence of trigger factors, premonitory symptoms, non-headache symptoms during the headache and postdromal symptoms were obtained as part of a semi-structured interview.

Results Among 632 participants (mean age 44.6 ± 12.0 years; 89% female), the most frequent triggers were sleep disturbances (70.1%), stress (67.7%), and alcohol consumption (59.0%). Common premonitory symptoms included tiredness (39.9%), concentration difficulties (35.0%), and neck pain (33.2%). Significant associations were found between specific triggers and premonitory symptoms: bright light with premonitory photophobia (OR, 2.79; 95% CI, 1.90 to 4.12; P < 0.001), loud noise with premonitory phonophobia (OR, 4.26; 95% CI, 2.77 to 6.59; P < 0.001), and sleep disturbances with premonitory tiredness (OR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.15 to 2.64; P = 0.009). A positive association was seen between all examined premonitory and postdromal symptom (P < 0.05), except for tiredness (OR, 1.51; 95% CI, 0.89 to 2.57; P = 0.12).

Conclusion Our results reveal a notable overlap between specific migraine triggers and corresponding premonitory symptoms, implicating that some perceived triggers could be early signs of an impending attack. Moreover, the continuation of most premonitory symptoms into the postdromal phase suggest that migraine-related symptoms extend across a broader temporal continuum than previously recognized.

OP017 May differential blockade of αCGRP and βCGRP with receptor antagonists underly differences in the efficacy and side-effect profile of anti-migraine drugs?

D. M. Boucherie1, M. Pawlowsky1, D. Schutter1, A. van den Bogaerdt2, R. Dammers3, A. Vincent3, A. H. J. Danser1, A. Maassen van den Brink1

1Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Division of Pharmacology and Vascular Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, Rotterdam, Netherlands; 2ETB-BISLIFE, Heart Valve Department, Beverwijk, Netherlands; 3Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Department of Neurosurgery, Rotterdam, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP017

Objective Data on the effect of CGRP pathway blockers on αCGRP and βCGRP are heterogeneous. We aimed to characterize the blocking effect of the truncated antagonist CGRP8-37 in isolated human and porcine arteries across several vascular beds.

Methods Relaxation responses to αCGRP and βCGRP were measured in the absence or presence of CGRP8-37 in porcine coronary arteries (PCA), human coronary arteries (HCA), and human middle meningeal arteries (HMMA).

Results In distal PCA (n=10–11), αCGRP and βCGRP induced a similar, potent vasodilation (pEC50 8.4±0.4; Emax 87±30 and 91±23). In proximal PCA (n=6–7), αCGRP induced stronger vasodilation than βCGRP (pEC50 of 8.4±0.9 vs. 7.8±0.4, p=0.03; Emax of 84±17% vs. 67±17%, p=0.0009). CGRP8-37 (1 µM) was ~8x more potent at blocking functional responses to αCGRP (pKB 6.59±0.35) than βCGRP (pKB 5.71±0.51; p=0.01) in distal PCA (n=6). Surprisingly, no significant blocking effect was observed in proximal PCA (n=5–7). In HCA (n=5-6), 1 µM CGRP8-37 did not block relaxation to αCGRP or βCGRP. In proximal HCA, 3 µM CGRP8-37 was ~6x more potent at blocking αCGRP (pKB 6.37±0.70) than βCGRP (pKB 5.60±0.41; p=0.002), whereas it was equally potent at blocking αCGRP (pKB 6.06±0.60) and βCGRP (pKB 6.21±0.33) in distal HCA. In HMMA (n=7), 3 µM CGRP8-37 trended towards a ~3x higher potency on βCGRP (pKB 6.84±0.42) than αCGRP (pKB 6.39±0.42; p=0.07).

Conclusion CGRP8-37 acts differently in PCA vs. HCA and across vascular beds, indicating a system bias that warrants further pharmacological investigation. Mapping αCGRP and βCGRP functional differences upon CGRP receptor antagonism may clarify the efficacy and side-effect profiles of anti-migraine medications.Fig. 1 (abstract OP017).

OP018 Src family kinases-associated H3K27me3 regulation of C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2) gene expression in a rat model of migraine

Z. Gong1, M. Wang1

1Xi’an jiaotong-Liverpool University, Biological Sciences and Bioinformatics, Suzhou, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP018

Objective Src Family Kinases (SFK) are critical in neuroinflammation and were implicated in inflammatory gene expression via H3K4me3, a chromatin openness marker, as novel transcriptional regulators in migraine pathophysiology (unpublished). However, the role of repressive histone marks in these conditions remains elusive. This study investigates the involvement of H3K27me3 in CCL2 expression following cortical spreading depression (CSD) and the mechanistic involvement of SFK. Specifically: Examine CCL2 gene level and H3K27me3 enrichment at CCL2 promoter post-CSD; Assess gene levels of the key H3K27me3 histone-modifying enzymes in response to CSD; Determine relationships between H3K27me3 enrichment at CCL2 promoter with CCL2 gene level, SFK activity and H3K4me3 enrichment at the same loci.

Methods Adult male SD rats were used, with animal procedures approved by the university ethics panel and under national and provincial rules. Conclusion CSD reduces the SFK-associated H3K27me3 at the CCL2 promoter, facilitating transcription through chromatin de-repression. The findings bring a new insight into histone modification in migraine-related neuroinflammation.

OP019 RAMP1-dependent hormonal regulation of CGRP and its receptor in the trigeminal ganglion

L. Edvinsson1, A. Holm1

1Swedish headache society, Medicine, Lund, Sweden

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP019

Objective Menstrual migraine (MM) is a debilitating neurological disorder triggered by fluctuations in ovarian hormones, particularly estrogen. This study investigates how sex hormones regulate CGRP-related gene expression in the trigeminal ganglion (TG), with a focus on the receptor activity-modifying protein 1 (RAMP1), using both wild-type (WT) and Ramp1 knockout (KO) mice.

Methods We analyzed gene expression in the TG across the estrous cycle and following systemic estrogen or progesterone administration. Expression of Ramp1, Calca (encoding CGRPα), Calcrl (encoding CRLR), estrogen receptors, and related genes was assessed by RT-qPCR. WT and Ramp1 KO mice of both sexes were used to explore hormone-dependent gene regulation and RAMP1’s functional role.

Results Ramp1 expression varied across the estrous cycle, peaking in proestrus and declining in diestrus, inversely correlated with Calca. Calcrl levels remained unchanged. Ramp1 expression correlated significantly with Esr2 (encoding ERβ), suggesting estrogen receptor–mediated regulation. Estrogen treatment upregulated Ramp1 in both sexes; Calca was downregulated in females but upregulated in males. In Ramp1 KO mice, the cyclical variation of Calca, RAMP2, and Ramp3 seen in WT mice was absent, and basal Calca expression was elevated in males, indicating that RAMP1 is essential for hormonal regulation of the CGRP system. Additionally, our findings support a role for estrogen-driven epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation, in the long-term regulation of Ramp1.

Conclusion RAMP1 as a key mediator linking hormonal fluctuations to CGRP signaling in the TG. Hormone-dependent gene expression changes were sex-specific and disrupted in Ramp1 KO mice, supporting its role in migraine susceptibility. We provide mechanistic insight into hormonal migraine and suggest that both acute hormone signaling and long-term epigenetic regulation shape individual sensitivity to CGRP-based therapies.

OP021 Mesocorticolimbic functional connectivity dysregulations in chronic and episodic cluster headache patients

A. Nigri1, G. Demichelis1, D. Fedeli1, G. Ciullo1, J. P. Medina Carrion1, R. Gianeri2, A. Deruti1, M. Grisoli1, B. Becker3, S. Usai4, L. Chiapparini5, A. Erbetta1, A. Cecchini Proietti4, L. Giani6, S. Ferraro3, M. Leone4

1IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, Neuroradiology Unit, Milan, Italy; 2Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Genoa, Italy; 3University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China; 4IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, Neuroalgology Unit and Headache Center, Milan, Italy; 5Fondazione IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo, Pavia, Italy; 6Istituti Clinici Scientifici Maugeri IRCCS, Milan, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP021

Objective CH is a primary headache disorder characterized by short-lasting, strictly unilateral craniofacial pain with autonomic symptoms. Converging evidence suggests that alterations in the hypothalamus and dopaminergic mesocorticolimbic system may contribute to the onset and chronification of pain disorders. To investigate functional connectivity alterations within the mesocorticolimbic system in both episodic (eCH) and chronic (cCH) cluster headache.

Methods We enrolled 68 adult CH patients (23 cCH, 45 eCH) and 26 healthy controls (CTRL), who underwent 3T resting-state fMRI. Functional data were analysed with CONN toolbox; images of patients with right-sided attacks were flipped to the left. Region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI analyses, with age and sex as covariates, included the following regions: frontal cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, nucleus accumbens, ventral tegmental area (VTA), and hypothalamus. Results Both eCH and cCH patients showed significant functional connectivity alterations compared to CTRLs. OP022 Treatment of chronic cluster headache with occipital nerve stimulation: A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial

I. S. Fogh-Andersen1,2, J. C. H. Sørensen1,2, A. S. Petersen3, R. H. Jensen3, K. Meier1,2,4

1Aarhus University Hospital, Department of Neurosurgery, Aarhus, Denmark; 2Aarhus University Hospital, Center for Experimental Neuroscience (CENSE), Department of Clinical Medicine, Aarhus, Denmark; 3Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Glostrup, Denmark; 4Aarhus University Hospital, Department of Anesthesiology, Arhus, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP022

Objective ccipital nerve stimulation (ONS) has shown promising results in attack prevention in patients with CCH, but evidence from controlled trials is scarce. Conventional (tonic) ONS elicits paresthesia, hampering blinded comparison to placebo. Using paresthesia-free burst ONS, we conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial.

Methods The study is an investigator-initiated, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial involving patients with CCH. It comprised a four-week baseline, a 12-week trial with transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, ONS implantation, a 12-week randomized, double-blind burst ONS treatment period, and a 12-week open-label tonic ONS treatment period. The primary outcome was the proportion of participants reporting a ≥30% reduction in attack frequency in the randomized and open-label trial phases.

Results Thirty-eight patients underwent ONS implantation and were randomly assigned to burst ONS (n=19) or placebo (n=19). After the randomized trial phase, the proportion of ≥30% responders was 18.81% (95%CI 0.28%-37.87%) in the burst ONS group and 50.02% (95%CI 26.87%-73.09%) in the placebo group. The likelihood of reaching the primary endpoint was 31.20% (95%CI 1.29%-61.23%, p=0.042) higher in the placebo group. After the open-label phase, 42.09% (95%CI 19.91%-64.34%) in the burst ONS group and 51.11% (95%CI 27.32%-74.88%) in the placebo group had ≥30% frequency reduction.

Conclusion ONS reduced attack frequency but was not superior to placebo. The results indicate that a part of the preventive effect of ONS may be attributed to a placebo response and call for attention to sufficient placebo control when planning further studies.

Objective Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is a neurometabolic disorder in which disease activity is linked to weight change. Methods This is an open-label randomized controlled trial conducted at two tertiary Danish headache centers. Lumbar OP nearly normalized by both strategies. Final conclusions on the eligibility and superiority of GLP1-RA in IIH await effects on headache, quality of life and long-term outcomes.

OP024 Alterations in gut microbiota and the endocannabinoid system in an animal model of chronic migraine

S. Facchetti1,2, C. Demartini1, M. Francavilla1,2, R. Greco1, C. Tassorelli1,2

1IRCCS Mondino Foundation, Pavia, Italy; 2University of Pavia, Department of Brain and Behavioral Sciences, Pavia, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP024

Objective The endocannabinoid system (ECs) is a complex cell-signalling system present in the nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. It regulates inflammatory responses and intestinal homeostasis via interactions with the gut microbiota, ultimately influencing brain function indirectly through gut-derived circulating factors and directly via vagus nerve signalling. Increasing evidence suggests a role for ECs in chronic migraine. This study assessed whether gut dysbiosis is associated with ECs alterations, centrally and peripherally, in a chronic migraine-like animal model induced by repeated nitroglycerin (NTG) administration.

OP025 Identifying candidate molecular biomarkers in idiopathic intracranial hypertension patients

L. J. Hill1, G. Begum1, J. Hubbard1, C. Mugo1, H. Botfield1, H. Lyons1, M. Thaller1, M. Sassani1, A. Yiangou1, O. Grech1, J. L. Mitchell1, S. P. Mollan1, A. J. Sinclair1

1University of Birmingham, Birmingham, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP025

Objective Idiopathic Intracranial hypertension (IIH) is a neurological disease associated with obesity and raised intracranial pressure (ICP) often causing severe headaches, visual loss and reduced quality of life. IIH is frequently misdiagnosed, with confirmation requiring invasive lumbar puncture. Monitoring disease progression is also complex, involving repeated visual assessments and sometimes further lumbar punctures. A reliable, non-invasive diagnostic and monitoring tool remains an unmet need. This study aimed to identify candidate serum microRNA (miRNA) markers in adults with active IIH.

Methods Serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples (n=9) were collected from patients with active IIH and 12 months later during disease remission induced by bariatric surgery. RNA was isolated, converted to cDNA and analysed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) using a 40- miRNA panel. Candidate serum miRNAs were also assessed in control participants with obesity and with migraine. Candidate miRNAs identified in patients with active IIH were evaluated against clinical characteristics.

Results Serum miRNAs (5/40) expression was significantly lower in active IIH patients compared to when in remission. Of these, hsa-miR-16-5p (p<0.0001) and hsa-miR-7-5p (p=0.0032) were significantly lower in active IIH compared to patients with obesity. hsa-miR-16-5p (p=0.0354) and hsa-let-7a-5p (p=0.0310) were significantly raised in CSF of patients with active IIH compared to in remission. hsa-miR-16-5p in serum and CSF significantly correlated with ICP (p<0.0001, p=0.046) and papilledema (p=0.0346, p=0.0241).

Conclusion We have identified two potential candidate miRNA biomarkers (hsa-miR-16-5p and hsa-miR-7-5p) in the serum of patients with active IIH which have a high degree of sensitivity and are associated with clinical measures of disease activity. These results are the first step towards developing a less invasive diagnostic and monitoring biomarker which would lead to a step change in patient care.

OP028 Profiles of migraine patients treated with triptan: A study based on data from the French nationwide claims database

X. Moisset1,2, M. Lantéri-Minet3, C. Lucas4, M. Dalichampt5, J. Mawet6

1CHU Clermont-Ferrand, Neurology, Clermont-Ferrand, France; 2Université Clermont Auvergne, Clermont-Ferrand, France; 3Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Nice, Pain Department and FHU InovPain, Nice, France; 4Lille University Hospital, Pain Unit, Neurosurgery Department, Lille, France; 5Regional Health Observatory, Pays de la Loire, Nantes, France; 6Lariboisière Hospital, AP-HP, Emergency Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Paris, France

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP028

Objective Although recommendations for the diagnosis and management of migraine have been published, it is managed in a very heterogeneous way. Here, we describe the profiles and care pathways of migraine patients treated with triptan in France.

Methods Retrospective cohort study of migraine patients treated with at least one triptan, identified in the 2/100th French Nationwide claims database (ESND) from 2016 to 2021 and analysed from 2006 to 2022.

Results Among the 37,884 migraine patients identified, 76% were women and 30% were covered by Universal Complementary Health Insurance. The mean age was 36.6 years at the first triptan. This initial prescription was issued by a general practitioner in 91% of cases and by a neurologist in 4%. Among patients treated with triptans for less than 4 months (39%), 66% received concomitant analgesics, mainly non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, 43%), and 18% received weak opioids. In patients treated for more than 4 months (61%), co-dispensing of analgesics was observed in 94% of cases, mainly paracetamol (87%) and NSAIDs (85%), while 51% received weak opioids. The management of migraine patients evolved following triptan initiation. In the year preceding the first triptan dispensing, NSAIDs were prescribed to 52% of patients, increasing to 89% in the following year. A similar trend was observed for weak opioids (30% before vs. 73% after) and strong opioids (1% before vs. 7% after). Preventive migraine therapies were dispensed to 9% of patients prior to triptan initiation and to 39% thereafter. Additionally, the proportion of patients with at least one sick leave increased from 43% to 52% post-initiation.

Conclusion We highlight here the heterogeneous management of triptan users in France and the change of care pathways after the first triptan dispensing.

OP029 Investigation of the relationship between weather and headache attacks: Smartphone application data analyzed with artificial intelligence

M. Katsuki1,2,3,4, M. Tatsumoto5,6, K. Kimoto7, T. Iiyama8, M. Tajima8, N. Iwami8, T. Miyamoto8, K. Suzuki6, T. Shimazu9, S. O’Connor2, K. Moran2,3,10

1Nagaoka University of Technology, Physical Education and Health Center, Niigata, Japan; 2Dublin City University, School of Human and Health Performance, Dublin, Ireland; 3Dublin City University, Insight Science Foundation Ireland Research Centre, Dublin, Ireland; 4Saitama Medical University, Department of Biostatistics, Saitama, Japan; 5Canon Marketing Japan Inc, Canon Marketing Japan Inc, Tokyo, Japan; 6Dokkyo Medical University, Department of Neurology, Tochigi, Japan; 7Nanao Hospital, Department of Neurology, Ishikawa, Japan; 8BellSystem24, Zutool, Tokyo, Japan; 9Saitama Neuropsychiatric Institute, Department of Neurology, Saitama, Japan; 10Maynooth University, Department of Sport Science and Nutrition, Maynooth, Ireland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP029

Objective To investigate the relationship between weather and headache attacks using big data from smartphone app combined with AI.

Methods Using data from January to December 2023, we selected users who had used triptans or lasmiditan at least once and recorded headaches on 1–14 days per month, identifying them as having episodic migraine. We applied a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) to estimate hourly headache occurrences (records/hour) based on various weather variables: barometric pressure (hPa), temperature (℃), humidity (%), precipitation (mm/hour), sunlight duration (hours), wind speed (m/s), the pressure change from 6 h earlier, and the 6 a.m. barometric pressure on the day of the headache, the following day, and two days later. These variables were selected based on prior research. Additionally, following our previous study, we categorized 6-day time-series barometric pressure patterns (4 days before and 2 days after the headache record) into four types (Types I–IV) using one-to-one Euclidean clustering (Fig. 1 A-F). Random effects in the model included age, sex, season, time of day, and regional climate classification.

Results Among the 10,248 users included (321,709 headache records), the average age was 41.2 years (SD 10.8), and 92.5% were female (n = 9,479). The GLMM revealed significant associations between increased hourly headache frequency and multiple weather variables: higher rainfall, longer sunlight exposure, stronger wind, lower barometric pressure compared to 6 h earlier, and lower pressure at 6 a.m. the following day. Barometric pressure patterns classified as Type I (persistently low), Type II (dropping around the headache), and Type IV (persistently high) were also linked to more frequent headache reports.

Conclusion This real-world big data analysis demonstrated that several weather conditions—including rain, sunshine, wind, and falling barometric pressure—are significantly related to hourly headache occurrence.Fig. 1 (abstract OP029).

OP030 Ultrasound-guided dry needling of suboccipital muscles: Precision targeting of myodural trigger points and correlated biomarkers in headache disorders

R. Bubnov1, L. Kalika2, Y. Brosgol3

1Clinical hospital Pheophania, Kyiv, Ukraine; 2New York Dynamic Neuromuscular Rehabilitation & Physical Therapy, New York, NY, USA; 3New York Dynamic Neuromuscular Rehabilitation & Physical Therapy, New York, NY, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP030

Objective Tension-type headaches (TTH) and migraines are often linked to central sensitization and myodural dysfunction. The suboccipital muscles—particularly the obliquus capitis inferior (OI) and superior (OS)—form a functional myodural bridge that influences cerebrospinal fluid dynamics. Tiny myofascial trigger points within these muscles can significantly alter muscle tone and dural mechanics. Precise ultrasound-guided dry needling (US-DN) combined with advanced imaging biomarkers may offer a novel treatment and monitoring approach. To evaluate the effects of ultra-precise US-DN on headache symptoms, myodural biomechanics, and to explore the correlation between shear wave elastography (SWE) and spinal dural oscillations.

Methods Sixteen patients (6 migraine, 10 TTH) received US-DN targeting 1–3 mm trigger points in the OI and OS muscles. Needle placement was confirmed with real-time B-mode ultrasound. Muscle stiffness was quantified using SWE with a 2–3 mm ROI. Spinal dural oscillations at C1–C2 were captured via M-mode ultrasonography. Ophthalmic artery Doppler and superb microvascular imaging (SMI) assessed vascular and microvascular changes.

Results Trigger points within the suboccipital muscles showed markedly increased stiffness on SWE (6 m/s) versus adjacent normal tissue (1–3 m/s). Following pinpoint US-DN, stiffness values normalized to 2–3 m/s, in parallel with a reduction in high-frequency spinal oscillations (from 160 to 320 Hz to ~80 Hz). This strong correlation suggests SWE and oscillation frequency are reliable, complementary biomarkers of muscle tone and dural stress. SMI revealed no detectable microvascularity in the trigger areas. DN of the OS muscle also reduced referred TMJ-associated migraine symptoms.

Conclusion SWE and spinal dural oscillations are highly correlated and offer a combined biomarker system to guide and monitor treatment. US-DN represents a precise, personalized approach for managing headaches linked to myodural dysfunction and central sensitization.Fig. 1 (abstract OP030).

.

OP031 Tolerability, safety, and efficacy of atogepant versus topiramate in participants requiring preventive treatment for migraine: Results from the head-to-head TEMPLE trial

U. Reuter1,2, A. van Dycke3, S. J. Tepper4, M. K. Farkas5, G. Forero6, L. Luo6, H. Guo6, E. Cohen6, K. Nagy6

1University Hospital Greifswald, Greifswald, Germany; 2Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Berlin, Germany; 3General Hospital Sint-Jan Bruges, Department of Neurology, Brugge, Belgium; 4The New England Institute for Neurology and Headache, Stamford, CT, USA; 5Semmelweis University, Pediatric Center, Budapest, Hungary; 6AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP031

Objective We compared the tolerability, safety, and efficacy between atogepant (ato), an oral calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonist, and topiramate (topi) in participants requiring preventive migraine treatment.

Methods TEMPLE was a 24-week, randomized, double-blind (DB), double-dummy, active controlled trial with a 52-week open-label safety extension to evaluate tolerability, safety, and efficacy of atogepant 60 mg once daily (QD) compared to the highest tolerated dose of topiramate (50, 75, or 100 mg/day) for preventive treatment of migraine in participants with episodic or chronic migraine. Conclusion Atogepant 60 mg QD demonstrated superior tolerability and efficacy compared with topiramate. Atogepant was generally safe and well tolerated and no new safety signals were identified.

OP036 Toward human-relevant models of migraine: Exploring vascular signaling in endothelial cells

V. Gkouzioti1, W. Winter2, G. K. Wardhana3, A. Abdollahzadeh4, F. van den Hil5, V. Orlova5, R. Giniatullin4, T. L. Costa3, M. Mastrangeli3, A. M. J. van den Maagdenberg1,2, J. P. Frimat2

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Leiden University Medical Center, Human Genetics, Leiden, Netherlands; 3Delft University of Technology, Microelectronics, Delft, Netherlands; 4University of Eastern Finland, A.I. Virtanen Institute for Molecular Sciences, Kuopio, Finland; 5Leiden University Medical Center, Anatomy and Embryology, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP036

Objective The vascular system plays a key role in migraine pathophysiology, though mechanisms remain unclear. The interaction between CGRP, a major migraine mediator, and Piezo1, a mechanosensitive channel, remains unexplored. Human iPSC-derived endothelial cells (hiPSC-ECs) offer a relevant model to study vascular signaling. Focused ultrasound (FUS) is a promising non-invasive neuromodulation tool to study mechanosensitive channels. Using a custom miniaturized FUS generator, we examined Piezo1 responses to ultrasound to explore the role of Piezo1 in migraine-relevant pathways.

Methods Intracellular calcium (Ca²⁺) activity was assessed in hiPSC-ECs after stimulation with Yoda1, a Piezo1 agonist, with or without CGRP co-treatment. To investigate downstream effects, we performed immunostaining for paxillin to assess focal adhesion (FA) formation. This effect was blocked by the CGRP receptor antagonist BIBN4096, confirming specificity. CGRP sensitization also increased the size of paxillin-positive FAs. In contrast, FUS did not activate Piezo1 in HUVECs, likely due to suboptimal acoustic conditions. However, Yoda1-induced activation triggered clear Ca²⁺ responses, confirming Piezo1 involvement.

Conclusion These findings suggest CGRP–Piezo1 crosstalk in hiPSC-ECs, supporting their use in migraine-related vascular modeling. While FUS did not activate Piezo1 in HUVECs, chemical activation confirmed its Ca²⁺-dependent role.

OP037 Beyond CGRP receptor blockade: Exploring the mechanisms of traditional migraine prophylactic drugs propranolol and candesartan

T. T. Liu1, D. M. Boucherie1, S. P. Zhang2, S. J. Wang3,4, J. C. Yen2, S. P. Chen5,6, A. Maassen van den Brink1

1Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Internal Medicine, Rotterdam, Netherlands; 2National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Pharmacology, Taipei, Taiwan; 3Taipei Veterans General Hospital, Department of Neurology, Taipei, Taiwan; 4National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Medicine, Taipei, Taiwan; 5National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Clinical Medicine, Taipei, Taiwan; 6Taipei Veterans General Hospital, Translational Research, Taipei, Taiwan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP037

Objective The mechanisms by which traditional prophylactic medications exert their effects in migraine prevention remain incompletely understood. This study aims to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of two commonly used agents, propranolol and candesartan.

Methods We examined the mechanisms by which propranolol and candesartan prevent migraine in two experimental models. First, CGRP receptor involvement was assessed using isolated distal porcine (PCA) and human coronary artery (HCA) segments (1–2 mm internal diameter) mounted on a Mulvany myograph system. After precontraction using 30 mM KCl, dose-response curves to αCGRP and capsaicin were obtained in the presence or absence of propranolol and candesartan. Secondly, cortical spreading depression (CSD) susceptibility, representing the pathophysiological basis of migraine aura, was examined using a KCl-induced (1 M) CSD model in rats. In CSD model, topiramate and amlodipine were also studied.

Results In porcine and human coronary arteries, propranolol and candesartan did not notably shift the dose–response curves of αCGRP-induced vasodilation (pEC50: 8.2±0.63 for PCA; 8.7±0.41 for HCA) at clinically relevant concentrations (20–400 nM for propranolol; 3.3–540 nM for candesartan), nor did they affect capsaicin-induced vasodilation (pEC50: 5.47±0.88 for PCA; 4.46±1.84 for HCA), the latter representing a CGRP-independent pathway. However, candesartan (1 mg/kg/day, 3 weeks) inhibited KCl-induced CSD frequency by 23.81%. Topiramate reduced CSD frequency by 28% at 80 mg/kg and by 30% at 200 mg/kg. In contrast, amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker without migraine prophylactic effects, showed no effect on CSD frequency.

Conclusion These findings suggest that propranolol and candesartan may not exert their prophylactic effects via direct antagonism of CGRP receptors. Instead, inhibition of CSD may represent a mechanism underlying their prophylactic actions. Their potential presynaptic effects on endogenous CGRP release remain to be investigated.

OP038 The contribution of menstrual migraine to risk for Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular disease

1Mayo Clinic, Neurology, Phoenix, AZ, USA

Objective The relationship between migraine and increased risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease (CVD) is well established, particularly in those with migraine with aura. .

OP039 Discriminating migraine aura from transient ischemic attack using MRI-based oxygen metabolism mapping

P. Pernot1, A. Bani-Sadr2,3, E. Ong1,4, T. H. Cho1,4, Y. Berthezene2,3, G. Demarquay5,6, M. Hermier2

1Hospices Civils de Lyon, Department of Stroke Medicine, Bron, France; 2Hospices Civils de Lyon, Department of Neuroradiology, Bron, France; 3Université Claude Bernard Lyon I, CREATIS Laboratory, INSERM U1294, Villeurbanne, France; 4Université Claude Bernard Lyon I, CarMeN Laboratory, IRIS, INSERM U1060/INRA U1397, Bron, France; 5Hospices Civils de Lyon, Neurophysiology & Epilepsy Unit, Bron, France; 6Université Claude Bernard Lyon I, NeuroPain Lab, Inserm U1028, CNRS UMR5292, Lyon, France

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP039

Objective Migraine aura is a common acute stroke mimic. Distinguishing between migraine aura (MA) and ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) based solely on clinical presentation can be challenging. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using routine protocols may not definitely differentiate MA from TIA. However, recent advances in the post-processing of dynamic susceptibility-weighted (DSC) perfusion MRI now enables an estimation of cerebral oxygen metabolism. This study aimed to investigate the impact of cerebral oxygen metabolism maps on the differential diagnosis between MA and TIA.

Methods We performed a retrospective study of patients admitted to the Lyon Stroke Center from the period 2012–2024. Patients who underwent an emergency MRI during initial assessment and received a final diagnosis of either MA or TIA were included.

Results This study included 53 patients: 39 with a final diagnosis of MA and 14 with TIA. Patients with migraine aura showed significantly higher oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) values within the regions of clinical interest compared to TIA patients. Median OEF change was +14.84% in the MA group versus -1.65% in the TIA group (p<0.001). Cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) values did not significantly differ between the two groups (p=0.524). Normalized OEF ratio exhibited a significantly higher area the under curve than normalized cerebral blood flow (CBF, p=0.04) and CMRO2 (p=0.001) (Fig. 1). After adjustment for the time interval from symptoms onset to MRI, OEF remained an independent predictor of migraine aura (odds ratio: 5.43, 95% CI: [1.69, 9.54], p=0.04).

Conclusion Migraine aura was associated with a focal increase in OEF during the acute phase, that can be captured using routine DSC perfusion MRI.Fig. 1 (abstract OP039).
