OP040 Altered clock function in primary skin fibroblasts cultures derived from cluster headache patients

S. Spulber1, F. Jennysdotter Olofsgård1, A. Steinberg1, C. Ran1, A. Carmine Belin1

1Karolinska Institutet, Department of Neuroscience, Stockholm, Sweden

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP040

Objective Cluster headache (CH) is the most common form of autonomic trigeminal cephalalgia, and about 2/3 of all patients report symptoms with distinct circadian distribution. Primary skin fibroblasts in culture display robust oscillations in clock gene expression and have been used for investigating the mechanisms of action of drugs targeting the molecular clock. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of verapamil on molecular clock function.

Methods We have established primary fibroblast cultures from 14 CH patients and 10 controls. The cells were transfected with a reporter system expressing firefly luciferase driven by BMAL1 promoter, and the bioluminescence signal was monitored continuously for 5 to 10 consecutive cycles using photomultiplier tubes in photon counting mode. Around the time of the second circadian trough in bioluminescence, verapamil (L-type calcium channel blocker; 100 microM) or an equivalent volume of sterile PBS was added to each culture dish. The signals recorded before and after treatment were fitted with sinusoids with exponential decay independently, and the effects of treatment were evaluated as deviations from the signal predicted by baseline parameters.

Results In fibroblasts isolated from control subjects, PBS treatment re-entrained circadian oscillations in clock gene expression and verapamil treatment led to a more robust re-entrainment associated with faster decay of oscillations in bioluminescence signal. The circadian period was not significantly changed by either treatment. Fibroblasts isolated from CH patients were virtually undistinguishable from controls in baseline conditions. Verapamil treatment resulted in a less robust re-entrainment as compared to controls, and prolonged the circadian period.

Conclusion Our data points to a less robust molecular clock in primary fibroblasts isolated from CH patients as compared to controls, and verapamil treatment makes cell populations more susceptible to external entrainment.

OP041 Effectiveness of laser acupuncture on sleep quality in patients with chronic migraine: A randomized, sham-controlled, single-blind trial

C. C. Chung1, C. H. Chou2, C. S. Wang2, H. Y. Wu1, Y. C. Liu1, W. L. Chen1, C. I. Tsai1, C. Y. Hsu3

1Taichung Veterans General Hospital, Traditional Chinese Medicine Department, Taichung City, Taiwan; 2Taichung Veterans General Hospital, The Department of Neurological Institute, Taichung City, Taiwan; 3Taichung Veterans General Hospital, Department of Medical Research, Taichung City, Taiwan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP041

Objective Our published randomized controlled trial (RCT) documented Laser acupuncture (LA) has shown efficacy in migraine prevention. However, its impact on sleep quality in patients with chronic migraine (CM) remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of LA in improving sleep quality among patients with CM.

Methods From April 2022 to January 2025, patients over 20 years old with CM who received LA as an add-on treatment were included in the experimental group, while the control group received sham treatment using an inactive laser device. Headache improvement was defined as a ≥30% reduction in the number of headache days by week 12 compared to baseline. Both groups were further stratified into subgroups based on whether this threshold was achieved. The primary outcome was the change in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores from baseline, assessed monthly. Evaluations were conducted at baseline, week 4, week 8, and week 12.

Results A total of 76 patients were included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. At baseline, there were no significant differences in PSQI scores among the four subgroups. The LA & ≥30% reduction group demonstrated a significant improvement in sleep quality, with PSQI scores decreasing from 18.8 ± 6.8 to 15.6 ± 8.2 at week 12 (p = 0.001), and the LA & <30% reduction group also showed improvement (p = 0.038).

Conclusion LA may have a beneficial effect on sleep quality in patients with CM, particularly among those who experience a ≥30% reduction in headache days. Further large-scale, multi-center studies are warranted to confirm these findings.Fig. 1 (abstract OP041).

.

OP042 White matter tract differences in persistent post-traumatic headache, migraine, and healthy controls: A diffusion tensor imaging study

R. Häckert Christensen1, H. M. Al-Khazali2, C. Gollion2, B. A. Chaudhry2, M. Ashina2, H. Ashina2

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Glostrup, Denmark; 2Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Glostrup, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP042

Objective Persistent post-traumatic headache (PPTH) frequently resembles migraine but may involve distinct white matter perturbations. We compared white matter fiber tracts among adults with PPTH, migraine, and healthy controls (HCs).

Methods This cross-sectional diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) study enrolled adults with PPTH, migraine, and HCs, who underwent a single 3T MRI session. Tract-based spatial statistics quantified white matter integrity. Outcome measures included fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AD), mean diffusivity, and radial diffusivity. Group comparisons used general linear models with threshold-free cluster enhancement and 5,000 permutations. Voxelwise significance was set at P < 0.05 after family-wise error correction, adjusting for age and sex. Post-hoc region-of-interest (ROI) analyses explored differences within significant regions.

Results Imaging data were available from 100 participants with PPTH, 293 with migraine, and 154 HCs. Compared to participants with migraine, those with PPTH exhibited higher FA and AD values in the posterior limb of the internal capsule and superior corona radiata (PFWE < 0.05), findings that were further confirmed by post-hoc ROI analysis relative to HCs (both P < 0.001). FA values within these tracts were positively associated with monthly migraine-like headache days (P = 0.043). In addition, participants with PPTH showed lower AD values within the corpus callosum compared to those with migraine (PFWE < 0.05), with similar post-hoc ROI differences relative to HCs (P = 0.002). Lower corpus callosal AD values were associated with greater post-concussive symptom severity (P = 0.036).

Conclusion PPTH is associated with distinct white matter alterations involving ascending somatosensory pathways and interhemispheric fibers. These alterations are associated with clinical symptom severity and differentiate adults with PPTH from those with migraine, suggesting trauma-induced maladaptive plasticity.

OP043 The PTHEENOT study: Feasibility of an early, interdisciplinary, non-pharmacological intervention for patients at risk of developing post-traumatic headache

S. Baatz1,2, C. Simonÿ2,3, T. Sejbæk1,2, H. Malá Rytter4,5,6, L. Schlosser Mose1,2

1University Hospital of Southern Denmark, Department of Neurology, Esbjerg, Denmark; 2University of Southern Denmark, Department of Regional Health Research, Odense, Denmark; 3Næstved, Slagelse, and Ringsted Hospitals, The Research and Implementation Unit PROgrez, Slagelse, Denmark; 4University of Copenhagen, Department of Psychology, Copenhagen, Denmark; 5University Hospital Bispebjerg-Frederiksberg, Department of Neurology, Bispebjerg-Frederiksberg, Denmark; 6Danish Concussion Center, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP043

Objective To evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of an early interdisciplinary intervention based on cognitive behavioral therapy and graded physical exercise for patients at risk of developing post-traumatic headache (PTH) 2-6 months following mild head trauma.

Methods This feasibility study evaluated the recruitment, retention, questionnaire comprehension, and the acceptability of a five-week group-based intervention initiated 2-6 months post-injury. The intervention included psychoeducational sessions, structured physical exercise, peer dialogue, and nursing support. Twelve patients aged 18-60 years (mean age 43), all with mild head trauma, were screened for eligibility. At the time of recruitment, all patients were working. Eight were enrolled in the study: three were on full-time sick leave, three part-time, and two working full-time. Six (75%) completed the intervention; two withdrew due to illness. Data were collected through focus group interviews. A qualitative content analysis was employed to systematically categorize and interpret participants experiences and evaluate the perceived feasibility and acceptability of the intervention.

Results Patients expressed high satisfaction with the intervention, valuing structured education, group discussions, and physical activity. Patients reported reduced headache frequency, improved sleep quality, and enhanced coping strategies. Based on patient feedback, nursing sessions were extended from 90 to 120 min. A follow-up session was also incorporated to help sustain newly acquired coping strategies. These adjustments will be implemented in the upcoming randomized controlled trial (RCT) design.

Conclusion The intervention was feasible and well-received, with promising indications of improved headache outcomes and coping abilities. The feasibility study has informed adjustments for the upcoming RCT. Early non-pharmacological interventions may contribute to reducing the risk of developing persistent PTH.

OP044 Kiss1 receptor as a novel target for migraine treatment

E. Rubio Beltran1, K. O’Byrne2, P. Holland1

1King’s College London, Headache Group, Wolfson Sensory Pain and Regeneration Centre, London, UK; 2King’s College London, Department of Women and Children’s Health, School of Life Course Sciences, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP044

Objective After puberty, a sharp increase in migraine prevalence is observed, especially in females, suggesting an interaction between the trigeminovascular system (TVS) and the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. Kisspeptin (KP), a hypothalamic neuropeptide, plays a key role in the onset of puberty. We have previously shown that KP administration sensitizes the TVS. The aim of the present study was to evaluate the expression patterns of the Kiss1 receptor (Kiss1R) in the rodent TVS and to assess the therapeutic potential of blocking Kiss1R with its antagonist p234 in preventing nitroglycerin-induced periorbital mechanical hypersensitivity.

Methods Adult C57BL6/J mice (n=12) were divided in two cohorts. One cohort was perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde, the trigeminal ganglia and trigeminal nucleus caudalis were isolated, cryosectioned and stained for Kiss1R using tyramide signal amplification. In the second cohort, orofacial mechanical withdrawal thresholds were assessed at baseline and after chronic administration of NTG (10 mg/kg) or vehicle (n=5 each), using von Frey filaments. On day 10, thresholds were evaluated after administration of p234 (6nmol/kg) at 60 and 120 min.

Results Kiss1R was widely expressed throughout the trigeminal ganglion and the dorsal horn of the trigeminal nucleus caudalis. Chronic NTG administration significantly reduced mechanical thresholds from day 5 (P<0.05). Administration of p234 restored the orofacial mechanical thresholds after 120 min, with no statistical difference observed between the NTG and vehicle groups (P>0.05).

Conclusion Our data highlight that KP can modulate trigeminal nociception, aligning with the increased migraine incidence observed after puberty. Targeting the KP signalling pathway may offer a promising therapeutic approach for migraine treatment.

OP045 Distribution of intranasal lidocaine and its effect on electrically-evoked calcium signals in mouse trigeminal ganglion neurons

L. Tiebl1, S. Belejova2, S. Soares1, B. Oehler3, H. J. Solinski1, M. Schmelz1, R. Carr1

1University Heidelberg - Medical Faculty Mannheim, MCTN - Experimental Pain Research, Mannheim, Germany; 2Heidelberg University Hospital, Department of Pharmacology, Heidelberg, Germany; 3University Medical Clinic Essen, Clinic for Anesthesiology and Intensive Care Medicine, Essen, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP045

Objective Intranasally (i.n.) applied lidocaine has shown promise in treating postdural puncture headache and has been explored as potential treatment for cluster headache and migraine. However, the mechanisms underlying its analgesic effects remain unclear. This study aimed to determine the concentration of lidocaine reached in relevant tissues after i.n. application and its impact on trigeminal ganglion (TG) neurons.

Methods We used a mouse model to investigate the distribution of lidocaine (10% w/v) after i.n. application, employing liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to measure lidocaine concentrations in various tissues. Additionally, we conducted calcium imaging experiments on acutely cultured murine TG neurons, using electrical stimulation to assess effects of different concentrations of lidocaine, encompassing the measured tissue concentrations, on neuronal excitability.

Results Results showed that 30 min to 2 h after i.n. application, lidocaine concentrations ranged from ~2 μM in plasma to ~60 μM in TG. Capsaicin-sensitive TG neurons tolerated repetitive electrical stimulation worse than other neurons and were more readily blocked by 100 μM lidocaine. Furthermore, these neurons displayed sustained increases in calcium signals when exposed to 10 μM lidocaine during repetitive stimulation, which failed to return to baseline levels.

Conclusion Our findings suggest that micromolar concentrations of lidocaine are reached in brain and TG within 30 min to 2 h after i.n. administration. These low concentrations may selectively affect depolarized trigeminal nociceptors, providing a potential mechanism for anti-headache effects of intranasally applied lidocaine.

OP046 Sexual dimorphism in the clonidine-mediated suppression of trigeminal nociception in wide dynamic range (WDR) neurons

A. González-Hernández1, G. López-Córdoba1, G. Martínez-Lorenzana1, M. Condés-Lara1

1Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Neurobiología, Querétaro, Mexico

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP046

Objective Behavioural experiments have shown that male rats are more sensitive to clonidine-induced antinociception than female rats. Interestingly, little is known about how neuronal nociceptive processing at the trigeminal level is affected in females (including the role of the α2A/2B/2C-adrenoceptors subtypes involved). Given that trigeminal second-order WDR cells play a crucial processing nociception from peripheral facial areas, this study aimed to investigate the impact of clonidine on the activity of trigeminal WDR cells in male and female rats.

Methods Extracellular single-unit recordings of trigeminal WDR cells were conducted in anaesthetised Wistar rats and examined in relation to discharges associated with Aδ- and C-fibres. The effect of local clonidine (3.1-31 nmol) on electrical periorbital-evoked firing of WDR cells was recorded. Furthermore, considering that at least three α2-adrenoceptor subtypes exist (α2A-, α2B- and α2C-adrenoceptors), blockade of these receptor subtypes using BRL 44,408 (α2A), imiloxan (α2B), and JP 1302 (α2C) was performed.

Results Clonidine inhibited neuronal firing associated with Aδ- and C-fibre activation in both sexes. This inhibition was observed in >50% of the recorded cells. The dose required to induce similar antinociceptive effects was higher in females (31 vs. 10 nmol). Moreover, clonidine-induced inhibition of Aδ- and C-fibre activity was reversed by BRL 44,408 in males. In contrast, in females, imiloxan and JP-1302 reversed the clonidine induced inhibition of Aδ- but not C-fibres.

Conclusion Clonidine-induced WDR antinociception is more pronounced in male than in female rodents. In males, clonidine-induced inhibition of Aδ- and C-fibre discharge relies on α2A-adrenoceptor activation. In females, the activation of α2B/2C-adrenoceptors appears to be significant for the inhibition of Aδ-fibre discharge by clonidine, but not for C-fibre discharge, suggesting that other mechanisms or receptors might be involved in females.

OP047 Patterns, efficacy, motivations and impact of therapeutic illicit drug use in cluster headache in the Netherlands: Results from a cross-sectional survey study

J. Jansen1,2, M. van Liefland3, C. Oosting4, W. Naber3, R. ter Heine2, W. Leen1, R. Fronczek3,5, C. Kramers2

1Canisius Wilhelmina Ziekenhuis, Neurology, Nijmegen, Netherlands; 2Radboud University Medical Center, Pharmacy, Pharmacology and Toxicology, Nijmegen, Netherlands; 3Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 4Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, Netherlands; 5Stichting Epilepsie Instellingen Nederland (SEIN), Sleep-Wake Centre, Heemstede, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP047

Objective People with cluster headache (CH) often experience limited efficacy and/or intolerable side effects of conventional treatments. Some turn to illicit drugs, reporting benefits. Existing survey studies lack detailed data on usage patterns, efficacy, motivations and impact. This study aims to address these gaps.

Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among CH patients recruited from two Dutch hospitals and patient organizations. The digital questionnaire covered CH characteristics, demographics, treatment history, attitudes toward drug use and therapeutic use details.

Results A total of 461 patients were analyzed (56% chronic CH), mean age 53.5±14.0 years. Nearly half (48.2%) reported lifetime drug use. Of these, 26.2% reported therapeutic use, 49.3% recreational use and 24.5% both. Among therapeutic users, the most frequently used substances were psilocybin (63.2%), cannabis (47.4%) and LSD (23.7%). Psilocybin and LSD were mainly used preventively, whereas cannabis was used equally as preventive and acute treatment. Among therapeutic users, preventive efficacy was reported by 59.3% for psilocybin, 54.9% for cannabis and 60.0% for LSD. In these, reported median attack reduction was 70%, 45%, and 75%, respectively. As acute treatment, 46.4% reported pain reduction with cannabis, describing a median 30% pain reduction with onset after 15 min. Therapeutic illicit drug use was most often discontinued because of insufficient efficacy (53.7%) or side effects (25.4%). Most patients reported no impact of therapeutic drug use on work/study, leisure activities or social relationships. When effects were reported, they were positive in ~90% of cases across all domains.

Conclusion Findings from this survey show that therapeutic illicit drug use is common among Dutch CH patients, especially with psilocybin, cannabis and LSD. The results highlight unmet treatment needs and possible efficacy. This supports the urgency of clinical trials into the potential therapeutic applications of these substances.

OP049 Steroid hormone dysfunction in female cluster headache patients

T. Lylloff1, A. S. Petersen1, N. Lund1, M. L. K. Søborg1, B. Styrishave2, R. H. Jensen1, C. S. J. Westgate1

1The Danish Headache Center, Rigshospitalet, Glostrup, Denmark; 2University of Copenhagen, Pharmacy, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP049

Objective Previous studies have shown alterations in steroid hormones in male cluster headache patients. This study aimed to examine serum steroid hormone levels in female cluster headache patients relative to healthy controls (n=19), to assess potential endocrine alteration.

Methods We performed targeted quantitative liquid chromatography tandem mass-spectrometry for 20 steroid hormones (corticosteroids, androgens, progestogens, and estrogens) in serum from adult female cluster headache patients, both chronic (n=28) and episodic (n=23) consisting of 18 paired samples in bout and remission, obtained from the Danish Cluster Headache Biobank in a prospective case-control study.

Results We found 9 differential steroids in chronic cluster, 8 in episodic in bout and 3 in episodic in remission, compared to controls. The stress hormone cortisol was lower in chronic (P=0.0022) and episodic in bout (P=0.0084). The progestogens pregnenolone and progesterone were lower in chronic (P<0.0001 and P=0.0012) and episodic in bout (P=0.0154 and P=0.0458) however, only pregnenolone was lower in episodic in remission (P=0.0153). The androgens dehydroepiandrosterone (P=0.0311) and androstenedione (P=0.0014) were lower in chronic cluster headache. No differences were found in steroid hormones in the paired analysis between episodic patients in bout and remission.

Conclusion Female cluster headache patients show a dysregulated steroid hormone profile with corticosteroids and progestogens being lower in the headache state of cluster headache. Furthermore, androgens were lower in chronic cluster headache patients. This highlights potential endocrine involvement in cluster headache and could underly the pathogenesis of cluster headache as well as suggest novel therapeutic pathways.

OP050 Dynamic changes in pain inhibition in episodic and chronic migraine: Evidence of CPM waning

F. van Welie1, R. van Welie1, A. Dahan2, M. van Velzen2, G. M. Terwindt1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Leiden University Medical Center, Anesthesiology, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP050

Objective More studies are needed to understand pain profiling in migraine. This study aimed to examine the changes in Conditioned Pain Modulation (CPM) along several repetitions across two types of migraine, episodic (EM) and chronic (CM) migraine.

Methods Fifty-seven migraine patients from the Leiden Headache Center were included: 28 with EM and 29 with CM. CPM was used to study the function of descending pain inhibitory pathways by administering a test stimulus (CPMheat or CPMelectrical) and a conditioning stimulus (cold) at 3 timepoints. Linear mixed effect models were fitted for all patient (migraine overall) and per diagnose (EM vs. CM). Importantly, a subgroup analysis was conducted including patients who demonstrated an effective CPM response at timepoint 1 (T1), to assess possible waning effects over repeated measurements (T2-T3).

Results In the overall migraine group, CPMheat remained stable across timepoints, with no significant differences between CM and EM groups. Patients with a normal CPM response at T1 showed a significant decline over repeated measurements, notably between T1–T2 (p = 0.04) and T1–T3 (p < 0.001). Age, sex, and stimulus-related factors (test temperature, condition stimulus) did not affect CPM responses. CPMelectrical showed similar patterns, with significant changes from T1 to T2 (p = 0.02) and T1 to T3 (p < 0.001).

Conclusion The observed waning of CPM suggests that even migraine patients with initially normal pain inhibition may experience progressive reductions in their descending pain inhibitory system over repeated or prolonged pain challenges.

OP051 Epidemiology and journeys of trigeminal neuralgia patients in UK

J. Zakrzewska1

1UCLH NHS Foundation Trust, Dental Medicine, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):OP051

Objective Determine the epidemiology of trigeminal neuralgia, how managed, use of machine learning to determine predictors and potential effects on treatment.

Methods Data obtained from Clinical Practise Research Datalink kept by the NHS in the UK for a period of 25 years for all patients with Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) an ICD code of G50.0 and control data of patients with other forms of facial pain. These were then analysed by data analysts in consultation with an expert clinician.

Results Records of 48 K TN patients were obtained and 104 K control data. The incidence and prevalence were steadily rising till the onset of COVID. Overall prevalence of 0.08% as % of the population.thus 8 in every 10,000 people in UK have TN. The mean incidence is 0.11 in every 1000 person years. Females were more commonly affected, peak age late 60’s. Distribution was nationwide with most frequently affected group being Caucasian. There was significant co-morbidity with MS. The most frequently used medication was carbamazepine. 10% of patients had some surgical intervention which is considered low and probably related to coding issues. Machine learning established that in patients with TN there was a 16 times increased risk of developing trifascicular heart block.

Conclusion This data is in keeping with data from the UK disease atlas which suggests that TN may not qualify as a rare disease. There is evidence for increasing neurosurgical management given the potential long term effects of drugs and establishing national multidisciplinary centres to ensure TN patients gain faster access to services. Registries should be set up.

P001 Effectiveness of a mindfulness-based intervention in reducing headache frequency and emotional distress in patients with migraine: A pilot study

I. Martin Villalba1

1Hospital Clinic Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P001

Objective Migraine is a disabling neurological condition often linked to emotional distress such as anxiety and stress. While medications are standard treatment, mindfulness has emerged as a promising non-pharmacologic approach. This study aimed to assess the impact of an 8-week mindfulness-based group intervention on headache frequency, anxiety, and perceived stress in migraine patients.

Methods Twenty-eight adults diagnosed with migraine were recruited from a neurology outpatient clinic. Participants attended an 8-week mindfulness-based program adapted from MBSR, led by a clinical psychologist. Headache frequency (monthly headache days), anxiety (GAD-7), and perceived stress (PSS-10) were assessed at baseline and post-intervention. Pre-post differences were analyzed using paired t-tests.

Results Participants showed a significant reduction in monthly headache days (mean reduction = 3.5 days; p < 0.01), anxiety levels (p < 0.01), and perceived stress scores (p < 0.01). No adverse effects were reported. The program had a high completion rate, with only 11% dropout.

Conclusion This pilot study suggests that mindfulness may be an effective and well-tolerated intervention for reducing headache frequency and emotional symptoms in migraine patients. Integrating mindfulness into multidisciplinary migraine care may enhance outcomes. Further controlled studies are needed to confirm these preliminary findings.

P002 Low-level 810 nm laser acupuncture for chronic migraine patient in change acute headache medication usage days: A follow-up phase of randomized controlled trial

Y. C. Liu1, C. H. Chou2, C. S. Wang2, H. Y. Wu1, C. C. Chung1, W. L. Chen1, C. I. Tsai1, C. Y. Hsu3

1Taichung Veterans General Hospital, Traditional Chinese Medicine Department, Taichung City, Taiwan; 2Taichung Veterans General Hospital, The Department of Neurological Institute, Taichung City, Taiwan; 3Taichung Veterans General Hospital, Department of Medical Research, Taichung City, Taiwan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P002

Objective Laser acupuncture (LA) has shown efficacy in migraine prevention in our previous published randomized Controlled trial (RCT). Our aim is to verify the efficacy of LA as preventive treatment for chronic migraine (CM) by a follow-up phase of our unpublished RCT (Registration Number: NCT06219694).

Methods Participants were randomly assigned to either the LA group or the sham treatment group. Both groups received eight treatments over one month, followed by a three-month follow-up period. After six months from the initial treatment, participants in the sham group received open label extension LA treatment, followed by an additional three-month follow-up. LA and open label extension LA were performed by LaserPen-Expert 511 A in 810 nm wavelength with an output power density of 5 W/cm², with the same acupoint. Each acupoint received 150 mW of output power in continuous mode for 30 s, delivering a stimulation energy of 4.5 J. The outcome was the change acute headache medication usage days in 3 months after receiving sham treatment or open label extension LA treatment.

Results This follow-up phase included 35 patients, 74.3% of whom were female, with a mean age of 43.00 ± 14.28 years and a mean headache duration of 14.71 ± 10.03 years. The acute headache medication usage day in baseline was 9.09 ± 9.56, and before open label extension laser acupuncture was 9.00 ± 9.48, which showed no statistical significant difference (p=0.501). The change acute headache medication usage days compared from baseline till 12 weeks was 0.00 ± 2.17; before open label extension laser to post open label extension laser 12 weeks was -3.94 ± 3.57; showed statistical significant difference (p<0.001).

Conclusion This follow-up phase of the RCT confirmed that LA is an effective preventive treatment for CM, significantly reducing acute headache medication usage days compared to the sham group.Fig. 1 (abstract P002).Fig. 2 (abstract P002).Fig. 3 (abstract P002).

P003 Impact of toothpaste cessation on migraine frequency and severity: A prospective analysis of pre and post-intervention outcomes

T. Mathew1, S. Bhardwaj1, A. Patil1, M. A. Kujur1, P. Paulraj1, A. Nanda1, E. Toppo1, P. Tigga1, M. George1, S. V. Nambiar1, P. Majumdar1, P. B. Karau1, S. Badachi1, S. Rs2, R. Nadig1

1St John’s National Academy of Health Sciences, Neurology, Bangalore, India; 2St. John’s Research Institute, Bengaluru, India

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P003

Objective Certain ingredients in toothpaste—such as nitrates, fluorides, and essential oils like eucalyptus and camphor—may trigger migraine attacks. We hypothesized that discontinuing toothpaste use could positively impact migraine frequency and severity.

Methods We prospectively enrolled 100 adult patients meeting ICHD-3 criteria for migraine or probable migraine. Patients with other primary or secondary headache disorders were excluded. Headache frequency, duration, intensity (on a 0–10 numerical rating scale), analgesic and balm usage were recorded in a headache diary. Follow-up interviews were conducted in person or by phone. Improvements began within 1–4 weeks and persisted at a mean follow-up of 30 weeks.

Conclusion Toothpaste cessation may significantly reduce migraine frequency, intensity, and medication use in affected individuals.

P005 Patient perspectives on physiotherapy interventions for migraine: A pre- and post- intervention qualitative study

M. Castaldo1, Z. Liang2, C. Scott2, F. Cabrera Manrique2, S. Kim2, C. Shun Lee2, B. Cheng2, C. Yiu Kwok2

1University of Parma, Parma, Italy; 2University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P005

Objective The aim of this study was to explore expectations and experiences of patients regarding physiotherapy management for migraine.

Methods Eleven out of 13 participants in a study on physiotherapy management for migraine were interviewed by an independent researcher over phone or videoconferencing using a semi-structured format before and after undergoing two months of physiotherapy treatments that included education, manual therapy and exercise. Over eight hours of interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed. Reflexive thematic analysis identified codes and key themes after five research team meetings.

Results All but one participant reported overall positive experience. Three themes were interpreted. Theme 1 was a gap in migraine management filled by physiotherapy. Participants expressed need for self-management strategies and information from a clinician who had time to understand validate their experience. They wanted assessment and treatment for neck pain and were interested in exploring non-pharmacological treatment. Theme 2 was that many outcomes mattered to patients. Participants had low expectations prior to physiotherapy, but after experiencing physiotherapy, all indicated that short term pain relief was important. Reduced duration, intensity and frequency of neck pain and headache were valued outcomes leading to perceived improved quality of life. Aggravation of symptoms was tolerated if there were immediate gains or clear understanding of why it was necessary. Some participants main goal was reduced medication use. Long term outcomes were not yet measured but participants expressed feeling positive and empowered. Theme 3 was about accessibility. Participants liked that physiotherapy sessions were longer and more frequent than visits to medical doctors. Exercise prescription and advice needed to be practical and take into account individuals busy routines.

Conclusion Patients want physiotherapy incorporated with usual care to improve symptoms and empower self-management.

P008 Younger age predicts greater improvement following placebo olfactory training in primary headache disorders

V. Faria1,2, B. Höfer1, M. Nicklas1, E. Moulton2, S. Holmes2, G. Gossrau1

1TU Dresden, Faculty of Medicine, Kopfschmerzambulanz, Universitätsschmerzcentrum, Medizinische Fakultät der TU Dresden, Universitätsklinikum Dresden, Deutschland, Dresden, Germany; 2Boston Childrens Hospital, Brain and Eye Pain Imaging Lab, Pain and Affective Neuroscience Center, Department of Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P008

Objective Primary headache disorders are highly prevalent and disabling, especially in children, yet treatment options remain limited. Evidence suggests placebo responsivity is higher in younger individuals. This study investigated whether age predicts changes in headache-related disability and frequency following placebo olfactory training, and whether sensory (olfactory) and physiological (pain sensitivity) changes are associated with symptom improvement.

Methods Data were pooled from two placebo-controlled olfactory training trials in pediatric and adult headache patients. Only participants in the placebo group (N = 73, age 6–55) were included. For 12 weeks, participants used odorless pens at home, believing they contained low-dose scents. Headache frequency and disability (MIDAS/PedMIDAS) were assessed pre- and post-intervention. Sensory outcomes included olfactory threshold and identification (Sniffin Sticks), and pain sensitivity (QST: mechanical pain threshold and sensitivity). Regression models tested age as a predictor of symptom change, controlling for baseline values. Spearman correlations assessed links between clinical outcomes and sensory/physiological changes.

Results At baseline, children (<18) reported more headache days and greater disability than adults (p < 0.001; p = 0.011). Overall, 60.3% showed ≥30% reduction in disability, and 37.0% in headache frequency. Age significantly predicted improvement in headache frequency (β = 0.320, p = 0.008), with younger patients benefiting more. Of the sensory/physiological measures, only improvement in odor identification correlated with reduced headache frequency (ρ = –0.241, p = 0.040).

Conclusion Younger age predicted greater placebo-related improvement in headache frequency. Enhanced odor identification may reflect mechanisms underlying clinical change. These findings highlight the role of developmental and sensory factors in placebo response among headache patients.

P009 Pressure pain threshold response to a maximal cardiopulmonary exercise test in episodic migraine: A pilot study

A. Rodrigues1,2, I. Meuwissen2, L. van Thillo2, T. van Malderen2, O. Verbraeken2, W. Hens3, T. Kelderman4, G. Vanderschueren4, D. Bevilaqua-Grossi1, W. de Hertogh2

1University of São Paulo, Health Sciences, Ribeirão Preto, Brazil; 2University of Antwerp, Antwerp, Belgium; 3Antwerp University Hospital, Antwerp, Belgium; 4Ziekenhuis Aan de Stroom, Neurology Department, Antwerp, Belgium

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P009

Objective Although exercise is often reported as a possible trigger for migraine attacks, it may also reduce pain through mechanisms such as the release of endorphins and the activation of endogenous pain modulation. This pilot study aimed to investigate changes in pressure pain thresholds (PPT) before and after a single Cardiopulmonary Exercise Test (CPET) in patients with episodic migraine, to explore the potential for exercise-induced hypoalgesia in this population.

Methods Sixteen adults diagnosed with episodic migraine participated. PPT was assessed bilaterally at the mid-point of the upper trapezius and the tibialis anterior muscles. Measurements were taken three times on each side using a digital pressure algometer (in Newton, N), and the average of both sides was used for analysis. Assessments were carried out before and after a CPET to determine the maximal aerobic capacity.

Results No significant changes in PPT were found in the upper trapezius (mean difference = 0.4 N; standard deviation (SD) = 4.4 N; p = 0.702). In contrast, a significant increase in PPT after the CPET was found on the tibialis anterior muscle (mean difference = -6.4 N; SD: 7.3 N; p = 0.003).

Conclusion A single CPET may induce hypoalgesia in the tibialis anterior muscle in patients with episodic migraine. However, the absence of hypoalgesia in the trapezius - a commonly sensitized area in migraine – suggests that these effects may be site-specific and indicate altered central pain modulation. Although it was not the focus of this study, future research should explore whether changes in PPT following maximal aerobic effort may help predict which patients will tolerate or benefit from exercise-based interventions.

P011 Retrospective analysis of acupuncture for migraine: A 150-patient study demonstrates 35% reduction in attack frequency compared to standard therapy

A. Tkachev1, D. Nikitishina1

1Klinika Tkacheva, Neurology, Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P011

Objective Migraine remains one of the most disabling neurological disorders, with many patients experiencing insufficient relief from pharmacological treatments alone. Acupuncture, as a component of integrative medicine, is increasingly used as an adjunct or alternative strategy, though large-scale clinical data remain limited. To evaluate the effectiveness of acupuncture in reducing the frequency and severity of migraine attacks in comparison to standard pharmacological therapy.

Methods This retrospective study analyzed clinical records of 150 patients diagnosed with episodic or chronic migraine who underwent acupuncture treatment at a specialized neurology center between 2021 and 2024. Patients were matched with controls who received standard pharmacologic management alone. The primary outcome was the change in monthly migraine days over a 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included intensity (VAS scale) and acute medication usage.

Results Patients receiving acupuncture experienced a 35% greater reduction in monthly migraine frequency compared to the standard therapy group (p < 0.01). Improvements were also noted in headache intensity and reduced reliance on abortive medications. No serious adverse effects were reported.

Conclusion This retrospective analysis suggests that acupuncture may offer a significant therapeutic benefit in migraine management, with a marked reduction in attack frequency. Further randomized prospective trials are warranted to confirm these findings and clarify mechanisms of action.

P012 Effects of dry needling of the obliquus capitis Inferior in patients with cervicogenic headache and upper cervical dysfunction: An exploratory randomized sham-controlled trial

M. Chys1, K. de Meulemeester1, M. de Sloovere1, I. de Greef1, B. Cagnie1

1Ghent University, Rehabilitation Sciences, Ichtegem, Belgium

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P012

Objective Cervicogenic headache (CeH) is linked to upper cervical dysfunctions. The obliquus capitis inferior (OCI) muscle may contribute to restricted cervical rotation at the C1-C2 level, altered proprioception and pain. Dry needling (DN) of the OCI is hypothesized to target these dysfunctions. The aim of this study is to investigate whether a single intervention combining DN and manual therapy (MT) compared to sham needling (SN) and MT, improves C1-C2 rotation, functional, headache-related, and psychological outcomes in a subgroup of CeH patients with a positive cervical flexion-rotation test (CFRT).

Methods Thirty-four participants were randomly assigned to: (1) DN + MT or (2) SN + MT. The primary outcome was C1-C2 rotational mobility. Secondary outcomes included headache-related parameters (frequency, intensity, duration and perceived effect), functional parameters (cervical mobility, pain pressure thresholds, motor control and proprioception) and psychological parameters (central sensitization, pain catastrophizing, coping strategies and kinesiophobia), outcomes were re-evaluated at one-week follow-up.

Results Linear mixed-effects models showed a significant and clinically relevant increase for the CFRT, in the DN group compared to the SN group post-intervention (mean difference [MD]: 4,51°; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 1,74 ; 7,28), which was maintained at the 1-week follow-up (MD: 5,44° ; 95% CI: 2,55 ; 8,33). No clinically relevant changes were observed in other functional, headache-related or psychological parameters.

Conclusion Targeting the OCI may be of added value in restoring atlanto-axial dysfunction. While short-term mobility gains were observed, a single intervention appears insufficient to impact other functional or psychological outcomes. Future research involving larger samples should examine DN effects as part of a multimodal treatment with long-term follow-up.

P013 Psychological comorbidities and non-pharmacological treatment strategies in cluster headache: Insights from a qualitative study on patient experiences

L. Jabbarian1, P. Zolfaghari1, D. Ramanagoudra2, A. Burak1, W. Al Haj Ali1, F. van Loon1, A. Özsert1, A. van der Vliet1

1Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Rotterdam, Netherlands; 2MyClusters BV, Amsterdam, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P013

Objective Cluster headache (CH) is a rare but excruciating neurological condition, often referred to as “suicide headache” due to its extreme pain and associated psychological distress. This study aimed to explore the lived psychological impact of CH and to examine how patients manage these challenges through non-pharmacological means, while identifying gaps in care—particularly those affecting quality of life in- and outside acute attack periods.

Methods A qualitative study was conducted through semi-structured interviews with individuals diagnosed with CH, recruited via patient networks and social media in the Netherlands. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, anonymized, and analyzed using inductive coding.

Results Participants (n=18) reported a high prevalence of psychological complaints, notably anxiety (95%), fatigue (72%) and sleep disturbances (55%). Addressing the patient’s quality of life outside of attack periods is crucial for comprehensive, patient-centered CH management.

P015 Patient experiences and preferences for non-oral acute migraine treatments: A discrete choice experiment

L. Hubig1, T. Smith2, L. Abraham3, J. Coulter4, K. Hygge Blakeman5, J. C. Cappelleri4, E. Agarwal4, S. H. Lo1

1Acaster Lloyd, London, UK; 2Study Metrix, St. Peters, MO, USA; 3Pfizer R&D UK Ltd., Sandwich, UK; 4Pfizer, Inc., New York, NY, USA; 5Pfizer AB, Stockholm, Sweden

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P015

Objective The study aimed to examine heterogeneity in patients’ preferences for attributes associated with non-oral acute migraine treatments.

Methods Adult migraine patients who, in the last 3 months, used two or more acute migraine medications and who either had used a non-oral treatment or were not satisfied with their current treatment were recruited in the United States and Germany. Participants completed an online survey with a discrete choice experiment where they were asked to choose between pairs of hypothetical treatments characterised by 8 attributes (pain freedom at 2 h, pain relief at 15 min (mins), return to normal function at 30 min, mode of administration, drug- and administration-related side effects, maximum monthly dose, treatment window) in a series of questions. Latent class analysis (LCA) was used to identify unique preference classes. Relative importance (RI) was estimated for each attribute for each class and expressed as a percentage of overall importance of all attributes for the class.

Results A total of 304 respondents completed the survey (n=152 per country). LCA identified two preference classes of approximately equal size. The most important attribute for Class 1 was mode of treatment administration (RI:30.9%; 95%CI: 20.2-36.5), followed by drug-related side effects (RI:23.6%; 95%CI: 14.2-27.4) and normal function at 30 min (RI:14.6%; 95% CI:8.8-20.1]. For Class 2, the most important attribute was pain freedom at 2 h (RI:33.6%; 95%CI:28.3-36.2) followed by drug-related side effects (RI:19.3%; 95%CI:13.5-22.7) and pain relief at 15 min (RI:8.6%; 95%CI:13.6; 21.8). Class membership was not explained by observable patient clinical or demographic characteristics.

Conclusion Respondents differed in their preferences for acute migraine treatment attributes, highlighting the need for patient involvement in treatment decisions. Mode of administration and speed of response may be the driving factors defining different groups of patients.

1Neurology Clinic Nis, Nis, Serbia

P017 Translation and validation of the Dutch Cluster Headache Impact Questionnaire (CHIQ)

P. van Tilborg1, W. Naber1, H. Kempers1, R. Brandt2, R. Fronczek1,3

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2The Migraine Clinic, Amsterdam, Netherlands; 3Stichting Epilepsie Instellingen Nederland (SEIN), Heemstede, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P017

Objective Cluster headache (CH) can severely impact Quality of Life (QoL). Studies suggest factors beyond attack frequency can affect QoL, indicating the importance of assessing QoL in drug trials. Previously, we translated the Cluster Headache Quality of Life scale (CHQ). This study translated and validated the Cluster Headache Impact Questionnaire (CHIQ), so both questionnaires can be used complementary.

Methods Patients were recruited from the LUMC-CH database. The TRAP-D method (Translation, Review, Adjudication, Pretesting and Documentation) was used to translate the CHIQ from English to Dutch. The original translation was completed by n=32. Question clarity was discussed in a phone interview. A new group (n=39) completed the revised CHIQ twice (2-day interval) for test-retest validation. Results included internal validity (Cronbach’s Alpha) and reproducibility (Intraclass Correlation Coefficient; ICC). To determine convergent validity (Spearman correlation), all patients completed 3 other questionnaires once – the CHQ, Headache Impact Test (HIT-6) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS).

Results 71 patients were included (47% male; 86% chronic CH). One minor change was made to the translation after pre-testing. The CHIQ took a median of 5 min (IQR: 4, 9) to complete and most (84%) found it not burdensome at all. Internal validity (Cronbach’s Alpha 0.92) and test-retest reliability (ICC 0.78; 95% CI 0.479, 0.898) were excellent. The mean difference between the 2 CHIQ-assessments was 2.36 ± 4.06. Convergent validity was very strong with CHQ (ρ: 0.86) and HIT-6 (ρ: 0.81), and strong with HADS (ρ: 0.65).

Conclusion The Dutch CHIQ is a valid, reliable tool for assessing CH’s impact on QoL. It aligns with general QoL scales but specifically addresses CH related issues. Its short completion time and negligible burden make it a practical instrument for clinical care and standardized QoL assessment in international trials. Combined, the CHQ and CHIQ offer a comprehensive QoL assessment in CH.

H. Genç1, R. Ghouri2, A. Özge3, H. Bolay2, P. Y. Dikmen4, E. Ekizoğlu5, A. A. Ozdemir6, B. Tasdelen7, E. Y. Uc8, B. Baykan9, M. D. S. Group1

1Gaziantep City Hospital, Health Application and Research Center, Neurology Clinic, Gaziantep, Turkey; 2Gazi University, Department of Neurology, NÖROM, Ankara, Turkey; 3Mersin University, Faculty of Medicine, Department of Neurology, Mersin, Turkey; 4Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University, Department of Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey; 5Istanbul University Istanbul Faculty of Medicine, Department of Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey; 6Mersin University, Faculty of Medicine, Department of Medical Education, Mersin, Turkey; 7Mersin University, Faculty of Medicine, Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, Mersin, Turkey; 8University of Iowa Hospitals & Clinics, Department of Neurology, Iowa City, IA, USA; 9EMAR Medical Center, Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey

Objective To evaluate headache characteristics during driving in individuals with migraine and their impact on driving cessation.

We employed a Structural Equation Model (SEM) to identify the variables that influence driving cessation.

The headache frequency was higher in patients with CM vs. EM (21.78% vs. 9.48%, p<0.001), VM vs. no VM (16.93% vs. 12.86%, p=0.032), but no difference was observed between MaA vs. MwoA (13.54% vs. 12.85%, p=0.639). The severity of pain and HIT-6 scores experienced during driving were higher in patients with MwA, CM, and VM (all, p<0.05). 1% of patients with MwA, 6% of those with CM, and 2% of those with VM ceased driving due to migraine. ROC curves using HIT-6 cut-offs showed a significant impact of migraine severity on driving cessation in different subtypes of migraine, except VM. SEM revealed the differential impact of various factors (e.g., migraine subtypes and severity, accompanying symptoms, driver road condition sensitivity characteristics) on driving cessation.

Conclusion Patients with chronic migraine and vestibular migraine are more prone to experience headaches during driving. High-severity migraines can be associated with driving cessation. Increased awareness of the impact of migraines on driving is necessary to enhance the functional abilities and quality of life of patients.Fig. 1 (abstract P018).

P021 Comparison of disability levels between primary and secondary headaches – An online survey in Brazil

A. Rodrigues1,2, J. Pradela1, G. F. Carvalho3, C. F. Pinheiro-Araújo1, F. Dach1, D. Bevilaqua-Grossi1

1University of São Paulo, Health Sciences, Ribeirão Preto, Brazil; 2University of Antwerp, Antwerp, Belgium; 3Furtwangen University, Freiburg, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P021

Objective To verify the impact and disability between primary (PH) and secondary headaches (SH), using the Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) and the Headache Disability Index-Brazil (HDI) questionnaires.

Methods This cross-sectional online survey included headache sufferers in Brazil between Feb/2022 to Dec/2024. Participants were recruited via a tertiary hospital with a headache clinic and on social media. Self-reported data included headache diagnosis, monthly frequency and intensity (0-10). Diagnoses were categorized as PH or SH per ICHD-III. All participants completed the HIT-6 and HDI. HIT-6 disability was classified as: little/no impact (<49), some (50–55), substantial (56–59), and severe (60–78). HDI categories were based on sample percentiles: mild (<40.0), moderate (40.1–82), and severe (>82).

Results Among 541 participants, 466 (86.1%) had PH and 75 (13.9%) SH. Regarding HDI, SH had a higher proportion of mild disability (41.3% vs. 22.7%; p = 0.001), while PH had a higher proportion of moderate disability (57.3% vs. 36.0%).

Conclusion There were no differences in total impact or disability scores between primary and secondary headache subgroups. However, a higher proportion of individuals with primary headaches reported severe impact on both the HIT-6 and HDI questionnaires. This highlights the burden that these disorders impose on patients’ daily functioning. Nevertheless, these data should be interpreted with caution due to the difference in sample size between the groups.

P022 Psychometric evaluation of HALT and HURT in European Portuguese-speaking patients with migraine

M. Plácido1,2, P. A. Laires1, L. Ferreira3,4, B. Santos2, R. Paizinho2, R. Gil-Gouveia5,6

1NOVA National School of Public Health, Public Health Research Centre, Comprehensive Health Research Center, Lisbon, Portugal; 2MiGRA Portugal - Portuguese Migraine and Headache Patients’ Association, Lisbon, Portugal; 3University of Algarve – ESGHT, Research Centre for Tourism, Sustainability and Well-Being (CinTurs), Faro, Portugal; 4Centre for Innovative Biomedicine and Biotechnology, Coimbra, Portugal; 5Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 6Universidade Católica Portuguesa, Center for Interdisciplinary Research in Health, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P022

Objective Headache-Attributed Lost Time (HALT) and Headache Under-Response to Treatment (HURT) were developed by Lifting The Burden global campaign against headache. P028 Does heterogeneity in patient population, study design, and endpoint definitions affect indirect comparisons of acute migraine treatments? A methodological assessment

R. B. Lipton1, P. Cowley2, E. Benbow3, T. Reason3, A. Hatswell2, A. Jenkins4, L. Abraham4, P. Saccone5, H. Chu5, T. Fullerton5, C. Tassorelli6

1Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Department of Neurology, New York, NY, USA; 2Petauri Evidence, Nottingham, UK; 3Estima Scientific, London, UK; 4Pfizer, Ltd., HTA, Value and Evidence, Tadworth, UK; 5Pfizer, Inc., New York, NY, USA; 6University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P028

Objective Indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) can be used to summarize and compare results across studies, based on the assumption that the placebo response adjusts for differences among studies. We sought to identify factors that influence heterogeneity in an ITC of acute treatments for migraine and to determine if adjustment for those factors influences the results.

Methods A review of recently published ITCs was conducted, followed by a thorough examination of individual studies. We focussed on a recently published ITC [1] based upon a comprehensive evidence base, publicly available details of analyses and the decision to analyse treatments individually (rather than at the class level).

Results Review of individual studies found substantial heterogeneity across trials, including differences in: pain intensity of treated migraine attacks, patterns of prior/concomitant migraine medication use, co-primary endpoint designation, and tools used to capture them (paper diaries or e-diaries). Despite the substantial heterogeneity observed no attempts to control for systemic differences were identified in the main analyses of published ITCs [1-5]. Extension of the analyses conducted by Karlsson et al. [1] demonstrated an approximate doubling of placebo response rate over the review period, consistent with Thokagevistk et al. [6] who reported changes in the relative effect of sumatriptan over time.

Conclusion ITCs of acute migraine trials, sometimes conducted decades apart, acknowledge heterogeneity but did not attempt to statistically adjust for it. More sophisticated analytical approaches are needed to obtain unbiased and reliable estimates of indirect comparative effectiveness.

P032 Clinical and therapeutic profiles of patients with chronic daily headache in a tertiary headache center

G. Cabral1

1Hospital Egas Moniz, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P032

Objective To characterize patients diagnosed with chronic daily headache (CDH) and describe their clinical features, comorbidities, and responses to treatment.

Methods We performed a retrospective review of consecutive patients who fulfilled International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3) criteria for CDH and were seen at a tertiary headache clinic between 2018 and 2024. Results Ninety-five patients were included (mean age ± SD, 48.8 ± 17.4 years; 80% women). Headache onset occurred before age 50 in most cases. Conclusion Patients with CDH referred to a tertiary center often have multiple comorbidities, high rates of medication overuse, and significant psychiatric burden. P033 Atogepant reduce psychological dependence to acute treatments evaluated with the Leeds dependence questionnaire (LDQ): A prospective observational study

LDQ scores were measured at baseline and week 12. Monthly headache days, acute medication numbers (AMNs), and days of use (AMDs) were recorded. A linear mixed-effects model was used to assess LDQ score changes over time, adjusting for MO status, MOH diagnosis and psychiatric comorbidities.

Results The LDQ total score significantly decreased from 7.95 ± 5.79 to 6.42 ± 5.08 (mean change –1.53; p = 0.032). Three LDQ items, loss of control, compulsive use, and psychological distress, showed significant improvement. Mixed-effects modeling confirmed a significant effect of treatment (p = 0.022), independent of MO status or psychiatric conditions. LDQ changes did not correlate significantly with AMNs, AMDs, or MHDs.

Conclusion Atogepant significantly reduced psychological dependence on acute migraine medications in a real-world setting. This effect was independent of MO or psychiatric comorbidities and not directly related to medication intake reduction. These findings suggest preventive therapy may improve behavioral dimensions of migraine and support the use of LDQ in routine clinical care.Fig. 1 (abstract P033).Fig. 2 (abstract P033).

P034 Protective effect of headache in patient with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage

A. Revurko1, Y. Solodovnikova1, K. Yarova1, A. Son1

1Odesa National Medical University, Neurology and Neurosurgery, Odesa, Ukraine

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P034

Objective Thunderclap headache is one of the most common symptoms among patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). It may be caused by inflammation of brain arteries, irritation of the meninges by blood, intracranial pressure changes, and possibly neuropathic factors. We aimed to explore a connection between headache and the clinical course of aSAH.

Methods The study included medical records of 421 patients with aSAH divided into two groups: (1) with headache at admission and (2) without headache. The following methods were used for statistical analysis: Chi-square test-test, binomial logistic and linear regression.

Results Surprisingly, no statistically significant association was found between headache and meningeal signs (Chi-square test=0.217; df=1; p=0.642). However, patients presenting with headache had significantly lower odds of developing paresis (OR=0.175; CI=0.097–0.313; p<0.001), a presence of Babinski sign (OR=0.139; CI=0.077–0.25; p<0.001), and oculomotor dysfunction (OR=0.271; CI=0.148–0.498; p<0.001). Headache at admission also correlated with milder clinical severity on the modified WFNS scale (OR=0.052; CI=0.028–0.096; p<0.001), shorter duration of lumbar drainage placement (p<0.001), and a 64.6% reduction in mortality risk (OR=0.354; CI=0.202–0.621; p<0.001).

Conclusion Headache at admission in patients with aSAH was associated with a more favourable clinical course. The presence of headache correlated with significantly lower odds of paresis, Babinski sign, and oculomotor dysfunction. Additionally, headache was associated with lower WFNS severity scores, shorter lumbar drainage duration, and reduced mortality risk.

P037 Relationship between cycling of traditional oral generic preventive medications and patient-reported outcomes: Multicountry results from the CaMEO-l study

M. Lantéri-Minet1, K. M. Fanning2, B. Dabruzzo3, E. Leroux4, M. Matharu5, F. Sakai6, S. Musson3, P. Gandhi3, K. Carr3, Z. Katsarava7,8

1CHU & Côte Azur University, Nice, France; 2MIST Research, Wilmington, NC, USA; 3AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA; 4McGill University, Montréal, Canada; 5Institute of Neurology, London, UK; 6SIHC, Saitama, Japan; 7Christian Hospital, Unna, Germany; 8UDE, Essen, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P037

Objective Oral generic preventive medications (OGPMs) are often associated with suboptimal efficacy, contraindications, or side effects, leading to high discontinuation rates and cycling through additional OGPMs. We evaluated the relationship between the number of traditional OGPMs taken and patient-reported outcomes among Chronic Migraine Epidemiology and Outcomes-International (CaMEO-I) study respondents from non-US countries.

1LMU Munich, Munich, Germany; 2LMU Munich, Munich, Germany; 3School of Medicine and Health, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Neuroradiology, Munich, Germany; 4TUM Neuroimaging Center, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; 5Hegau-Jugendwerk, Neurological Hospital and Rehabilitation Center for Children, Adolescents and Young Adults, Gailingen, Germany; 6University Hospital Ulm, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology, Ulm, Germany

P040 Elevated symptoms of burnout in a cluster headache cohort

F. Jennysdotter Olofsgård1, C. Ran1, S. Spulber1, A. Steinberg1,2, C. Sjöstrand3, E. Waldenlind4,2, M. Lantz3, A. Sundholm1,2, M. Söderström4,5, A. Dahlgren4,5, A. Carmine Belin4,5

1Karolinska Institutet, Department of Neuroscience, Stockholm, Sweden; 2Karolinska University Hospital, Department of Neurology, Stockholm, Sweden; 3Danderyd Hospital, Department of Clinical Sciences, Stockholm, Sweden; 4Karolinska Institutet, Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Stockholm, Sweden; 5Stockholm University, Department of Psychology, Stockholm, Sweden

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P040

Objective People with cluster headache suffer daily headache attacks of extreme intensity during active bouts. The attacks, which commonly occur at night, greatly impact sleep and quality of life for those affected. Symptoms of burnout are categorized as a depletion of a person’s energy reserves, affecting daily functioning, and may occur in any context of life. We hypothesize that the symptoms of cluster headache increase the risk for burnout during active bouts.

Methods To investigate the extent of burnout in a Swedish cluster headache cohort, 701 study participants with cluster headache were invited to answer the Shirom-Melamed Burnout Questionnaire. Scores for burnout were compiled and compared between study participants in active bout and remission using logistic regression. Additionally, in-depth analysis of clinical characteristics was performed with the aim of identifying risk factors for burnout.

Results A total of 284 individuals with cluster headache were included in the final analysis. Symptoms of burnout were commonly observed in people with cluster headache. In an active bout, 67.6% (n = 50) of the study participants scored above 3.75, which is indicative of having a risk for burnout, as compared to 39.5% (n = 83) of the study participants in remission. Regression analysis further showed that symptoms of burnout decrease with the number of years since the last active bout. Female study participants were at higher risk for burnout than males.

Conclusion We observed a high degree of symptoms of burnout people with cluster headache, especially in active bout. These data suggest that the risk for symptoms of burnout is substantial in cluster headache and should be assessed when managing cluster headache patients in the healthcare system.

P041 A rare case of spontaneous intracranial hypotension complicated with intracranial hypertension

B. Pirlog1, L. Neumann2, G. Tuloup1, C. Roos1

1APHP, Lariboisiere Hospital, Headache Emergency Department, Paris, France; 2Hôpital Delafontaine - Saint-Denis, Paris, France

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P041

Objective Can intracranial hypertension complicate spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH)?

Methods We report the case of a 27-year-old woman who presented to our department for an unusual headache.

Results In June 2019, she presented to the Headache Emergency department for postural headache after a moderate cranial trauma. Brain MRI confirmed signs of SIH, and the spinal MRI found an anterior epidural fluid collection at C6-T1 (Fig. 1). An epidural blood patch(EBP) was performed one month after symptom onset, resulting in initial improvement. However, due to a recurrence of postural headache, a second EBP was performed 2 months later. The patient experienced resolution of orthostatic headaches but continued to report headaches during forward-bending movements. Brain MRI performed in 2022 revealed indirect signs of SIH, and the spinal MRI still found anterior epidural fluid collection. In 2023, she presented with an unusual headache that persisted while lying down, accompanied mainly by tinnitus in the left ear. An AngioCT revealed a diminution of the transvers sinus, and a lumbar puncture found an opening pressure of 35 cmH20. No other abnormalities were found in her MRI (Fig. 2), and no papillary oedema was found. We later understood that the patient was using retinoids to treat eczema. The patient was advised to discontinue retinoids and was started on acetazolamide. Due to a favorable outcome, normal opening pressure and ophthalmologic examination the treatment was stopped after two months. The patient continues to experience headaches when leaning forward, with recurrent signs of SIH on brain MRI, and a persistent anterior epidural collection on spinal MRI. Due to pregnancy, the search for a dural leak and consideration of surgical treatment have been delayed. patient gave her informed consent to publish their details.

Conclusion We report a rare case of spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) complicated by secondary intracranial hypertension attributed to retinoid therapy for eczema.Fig. 1 (abstract P041).Fig. 2 (abstract P041).

Objective Rimegepant (RIM) is approved for both acute and preventive migraine treatment. P046 Retrospective study of trigeminal neuralgia: Analysis of 100 episodes managed in the emergency department

D. S. Gómez de la Torre Morales1, M. Ravelo León1, B. Rodríguez García1, J. A. Aguilera Aguilera1, J. S. Rodríguez Carrillo1, I. Díaz Díaz1, M. Luz Esteve1, Á. Criado Antón1, S. Borja Andrés1, L. López Mesonero1

1Complejo Asistencial Universitario de Salamanca, Neurology, Salamanca, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P046

Objective To analyze the diagnostic and therapeutic approach in patients presenting with suspected trigeminal neuralgia at the Emergency Department of the Salamanca University Hospital Complex.

Methods A retrospective observational study was conducted between May 2023 and March 2025, including patients discharged from the Emergency Department with a diagnosis of trigeminal neuralgia. Clinical and demographic variables were collected. We analysed the treatments administered in the emergency setting, subsequent referrals for specialist follow-up, treatment response, and the complementary tests performed.

Results A total of 100 episodes of trigeminal neuralgia were analyzed, corresponding to 74 patients, with a mean age of 57.6 years (64% female). Neurology was consulted in 41% of cases. The most frequently prescribed treatment by neurologists was lacosamide, with a pain relief rate of 84.6%, whereas emergency physicians predominantly administered paracetamol, NSAIDs, and opioids. Conclusion Trigeminal neuralgia poses a significant challenge in the emergency setting, with considerable heterogeneity in both its diagnostic and therapeutic management, and a high proportion of initial diagnoses not subsequently confirmed. This study underscores the importance of neurological assessment in the emergency department and the need for close follow-up to optimize symptom control.

Results Seventy-five participants were included in this early analysis. Mean (±SD) age was 45 (±9) years, and 69/75 (92%) were females. Fifty-four of 75 (72%) participants had chronic migraine, and 44/75 (59%) received other anti-CGRP(s) before eptinezumab. At Month 3, 46% (n=33/71) and 32% (n=23/71) of participants experienced ≥30% and ≥50% MMD reduction, respectively. The change from baseline in MMDs was particularly pronounced in participants naïve to anti-CGRP(s) at the time of eptinezumab initiation. Additionally, significant reduction was observed in HIT-6 total score at Month 3 (change from baseline: –4.65; 95% CI: –6.17, –3.12; p<0.01; n=57). Six-month data for participants achieving this milestone will be presented in the poster.

Conclusion: This early analysis showed the effectiveness of eptinezumab for migraine prevention in a real-world setting in Spain.

P049 Consistency of effect of rimegepant as an acute treatment for migraine attacks: Data from a prospective, real-world study

W. Kang1,2, P. Huang1,2

1Ruijin Hospital Affiliated Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China; 2Ruijin-Hainan hospital Shanghai Affiliated Jiao Tong University School of Medicine (Hainan Boao Research Hospotal), Boao, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P049

Objective This prospective, real-world study aimed to evaluate the consistency of rimegepant’s efficacy as an acute treatment for migraine across three separate attacks among Chinese patients.

Methods This was a single-arm, prospective, real-world study (NCT05709106). Adults diagnosed with migraine (with or without aura) in accordance with the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd Edition (ICHD-3) and prescribed rimegepant as part of the routine treatment were screened for this study. In this report, percentages of participants achieving pain freedom, freedom from the most bothersome symptom (MBS) and normal function at 2 h post-dose were evaluated for each attack and in ≥2/3 attacks.

Additionally, 35.8% of participants achieved pain freedom at 2 h post-dose in ≥2 of 3 attacks, 65% achieved MBS freedom, and 50% achieved normal function (Table 1).

Conclusion These results confirm the good real-world efficacy of rimegepant and further demonstrate consistency of response across multiple attacks.Fig. 1 (abstract P049).

P050 Insomnia and sleep quality in patients with treatment-resistant chronic migraine

M. d. l. N. Fabregat Fabra1, S. Fernández1, M. T. Marco1, M. A. Sosa1, A. Grajea1, D. Asin1, I. Víctor Obach2, B. Víctor Obach1

1Hospital Clinic, Headache Unit, Barcelona, Spain; 2University of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P050

Objective Treatment-resistant chronic migraine (TRCM) is a complex condition often complicated by sleep disturbances, which exacerbate disability and reduce quality of life. Standardized assessments of sleep comorbidities in this population remain limited. To evaluate sleep disorder prevalence in TRCM patients refractory to ≥3 oral preventives and botulinum toxin using validated scales.

Methods This prospective observational study included 164 adults with TRCM (mean age 48.3 years, 86.5% women) from our headache unit. Sleep quality, insomnia, and daytime sleepiness were assessed via Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS). Clinical and demographic variables, including prior Botox use (37.3% discontinued, 7.5% naïve) and concurrent anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (most patients), were analyzed descriptively.

Results Poor sleep quality (PSQI >5) affected 77%, excessive daytime sleepiness (ESS >10) 21%, and clinically significant insomnia (ISI ≥15) 95%. Functional impairment was notable: 60% reported work/social difficulties (PHQ-9), with 37% describing severe limitations. Comorbid sleep disorders were rare: obstructive sleep apnea (3%), restless legs syndrome (12.5%), and sleepwalking (2.4%). Antidepressant use was reported in 33.3% of cases.

Conclusion Sleep disturbances, particularly insomnia, are highly prevalent in TRCM, despite low rates of other sleep disorders. The high rates of functional impairment and antidepressant use highlight the need for integrated psychiatric and sleep-focused interventions in this population.

P051 Consistency of response to rimegepant for the acute treatment of migraine: A population and participant-level analysis of a prospective real-world observational study (CONFIDENCE)

L. Abraham1, A. Urani2, G. Lambru3, R. B. Lipton4, P. J. Goadsby5, P. Pozo-Rosich6, K. M. Fanning7, F. Dai8, K. Hygge Blakeman9

1Pfizer R&D UK Ltd., Tadworth, UK; 2Aptar Digital Health, Paris, France; 3The Headache and Facial Pain Service, Guy’s and St. Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK; 4Montefiore Medical Center and Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, New York, NY, USA; 5King’s College Hospital, NIHR King’s Clinical Research Facility, London, UK; 6Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Headache Unit, Neurology Department, Barcelona, Spain; 7MIST Research, Wilmington, NC, USA; 8Pfizer, Inc., New York, NY, USA; 9Pfizer AB, Stockholm, Sweden

Objective Evaluate the real-world consistency of response to rimegepant (RIM) 75 mg for the acute treatment of migraine.

P052 Prospective, real-world evidence of meaningful pain relief, return to function, and satisfaction among patients with migraine on acute rimegepant treatment alone or with concomitant preventive migraine medication

K. Hygge Blakeman1, A. Urani2, G. Lambru3, R. B. Lipton4, P. J. Goadsby5, P. Pozo-Rosich6, T. J. Schwedt7, K. M. Fanning8, L. Abraham9

1Pfizer AB, Stockholm, Sweden; 2Aptar Digital Health, Paris, France; 3The Headache and Facial Pain Service, Guy’s and St. Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK; 4Montefiore Medical Center and Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, New York, NY, USA; 5King’s College Hospital, NIHR King’s Clinical Research Facility, London, UK; 6Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Headache Unit, Neurology Department, Barcelona, Spain; 7Mayo Clinic, Neurology, Scottsdale, AZ, USA; 8MIST Research, Wilmington, NC, USA; 9Pfizer R&D UK Ltd., Tadworth, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P052

Objective This analysis of a prospective, observational, real-world study (NCT06467370) assessed the effectiveness of acute rimegepant (RIM) treatment in patients with migraine across 4 subgroups: (1) no concomitant preventive medication (RIM-only); (2) oral migraine preventive medications (OMPMs), (3) onabotulinumtoxinA (BTX) and (4) anti-calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) monoclonal antibodies (mAbs).

Methods Adults with 3–14 headache days and in the prior 30 days and planning to use RIM over the next 30 days were enrolled via the Migraine Buddy® app. No study treatment was provided. Results Responses from 416 patients (RIM-only [n=66] or RIM with OMPMs [n=69], BTX [n=140], or anti-CGRP mAbs [n=141]) who used RIM to treat ≥1 migraine attack were analyzed. Conclusion Patients treating migraine attacks with RIM, independent of preventive treatment use, reported meaningful pain relief, a return to normal function, and high satisfaction. It is unclear if the differences between the subgroups is based on selection bias or if there is a difference in acute RIM effectiveness with prevention use.

P053 Efficacy of atogepant on migraine headache severity in episodic migraine stratified by patient impression of disease improvement: A post-hoc analysis of the 12-week ADVANCE and 52-week open-label trials

1WVU Headache Center, Morgantown, WV, USA; 2Rehabilitation and Neurological Services, LLC, Huntsville, IL, USA; 3University of Miami, Miller School of Medicine, Miami, FL, USA; 4Thomas Jefferson University, Jefferson Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Philadelphia, PA, USA; 5AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA; 6MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, Washington, D.C., USA

P054 Effectiveness and satisfaction with eptinezumab for the preventive treatment of migraine in patients under routine clinical practice in Spain: EPIC study

1Hospital Universitario La Paz, Madrid, Spain; 2Marqués de Valdecilla University Hospital, Santander, Spain; 3Lundbeck Spain, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P054

Objective To describe the perceived effectiveness and satisfaction of neurologists with eptinezumab as a migraine preventive treatment in routine clinical practice, and to analyze the sociodemographic and clinical profiles of patients.

Methods National, observational, study based on aggregated data from patients with high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM) or chronic migraine (CM), through a structured questionnaire specifically developed for this study and addressed to neurologists.
