P055 Evaluation of real-world effectiveness of acute migraine treatment: Results from DREAM, a nationwide population study on 58,000 people

H. Winther Schytz1, D. S. Hauberg2, U. S. Lønberg2, A. Jenkins3, L. Abraham3, K. Hygge Blakeman4, M. Spanggaard5, J. Olsen5, C. Bach5, T. F. Hansen1

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2Pfizer Aps, Ballerup, Denmark; 3Pfizer R&D UK Ltd., Tadworth, UK; 4Pfizer AB, Stockholm, Sweden; 5EY Parthenon, Frederiksberg, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P055

Objective What is the effectiveness of acute migraine treatments and impact on return to normal function reported by patients in Denmark?

Methods The nationwide DREAM (Danish REgistry Analyses of Migraine) study combined data from Danish national health registers with a survey consisting of 87 questions on experience with acute and preventive migraine medications. All Danish residents ≥ 18 years having redeemed a triptan prescription or diagnosed with migraine (ICD-10: G43) between Jan 2021 – Dec 2023 were invited. With the European Headache Federation consensus statement on effective treatment of acute migraine medication in mind, we evaluated the effectiveness of acute treatments to treat the most recent migraine attack (any severity, ≤3 months prior) defined as: (1) pain freedom or pain relief within 2 h, lasting at least 24 h, (2) no or minimal migraine accompanying symptoms within 2 h, (3) no side effects. As return to normal function is a goal of acute treatment and important to patients we asked respondents about their ability to return to normal function at 2 h after taking medication.

Results Of the 144,323 people invited, 58,317 (40%) responded, of which 50,857 reported having a migraine diagnosis from a physician (migraine population (MP), 83% women, mean age 50.0). Of the 38,981 people in the MP treating a migraine attack within 3 months, only 14,021 (36%) reported effective treatment, with only 8,422 (60%) of these returning to normal function within 2 h.

Conclusion Only about 1 in 5 people treating a migraine attack achieved both effective treatment and the ability to return to normal function at 2 h, indicating that the majority of patients using acute treatments still experience a significant burden from migraine and could benefit from strategies for treatment optimization.

P056 Migraine related sick leave among people with effective treatment of migraine: Results from DREAM, a nationwide population study

H. Winther Schytz1, D. S. Hauberg2, U. S. Lønberg2, A. Jenkins3, L. Abraham3, K. Hygge Blakeman4, M. Spanggaard5, J. Olsen5, C. Bach5, T. F. Hansen1

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2Pfizer Aps, Ballerup, Denmark; 3Pfizer R&D UK Ltd., Tadworth, UK; 4Pfizer AB, Stockholm, Sweden; 5EY Parthenon, Frederiksberg, Denmark

Objective What is the impact of acute migraine treatment on days of sick leave reported by patients in Denmark?

The distribution of days of sick leave of people with and without effective treatment is presented in Fig. 1.

Conclusion People with migraine reporting effective treatment of their most recent migraine attack had significantly fewer days of migraine related sick leave than people without effective treatment, suggesting an important benefit of optimized treatment to patients and society. P057 Burden of self-reported migraine in the Pfizer Ireland workforce – A cross-sectional study

G. Dooley1, K. Nakajima2, S. Patten1, S. Chern Chuan3, F. Dai4, A. Turko3

1Pfizer Healthcare Ireland, Dublin, Ireland; 2Pfizer, Inc., São Paulo, Brazil; 3Pfizer, New York, NY, USA; 4Pfizer, Inc., Groton, CT, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P057

Objective To estimate the prevalence and evaluate the impact of migraine on workplace productivity among employees of Pfizer Ireland.

Methods An online anonymous survey was administered to all Pfizer Ireland employees between February and March 2025 to collect data on demographics, migraine history and work productivity. Participants with self-reported migraine were assessed using the ID-Migraine™ screening tool (MST) and further completed the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI-migraine) questionnaire to quantify productivity impact of migraine.

Results Of 6,517 Pfizer Ireland employees, 1,131 (17.4%) participants completed the survey, with 51.4% being male, and 56.3% being 30 to 49 years of age. The prevalence of self-reported migraine was 33.1% (N=374), and 38.6% (N=437) based on the MST. Conclusion The migraine prevalence among Pfizer employees was higher than the observed globally, probably as employees with migraine felt more engaged to participate in the study. Migraine impairs work productivity for most migraine sufferers, highlighting a need for support and treatment optimization, benefiting both individuals and the organization.

P058 Chronic migraine progression and persistence: Results from the chronic migraine epidemiology and outcomes (CaMEO) study

R. B. Lipton1, K. M. Fanning2, P. Pozo-Rosich3, K. C. Brennan4, R. Burstein5, J. H. Smith6, I. Shakhmantsir6, B. Dabruzzo6, R. Bostic2, D. C. Buse1

1Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York, NY, USA; 2MIST Research, Wilmington, NC, USA; 3Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Barcelona, Spain; 4University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA; 5Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA; 6AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P058

Objective Migraine progression is typically defined by the episodic (EM) to chronic migraine (CM) transition, precluding progression of CM. Using the CaMEO study, we evaluated 2 different definitions of migraine disease progression, based on changes in either monthly headache days (MHDs) or in Migraine Disability Assessment Scale (MIDAS) scores.

Methods The CaMEO Study (NCT01648530) was a longitudinal web-based survey, evaluating migraine disease state every 3 months for up to 1 year in a representative sample of people with migraine (US population). Eligible respondents met an ICHD-3 definition for CM at baseline and provided assessments at baseline, 3, 6, 9 and/or 12 months. Disease progression was defined as an increase of ≥5 MHDs or ≥5 MIDAS points from baseline to any follow-up timepoint; persistence required maintaining progression at subsequent timepoints for ≥6 months. External validators included the Migraine Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (MSQv2.1), a depression screener (PHQ-9), and an anxiety screener (GAD-7).

Results 342 eligible respondents with CM had a baseline median of 19.3 (Q1-15.9, Q3-21.7) MHDs and a median MIDAS score of 30.0 (Q1-13, Q3-65). 16.4% (n=56) of respondents progressed based on an increase of ≥5 MHDs, and 27.2% (n=93) based on an increase of ≥5 MIDAS points. In total, 34.5% (n=118) of respondents progressed and 7.3% (n=25) progressed and persisted based on ≥1 of these 2 disease progression definitions. The subgroup with disease progression demonstrated lower quality of life on MSQv.2.1 and higher rates of depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety symptoms (GAD-7).

Conclusion CM is a sometimes-progressive disorder. Novel definitions of progression characterize the disease state dynamics of people with CM, underscoring the need for CM treatment optimization.

P061 Fremanezumab helps in long-term migraine prevention in children – Real-world evidence

A. K. Lindén1, M. Raisio2, S. Kuusela2, M. Pohjanpää2, S. Vuolle2, E. Riuttanen2, H. Alanen2, S. Palmu2

1Tampere University, Faculty of Medicine and Health Technology, Tampere, Finland; 2Tampere University and Tampere University Hospital, Pediatric Early Phase Trials Unit, Tampere, Finland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P061

Objective There is a significant need for effective and well-tolerated medicines in the prevention of migraine in children. The purpose of this retrospective study is to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of fremanezumab in real world setting.

Methods The study population consists of 18 patients who had participated in a clinical trial investigating the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fremanezumab, and who demonstrated clinical benefit. Effectiveness was evaluated using the pedMIDAS disability scale and changes in the number of headache days. Safety was assessed through adverse effectsand changes in laboratory tests (serum chemistry, hematology, and coagulation) or ECG. A physical examination was performed at every third injection.

Results The mean age of participants was 14.6 years (11.7 to 17.7 years). Of these, ten were females. Half of the children had episodic migraine, and the remaining with chronic migraine. The number of fremanezumab injections received varied from 12 to 36, with monthly injections of 225 mg. AEs were reported in 13 patients (72%). These included redness, swelling or pain at the injection site and were not considered as clinically significant. No severe adverse effects were reported. No clinically significant findings were noted in ECGs, laboratory values, or during physical examinations. Two participants discontinued the treatment due to lack of efficacy. Quality of life improved by at least one pedMIDAS grade in 14 participants, deteriorated in one, and remained unchanged in 3 participants. Mean total PedMIDAS-score changed from 67.9 at baseline to 50.6 at follow-up (p=0.134) and the mean reduction was 17.3 points. The mean number of headache decreased from 15.3 to 9.8 days in the latest recording (p=0.027), mean reduction of 5.5 days.

Conclusion Fremanezumab showed a favourable safety profile and was associated with clinically meaningful reductions in headache frequency in children and adolescents with migraine in a real-world setting.

P063 The PopHEAD study: Prevalence of headache disorders in Norway, results from a population based cross-sectional study

M. Argren1,2,3, H. Engstrand1,2,3,4, A. K. Husøy3,5,6, E. S. Kristoffersen3,7,8, M. Toft1,2, A. H. Pripp9,10, J. A. Zwart1,3,4, B. Winsvold1,2,3

1University of Oslo, Faculty of Medicine, Oslo, Norway; 2Oslo University Hospital, Neurology, Oslo, Norway; 3Norwegian Centre for Headache Research, NTNU Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway; 4Oslo University Hospital, Research and Innovation, Oslo, Norway; 5St. Olavs University Hospital, Department of Neurology and Clinical Neurophysiology, Trondheim, Norway; 6Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Department of Neuromedicine and Movement Science, Trondheim, Norway; 7Health Services Research Unit, Dept. of neurology and clinical neurophysiology, Lørenskog, Norway; 8University of Oslo, Department of General Practice, Oslo, Norway; 9Oslo University Hospital, Research support services, Oslo, Norway; 10Oslo University Hospital, Oslo Centre of Biostatistics and Epidemiology, Oslo, Norway

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P063

Objective Reliable prevalence estimates of headache disorders are essential for public health planning. Despite previous large-scale studies, there is a lack of validated and up-to-date prevalence estimates from population-representative populations in Europe. Here, we aimed to estimate the one-year prevalence of the major headache disorders in Norway using a validated diagnostic tool.

Methods PopHEAD is a population-based Norwegian cross-sectional study. A random sample of 28,753 individuals aged 18–70 years was invited to complete a digital version of the Headache-Attributed Restriction, Disability, Social Handicap and Impaired Participation (HARDSHIP) questionnaire, adapted and translated into Norwegian and later validated. Headache diagnoses were made using a standardized algorithm based on International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) criteria. Prevalence estimates were calculated as crude proportions with 95% confidence intervals and sequentially adjusted for age and sex, measurement error and selection bias.

Results A total of 8,265 participants (3,344 men and 4,921 women; mean age 47.3 years) responded. The crude one-year prevalence was 29.6% for migraine (36.5% in women, 19.4% in men), 52.7% for Tension type headache (TTH) (51.4% in women, 54.6% in men), and 5.1% for medication overuse headache (MOH) (6.5% in women, 3.1% in men). After adjusting for age, sex, measurement error, and selection bias, the final estimated prevalence was 20.3% for migraine, 47.9% for TTH, and 5.9% for MOH. Migraine prevalence estimates were higher among participants with lower income and education, while TTH estimates were higher in those with higher socioeconomic status. MOH prevalence was highest in participants aged 26–45 and those with lower education.

Conclusion The PopHEAD study provides updated, validated and bias-adjusted prevalence estimates for migraine, TTH and MOH in the Norwegian adult population. These data may inform health resource allocation for headache management in similar populations.

P064 Identifying risk markers for high likelihood of triptan-refractory migraine among first-time users: A real-world retrospective cohort study

Y. Barer1, M. Hoshen1, S. Gazit1, M. Tirosh2, D. Davidovici2, E. Domany3, A. Mosek4

1Maccabi Institute for Research and Innovation, Maccabi Healthcare Services, Tel Aviv, Israel; 2Pfizer Pharmaceuticals, Herzeliya, Israel; 3Headache Clinic Rambam Medical Center, Department of Neurology, Haifa, Israel; 4Headache and Facial Pain Clinic, Hod Hasharon, Israel

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P064

Objective The European Headache Federation defines triptan-refractory status as failure of ≥3 triptans, including ≥1 subcutaneous formulation. We aimed to identify patients with high probability of triptan-refractory migraine, and to assess clinical features that may have predicted treatment refractoriness.

Methods This retrospective cohort study utilized deidentified data from the second-largest healthcare provider in Israel and identified members aged ≥21 years with first triptan dispensation during 2012-2022. Users were classified as “presumed triptan-refractory migraine” if they used and discontinued ≥3 different generic triptan ingredients. Delivery system was not regarded due to the low prevalence of use with subcutaneous formulations in Israel. Conversely, users were classified as “presumed non triptan-refractory migraine” if they used 1/2 generic ingredients regardless of discontinuation status, or they used 3 generic ingredients without discontinuation. Stepwise logistic regression was used to identify predicting features for triptan-refractory migraine.

Results We identified 1303 (3%) patients with presumed triptan-refractory migraine and 39,994 (97%) with presumed triptan non-refractory migraine. Compared to individuals aged 26-35 years, younger patients (20-25 years) had a 30% higher probability of experiencing triptan refractory migraine. Conversely, older patients showed decreased probability: 30% lower among patients aged 46-55 years and 64% lower among patients aged 56 years and older. Female sex, medium-high socioeconomic status, prior diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome and overactive bladder were associated with an 19%, 35%, 33% and 55% higher probability of triptan refractory migraine, respectively.

Conclusion This study estimate that approximately 3% of treated patients develop triptan-refractory migraine with a predominance of young females from medium-high socioeconomic status. Further studies are warranted.

P065 Triptans treatment patterns among first-time users: A real-world retrospective cohort study

Y. Barer1, M. Hoshen1, S. Gazit1, M. Tirosh2, D. Davidovici2, E. Domany3, A. Mosek4

1Maccabi Institute for Research and Innovation, Maccabi Healthcare Services, Tel Aviv, Israel; 2Pfizer Pharmaceuticals, Herzeliya, Israel; 3Headache Clinic Rambam Medical Center, Department of Neurology, Haifa, Israel; 4Headache and Facial Pain Clinic, Hod Hasharon, Israel

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P065

Objective Migraine is a prevalent and debilitating neurological disorder with substantial impact on an individual quality of life and on the healthcare system. Triptans have been established as the standard of care for moderate-to-severe acute migraines for over two decades. This study aims to evaluate real-world triptan treatment patterns.

Methods This retrospective cohort study utilized deidentified data from the second-largest healthcare provider in Israel and identified members aged 21 years or older who had a first triptan dispensation between 2012 and 2022 (i.e., index-date). The end of follow-up was December 2023. Triptan discontinuation was defined as the absence of additional dispensations between the last dispensation date (plus 90 days) and the end of follow-up, except where treatment cessation was due to contraindications. Time to discontinuation was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method.

Results We identified 41,297 adults with a first triptan dispensation (median age at index-date: 38.4 years [inter-quartile range: 28.2,48.0], 75.6% females). Among those, 28,920 (70%) discontinued their triptan use with median time to discontinuation of 7.8 months (95% CI: 7.2-8.4). After excluding 19,904 (48%) with only a single dispensation, 12,185 out of 21,393 individuals (56.9%) discontinued use, with an overall median treatment time of 4.6 years (95% CI: 4.5-4.7). Approximately 25% of triptan users purchased more than one generic ingredient and 14.8% more than two.

Conclusion This study indicates a high discontinuation rate. This may suggest potentially suboptimal response or tolerability issues with the current standard of care.

P066 Do migraine and tension-type headache affect cardiac structure and function? Findings from the HUNT population-based study

S. Giri1,2, H. Dalen3,4,5, E. A. Tronvik1,2,6, B. M. Nes3,4, H. Ellekjær1,7, K. Hagen1,2,8

1Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Department of Neuromedicine and Movement Science, Trondheim, Norway; 2Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Norwegian Centre for Headache Research (NorHead), Trondheim, Norway; 3Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Department of Circulation and Medical Imaging, Trondheim, Norway; 4St. Olavs University Hospital, Clinic of Cardiology, Trondheim, Norway; 5Nord-Trøndelag Hospital Trust, Department of Medicine, Levanger, Norway; 6St. Olavs University Hospital, Department of Neurology and Clinical Neurophysiology, Trondheim, Norway; 7St. Olavs University Hospital, Stroke Unit, Department of Internal Medicine, Trondheim, Norway; 8St. Olavs University Hospital, Clinical Research Unit, Trondheim, Norway

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P066

Objective To evaluate whether primary headache disorders, especially migraine and tension-type headache (TTH), are associated with alterations in cardiac structure and function.

Methods We analyzed data from the HUNT4 study (2017-2019), a population-based cohort study in Norway. Of 5,752 individuals aged ≥20 years randomly selected for echocardiography, 2,039 participants with complete headache and echocardiographic data were included. Individuals with prior stroke, myocardial infarction, or heart failure were excluded. Headache types were classified using validated questionnaires. Cardiac structure and function were assessed by echocardiography. Associations were analyzed using adjusted linear regression models.

Results Among 2,039 participants, two third were women and under 65 years. Compared to those without headache, individuals with migraine (n=150) and TTH (n=286) had 4-15% and 4-8% smaller cardiac volumes, respectively. Adjusted β-coefficients for left ventricular end diastolic volume were -2.62 (95% CI, -7.01 to 1.76) for migraine, -4.04 (95% CI, -6.87 to -1.20) for TTH, and -1.29 (95% CI -5.23 to 2.63) for unclassified headaches. Stroke volume was numerically lower in migraine (-1.56 ml) and TTH (-1.76 ml), with greater but non-significant reductions in men (-2.48 ml for migraine; -3.46 ml for TTH). Diastolic early mitral inflow (E-wave) was lower in the migraine (-2.24, 95% CI -5.24 to 0.76), but this also did not reach statistical significance. Myocardial and tricuspid regurgitation velocities did not differ between the headache groups.

Conclusion Our findings suggest a potential association between TTH and subclinical changes in left ventricular volumes. Further studies are needed to confirm these observations and explore their clinical relevance.

P067 Tolerability sof witch from erenumab to fremanezumab in adults with chronic migraine

F. M. Amin1, T. Linnet1, C. K. Collum1, T. P. Do1, S. Younis1

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Glostrup, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P067

Objective Although erenumab and fremanezumab are effective for migraine prevention, it remains unclear whether patients who experience adverse events (AEs) on erenumab can tolerate fremanezumab. Erenumab targets the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor, while fremanezumab targets the ligand. Despite this distinction, switching treatment due to AEs is often not reimbursed, based on the assumption of class-wide intolerance. This study evaluated tolerability of switching from erenumab to fremanezumab in patients with chronic migraine who experienced AEs on erenumab.

Methods We analyzed data from patients with chronic migraine who discontinued erenumab due to AEs and subsequently received at least three months of fremanezumab. AEs were recorded before and after switching.

Results In total, 94 patients (median age: 50 years) were included. Hereof, only 29 (31%) patients experienced treatment-emergent AEs after switching. Constipation was the most common AEs on erenumab (n=74, 79%), which reduced to only 12% (n=9) of patients after switching to fremanezumab. No patients discontinued fremanezumab during the study period due to AEs.

Conclusion Switching from erenumab to fremanezumab due to adverse events was well-tolerated, particularly among patients with erenumab-induced constipation. These findings support the clinical utility of switching therapies based on tolerability issues and highlight the importance of individualized strategies in migraine management.

P068 Real-world effectiveness of eptinezumab in migraine patients with prior preventive migraine treatment failures: Preliminary results from a general neurology unit in Greece

E. Karamolegkos1, E. Andreadaki1, A. Habipi1, X. Kakaflikas1, I. Triantafiloy1, N. Markos1, V. Vagenas1

1G.O.N.K Hospital, Neurology, Athens, Greece

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P068

Objective To evaluate the real-world effectiveness of eptinezumab for migraine prevention in a hospital-based setting.

Methods This retrospective observational analysis included 25 adult patients with migraine who received at least one dose of eptinezumab 100 mg. Effectiveness was assessed by changes in Monthly Migraine Days (MMDs), ≥50% and ≥75% Migraine Responder Rates (MRRs), reduction in average pain severity, resolution of the Most Bothersome Symptom (MBS), days of acute medication use, and Patient-Reported Outcomes (HIT-6 and MIDAS).

Results Patients had a mean migraine history of 26 years, 10 MMDs at baseline, average pain severity of 8/10, and used acute medication on 9 days/month. Prior treatments included traditional preventives (68%), botulinum toxin (56%), while 60% were anti-CGRP naïve. Mean baseline HIT-6 and MIDAS scores were 65 and 77, respectively, indicating severe impact and disability. By day 15, 96% of patients reported clinical improvement. At day 30, 92% experienced significant improvement or resolution of their MBS, with pain being the most frequently reported. Mean MMDs decreased from 10 to 2, and pain severity from 8 to 4. At 3 months, benefits were sustained: patients reported 3 MMDs, pain severity of 4/10, and acute medication use on 3 days/month., Overall, 88% of patients achieved a ≥50% response at 3 months.

Conclusion Eptinezumab demonstrated rapid and sustained effectiveness in reducing migraine frequency, severity, and associated disability in a real-world clinical setting. Improvements were reported by the majority of patients within 15 days of treatment initiation and were maintained over the first 12 weeks.

P069 Final Italian analysis of the PEARL study: 24 months of fremanezumab treatment on quality-of-life outcomes

M. Silvestro1, E. Cresta2,3, E. Reggio4, F. L. Castro5, S. Usai6, P. Kokturk7, M. Bartolini8

1University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Department of Advanced Medical and Surgical Sciences, Naples, Italy; 2S. Maria Hospital, Headache Center, Neurology and Stroke Unit, Department of Neurosciences, Terni, Italy; 3University of Perugia, Neurologic Clinic, Perugia, Italy; 4G. Rodolico-San Marco Hospital, University of Catania, Department of Neurology, Catania, Italy; 5AOU Policlinico di Modena, Digital and Predictive Medicine, Pharmacology and Clinical Metabolic Toxicology-Headache Center and Drug Abuse-Laboratory of Clinical Pharmacology and Pharmacogenomics, Department of Specialist Medicines, Modena, Italy; 6Headache Unit, Department of Clinical Neuroscience, C. Besta Neurological Institute and Foundation, Milan, Italy; 7Teva Pharmaceuticals Europe B.V., Amsterdam, Netherlands; 8Marche Polytechnic University, Neurological Clinic, Ancona, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P069

Objective The impact of migraine extends beyond headache frequency, affecting various domains of an individual’s life, including their ability to work, socialize, and perform daily living activities, particularly for those with chronic migraine (CM). In this sub-analysis of the 24-month, prospective, observational Pan-European Real Life study (PEARL; EUPAS35111), we assessed the effectiveness of fremanezumab on quality-of-life outcomes in a cohort of adult participants with episodic migraine (EM) or CM treated in Italy according to routine clinical practice.

Methods Participants were enrolled across 30 headache centers in Italy. Endpoints included: the proportion of participants reaching ≥50% reduction from baseline in Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS) score, mean change from baseline in MIDAS and 6-Item Headache Impact Test (HIT-6) scores, all measured at Months 12 and 24, and the proportion of participants with CM reverting to EM by Month 24.

Results In total, 354 participants were enrolled from Italian centers and included in the effectiveness analysis. In participants with data available, 75.0% (EM, 78.7%; CM, 73.2%) at Month 12 (n=288) and 66.7% (EM, 73.3%; CM, 63.3%) at Month 24 (n=45) reached a ≥50% reduction in MIDAS score. Improvements in MIDAS scores were observed at Month 12 (mean change from baseline −68.4 [EM, −52.0; CM, −76.4]), and at Month 24 (mean change from baseline −78.5 [EM, −63.0; CM, −86.0]), both in participants with EM and CM. Impact of headache, assessed by HIT-6 score, reduced at Month 12 (mean change from baseline −11.1 [EM, −10.7; CM, −11.2]), and Month 24 (mean change from baseline −13.0 [EM, −13.3; CM, −12.9]). In total, 71.9% of participants with CM at baseline had reverted to EM at Month 12 (0–7 monthly migraine days [MMD], 53.1%; 8–14 MMD; 18.8%), and by Month 24, the proportion was 86.7% (0–7 MMD, 66.7%; 8–14 MMD; 20.0%).

Conclusion Fremanezumab treatment was associated with improvements in MIDAS and HIT-6 scores over 24 months in participants with EM and CM.

P070 The prevalence and characteristics of interictal headaches in people with cluster headache

P. van Tilborg1, W. Naber1, E. Numan1, R. Brandt1,2, R. Fronczek1,3

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2The Migraine Clinic, Amsterdam, Netherlands; 3Stichting Epilepsie Instellingen Nederland (SEIN), Heemstede, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P070

Objective Cluster headache (CH) patients often report interictal headaches (IH). Due to relatively limited knowledge on IH, we aimed to explore their prevalence and characteristics in CH.

Methods All 912 CH patients in our database were invited to complete a single e-survey on their CH attacks (CHA) and, if present, IH (headache between CHA, not better explained by another ICHD-3 diagnosis). We distinguished 2 IH patterns: continuous pain (shadow headache; SH) and short-lasting pain (shadow attack; SA). Participants rated impact on quality of life (QoL; 10-point scale) for each headache subtype. Descriptive statistics and logistic regression were performed.

Results 529 patients completed the survey. 275 (53%) reported one or both IH types (SH: n=134 [25%]; SA: n=191 [36%]). IH prevalence was higher in women (β=1.53; 95% CI 1.00-2.32; P=0.05) and those with self-reported comorbid primary headaches (β=3.57; 95% CI 2.20-5.93; P<0.001), and lower with increasing age (β=0.971; 95% CI 0.96-0.987; P<0.001). Headache characteristics differed in SH and SA vs. CHA (Fig. 1). SH and SA were more often bilateral (38% & 37% vs. 1%), frontal and occipital (44% & 56% vs. 24%; 43% & 55% vs. 14%) instead of orbital (49% & 35% vs. 82%), all P<0.001. SH and SA were dull/nagging (46% & 43%) rather than stabbing in CHA (87%), less severe (NRS 5 [IQR 4-6] vs. 9 [9-10]) and less often accompanied by autonomic symptoms and restlessness (28% & 29% vs. 96%; 33% & 33% vs. 92%), all P<0.001. SH and SA impacted QoL less than CHA (5 [IQR 3-7] and 4 [2-6] vs. 8 [6-9]). In the SH group, 25 (19%) used analgesics ≥10 days/month (excluding triptans taken for CHA).

Conclusion The presentation of IH is less distinct than CHA, though some patterns were found. While SH may indicate medication overuse headache in some, in our cohort most used analgesics <10 days/month. We propose both IH forms are part of the CH phenotype. The high prevalence and moderate impact on QoL highlight the need to recognize IH. Our findings can aid physicians to identify IH.

P072 Treatment patterns in the ContemporAry ProspecTive Understanding of migraine Real-world Evidence (CAPTURE) study

C. Tassorelli1, M. Matharu2, J. Ailani3, M. Lantéri-Minet4,5, J. Lam6, Y. Liu7, H. Ha6, L. Delahaye8, P. Pozo-Rosich9

1University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy; 2Institute of Neurology, London, UK; 3Georgetown University Hospital, MedStar, Washington, D.C., USA; 4CHU & Côte Azur University, Nice, France; 5Auvergne University, INSERM U1107 Migraine and Trigeminal Pain, Clermont-Ferrand, France; 6AbbVie, Toronto, Canada; 7AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA; 8AbbVie, Rungis, France; 9Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P072

Objective To describe patterns of medication use for migraine over the first 12 months of the ContemporAry ProspecTive Understanding of Migraine Real-world Evidence (CAPTURE) study.

Methods CAPTURE is a 2-year, international, prospective, longitudinal, observational study of disease burden and treatment patterns among patients with migraine currently consulting at specialty clinics. Participants aged ≥18 years with a migraine diagnosis for ≥1 year who used ≥1 migraine medication and experienced ≥4 MHDs in the 3 months before screening were stratified by headache frequency during 30-day screening: 4–<8 MHDs (Cohort 1), 8–<15 MHDs (Cohort 2), and ≥15 MHDs (Cohort 3). Assessments were current migraine treatment(s)/duration, new treatment(s), changes in current treatment, switching (initial-subsequent/monotherapy-combination therapy), and acute medication overuse.

Results The population (N=555; Cohort 1=139, Cohort 2=251, Cohort 3=165) was aged 41.4-43.0 years, >83% female, and >94% White. The percentage of participants who switched from initial treatment to subsequent treatment and from monotherapy to combination therapy was generally low (<8%), being higher for acute medications (≤7.9%) than for preventive medications (≤6.0%). A substantial decrease from baseline in the percentage of overusers at Month 12 was observed in Cohorts 2 and 3: 19.1% to 8.1%, and 63.0% to 31.7%, respectively. Overuse occurred in <6% of participants in Cohort 1.

Conclusion Through Month 12, acute medication overuse decreased in both Cohorts 2 and 3, being more marked in the latter. Cohort 2 switched more frequently preventive treatments. These snapshot findings suggest that the completed CAPTURE study may provide novel insights into migraine treatment patterns, helping to characterize migraine burden.Fig. 1 (abstract P072).Fig. 2 (abstract P072).

P073 Use of eptinezumab in refractory chronic migraine: Real-world experience from the Glasgow headache service

M. Lowe1, G. Gorrie1, S. Miller1, A. Tyagi1, K. Dani1

1Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, Neurology, Glasgow, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P073

Objective Eptinezumab is an intravenously administered monoclonal antibody (MAb) targeting the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) ligand. We report our experience using eptinezumab in a cohort of patients with refractory chronic migraine.

Methods We retrospectively reviewed medical records and headache diaries for 38 patients who received eptinezumab in our service between October 2023 and February 2025. All patients received 100 mg eptinezumab initially, some patients later received 300 mg. Monthly (28 day) headache diaries were collected at baseline and over 2-3 months post-treatment. Headache days (HD) were classified as severe (SHD) if the average pain rating (numeric rating scale) was 7 or greater. Monthly HDs and SHDs were averaged over the available follow up period. Treatment response was defined as a 30% reduction in HDs or a 50% reduction in SHDs compared to baseline.

Results All patients had tried or had contraindications to at least 6 preventative treatment classes; 97% had previously received CGRP targeting treatment; 97% had previously received botulinum toxin; and 71% met the European Headache Federation definition of refractory migraine. Complete headache diary data was available for 33 patients: at 2-3 months follow up after 100 mg IV eptinezumab, 18 (55%) met criteria for a positive response. Mean reduction in HDs was 5.1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 3.0-7.1), and in SHDs was 5.6 (95% CI 3.4-7.7). 27 patients (71%) continued eptinezumab after the initial 3-month trial. 20 received further doses of 100 mg, whilst 7 received the 300 mg dose. At the time of review, 22 patients remained on treatment (mean duration 348 days, range 95-498 days).

Conclusion Eptinezumab appears to be a reasonable treatment option in refractory migraine, even after poor response to prior CGRP-targeting treatment. Our study has limitations; most significantly its retrospective and uncontrolled nature and the lack of headache diary data after 3 months to corroborate reported longer-term response.Fig. 1 (abstract P073).

P074 Use of eptinezumab or an alternative subcutaneous CGRP-targeting monoclonal antibody after non-response to two prior CGRP targeting treatments: A real-world observational evaluation

M. Lowe1, S. Miller1, G. Gorrie1, A. Tyagi1, K. Dani1

1Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, Neurology, Glasgow, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P074

Objective Multiple treatments targeting the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) pathway have been developed for the preventative treatment of migraine. Real world data suggest that an alternative CGRP targeting treatment can be effective if a patient does not respond to a first. We present our experience comparing the use of eptinezumab, an intravenously administered monoclonal antibody (MAb) targeting CGRP, or an alternative subcutaneous (SC) CGRP-MAb after failure of 2 prior CGRP targeting treatments.

Methods We identified 43 patients who had received a third CGRP-MAb after non-response to 2 prior CGRP targeting treatments; 22 received a third SC MAb (11 galcanezumab, 10 fremanezumab and 1 erenumab) and 21 received eptinezumab. Their medical records and headache diaries were retrospectively reviewed. Monthly headache diaries were collected at baseline and 3 months post-treatment. Headache days (HD) were classified as severe (SHD) if the average pain rating was 7 or greater. Treatment response was defined as a 30% reduction in monthly HDs or a 50% reduction in SHDs.

Results Patients receiving eptinezumab or a third SC MAb had no significant differences in age, gender, baseline HDs/SHDs, number of prior preventative treatment trials or medication overuse. Complete headache diary data were available for 19 patients in each group. 12/19 (63%) met criteria for positive response with eptinezumab; 6/19 (32%) met criteria for positive response with a third SC MAb. Reduction in HDs after treatment was 7.0±1.4 (mean±SEM, p<0.01) with eptinezumab and 0.4±0.6 (p=0.54) with a third SC MAb. Reduction in SHDs after treatment was 6.6±1.5 (p<0.01) with eptinezumab and 1.9±1.8 (p=0.29) with a third SC MAb.

Conclusion After non-response to 2 CGRP targeting treatment, eptinezumab resulted in a significant reduction in HDs/SHDs. Use of a third SC MAb did not result in a significant reduction in HDs/SHDs, with lower overall positive response rates. Our evaluation is limited by its uncontrolled, observational nature.Fig. 1 (abstract P074).

P075 Associations between headache prevalence and use of conventional and heated tobacco products and passive smoking: A cross-sectional study based on the Japan ‘Society and New Tobacco’ Internet Survey (JASTIS)

M. Katsuki1,2,3,4, M. Tatsumoto5,6, K. Suzuki6, T. Shimazu7, Y. Matsumori8, Y. Fuse9, T. Ward3, S. O’Connor2, K. Moran2,3,10, T. Tabuchi11

1Nagaoka University of Technology, Physical Education and Health Center, Niigata, Japan; 2Dublin City University, School of Human and Health Performance, Dublin, Ireland; 3Dublin City University, Insight Science Foundation Ireland Research Centre, Dublin, Ireland; 4Saitama Medical University, Department of Biostatistics, Saitama, Japan; 5Canon Marketing Japan Inc, Canon Marketing Japan Inc, Tokyo, Japan; 6Dokkyo Medical University, Department of Neurology, Tochigi, Japan; 7Saitama Neuropsychiatric Institute, Department of Neurology, Saitama, Japan; 8Sendai Headache and Neurology Clinic, Sendai, Japan; 9Graduate School of Medicine and School of Medicine, Chiba University, Department of Artificial Intelligence Medicine, Chiba, Japan; 10Maynooth University, Department of Sport Science and Nutrition, Maynooth, Ireland; 11Graduate School of Medicine, Tohoku University, Division of Epidemiology, School of Public Health, Sendai, Japan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P075

Objective Heated tobacco products (HTPs) are novel nicotine delivery systems that heat tobacco leaves without combustion. While the association between conventional cigarette smoking and headache disorders has been well documented, evidence regarding HTP use remains limited. This study aimed to examine whether HTP use is associated with the prevalence of chronic headaches in a large Japanese cohort.

Methods We utilized data from the Japan “Society and New Tobacco” Internet Survey (JASTIS), a nationally representative, ongoing internet-based cohort initiated in 2015 to monitor trends in tobacco product use. Participants were recruited from a panel of over 2 million individuals. In the 2025 wave, 23,228 respondents with complete and valid data were included from the initial 28,000 participants. Headache prevalence was assessed by the question, “Have you experienced headaches in the past year?“—with responses of “occasionally” or “frequently” categorized as positive. Multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and clinical variables.

Results Current (OR: 1.71; 95% CI: 1.44–2.03) and former (OR: 1.54; 95% CI: 1.37–1.73) cigarette smokers showed significantly increased odds of reporting headaches. Current HTP users also demonstrated a modest but significant association (OR: 1.15; 95% CI: 1.01–1.32). Additionally, 16% of participants reported experiencing headaches following passive exposure to cigarette or HTP smoke.

Conclusion Current and former use of conventional cigarettes was significantly associated with increased headache prevalence, and a smaller yet significant association was observed for HTP use. These findings suggest that, despite perceptions of reduced harm, HTPs may still contribute to headache development through exposure to nicotine and other volatile compounds.

P077 “Migraine and I” – Small project for big changes?

V. Kosta1, L. Topic2,3, A. Banovic2,3, M. Jerkovic2,3, J. Krka2,3, M. Pervan2,3, J. Rakuljic Zelov2,3, K. Caljkusic1, J. Gulisija1, M. Jelavic1, Z. Nikolic1, T. Pijerov1

1University Hospital of Split, Department of Neurology, Split, Croatia; 2Croatian Medical Student International Committee (CroMSIC), Split, Croatia; 3University of Split, School of Medicine, Split, Croatia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P077

Objective Migraine is one of the most common neurological conditions and one of the leading causes of disability among working-age population. Only minority of patients are receiving proper care. The aim of our project “Migraine and I” was to enhance the knowledge of medical students about migraine and to identify migraine enthusiasts among them who could deepen their understanding and subsequently educate their peers.

Methods Neurological team, consisted of two neurologist and three neurology residents, have designed five short lectures about migraine. Topics have covered the burden of migraine, pathophysiology, clinical picture, differential diagnosis and approach to a patient with migraine. Participating medical students completed pre - and post - lecture questionnaires and knowledge tests to assess learning outcomes.

Results Thirty students (79% of them were female), that had already finished a neurology course, have attended our lectures. Baseline knowledge was limited, with an average correct response rate of 29.9%. Following the lectures series, this rate significantly increased to 60%. Students were very satisfied with the lectures; 86.7% of them rated lectures as great. Six highly motivated students joined our team to continue lecturing and participating in various migraine-related initiatives.

Conclusion Extracurricular lectures can greatly improve the knowledge about migraine among young future doctors, but the problem is the lack of interest for them. Only 13% of students who were invited have attended lectures. Finding the way how to attract much more students would make a difference. Nevertheless, working in small, motivated groups has proven to be highly effective and productive.

P078 AI-powered simulated patients with automated feedback for enhancing headache history-taking skills: A convergent mixed-methods study

K. Sindhvananda1, K. Ruengwattanachot1, S. Leksuwankun2, T. Pongpitakmetha3, A. Hiransuthikul3, P. Anukoolwittaya3, P. Panjasriprakarn1

1Faculty of Medicine at Chulalongkorn University, Division of Integrated Innovation and Digital Technologies Affairs, Bangkok, Thailand; 2Faculty of Medicine at Chulalongkorn University, Department of Pharmacology, Bangkok, Thailand; 3Faculty of Medicine at Chulalongkorn University, Comprehensive Headache and Orofacial Pain (CHOP) Research Group, Bangkok, Thailand

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P078

Objective Headaches are a common but diagnostically challenging, relying heavily on patient history. However, medical students often struggle due to limited case exposure and feedback. Conclusion AISPs with automated feedback show strong potential as scalable tools for improving clinical skills in headache education and may effectively complement traditional teaching.Fig. 1 (abstract P078).

P079 Improving headache care through specialized education

L. J. Zavala1, H. Winther Schytz1, R. H. Jensen1

1University of Copenhagen, Department of Neurology, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P079

Objective Headache disorders affect 40% of the global population but remain underdiagnosed and untreated due to limited specialist access. This gap highlights the need for structured educational programs to improve healthcare professionals’ skills in headache diagnosis and management. We aimed to explore the impact of an academic master’s program on graduates’ careers, work status, and educational needs.

Methods In this observational cross-sectional study performed between July and September 2024, 88 Master of Headache Disorders (MHD) graduates from the University of Copenhagen were invited to complete an anonymous online survey assessing career impact and educational needs.

Results 80 graduates (91% response rate) across cohorts from 2018 (MHD1) to 2024 (MHD4) were analyzed, representing 36 countries; 63% were female, and 43% aged 35-44 Before enrollment, the majority held bachelor’s or master’s degrees, predominantly in neurology (48%), nursing (13%) and physiotherapy (8%). P081 Development and evaluation of a behavioral training program for the reduction of migraine attacks in patients in the primary care setting

A. Wolfram1

1MVZ München Süd Harras, Academic Family Practice of the Ludwig-Maximilians University Munich, Munich, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P081

Objective According to the AWMF (German Society for Neurology) guidelines for the treatment and prophylaxis of migraine, patients with frequent migraine attacks with pronounced symptoms should be offered not only medication-based migraine prophylaxis but also behavioral modification training. The goal was to reduce the frequency of migraine attacks per month.

Methods Based on the recommendation of the guidelines, a training system for behavior modification was designed. Psychological methods such as education, self-observation, relaxation techniques, mindfulness, endurance sports, as well as recommendations for low-sugar, low-fat and ketogenic diets and the reduction of processed foods were implemented.The program was evaluated in patients who had been in neurological treatment for 3 years or more and who had established medication-based migraine prophylaxis. The patients received the training using information resources. The evaluation was based on a questionnaire that included, among other things, acceptance, teaching quality and motivation, as well as the frequency of migraine attacks.

Results The process evaluation shows a high level of acceptance and a measurable effect in terms of extrinsic and intrinsic motivation for the training material. The frequency of migraine attacks was reduced from 4 to 6 times a month to 1-3 times a month three months after the start of the program. 40% of the subjects stated that they no longer had migraine attacks three months after using the program and training material.

Conclusion The recommendations of the information tool were understandable and could be implemented. The psychological methods for self-observation and mindfulness, endurance sports and the nutritional recommendations could be implemented. The questionnaire was partly considered too extensive. The program is an effective tool for learning behavior modification for migraine as an accompanying measure to medication-based prophylaxis.Fig. 1 (abstract P081).Fig. 2 (abstract P081).

P082 What patients want: A qualitative study on an information resource on migraine

M. Castaldo1, Z. Liang1, G. Williams1, S. Watson1, C. Haynes1, Z. Diamond1

1University of Parma, Department of Medicine, Parma, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P082

Objective The aim of this study was to explore patient preferences and perspectives on a migraine information resource to be used in clinical settings.

Methods Seven individuals with migraine participated in two-hour focus groups to refine a digital information resource they received during participation in a study on individualized physiotherapy management. A physiotherapist experienced in managing patients with headache facilitated discussion regarding content, format and delivery of information. The sessions were audio-recorded and transcribed. Reflexive thematic analysis was performed to refine codes and interpret key themes from the data.

Results Four themes were interpreted. Theme 1 was that the science mattered. Participants wanted evidence-based, neuroanatomical and physiological information to explain what migraine is, why they experience those symptoms, and how to self-manage. Theme 2 was validation. Knowledge of migraine enabled self-compassion, reflection and acceptance which led to better self-management strategies such as pacing, exercise and stress relief. External validation from others through sharing of knowledge further encouraged these strategies. Theme 3 described tailoring of information for the population and the individual. This meant that the clinician delivering information needed a thorough understanding of each patient’s experiences and circumstances so as to individualise content, delivery and pacing of information. Theme 4 was empowerment and positivity: it relates to the positivity participants wanted projected by the information and the empowerment they gained from it. Participants wanted migraine described as a condition that can be managed and quality of life improved, not a “disability”. Knowledge gave a sense of control. Self-management strategies with personal relevance were empowering.

Conclusion Patients want scientific, validating, positive and relatable information that will empower self-management in migraine.

P083 Coping and pain catastrophizing in migraine patients and their mothers: A comparison between mothers with and without migraine

M. Proietti Checchi1, S. Tarantino1, F. Ursitti1, G. Monte1, G. Sforza1, A. Borrelli1, M. Valeriani1,2,3, L. Papetti1

1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Developmental Neurology, Rome, Italy; 2University of Rome Tor Vergata, Child Neurology and Psychiatry Unit, Rome, Italy; 3Aalborg University, Translational Pain Neuroscience and Precision Medicine, CNAP, Dept. of Health Science and Technology, Aalborg, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P083

Objective We aimed to:1) explore coping strategies and pain catastrophizing in children and their mothers, and their association with (a) headache frequency and (b) pain intensity; 2) compare coping and catastrophizing between patients and mothers (with and without migraine), analyzing relationships across subscales.

Methods We included 166 children (m.a 12.2 ± 2.6 years) with migraine, and their mothers. Patients were categorized by:1) daily, high and low frequency; 2) severe and mild pain intensity; and 3) children of mothers with and without migraine. Pain catastrophizing was assessed using the PCS/PCS-C (Pain Catastrophizing Scale/Child), while coping strategies were evaluated using the PPCI (Children’s Coping Strategies to Physical Pain) and the CSQ-R-I (Coping Strategies Questionnaire-Revised, Italian version).

Results Children with daily headache showed higher scores in “Total PCS-C” (0.038) and “Helplessness” (0.015). Their mothers showed higher scores in “Self-Statement” (0.050). Mothers of children with severe pain had higher scores in “Magnification” (0.011) and lower scores in “Ignoring Pain Sensations” (0.029). Children of migraine mothers had higher “Problem Solving” scores (0.047). No significant differences were observed between mothers with and without migraine, but “Magnification” in non-migraine mothers correlated with children’s “Rumination“(0.049), “Helplessness“(0.028), and “Catastrophizing“(0.009).

Conclusion Children with daily headache exhibit greater pain catastrophizing and helplessness. Migraine severity is linked to maladaptive coping strategies in mothers, which, in non-migraine mothers, correlate with similar maladaptive strategies in their children. While no significant differences were found between mothers with and without migraine, children of migraine-affected mothers showed a greater tendency toward problem-solving, suggesting adaptive traits that may be learned or inherited.

P085 Comparison of pain characteristics and activity patterns in migraine patients with and without cervical dysfunction – A descriptive preliminary study

E. S. Dusgun1, H. Altay2, Ş. Toprak Çelenay3

1Fenerbahce University, Physiotherapy, Istanbul, Turkey; 2Mardin Artuklu University, Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation, Mardin, Turkey; 3Ankara Yildirim Beyazit University, Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation, Ankara, Turkey

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P085

Objective This study aimed to compare pain characteristics and activity patterns in migraine patients with and without cervical dysfunction.

Methods A total of 88 individuals diagnosed with migraine were included and classified into two groups based on cervical dysfunction status: Cervical Dysfunction group (CD group; n = 45; median age: 24.0 [IQR: 18.0–50.0]) and Non-Cervical Dysfunction group (Non-CD group; n = 43; median age: 21.0 [IQR: 18.0–50.0]). Cervical dysfunction was assessed using the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire. Pain characteristics (frequency, intensity, duration) over the past month were recorded. Activity patterns were evaluated with the Patterns of Activity Measure-Pain, including Avoidance, Overdoing, and Pacing subscales.

Results The pain frequency was significantly higher in the CD group compared to the Non-CD group (p = 0.015). However, no statistically significant differences were found between groups for pain intensity (p = 0.516) and duration (p = 0.166). Overdoing scores were significantly higher in the CD group (p = 0.008), while Avoidance (p = 0.844) and Pacing (p = 0.933) scores showed no significant differences (Fig. 1).

Conclusion These findings suggest that although pain intensity and duration were similar between groups, increased headache frequency and higher Overdoing scores in the CD group may reflect a maladaptive pain response. Evaluating cervical musculoskeletal involvement appears relevant in migraine care. Recognizing pain activity patterns -especially Overdoing- can guide patient education and self-management approaches. Supporting patients in modifying these behaviors may help reduce pain intensity and enhance functional outcomes. Future research should explore how such strategies can be effectively integrated into clinical practice.Fig. 1 (abstract P085).

P086 Understanding patient perceptions of migraine provocation models: A call for awareness and ethical engagement

M. Al-Afraji1, L. Pellesi1

1University of Southern Denmark, Odense, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P086

Objective Human provocation models are a cornerstone of migraine research, enabling the study of pathophysiological mechanisms and the identification of novel therapeutic targets. However, these studies involve the intentional induction of migraine attacks, which may raise ethical concerns. Despite their widespread use in countries like Denmark, little is known about how patients perceive these models or whether cultural differences affect their acceptance. This study aimed to explore and compare the perspectives of Danish and Italian individuals with migraine regarding provocation models.

Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey among Danish and Italian individuals with migraine, using Facebook-based recruitment (Fig. 1). A total of 268 Danes and 146 Italians responded to a questionnaire exploring awareness, attitudes, ethical concerns, willingness to participate, trust in researchers, and preferences for alternative research approaches.

Results Awareness of provocation models was significantly higher in Denmark (28%) than in Italy (2%). Despite limited prior knowledge, participants recognized the scientific value of such studies. Key concerns included the risk of severe migraine attacks, inadequate pain relief, and long-term effects. Willingness to participate was conditional, and ethical acceptability was recognized when strict guidelines were followed. Notably, Danish respondents expressed greater trust in researchers, while Italian respondents showed stronger preference for alternative research methods.

Conclusion This study reveals a need for better patient education and communication around provocation studies. Addressing ethical concerns is critical not only to facilitate research participation, but also to reduce stigma and build public trust.Fig. 1 (abstract P086).

P087 Stigma in migraine: Preliminary results from the Studio Emicrania Maugeri (SEM) project

L. Giani1, C. Lunetta1

1Istituti Clinici Scientifici Maugeri IRCCS Milano, Neurological Rehabilitation, Milan, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P087

Objective We assessed the experience of stigma related to migraine in healthcare workers using the Migraine-related Stigma (MiRS) scale [1].

Methods The Studio Emicrania Maugeri (SEM) is an observational study aimed at evaluating the prevalence and characteristics of migraine among healthcare workers. Maugeri is a healthcare organization comprising 25 clinical sites in Italy. All the employees (4050 persons) were invited to answer to an anonymous web questionnaire about headache. Participants who consented and reported experiencing headaches at least once per year completed the Italian Version of the “ID Migraine” [2] for migraine screening, and a literal translation of the MiRS questionnaire to evaluate the frequency of experienced migraine-related stigma.

Results A total of 783 persons answered the questionnaire, of which 363 with a positive migraine screening completed the MiRS questionnaire. The majority of respondents (57%) reported experiencing stigma rarely or sometimes, while 33% reported never experiencing stigma. However, a notable proportion (10%) reported experiencing some kind of stigma often or very often.

Conclusion These preliminary results confirm the importance of addressing stigma in migraine and suggest the need for targeted interventions to reduce its impact in occupational settings even among healthcare workers.

P088 Assessing migraine awareness in adolescents: Insights for developing preventive and educational programs

G. Fiorentini1,2, G. Egeo1, C. Aurilia1, P. Barbanti1,2

1IRCCS San Raffaele, Rome, Italy; 2San Raffaele University, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P088

Objective The aim of this study was to assess the level of awareness about migraine among high school students, to explore the potential impact of preventive and educational interventions in this population.

Methods A 20-item questionnaire was developed, covering four domains: disease knowledge, stereotypes and stigma, impact on quality of life, and use of healthcare resources. It was administered to 63 fourth-year students from a high school in Rome. Responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics.

Results The student population comprised 38 males and 25 females, aged 17–18 years. Most students (88.9%) recognized characteristic migraine symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia. However, only 25.4% identified migraine as a brain disorder and 46% expressed uncertainty about its curability. Regarding stereotypes, 87.3% rejected the idea that “all headaches are the same”. Nevertheless, many still perceived absenteeism from school (44.5%) or social events (30.2%) due to migraine attacks as excessive. More than half (55.6%) reported concern that their pain might not be taken seriously, and 20.6% anticipated difficulties in discussing it with others. Concerning healthcare, 71.4% acknowledged the risk of medication overuse, while 33.3% considered diagnostic imaging necessary to confirm a migraine diagnosis, reflecting partial and sometimes distorted views of clinical management.

Conclusion This study highlights existing gaps in migraine knowledge among adolescents, alongside persistent stereotypes and stigma that may hinder appropriate healthcare use. These findings underscore the importance of implementing preventive and educational programs in schools to enhance awareness and promote healthier behaviors. Limitations include the exploratory nature of the study and the lack of formal validation of the questionnaire, which calls for further research to refine the assessment tools and confirm these preliminary results.

P089 Awareness of medication overuse headache in Hungary: Survey among pharmacists and the general population

K. Gecse1,2,3, R. Kovacs-Vincze1,4, G. Juhasz1,2,3

1Semmelweis University, Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Department of Pharmacodynamics, Budapest, Hungary; 2Semmelweis University, NAP3.0-SE Neuropsychopharmacology Research Group, Hungarian Brain Research Program, Budapest, Hungary; 3Semmelweis University, Center of Pharmacology and Drug Research & Development, Budapest, Hungary; 4Glória Pharmacy, Budapest, Hungary

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P089

Objective Although medication overuse headache (MOH) represents a significant burden, awareness of the condition remains limited worldwide. Pharmacists may play a role in counselling patients about appropriate medication use, yet their level of knowledge on MOH has not been comprehensively evaluated.

Methods Our objective was to assess the knowledge of MOH among pharmacists and the general population in Hungary using an online survey about MOH.

Results The pharmacist survey was completed by 116 pharmacists (76.7% female) working in Hungarian community pharmacies. The majority (62.1%) reported being asked for advice about headache at least daily. However, 41.4% had never heard of MOH. Among those familiar with the condition, most (80.9%) had learned about it during university studies or continuing education. Regarding medications associated with MOH, the most frequently recognized was non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, 88,8%), only 23,3% mentioned that triptans could be overused. In the general population survey, 579 volunteers (75% female) participated. Only 25.2% had ever heard of MOH, and 70% were unaware of which analgesics could contribute to its development. Among those who were aware that analgesics could cause headaches, 48.2% had learned about it through healthcare education or work, 25.3% via media, and only 21.8% had heard about it from a pharmacist. This percentage is still higher than the proportion informed by their physician (17.1%).

Conclusion Awareness of MOH in Hungary is insufficient among both pharmacists and the general population. Although pharmacists showed higher awareness than general population, substantial knowledge gaps remain. Most pharmacists would suggest patients to ask headache specialists help, highlighting their pivotal role in early detection. Targeted educational programs for pharmacists, as well as public health campaigns, are essential to improve prevention and reduce the burden of MOH., Funding: EKOP-2025-624, Anna Richter Award, Hungaropharma Scholarship.

Objective To evaluate the 24-week impact of eptinezumab versus placebo on electronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs) in adults with chronic migraine (CM) and medication-overuse headache (MOH) who received patient education.

R. H. Jensen1, C. Lundqvist2, H. Winther Schytz1, C. Tassorelli3, F. Vernieri4, M. Lantéri-Minet5, G. M. Terwindt6, A. Blumenfeld7, S. J. Tepper8, M. K. Josiassen9, G. Jansson9, A. Ettrup9, A. Mittoux9, R. B. Lipton10

Objective To evaluate the 24-week efficacy and safety of eptinezumab in adults with chronic migraine (CM) and medication-overuse headache (MOH) who also received patient education.

Methods RESOLUTION was a phase 4 clinical trial (NCT05452239) including a 12-week double-blind placebo-controlled period and 12-week open-label extension (OLE). P095 Efficacy and safety of combination of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies and onabotulinumtoxinA in chronic migraine treatment: A systematic review and meta-analysis

A. Putra1,2, H. C. Kusuma2, I. S. Madjid1, H. R. Sofyan1, J. F. A. Barus2, S. B. Tjahaja2, I. Samuel2, J. Congdro2, J. K. Sindaka2, J. Julianty2, V. G. Wijaya2, M. Y. Putri1, W. A. Isaac1, S. A. S. Simatupang1, A. R. Faiq1, S. Rizqi1, T. Aninditha1

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P095

Objective Migraine is a common, disabling disorder with CGRP as a key therapeutic target. OnabotulinumtoxinA, which inhibits CGRP release from unmyelinated C nociceptive fibers, and anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), which selectively block CGRP-receptor interaction at meningeal vessel walls, peripheral sites and along Aδ fibers offer preventive options for chronic migraine (CM). While combining may improve outcomes, their interaction—additive or synergistic—remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses current evidence on their combined use for CM prevention and treatment.

Methods Following PRISMA 2020, PubMed, ProQuest, Lancet, EBSCO, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched (past 10 years). Eligible randomized and observational studies reported monthly migraine days (MMD), monthly headache days (MHD), and adverse events. Pooled analyses employed random-effects models; risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2.0/ROBINS-I and funnel plot, and GRADE analysis was done independently.

Results 5 studies (n=615, all with diagnosis of CM) were included, comparing three combination regimens to onabotulinumtoxinA monotherapy. Erenumab + onabotulinumtoxinA showed significant reductions in MHD (-5.53 days; 95% CI: -7.76, -3.30; p<0.00001, low certainty) and MMD (-4.42 days; 95% CI: -6,28, -2.56; p<0.00001, low certainty) compared to onabotulinumtoxinA alone. Safety profiles were favorable with no serious adverse events reported.

Conclusion Combining anti-CGRP mAbs with onabotulinumtoxinA appears to be a promising approach for CM prevention. Although current safety data are limited, the reported adverse events have generally been mild. Further research is needed to establish its safety, efficacy, and optimal protocols in episodic and chronic migraine populations.Fig. 1 (abstract P095).Fig. 2 (abstract P095).Fig. 3 (abstract P095).

P096 Association between the clinical profile of patients with trigeminal neuralgia and treatment resistance: Case series analysis

A. Martins1, G. Teles1, M. Viana Baptista2, G. Cabral1

1Hospital Egas Moniz, Lisbon, Portugal; 2NOVA Medical School, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Neurología, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P096

Objective Is There an Association Between the Clinical Profile of Patients with Trigeminal Neuralgia and Treatment Resistance?

Methods This retrospective study included all patients diagnosed with Trigeminal Neuralgia (TN) seen at the Headache Outpatient Clinic of Hospital Egas Moniz between January 2024 and April 2025. A total of 51 patients met the inclusion criteria. Demographic, clinical, and imaging data were collected. Statistical analysis was conducted using IBM SPSS version 29.0. Non-parametric tests were applied because the variables had a non-normal distribution. Treatment resistance was defined as the use of three or more medications.

Results The sample consisted of 66.7% female patients, with a mean age at symptom onset of 60.2 ± 17.0 years. MRI was performed in 35 patients, with abnormalities detected in 65.7% of cases. No significant associations were found between MRI findings and the side or location of pain, neurological signs, disease relapse, botulinum toxin usage, or surgical interventions. TN was classified as classical (40%), idiopathic (50%), and secondary (10%). The average number of medications prescribed was 2.7 ± 1.3. There was no significant association between the number of drugs and disease duration or age at symptom onset. Although the number of medications did not differ significantly across TN subtypes, patients with secondary TN tended to require more medications (mean: 4.3). In a small subgroup (n = 3), satisfactory pain control was achieved using lacosamide in combination with another medication.

Conclusion In patients with TN, no clinical or imaging variables were significantly associated with treatment resistance. These findings suggest that standard clinical characteristics may not fully explain therapeutic response, emphasizing the need for individualized treatment strategies and further research into predictive biomarkers. Preliminary observations also support further investigation of lacosamide as a potential first-line treatment option.

P097 Evaluating the efficacy of combined treatment in patients with Persistent Idiopathic Facial Pain (PIFP)

L. Rukhadze1, G. Chakhava2, G. Matchavariani1, D. Tabatadze1

1Central University Hospital After Acad. N. Kipshidze, Neurology, Tbilisi, Georgia; 2Multiprofile Clinic Consilium Medulla, Neurology, Tbilisi, Georgia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P097

Objective Persistent idiopathic facial pain (PIFP) (previously known as atypical facial pain) is characterized by persistent facial and/or oral pain in the absence of a neurologic deficit. Due to the lack of the large-scale multi-center randomized control trials, current guidlines for the treatment regimen are limited in terms of evidence quality. Our main goal was to assess the effectiveness of the combined treatment with antidepressant and an antiseizure medication, based on patient feedback collected during clinical follow-up.

Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 9 patients meeting diagnostic criteria for PIFP. P098 Trigeminal neuralgia secondary to posterior fossa arteriovenous malformation and hydrocephalus: A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge

J. M. Ferreira Machado1, A. L. Neves2, B. Barreto2, A. Gomes3, S. Moreira1, A. Ferreira3

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Matosinhos - Hospital Pedro Hispano, Neurología, Senhora da Hora, Portugal; 2Unidade Local de Saúde de São João - Hospital São João, Neurología, Porto, Portugal; 3Unidade Local de Saúde de São João - Hospital São João, Neurocirugía, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P098

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Classical trigeminal neuralgia typically results from neurovascular compression at the root entry zone of the trigeminal nerve, most commonly by the superior cerebellar artery (SCA). Although rare, the concomitant presence of a posterior fossa arteriovenous malformation (AVM) can underlie this condition, adding diagnostic and therapeutic complexity.

Methods Clinical case.

Results A 32-year-old woman presented with paroxysmal facial pain in the right V3 territory, described as brief, electric shock-like episodes triggered by touch, chewing, and speech, with progression to eight daily episodes within one month. Neurological examination revealed macrocephaly, inattention, gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus, generalized hyperreflexia, and broad-based gait. Brain CT showed hydrocephalus with sulcal effacement. CT angiography revealed a large posterior fossa AVM (Spetzler-Martin grade V) centered in the superior vermis. MRI confirmed compression of the right trigeminal nerve by an ectatic SCA and periventricular edema due to chronic hydrocephalus. Angiography identified multiple arterial feeders (SCAs, PICAs) and venous aneurysms causing brainstem molding. Carbamazepine 200 mg every 8 h led to full pain resolution within 48 h. Due to its size and complexity, the AVM was deemed inoperable. The clinical picture was attributed to decompensation of chronic hydrocephalus, and placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt resulted in marked improvement of gait and balance. Three months post-discharge, medical therapy was successfully withdrawn.

Conclusion This case illustrates a rare presentation of trigeminal neuralgia secondary to a large posterior fossa AVM, associated with decompensated chronic hydrocephalus. Although there was a favorable response to initial medical and surgical management, the case underscores the need for careful consideration of alternative therapeutic strategies should symptoms recur in a patient with an inoperable AVM.

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P099

Objective The study aimed to investigate the predictive factors of response to Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)–targeted therapies in patients with migraine and multiple sclerosis (MS).

Methods This retrospective, multicenter study (17 Italian MS centers) included patients with MS treated with anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) or gepants, combined with disease-modifying treatments (DMTs), on a stable DMT regimen for at least three months before the anti-CGRP targeted therapy initiation and a minimum follow-up period of three months for the concomitant treatment. Collected MS data included age at onset, prior and current DMT, EDSS score, MRI activity, and clinical relapses. Collected migraine data included monthly headache days (MHDs) before and at last follow-up, disease duration, age at onset, type, and duration of anti-CGRP mAb treatment. A multivariate linear regression model was then used to examine the associations between predictor variables and treatment response (MHD delta from baseline to last follow-up).

Mean MS age onset was 28.33±9.11 years while mean migraine age onset was 19.04±8.12 years. At baseline, the mean MHDs was 20.5±7.05. Mainly used DMTs were ocrelizumab (25.5%), natalizumab (19.1%), and dimethyl fumarate (17.0%), while anti-CGRP treatments included anti-CGRP mAbs (95%) and atogepant (5%). Conversely, longer MS duration was linked to reduced benefit (β=–0.749, p=0.02).

Conclusion We confirm the safety of combined DMT and CGRP treatments in patients with both conditions. Timely and tailored therapy should be planned early in MS disease course to achieve the best outcomes.

P100 Super-refractory cerebrospinal fluid hypotension headache: A case report

G. Diniz Pinho1, J. Bonifácio Vítor1, I. Brás Marques1, B. Santiago2, S. Nunes Oliveira1

1Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Neurosurgery, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P100

All patients gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Dural tears/subarachnoid-venous communications may cause cerebrospinal fluid hypotension (CSFH). Though rarely severe, extreme measures with anecdotal evidence may sometimes be needed.

Methods Case-report.

Results A 74-year-old woman with no trauma history had acute intense orthostatic headache. Brain CT revealed pachymeningeal enhancement and bilateral 10 mm subdural effusions. She was given paracetamol, caffeine and fluids. MRI revealed C6-7, D3, D8-11, L3 and S1-2 spinal nerve root cysts. Poor response prompted lumbar blood patch (BP). Confusion and obtundation were noted even prior, followed by coma in the subsequent hours. A 2nd CT showed convexity effusion enlargement and de novo 9 mm falcine hemorrhage with cerebellar tonsil herniation. She was ventilated after antiseizure therapy failed. EEG showed diffuse slowing. Trendelenburg positioning and vigorous L3-4 intrathecal saline administration were tried after demonstrated negative pressure upon subarachnoid space catheterization, with marked consciousness improvement in 48 h. Upright headache recurred, however, and CT myelography showed an active D11 CSF leak and distant bilateral kidney enhancement, suggestive of a CSF-venous fistula. A 2nd dorsal BP was performed. However, prostration ensued so more fluid was instilled at the catheter site, and digital subtraction myelography revealed another major lumbar CSF leak at the catheter placement site. It was surgically closed, a new catheter was placed at L2 with maintained 30cmH2O pressure post-fluids, and a final target epidural patch was done to the high-flow CSF from a mixture of iodine contrast, autologous blood and fibrin glue. The patient regained full consciousness and tolerated progressive standing, headache-free.

Conclusion This case highlights the complex management of BP-refractory CSFH. Coma precipitated intrathecal fluid reposition, which is rarely reported but may have allowed our patient time for further investigation, though with complications, before definite leak closure.

P101 Middle meningeal artery lidocaine infusion for refractory migraine: First case report in Portugal

S. Moreira1, A. Costa1, J. M. Araújo1, J. M. Amorim2, S. Varanda1

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Neurology, Braga, Portugal; 2Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Neuroradiology, Braga, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P101

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Refractory migraine is a disabling and hard-to-treat condition. Middle meningeal artery (MMA) lidocaine infusion may be a treatment option.

Methods Case report.

Results A 42-year-old man with episodic migraine since the age of 20 developed chronic daily bifrontal headaches, pressure-like, associated with photophonophobia, kinesiophobia, and anorexia. The condition was further complicated by medication-overuse headache, resulting in multiple hospital admissions. Various pharmacologic classes were tried without benefit: antihypertensives and calcium channel blockers (propranolol, candesartan, flunarizine), antiepileptics (valproic acid, topiramate, oxcarbazepine), antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, venlafaxine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, clomipramine), other preventives (prednisolone, oxitriptan, melatonin), cycles of botulinum toxin (PREEMPT protocol), monoclonal antibodies (galcanezumab, fremanezumab, erenumab), and atogepant. At the time of the procedure, the patient was on eptinezumab 100 mg and botulinum toxin every three months but continued to have daily headaches, with severe intensity and reliance on eletriptan for acute relief. A selective lidocaine infusion into both middle meningeal arteries was performed under angiographic guidance resulting in immediate and sustained reduction in headache intensity, fewer migraine days, and decreased eletriptan use. HIT-6 score improved from 67 to 55 at 30-day follow-up. MIDAS assessment will be more informative after longer follow-up. No adverse events occurred.

Conclusion MMA lidocaine infusion has been described in few cases, and this is, to our knowledge, the first reported in Portugal. It constitutes an invasive therapeutic approach that should be considered only as a rescue option for carefully selected patients with severely refractory migraine. Further studies and long-term follow-up are needed to assess efficacy and safety.

P103 Real-world evidence of monoclonal antibodies use in refractory migraine patients on polytherapy: Insights from a headache center

B. Martins1,2, I. Brás Marques3, E. Parreira3,4, A. L. Neves1,2, C. Correia1,2, R. Gil-Gouveia3

1Unidade Local de Saúde de São João, E.P.E., Neurology, Porto, Portugal; 2Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade do Porto, Departamento de Neurociências Clínicas e Saúde Mental, Porto, Portugal; 3Headache Center, Hospital da Luz, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 4Unidade Local de Saúde de Amadora/Sintra, Amadora, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P103

Objective Preventive polytherapy is often used in refractory migraine, despite limited evidence and potential drug interactions. We aimed to examine the impact of initiating monoclonal antibodies (MAbs) on polytherapy migraine regimens.
