Conclusion In this sample, MAbs proved to have beneficial effects not only by diminishing the necessity for preventive polytherapy in patients with refractory headache but also by ameliorating the impact and disability associated with migraine.

P104 Clinical outcomes of botulinum toxin type A in chronic migraine: Real-world data from Unidade Local de Saúde de Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro

J. Pona-Ferreira1, A. Costa1, M. Perdicoúlis1, R. Raimundo1, A. Matas1, A. G. Velon1

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro, Neurology, Vila Real, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P104

Objective Chronic migraine is a disabling neurological disorder defined by ≥15 headache days per month. OnabotulinumtoxinA is the first neurotoxin specifically approved for its prophylaxis. P106 Octreotide in the management of pharmacoresistant idiopathic intracranial hypertension: A case report

S. Bueso Diaz1, F. J. Alberola Amores1

1Hospital General Universitario de Elche, Neurología, Lorca, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P106

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) is a condition with unknown pathophysiology, involving factors such as obesity, growth hormone (GH) production, increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production, and impaired reabsorption, which lead to symptoms like headache and visual acuity loss. First-line pharmacological treatment includes acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production, along with topiramate or diuretics. Alternatives include GLP-1 receptor analogs, 11B-HSD1 inhibitors, and octreotide.

Methods We present the case of a 34-year-old obese woman diagnosed with IIH, treated with furosemide and topiramate, with poor response and limiting side effects. She refused a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, so treatment with octreotide was started at 0.2 mg/24 h for 5 days, then 20 mg/month for 6 months.

Results Octreotide acts as a somatostatin receptor agonist in the choroid plexus, decreasing CSF production and inhibiting GH and IGF-1. One month after treatment initiation, clinical improvement and resolution of papilledema were observed, which persisted after discontinuing treatment at 6 months.

Conclusion Treatment-refractory IIH presents a therapeutic challenge. Octreotide is a promising alternative with favorable outcomes, expanding therapeutic options for this condition.

P107 Inhaled Acetylsalicylic Acid (ASA) reaches therapeutic blood levels and effectively blocks cyclooxygenase enzymes

S. Canisius1, W. Timmer2, K. Kaiser3, K. Nocker1, A. Fischer4

1AspiAir GmbH, Gemünden, Germany; 2Nuvisan GmbH, Neu-Ulm, Germany; 3Ratatoa GmbH, Oberwil, Switzerland; 4Activoris Medizintechnik GmbH, Gemünden, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P107

Objective ASA has antithrombotic and analgetic effects, however when administered orally exhibits numerous gastrointestinal side effects, which limits the dose. Orally inhaled ASA avoids these side effects and utilizes the lung as a safe route of administration. While the GI side effects can also be avoided with intravenous (i.v.) administration, inhaled ASA would allow for flexible self-treatment by the patient, at home or on the road. The purpose of this study was to compare the PK of different inhaled doses of ASA to i.v. administration.

Methods In a multiple cross-over study in healthy subjects, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamic effects of inhaled ASA, applied with a newly developed mesh inhaler device (ASCOT® inhaler), were investigated and compared to ASA i.v. In total, 16 healthy subjects received 4 different single doses of inhaled ASA (250 mg, 500 mg, 750 mg at 87.5 mg/mL) and one intravenous dose of ASA (500 mg at 87.5 mg/mL) in a randomized 4-times cross-over design. In a separate study part, 500 mg ASA at 158.7 mg/mL were inhaled by 12 subjects. Blood levels of ASA and salicylic acid (SA), as well as Thromboxane B2 (TxB2) were measured over a period of 24 h post-dose.

Results Inhalation was safe and well tolerated. Measured PK profiles showed a good dose-exposure relationship. Typical adverse events observed, such as coughing or sore throat, were mainly mild and dependent on the dose and the inhaled concentration of ASA. Pharmacokinetic analyses showed a rapid bioavailability of 62% of the delivered dose. The decrease in TxB2 levels with inhalation was similar to i.v. treatment 30 min post-dose. This effect remained even after 24 h.

Conclusion Inhaled ASA is safe, and the PK data supports the approach. The rapid and consistent decrease of TxB2 levels point towards a similar beneficial effect on pain compared to the standard i.v. treatment. Further studies should be carried out in patients to confirm the initial results.

P109 Trigeminal neural and hemifacial spasm – An uncommon association

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro, Neurology, Vila Real, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P109

Objective To describe a case of concurrent trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm caused by trigeminal neurovascular contact and to discuss the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms.

Methods Patient gave their consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

A 61-year-old female presented with a 3-year history of recurrent electric shock-like pain attacks in the left hemiface, along the maxillary and mandibular trigeminal nerve branches’ distribution. The pain usually lasted a few seconds and recurred multiple times a day. Some episodes were triggered by talking and touching the face.

Results The neurological examination showed a left-sided hemifacial spasm. The MRI showed a point of contact with the anterior inferior cerebellar artery in the prepontine cistern. P110 What happens to bone in chronic migraine patients after one year of anti-CGRP therapy? A prospective study of bone metabolism markers and densitometric parameters

L. de La Guerra-Sasián1,2, G. Gárate1,2, M. Haro1,2,3, A. Maiztegi-Azpitarte2, M. T. García-Unzueta2, J. L. Hernández1,2,3, J. M. Olmos1,2,3, C. Valero2, V. González Quintanilla1,2, J. Pascual Gómez1,2,3

1Marqués de Valdecilla Health Research Institute (IDIVAL), Santander, Spain; 2Marqués de Valdecilla University Hospital, Santander, Spain; 3Universidad de Cantabria, Santander, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P110

Objective CGRP is a known modulator of bone homeostasis. We prospectively investigated the evolution of bone metabolism and density in chronic migraine patients during their first year of monoclonal anti-CGRP antibody (mAb-CGRP) treatment.

Methods Sixty (60) patients with chronic migraine were recruited. Biochemical markers of bone formation (P1NP) and resorption (CTX) were measured at baseline (M0), three (M3), and twelve (M12) months after starting mAb-CGRP therapy. Scans were performed at M0 and M12 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, and total hip to determine the bone mineral density (BMD). T-scores were calculated for all sites. Analyses were stratified by menopausal status.

Results P1NP levels showed a non-significant downward trend over time (M0: 40.4 [32.7–59.5] μg/L; M3: 38.8 [28.2–51.7] μg/L, p > 0.999; M12: 37.8 [29.7–51.1] μg/L, p > 0.999). Similarly, CTX levels remained unchanged (M0: 0.324 [0.254–0.446] pg/mL; M3: 0.322 [0.228–0.443] pg/mL, p > 0.987; M12: 0.278 [0.200–0.483] pg/mL, p > 0.999). Lumbar spine bone mineral density significantly declined after one year (M0: 0.979 [0.897–1.041] g/cm²; M12: 0.949 [0.873–1.014] g/cm², p = 0.001), with a corresponding decrease in lumbar T-scores (M0: –0.9 [–1.6–0.0]; M12: –0.9 [–1.6–(–0.3)], p = 0.003). When stratified by menopausal status, this decline remained significant only among postmenopausal women (n = 23; p = 0.004 for bone mineral density, p = 0.005 for T-score). No significant changes were observed at femoral neck or hip sites.

Conclusion One year of mAb-CGRP treatment may negatively affect bone formation, particularly in postmenopausal women with chronic migraine. While no significant alterations were observed in biochemical markers, bone density findings suggest localized bone loss at the lumbar spine. These preliminary results underscore the importance of bone health surveillance and preventive strategies in women receiving long-term anti-CGRP therapies.

Work supported by grants PI21/00532 and PMP22/00183.

P113 Synergistic antimigraine effects of lisinopril and memantine associated with an improved therapeutic index

S. Farkas1,2, C. Horváth3, I. Kis-Varga3, C. Csekő3, É. Makó3, A. DiCamillo4, T. Kitka1, Z. Péterfi1,2

1VRG Therapeutics Ltd., Budapest, Hungary; 2Novamigra Therapeutics, Budapest, Hungary; 3Gedeon Richter Plc, Budapest, Hungary; 4Melior Discovery, Inc., Exton, PA, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P113

Objective Despite available treatments, many migraine patients experience suboptimal response or tolerability issues. Combining agents with complementary neurological and vascular mechanisms may offer improved outcomes in preventive therapy. This study evaluated the pharmacodynamic interaction between lisinopril and memantine, both of which have shown efficacy in randomized controlled trials and are used off-label for migraine prophylaxis.

Methods The efficacy of lisinopril and memantine, administered alone and in combination (1:1 dose ratio), was tested in two rat models of migraine involving chronic trigeminovascular sensitization: (1) partial infraorbital nerve ligation (pIONL) and (2) repetitive dural inflammatory soup infusion (rDISI). Orofacial or periorbital tactile allodynia was measured using von Frey filaments. Additionally, pharmacodynamic interactions on blood pressure and heart rate were assessed in awake, unrestrained rats via cardiovascular telemetry. Dose–response curves were generated and compared.

Results In the pIONL model, both drugs reversed allodynia in a dose-dependent manner, while the combination produced a five-fold leftward shift in the dose–response curve, indicating synergy. In the rDISI model, lisinopril reversed allodynia in a dose-dependent manner, whereas memantine alone had only minimal effect. However, when co-administered, memantine markedly potentiated the effect of lisinopril, enabling a ten-fold dose reduction. Cardiovascular telemetry confirmed lisinopril’s expected effects: blood pressure reduction and dose-dependent reflex tachycardia. Memantine had no cardiovascular effects and did not alter lisinopril’s profile in combination.

Conclusion Lisinopril and memantine exhibit strong pharmacodynamic synergy in migraine models without adverse or amplifying cardiovascular effects. This combination may offer enhanced efficacy with a favourable side effect profile, supporting its potential utility in migraine prophylaxis.

Neurologia AOU “SS. Antonio e Biagio e Cesare Arrigo”, Alessandria, Alessandria, Italy; 20University of Siena, Department of Medical, Surgical and Neurological Sciences, Siena, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P115

Objective To assess whether the timing of atogepant administration influences its tolerability and effectiveness over 12 weeks in patients with episodic and chronic migraine in a real-world setting.

Methods This is a post-hoc analysis of the first 12 weeks of the STAR study, a prospective, multicenter study in Italy evaluating atogepant 60 mg for migraine prevention. Data were collected at baseline (T0) and after 12 weeks (T3). Patients were grouped by administration timing (morning vs. evening). Changes in monthly headache days (MHDs), migraine days (MMDs), and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were assessed. Tolerability was evaluated via adverse events (AEs). Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were used.

Results 81 patients (86% females, mean age 50.8±13.7) were included. At T3, MMDs dropped from 16.6 to 9.7 (p<0.001) and MHDs from 19.2 to 10.7 (p<0.001); 60% achieved ≥50% reduction in MMDs. AEs occurred in 43% of patients. Atogepant was taken in the morning by 57% and evening by 43% of patients. No significant differences in MMDs, MHDs, or AEs emerged between groups. Evening users had higher baseline MIDAS scores (70.0 vs. 39.9), but showed a greater reduction (F(1,63)=6.29, p=0.015), with similar final scores at T3 (25.1 vs. 23.9).

Conclusion Timing of atogepant administration (morning vs. evening) did not affect overall effectiveness or tolerability. However, a greater MIDAS score reduction in evening users was observed. Whether this reflects a pharmacodynamic advantage or a ceiling effect remains unclear. Long-term and dedicated studies are needed to evaluate and confirm these findings.

P116 Low sodium oxybate use for nocturnal cluster headache: Efficacy, tolerability and safety – A phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, bi-center study

M. van Liefland1, P. van Tilborg1, W. Naber1, C. Kramers2, G. J. Lammers1, H. M. Thrainsson3, Z. Zhang3, R. Khatami3,4, R. Fronczek1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Radboud University Medical Center, Pharmacology-Toxicology, Nijmegen, Netherlands; 3Clinic Barmelweid, Sleep, Medicine & Epileptology, Barmelweid, Switzerland; 4Inselspital, University Hospital Bern, University of Bern, Department of Neurology, Bern, Switzerland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P116

Objective Cluster headache (CH) is characterized by severe headache attacks that typically occur during sleep. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy, tolerability and safety of low sodium oxybate (LXB) for nocturnal attacks in patients with chronic cluster headache (CCH). Methods In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, bi-center trial, patients (18–75 years) with CCH and ≥4 nocturnal attacks per week will be enrolled. Conclusion This is the first randomized, placebo-controlled trial investigating LXB for nocturnal CH. P118 Trigeminal neuralgia secondary to giant saccular aneurysm/endovascular procedure – Is lidocaine block an old treatment with a new indication?

M. Pereira1,2, A. I. Gonçalves1, A. Silva3, H. Mota Dória3, R. Pestana4, T. C. Aguiar1

1Hospital Dr. Nélio Mendonça - Centro Hospitalar do Funchal, Serviço Regional de Saúde da Madeira – Portugal, Serviço de Neurologia, Funchal, Portugal; 2Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Instituto de Fisiologia, Lisbon, Portugal; 3Hospital Dr. Nélio Mendonça - Centro Hospitalar do Funchal, Serviço Regional de Saúde da Madeira – Portugal, Serviço de Neurorradiologia, Funchal, Portugal; 4Hospital Dr. Nélio Mendonça - Centro Hospitalar do Funchal, Serviço Regional de Saúde da Madeira – Portugal, Serviço de Neurocirurgia, Funchal, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P118

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Trigeminal neuralgia is a chronic facial pain syndrome characterized by sudden, intense, and electric shock-like episodes, typically unilateral, affecting one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve. In most cases, it is idiopathic, but a subset is secondary to structural lesions such as brain tumors, demyelinating disease, or vascular compressions—particularly aneurysms—only detectable through neuroimaging. Carbamazepine is the standard first-line treatment, although alternatives such as oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, or pregabalin may be considered in cases of intolerance or poor response.

Methods A 59-year-old woman presented with trigeminal neuralgia affecting the left V1–V2 territory. MRI revealed a giant saccular aneurysm of the left internal carotid artery’s communicating segment. She underwent endovascular treatment with simple coiling and was started on carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily. Two months later, she developed persistent pain and progressive bilateral visual impairment. MRI confirmed compression of both the trigeminal and optic nerves by the aneurysmal mass and coils. Due to poor control of pain (15 episodes/month) and intolerance to carbamazepine (ataxia, vertigo), eslicarbazepine was introduced. Trials with oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, pregabalin, and levetiracetam were ineffective and poorly tolerated. After 12 months, imaging showed a reduction in aneurysmal size and partial visual recovery. However, neuralgic episodes persisted (4/month, each lasting up to 2 days).

Results Given the refractoriness of symptoms, the patient was submitted to peripheral nerve block with 2% lidocaine at the auriculotemporal and supraorbital branches, resulting in marked improvement and a >50% reduction in frequency and severity of attacks.

Conclusion Peripheral nerve block with lidocaine is a safe, accessible, and effective option for symptom relief and should be considered in cases of secondary trigeminal neuralgia refractory to pharmacological treatment.

P120 Glymphatic dysfunction in migraine mice model

Z. Xiao1

1Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University, Neurology, Wuhan, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P120

Objective The glymphatic system is essential for waste removal in the central nervous system, facilitated by aquaporin-4 (AQP4) at the end of astrocytes. While the glymphatic system plays a role in various neurological diseases, its involvement in migraine remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the relationship between glymphatic dysfunction and migraine, providing potential targets for migraine prevention and treatment.

Methods The study used a nitroglycerin-induced migraine model in C57/BL6 mice. The glymphatic influx of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tracer was measured, and AQP4 expression and polarization were evaluated. The effect of glymphatic suppression via TGN-020 (an AQP4 blocker) on migraine pathology was also assessed.

Results In the migraine model, glymphatic influx of CSF tracer was reduced, accompanied by decreased AQP4 expression and impaired polarization, indicating glymphatic dysfunction. Further suppression of glymphatic function by TGN-020 aggravated migraine-related pathological changes in mice.

Conclusion Glymphatic dysfunction may worsen migraine pathology, with AQP4 being a potential therapeutic target for migraine.

P126 nAChR modulation as a potential target in post-COVID headache and fatigue syndrome: Preliminary observational findings

G. Waldmann1

1MEDICLIN, Mediclin Rehabilitation Center, Bad Düben, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P126

Objective A significant number of patients experience persistent symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Common complaints include long-lasting headaches—often stabbing and stress-sensitive—and fatigue with both somatic and cognitive elements, such as brain fog. When these symptoms co-occur with musculoskeletal pain, dyspnea, weakness, or cognitive deficits, the condition is referred to as Post-COVID Fatigue Syndrome (PCFS). The pathophysiology remains unclear but is likely related to altered neuronal signaling. Evidence suggests a dysregulation of excitatory and inhibitory intracortical networks (Versace, 2021). Excitatory transmission is mainly mediated by cation-permeable ion channels, particularly glutamatergic receptors (AMPA, NMDA, kainate) and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Acetylcholine plays a key role in central synaptic activity, autonomic regulation, and neuromuscular function. Central cholinergic systems modulate arousal, reward, cognition, and motor control (Gil 2018). Nicotine has been discussed as a protective factor in SARS-CoV-2 infection (Changeux 2020). It has been hypothesized that COVID-19 and PCFS may involve impaired nAChR signaling, potentially modifiable by nicotine agonists.

Methods We reviewed Post-COVID patient data from January 2020 to May 2025 at RC Bad Düben (n=302) with documented PCFS (n=228) and headaches (n=11), analyzing self-reported nicotine use.

Results Only 11% of PCFS patients reported nicotine use. Notably, none of the patients with combined PCFS and headache were smokers (0%). This rate is markedly lower than the smoking prevalence in the general German population (22%).

Conclusion These observations suggest a potential modulatory role of nicotine in post-COVID symptom expression. Preliminary experiences with nicotine patches have shown possible benefit. Controlled studies are needed to explore nAChRs as therapeutic targets in PCFS.

P127 The cogni̇ti̇ve burden of cervi̇cogeni̇c headache: Unexplored neurophysi̇ologi̇cal li̇nks

T. Dere1, B. N. Durukan1, H. Abakay1

1Yozgat Bozok University, School of Sarıkaya Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation, Sarikaya, Turkey

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P127

Objective It is well-established that chronic pain adversely affects cognitive functions such as attention, memory, and executive functions, particularly in conditions like migraine and tension-type headache. However, the cognitive profile associated with cervicogenic headache (CGH) remains poorly understood. Therefore, the aim of this review is to elucidate the cognitive impairment in individuals with CGH and to synthesize the underlying neurophysiological basis of this relationship based on the current literature.

Methods A literature search was conducted for the period 2015-2025 in the PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases. The search utilized the following keywords: “cervicogenic headache”, “cervicogenic chronic headache”, “cognitive impairment”, “cognitive dysfunction”, “cognitive disability”, “cognitive decline”, “attention”, “executive function”, and “mental deterioration”.

Results In cervicogenic headache, the neuroanatomical substrate involves interneurons within the trigeminocervical nucleus, which facilitate a sensory information exchange between the upper cervical spinal nerves and the trigeminal nerve. Specifically, afferent sensory signals travel within the dorsolateral tract and the substantia gelatinosa. This persistent nociceptive input is hypothesized to form the basis for central sensitization in chronic CGH, which in turn is thought to impact higher-order functions such as perception, executive functions, attention, and memory.

Conclusion Chronic pain resulting from CGH can lead to both anatomical and functional changes, while also imposing a significant cognitive load that potentially impairs parameters such as cognition, executive functions, memory, attention, and perception. P128 The transient receptor potential melastatin type 3 plays a critical role in light aversion

Z. Huang1,2, M. Wang1,2

1Xi’an jiaotong-Liverpool University, Suzhou, China; 2University of Liverpool, Institute of Systems, Molecular and Integrative Biology, Liverpool, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P128

Objective Transient receptor potential melastatin 3 (TRPM3) is a cation channel that contributes to activating trigeminal nerve fibres in neuropathic pain, While activation of trigeminal ganglion is essential for triggering light aversion behavior in mice. This project aims to identify whether TRPM3 contributes to light aversion behavior and explore its underlying mechanisms.

Methods Adult male C57BL/6J mice were used, and behavior procedures were approved by the University Research Ethics Review Panel and conducted following national and provincial guidelines. Light aversion was induced by intranasal injection of the TRPA1 activator, umbellulone. Mouse behavior was assessed by the total time they stayed in dark and light areas. qPCR and RNA-seq were used to detect Trpm3 gene expression and related microRNA levels in the TG. RNA interactions were identified by dual-luciferase reporter gene assay.

Results Inhibition of TRPM3 by intraperitoneal injection of ISO markedly reduced the total time in light and transition times of photophobia mice induced by umbellulone, indicating a crucial role of TRPM3 in mediating light aversion. In line with this, rapid induction of Trpm3 gene expression following light aversion was observed in the trigeminal ganglion, suggesting TRPM3 translational machinery activation. Such upregulation of Trpm3 gene expression following photophobia corresponds to a downregulated miR-196a-5p. Furthermore, dual-luciferase reporter gene assay identified sequence-based physical RNA interactions between miR-196a-5p and Trpm3 in HEK293 cells. These data revealed that the sustained Trpm3 transcript production is attributed to the repressed miR-196a-5p level following photophobia.

Conclusion TRPM3 plays a pivotal role in light aversion. TRPM3 channels would be a novel therapeutic target in preventing migraine-associated light aversion.

P129 Impaired venous outflow in migraine with and without aura: An MRV study

S. Braca1, C. V. Russo1, A. Miele1, A. Stornaiuolo1, G. Cretella1, C. Giannini1, R. de Simone1

1University of Naples “Federico II”, Department of Neuroscience, Reproductive Sciences and Odontostomatology, Naples, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P129

Objective Idiopathic intracranial hypertension without papilledema (IIHWOP) and migraine are almost clinically indistinguishable. Accumulating evidence suggests that impaired regulation of intracranial pressure (ICP), even if insufficient to cause overt intracranial hypertension (IIH), may represent a pathophysiological mechanism underlying migraine. Since venous sinus stenosis is the most prominent radiological marker of elevated ICP, this study aimed to quantify the degree of venous stenosis present in migraine patients to investigate this association.

Methods We enrolled 161 consecutive patients, classifying them into three clinical cohorts —IIH (n=36), migraine without aura (n=97), and migraine with aura (n=36) —and compared their results with those of 37 healthy volunteers. Venous outflow compromise was quantified for each transverse sinus and for the superior sagittal sinus as follows: luminal narrowing <33% scored 0, 33–66% scored 1, >66% scored 2, and complete flow interruption (“flow gap”) scored 3. One additional point was assigned when the confluence of sinuses showed torcular non-confluence. The distribution of these scores across the clinical groups was compared with the Kruskal-Wallis test.

Results Both migraine without aura (median=3, IQR=2–4; p<0.001) and migraine with aura (median=3, IQR=3–4; p<0.001) groups had significantly higher stenosis scores than controls (median=2, IQR=1–3). The difference between the two migraine subtypes did not reach statistical significance (p=0.774). As expected, patients with IIH demonstrated the highest stenosis scores (median=6, IQR=5–6), significantly exceeding all other groups (p<0.001).

Conclusion Migraine patients, both with and without aura, demonstrated significantly greater venous sinus stenosis compared to healthy controls. This finding suggests that impaired venous outflow and the consequent elevation in ICP, though insufficient to cause overt signs of IIH, might contribute to the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying migraine.

P130 A case report on the association of migraine with focal cortical dysplasia

M. Fila1, J. Krekora2, J. Blasiak3

1Polish Mother’s Memorial Hospital Research Institute, Lodz, Poland; 2Medical University of Lodz, Lodz, Poland; 3Mazovian University in Plock, Faculty of Medicine, Lodz, Poland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P130

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Migraine is associated with morphological alterations in the brain, cerebellum, and brainstem manifested as nontraumatic brain lesions, including deep white matter hyperintensities, infratentorial hyperintensities, infarct-like lesions in the posterior circulation territory, volumetric changes in the cortex, alterations in cytoarchitecture, and changes in the neuronal network. Variations in cortical thickness in migraine patients have been reported and are similar to focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) according to the criteria of the International League Against Epilepsy. The aim of this work is to argue for a causal relationship between FCD and migraine and analyze an associated case.

Methods A 29-year-old woman has been experiencing worsening headache attacks for nearly 20 years. She was diagnosed with high-frequency episodic migraine without aura and currently has 5 to 10 migraine headache days per month. An MRI was performed for examination.

Results Cortical neurons are implicated in migraine pathogenesis. The brain cortex exhibits several functional changes associated with migraine, such as cortical spreading depression (CSD), enhanced excitability, altered connectivity, and abnormal energy metabolism, which are underpinned by mitochondrial dysfunction in both interictal and ictal phases, suggesting a structural source. Structural alterations in the cortex were directly observed in migraine patients. An MRI of the case revealed signal abnormalities in the left occipital lobe, suggesting focal cortical dysplasia. A 3-month follow-up confirmed the initial diagnosis without any signs of change.

Conclusion Cortical changes in migraine patients align with the FCD criteria, but further research is needed to establish or exclude a causal relationship between them.

P131 Exploring the role of melatonin and its receptors in primary headache pathophysiology: Insights from the trigeminovascular system

A. Maddahi1, L. Edvinsson1, D. Krause1,2

1Lund University, Department of Clinical Sciences, Lund, Sweden; 2University of California at Irvine, Department of Pharmacology, Irvine, CA, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P131

Objective Primary headache disorders such as migraine and cluster headache show circadian patterns, potentially linked to melatonin, a hormone that regulates biological rhythms. Melatonin has shown promise as a treatment; however, its precise mechanisms particularly - its interactions with the trigeminovascular system (TVS) remain unclear. This study investigates the expression and localization of melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2 in key regions of the TVS.

Methods The hypothalamus, cerebral arteries, dura mater, trigeminal ganglion (TG), dorsal root ganglion (DRG), and sphenopalatine ganglion (SPG) were dissected from adult male and female rats. Immunohistochemistry and RT-qPCR were used to assess melatonin receptors expression.

Results MT1 and MT2 were differentially expressed in TG, DRG, and SPG. MT1 was widely distributed in the cytoplasm and nuclei of neurons and satellite glial cells (SGCs), while MT2 localized mainly in the cytoplasm of neurons, Aδ-fibers, and SGCs. MT1 co-localized with CGRP and RAMP1, whereas MT2 co-localized with RAMP1. In SPG, both receptors co-localized with the neuropeptides VIP and PACAP, indicating involvement in autonomic regulation. No significant sex differences were found, although MT1 levels were approximately twice higher than MT2 in TG. MT2 immunoreactivity in Aδ fibers were found throughout the dura mater. Only MT1 was present in cerebral vessels, localized mainly in the endothelial and smooth muscle cells. RT-qPCR confirmed higher MT1 expression in TG compared to MT2 and lower MT1 expression in the hypothalamus relative to TG.

Conclusion MT1 and MT2 receptors show distinct expression patterns within sensory and autonomic regions implicated in headache. The wider distribution and vascular presence of MT1 suggest a more prominent role in modulating trigeminovascular activity. These findings highlight potential mechanisms through which melatonin influences headache pathophysiology and support its future therapeutic use.

P133 Estradiol and other sex-hormones dynamics in menstrual migraine: Pathway analysis of hormonal fluctuations in a controlled cohort study

G. M. Terwindt1, B. van der Arend1, I. Verhagen1, D. van Casteren1, J. Goeman1, J. Laven1, A. Maassen van den Brink1, S. van den Berg1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P133

Objective Menstrual migraine (MM) is linked to hormonal fluctuations, but the precise role of sex hormones remains unclear. This study hypothesizes that women with MM experience a steeper decline in estradiol before menstruation.

Methods In this prospective cohort study, 28 women with MM and 18 healthy controls were followed over two menstrual cycles. Blood samples were collected on standardized cycle days based on the LH surge (day 0), specifically on days 1, 2, 3, 8, 10, 12, and 14 post-surge, covering mid- and late-luteal phases. The primary outcome was the peak estradiol level during the mid-luteal phase (day 8) and its subsequent decline from day 8 to day 14. Secondary outcomes included levels of other sex hormones such as steroids (progesterone, testosterone), gonadotropins, and androgens, as well as hormone pair ratios.

Results Women with MM had a 49% higher peak estradiol level during the luteal phase (1·49, 95% CI: 1·03–1·87, p=0·04) and a 90% greater decline from mid- to late-luteal phase compared to controls (1·90, 95% CI: 1·16–3·12, p=0·03). Secondary pathway analysis showed no differences in other sex hormones, although progesterone showed high variability and a peak difference of similar magnitude to estradiol.

Conclusion Women with MM have a higher peak estradiol and a more pronounced estradiol decline during the luteal phase compared to controls, indicating that interventions for women with MM need to focus on stabilizing estradiol fluctuations during the luteal phase for migraine attack prevention.

P134 Migraine attack incidence in relation to ovulation: A prospective cohort study

G. M. Terwindt1, I. de Boer1, B. van der Arend1, S. Bakker1, S. Cannegieter1, D. van Casteren1, I. Verhagen1, A. Maassen van den Brink1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P134

Objective Previous studies suggest the perimenstrual phase increases migraine risk without aura, while the link to the ovulatory phase remains unclear.

Methods We conducted a longitudinal cohort study among 554 women with migraine and a regular menstrual cycle. Participants completed a validated e-headache diary including also the menstrual cycle. Of these women, 31 (who participated in our Women Hormones Attacks and Treatment (WHAT)-hormone study) performed urine luteinizing hormone (LH) surge tests during two menstrual cycles to validate the estimation of the ovulation. The association between the ovulatory phase and migraine incidence was assessed using a mixed logistic model with patient as random effect, and the ovulatory and menstrual window as fixed effects. Secondary analyses included a case-crossover model and a self-controlled case series (SCCS) model to strengthen data robustness and control for time-invariant confounders.

Results E-diary data from 2,522 menstrual cycles, including 58 from the WHAT-hormone subgroup, were analyzed. Across all three statistical models, the ovulatory window showed no higher incidence of migraine (with or without aura) than other menstrual cycle days (mixed logistic model: OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.88–1.02; WHAT-hormone subgroup: OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.38–1.16). The perimenstrual window had the highest migraine incidence (SCCS model with luteal phase as reference: OR 2.57, 95% CI 1.51–4.39), followed by the follicular phase (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.02–2.80).

Conclusion There is no increased incidence of migraine attacks (with or without aura) during the ovulatory window in women, but a higher incidence during the follicular phase compared to the luteal phase was confirmed, potentially linked to lingering effects of perimenstrual estrogen decline.

P136 Right-sided predominance in primary stabbing headache: From a large consecutive case series in Korea

B. K. Kim1

1Nowon Eulji Medical Center, Neurology, Seoul, South Korea

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P136

Objective Right-sided pain predominance has been well-documented in cluster headache, and several studies suggest a similar lateralization tendency in migraine. However, pain lateralization in primary stabbing headache (PSH) has not been systematically investigated. This study aimed to evaluate the laterality of pain in PSH through a large consecutive case series.

Methods We consecutively enrolled new patients diagnosed with PSH at the Headache Clinic of Nowon Eulji Medical Center, Korea. The diagnosis of PSH was based on the criteria of the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3). Demographic characteristics (age, sex), clinical features (pain location, frequency, duration, and associated symptoms), and detailed pain lateralization (right, left, bilateral, side-shifting) were recorded through structured interviews and headache diaries. Patients with bilateral or alternating side pain were excluded from the lateralization analysis.

Results Among 815 patients diagnosed with PSH during the study period, 19 patients (2.3%) reported bilateral or side-shifting pain and were excluded. The final analysis included 796 patients with clearly lateralized pain. The cohort was predominantly female (557 women, 70.0%), with a mean age of 55.1 years (standard deviation 16.4; range 12–88 years). Right-sided pain was reported by 421 patients (52.9%), whereas 375 patients (47.1%) had left-sided pain. The difference in laterality was statistically significant (p = 0.042).

Conclusion In this large consecutive case series of PSH, right-sided pain was found to be more frequent than left-sided pain. These results suggest that lateralization patterns in PSH may reflect underlying hemispheric differences in pain processing or susceptibility. Further studies exploring neuroimaging correlates or neurophysiological mechanisms of PSH lateralization are warranted.

P137 Hormonal factors and the course of migraine in postmenopausal women: An observational study

M. Perdicoúlis1, J. Pona-Ferreira1, S. Lima1, A. Matas1

1ULSTMAD, Vila Real, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P137

Objective Migraine is known to be modulated by hormonal fluctuations throughout a woman’s life. However, the influence of hormonal events on the clinical course of migraine after menopause remains unclear. This study aims to characterise the hormonal history and the clinical course of migraine in women aged 60 years or older.

Methods Observational, cross-sectional study, conducted in a headache clinic between September 2024 and March 2025. Women diagnosed with migraine, with or without aura, and aged 60 years or older were included. The questionnaire was either applied in person or by telephone. Of a total of 33 eligible patients, 31 agreed to participate.

Results The median age was 66 years. The average age of menarche was 13 years, and menopause occurred on average at 49 years. 22,6% used hormone replacement therapy. After menopause, 64,5% of the patients reported and improvement of frequency and/or intensity of migraine attacks, while 25,8% reported worsening. Postmenopausal worsening was associated with higher disability scores (average MIDAS: 41 vs. 21, p=0,04) and higher anxiety scores (average HADS-A: 13 vs. 9; p=0,03). No significant differences were found regarding hormone therapy use or age at menopause. The prevalence of anxiety and/or depression, as measured by the HADS score, was high (51,6%), regardless of the clinical course.

Conclusion In this study, most women reported an improvement in migraine symptoms after menopause, consistent with literature data. However, a relevant subgroup of patients experienced worsening, which was associated with greater functional disability and higher anxiety burden. These results highlight the need for an individualised approach that considers not only hormonal factors but also the emotional and functional impact of the disease in postmenopausal women.

P139 Capsaicin induced cell death in primary cultured neurons

J. H. Lee1

1National Health Insurance Service Ilsan Hospital, Neurology, Goyang-si, South Korea

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P139

Objective To determine the effect of capsaicin to central nervous system, we prepared morphologic changes and biochemical assay were investigated in mouse primary cultured CNS neuron.

Methods The susceptability of capsaicin differs for different brain area. Cerebral cortex and hippocampus were more sensitive, and striatum, thalamus and midbrain area were less sensitive to capsaicin susceptability. After capsaicin treatment, cortical and hippocampal neurons were died in dose-and time-dependent manner. By observation of nuclear fragmentation of capsaicin treated neuron, it is thought that the type of cell death is apoptosis rather than necrosis. The capsaicin receptor immunoreactive cells were observed in the cortex and hippocampus. It is consistent with area of damaged neuron. Results These results indicated that capsaicin induced influx of cation ions. These results showed that capsaicin induced influx of Ca2+, followed by neuronal NOS is activated by Ca2+ and induced cell death. Also, the activity of caspase 3 was increased after capsacin treatment in the cortical and hippocampal neurons.

Conclusion These results demonstrate that capsaicin induced the apoptosis through acting with capsaicin receptors. Calcium influx due to capsaicin recptor activation may induce apoptosis, which is triggered the formation of peroxynitrite by activating NOS activity or is mediated by activating caspase 3 pathway.

P140 An unexpected side effect of a cardiac catheterization

S. Palma1, J. Almeida Ferreira1, A. Rachão1, B. Ferreira1, F. Antunes1, L. Pereira1

1Hospital Garcia de Orta, ULSAS, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P140

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective

Introduction

Visual aura-like phenomena, with or without headache, have been described in the context of endovascular procedures. Although rare, they have been reported following cerebral angiography, catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, patent foramen ovale closure, and varicose vein sclerotherapy.

Methods .

Results

Clinical Case

A 59-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and a history of ischemic heart disease underwent a diagnostic coronary catheterization. Minutes after the procedure, he experienced a disturbance in his right visual field resembling a “fortification spectrum,” accompanied by scintillating scotomas with centrifugal progression. He denied any personal or family history of migraine, neurological disease, or any other symptom. The episode was self-limited, resolving within approximately 20 min. Neurological examination at the time was unremarkable. About an hour later, he experienced a second, similar episode, which also resolved spontaneously. Brain MRI and electroencephalogram revealed no abnormalities. One year later, the patient remains asymptomatic, with no episodes of headache or migraine. A diagnosis of visual aura-like phenomenon following cardiac catheterization was established.

Conclusion Aura-like phenomena following endovascular procedures—particularly coronary catheterizations—are rare and clinically heterogeneous, making recognition and diagnosis challenging. It is essential to exclude other potential aetiologies, namely vascular or epileptic. The underlying pathophysiological mechanism remains unclear, but proposed explanations include microembolic events, the release of bubbles from the catheter, or the action of local inflammatory mediators or vasoactive substances. Despite their rarity, these phenomena appear to be benign, with recurrences seldom reported. Case reporting remains important to enhance understanding of their potential clinical implications.

Objective Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias are characterized by short-lasting, unilateral, and intensely painful headache attacks associated with autonomic symptoms. Although they may be secondary to structural lesions, establishing a causal relationship is often challenging.

P142 Do different types of migraines also mean different responses to triggers?

A. K. Szewczyk1, K. Mitosek-Szewczyk1, A. Brzozowska2, P. Lesiuk3, K. Nowomiejska3, R. Rejdak3

Objective To examine association between different migraine types (migraine with and without aura (MA, MO); low or high frequency episodic migraine (LFEM, HFEM) and chronic migraine (CM), as well as migraine time of appearance) and various habits.

P143 Novel morphological fractal dimension features as a biomarker for migraine classification: A support vector machine approach

C. W. Jao1, W. H. Chen1, Y. T. Wu1, J. H. Yeh1, V. Walsh1, T. H. Chen1, C. I. Lau1

1National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Institute of Biophotonics, Taipei, Taiwan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P143

Objective Diagnosing migraine is challenging because it relies on subjective, self-reported symptoms due to the lack of an objective neuroimaging biomarker. Advanced tools are needed to identify the subtle structural brain changes visible on MRI in migraine patients. This study investigated using Fractal Dimension (FD)—a sensitive metric quantifying brain complexity and morphology—combined with a Machine Learning (ML) model as a reliable, objective diagnostic biomarker.

Methods We analyzed axial MRI scans from 100 migraine patients (50 episodic, 50 chronic) and 100 matched healthy controls. All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal. The brain’s gray matter was parcellated into 68 regions of interest (ROIs) using the Desikan-Killiany atlas, and FD was calculated for each. We first performed group comparisons to find morphological differences. Then, the 68 sub-regional FD values were used as features in a Support Vector Machine (SVM) model to classify migraine patients from healthy controls.

Results FD measures successfully differentiated the groups. Migraine patients showed significantly decreased FD values in 17 ROIs compared to controls, primarily in the left hemisphere. Conclusion This pilot study demonstrates that FD is a potent neuroimaging biomarker for migraine. The FD-based SVM classifier achieved high diagnostic accuracy and provided valuable insights into sub-regional morphological alterations in the migraine brain. These findings hold significant promise for supporting objective clinical diagnosis and enabling future automated screening for migraine.

P144 Characterization of mental health in cluster headache a.k.a suicide headache

Objective Cluster headache is characterized by excruciatingly painful recurrent headaches and is sometimes referred to as suicide headache. While mental health issues significantly contribute to the burden of cluster headache, they remain understudied. Conclusion Our results show a strong inclination of individuals with cluster headache to resort to self-harm. P146 No differences in subcortical volume between people with and without migraine: A REFORM study

B. A. Chaudhry1, R. H. Christensen1, H. Ashina1, H. M. Al-Khazali1, T. M. Amin1, M. Ashina1, F. M. Amin1

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P146

Objective To determine whether the volume of specific subcortical structures differ between people with migraine and healthy controls, and whether these volumes vary across distinct migraine subtypes and phases.

Methods In this cross-sectional study at the Danish Headache Center in Denmark, conducted between January 2020 and December 2023, adult participants with migraine and age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent a single magnetic resonance imaging session at 3 Tesla. T1-weigthed scans were acquired to measure the volumes of subcortical structures using automated segmentation techniques. The structures analyzed included the thalamus, putamen, caudate nucleus, pallidum, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and hippocampus.

Results Imaging data from 295 participants and 154 healthy controls were included in the final analyses. No significant differences were observed between migraine participants and healthy controls in thalamic volume (migraine: 7243 ± 923 mm³ vs. healthy controls: 7350 ± 782 mm³; p = 0.774) or hippocampal volume (migraine: 4204 ± 398 mm³ vs. healthy controls: 4307 ± 446 mm³; p = 0.337). No differences were observed in any other subcortical structure. Likewise, different subgroup analyses revealed no volumetric differences in episodic vs. chronic migraine, migraine with aura vs. without aura, ictal vs. headache free, or between each migraine subgroup and healthy controls (all p > 0.05 after multiple comparison correction).

Conclusion In this large cross-sectional study, we found no evidence of subcortical volume differences between adults with migraine and healthy controls. Furthermore, no differences were found across migraine subtypes or phases. These findings indicate that subcortical volumetric measures are not suitable as imaging biomarkers of migraine. Future research should explore functional and metabolic alterations in subcortical structures to better understand the neurobiologic underpinnings of migraine.

P147 Investigation of the rimegepant effect on cerebral and extracerebral arteries – A longitudinal magnetic resonance angiography study

B. A. Chaudhry1, S. Younis1, F. M. Amin1

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P147

Objective To determine whether rimegepant induces vasoconstriction of cerebral or meningeal arteries during acute migraine attacks.

Methods This was a prospective, longitudinal study conducted at a single academic imaging center between January 12, 2024, and June 10, 2025. Results No significant vasoconstriction was observed in either artery following rimegepant administration. Rimegepant may offer a safer alternative to triptans for individuals with cerebrovascular risk.

P156 CEFALEAPP: An app for the diagnosis and treatment of migraine in primary health care

D. A. García-Estévez1, B. Garcia Pérez-Schofield2, N. Sabbagh-Casado1

1Universitary Hospital of Ourense, Neurology, Ourense, Spain; 2University of Vigo, Higher School of Computer Engineering, Ourense, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P156

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Among the factors of migraine chronification are the delay in the initiation of preventive drugs, with the consequent abuse of analgesics, and the trivialization of migraine in the population, mainly female, and this causes a delay in diagnosis. The end result is a significant number of years lived with disability. Our aim was to develop a digital application to support Primary Health Care (PHC) physicians in both the accurate diagnosis and early preventive treatment of migraine.

Methods We designed a rules-based artificial intelligence system to analyze patient responses to the ID-Migraine screener—a 3-question probabilistic tool for identifying migraine in primary care. The system determines whether a patient meets the International Headache Society diagnostic criteria for migraine (ICHD-3). If not, the app suggests an alternative diagnosis, such as tension-type headache. In addition, it includes an algorithm to guide the selection of preventive treatments based on the patient’s comorbidities. The application was developed in Java, with rules and associated data structured through XML files.

Results CefaleApp enables the diagnosis of migraine, tension-type, or mixed headaches; estimates migraine-related disability using HIT-6 and MIDAS scores; and generates tailored recommendations for preventive treatment considering comorbidities. Initial validation in patients newly diagnosed with migraine in a Neurology clinic showed perfect concordance with clinical assessment (correlation = 1.0).

Conclusion CefaleApp facilitates accurate clinical diagnosis of migraine in PHC settings and supports early, personalized preventive treatment. It is a digital tool for the clinical management of migraine. By leveraging artificial intelligence, it addresses the shortage of neurologists and empowers PHC providers in migraine management. CefaleApp enhances the quality of care by promoting preventive treatment in PHC, reducing migraine chronification, and improving patients’ quality of life.

P157 Tension-type headache vs. migraine: Role of ultrasound-guided dry needling in differentiation

R. Bubnov1, L. Kalika2, Y. Brosgol2

1Clinical hospital Pheophania, Kyiv, Ukraine; 2New York Dynamic Neuromuscular Rehabilitation & Physical Therapy, New York, NY, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P157

Objective Headache disorders affect billions globally, with tension-type headache (TTH) and migraine being the most common subtypes. Despite overlapping clinical presentations, they have distinct pathophysiological mechanisms, necessitating precise differentiation for effective management. Ultrasound (US)-guided dry needling (DN) has demonstrated efficacy in pain conditions, including headache and migraine. This study explores the role of US-guided DN in distinguishing TTH from migraine by evaluating specific US markers and their dynamics during treatment.

Methods Fifteen patients presenting with headache, vertigo, and central sensitization symptoms were enrolled. Based on diagnostic criteria, 5 were classified as definite migraine, 6 as clear TTH, and 4 as mixed/unknown cases. US-guided DN by R.Bubnov, aimed at restoring posture, targeted also trigger points in suboccipital muscles, focusing on structures attached to the dura mater. Real-time US imaging confirmed needle placement, M-mode visualization of dorsal and ventral root pulsations at C1-C2 was conducted. Ophthalmic artery Doppler assessments were performed pre- and post-treatment to analyze blood flow changes.

Results DN successfully inactivated trigger points in suboccipital, shoulder, and temporomandibular muscles, improving muscle contractility. Migraine patients exhibited significant central sensitization, with altered spinal root pulsations and enhanced retinal, ciliary, and ophthalmic artery blood flow. TTH patients showed relapse correlated with trigger point reactivation but exhibited less pronounced central sensitization. Occipitalis muscle DN may be valuable for TTH, while suboccipital DN remains essential for dura mater-related sensitization.

Conclusion US-guided DN aids in differentiating TTH from migraine by addressing trigger points and monitoring neuromuscular dynamics. M-mode ultrasound provides an objective tool for assessing spinal root oscillations, supporting targeted, personalized interventions.

P158 Ultrasound-guided dry needling approach for suboccipital muscles: A novel perspective on myodural modulation in headache disorders

R. Bubnov1, L. Kalika2

1Clinical hospital Pheophania, Kyiv, Ukraine; 2New York Dynamic Neuromuscular Rehabilitation & Physical Therapy, New York, NY, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P158

Objective Headache disorders, including tension-type headache (TTH) and migraine, are widespread and significant health concerns. The myodural bridge, connecting suboccipital muscles (obliquus capitis inferior and superior) to the spinal dura mater, is implicated in modulating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics and central sensitization. Ultrasound-guided dry needling (US-DN) targeting these muscles offers a potential approach for headache management.

Objective To assess the effects of US-DN on headache symptoms, spinal oscillatory patterns, and cerebrovascular dynamics.

Methods Ten patients (4 migraine, 6 TTH) were treated with US-DN following real-time diagnostic assessment. M-mode ultrasound visualized spinal root oscillations at the C1–C2 level as in [10.1177/03331024241280496#sec-206].

Results Pathological dural oscillation frequencies—often 2–3× the cardiac frequency (e.g., 160–240 Hz vs. normal ~80 Hz)—were detected, particularly in migraine and centrally sensitized states. US-DN targeting the IO and SO muscles led to normalization of these frequencies post-intervention, supporting the hypothesis of a resonance mechanism wherein muscle-induced dural tension alters the frequency of mechanical pulsations (figure). Additional Doppler assessment of the ophthalmic artery confirmed improved hemodynamics post-DN, aligning with symptom relief.

Conclusion These findings suggest that abnormal dural resonance, modulated by IO/SO tension, contributes to headache pathogenesis. Ultrasound-guided dry needling of the suboccipital muscles, particularly IO and SO, offers a promising personalized approach for treating headaches, especially those linked to central sensitization. Spinal duro-mechanical oscillation analysis via M-mode ultrasound may serve as a non-invasive biomarker for diagnosing and monitoring treatment efficacy.Fig. 1 (abstract P158).

Objective To assess rimegepant (Rim) for acute treatment of migraine in adults unsuitable for triptans (NCT05509400).

P163 Latent class analysis of headache disorders using population-based study: Searching for natural subgroups

W. Lee1, J. Yum1, S. J. Heo2, M. K. Chu3

1Yongin Severance Hospital, Yonsei University College of Medicine, Neurology, Yongin-si, South Korea; 2Yonsei University College of Medicine, Biostatistics Collaboration Unit, Department of Biomedical Systems Informatics, Seoul, South Korea; 3Severance Hospital, Yonsei University College of Medicine, Seoul, Korea, Neurology, Seoul, South Korea

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P163

Objective Headache disorders, despite their differing pathophysiologies, are currently diagnosed based on clinical criteria using ICHD-3. Migraine is typically characterized by unilateral, moderate to severe headache with nausea/vomiting and/or photophobia and phonophobia, whereas tension-type headache (TTH) is recognized as bilateral, non-pulsating, mild to moderate headache with few or no accompanying symptoms. However, ICHD-3–based diagnoses often present with overlapping symptoms or a wide variety of symptoms within a single diagnosis. This study aimed to identify natural subgroups of headache disorders and compare them with ICHD-3 diagnoses.

Methods The CHASE study is a population-based survey investigating headache and sleep. Categorical variables based on ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for migraine and TTH were analyzed using latent class analysis.

Results Among 1,938 individuals with headache, five latent classes were identified, comprising 619 (32.0%), 365 (18.8%), 491 (25.3%), 61 (3.1%), and 402 (20.7%) individuals, respectively.

Class 1: Mild, short-duration headaches without nausea, resembling primary stabbing headache or other headache disorders.

Class 2: Moderate to severe headache with typical migraine features.

Class 3: Mild to moderate headache with migraine features and short duration, resembling probable migraine.

Class 4: Moderate, bilateral, non-pulsating headaches lasting more than 4 h without nausea/vomiting, resembling TTH.

Class 5: Moderate headaches lasting less than 4 h, without nausea or vomiting, suggesting mild TTH or other headache types.

Conclusion Five natural subgroups of headache disorders were identified, reflecting migraine, TTH, and other headache types with varying severity and duration.Fig. 1 (abstract P163).

A similar trend was observed in DELIVER; 0.7% (100 mg), 2.4% (300 mg), and 0% (PBO) of participants had migraine freedom after Dose 1, increasing through the end of the trial. The proportion of participants with migraine freedom in PREVAIL increased from 9% (Dose 1) to 23% (Dose 8). During the PBO-controlled periods, the proportion of participants with ≥1 migraine-free month was 35% (100 mg), 40% (300 mg), and 22% (PBO) in PROMISE-2; DELIVER: 22%, 27%, and 8%.

Conclusion In people with CM and those for whom 2–4 prior preventive treatments failed, migraine freedom was observed in greater proportions of participants treated with EPTI than PBO. These proportions increased over long-term EPTI treatment, highlighting the build-up effect of continuous treatment.

P174 No additional benefit with detoxification strategies: A real world experience in 200 patients with chronic migraine and either simple or complex MOH treated with CGRP monoclonal antibodies

M. Silvestro1, I. Orologio1, P. Sozio1, V. Dortucci1, A. Tessitore1, F. Trojsi1, G. Tedeschi1, M. Siciliano1, A. Russo1

1University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Department of Advanced Medical and Surgical Sciences, Naples, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P174

Objective Although withdrawal from analgesics with or without detoxification strategy represented a mainstay in medication overuse headache (MOH) management, recent evidence supports that it is no longer beneficial when CGRP-targeting monoclonal antibodies (CGRP-mAbs) are employed. MOH could be stratified into simple and complex phenotypes according to different clinical parameters (i.e., amounts and class of analgesics, psychiatric comorbidities, history of relapse after withdrawal, symptoms of central sensitization and maladaptive anticipatory response to pain experience). P175 Improved workplace productivity following preventive migraine treatment with eptinezumab: Results from a phase 3 trial in a predominantly Asian population with chronic migraine

S. Yu1, Y. Matsumori2, B. K. Kim3, A. Gryglas-Dworak4, G. Giorgadze5, P. Pozo-Rosich6, M. K. Josiassen7, K. Ranc7, A. Ettrup7, B. Sperling7, A. Mittoux7, T. Takeshima8

1Chinese PLA General Hospital, Beijing, China; 2Sendai Headache and Neurology Clinic, Sendai, Japan; 3Eulji University School of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea; 4MIGRE Polish Migraine Center, Wroclaw, Poland; 5Aversi Clinic LTD, Tbilisi, Georgia; 6Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Quiron Hospital, Barcelona, Spain; 7H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark; 8Tominaga Hospital, Osaka, Japan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P175

Objective To evaluate the impact of eptinezumab versus placebo on migraine-related impairment in workplace productivity and overall activity in the phase 3 SUNRISE trial.

Methods The SUNRISE trial (NCT04921384) confirmed the migraine-preventive efficacy and safety of eptinezumab in participants with chronic migraine, predominantly from Asian countries. Adults (18–75y) diagnosed with chronic migraine were randomized 1:1:1 to 12-week double-blind treatment with IV eptinezumab 100 mg, 300 mg, or placebo. The patient-reported Migraine-specific Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire (WPAI: M) was captured at baseline and at Weeks 4, 8, and 12. P182 The effectiveness of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies in managing medication overuse headache in elderly patients

Y. Gil1

1St. Vincent’s Hospital, Neurology, Suwon, South Korea

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P182

Objective Despite the relatively low prevalence of headaches among the elderly, clinicians frequently encounter elderly patients suffering from headaches in clinical practice. A significant proportion of these patients have been exposed to medication overuse. Recently, anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy has been recommended as an effective treatment for medication overuse headache. The objective of this paper is to present cases that demonstrate the efficacy of this treatment approach in elderly patients.

Methods A prospective review of patient records highlighted two cases of elderly patients with medication overuse headache.

Results A 69-year-old woman with a history of migraine since her 20s visited the outpatient clinic. She had been taking a combination of analgesics for more than 15 days per month for over a year, and she had been taking analgesics daily for six months prior to this visit. She has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and her current headache is more like a chronic tension-type headache. In order to discontinue medication overuse, she was administered fremanezumab and prescribed oral steroids for a period of two weeks. The patient successfully discontinued the overused medication, and her headaches recurred only 1-2 times per month thereafter. The second patient is a 77-year-old woman who has had migraines since her 30s. To cease medication overuse, she received fremanezumab injections along with two weeks of oral steroids. One month after treatment, the patient’s headaches significantly improved, and she was able to quit analgesic use. Currently, she continues maintenance therapy with fremanezumab alone.

Conclusion These cases illustrate that anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy can be an effective treatment option for elderly patients with medication overuse headache. Further studies in older patients are encouraging.

P183 Thirteen-year trajectories of depressive and anxiety symptoms in individuals with and without migraine: The Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety (NESDA)

N. van Veelen1, K. Kaushik1, N. Pelzer1, B. Penninx1, G. M. Terwindt1, E. Giltay2

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Leiden University Medical Center, Psychiatry, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P183

Objective This study investigated 13-year trajectories of affective symptoms in individuals with and without migraine, both in those with and without an affective disorder at baseline.

Methods The NESDA cohort included 2,981 participants followed over 13-years across six data waves. Anxiety and depressive symptoms were assessed using the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) and Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (IDS). Participants were divided into two subgroups: those with and those without a current affective disorder at baseline, as diagnosed using the Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI). Linear mixed models analyzed symptom trajectories of the BAI and IDS by migraine status. Cox regression models estimated hazard ratios (HR) for onset and recovery from affective disorders (CIDI).

Results Among 2,578 participants (1,448 with and 1,130 without an affective disorder at baseline), 453 had migraine, 1,274 non-migraine headache, and 551 non-headache. At baseline, migraine was associated with over twice the odds of having an affective disorder (OR for anxiety: 2.34; 95% CI [1.87, 2.93]; OR for depression: 2.85; 95% CI [2.27, 3.58]). Migraine was associated with an increased risk of new-onset affective disorder (HR:1.83; 95%CI [1.32,2.53]) and reduced likelihood of recovery (HR:0.82; 95%CI [0.70,0.98]). Notably, more than 40% of migraineurs without an affective disorder at baseline developed anxiety of depression during follow-up.

Conclusion Migraine is linked to twice the baseline odds of anxiety or depression, greater long-term affective risk, and slower recovery from affective disorders. These findings underscore the importance of early identification and integrated treatment strategies for individuals with migraine.

P184 Does age impact headache diagnosis and migraine management in England? A retrospective cohort study of primary care medical records

D. P. Watson1, R. Pawinski2, M. Czachorowski2, M. Araghi2, C. Ellsbury2, A. M. Williams2, L. Camidge3, E. Rottier3, H. Gowman3, S. Law3, G. O’Neil2

Objective To examine diagnosis among people with headache in England by age and treatment patterns, including possible risk of medication overuse and titration of preventive medication, among people diagnosed with migraine by age.

Conclusion In older adults, 2 out of 3 patients with headache were not given a diagnosis. Older adults were also less likely to receive a triptan when diagnosed with migraine. Objective Medication-overuse headache (MOH) is globally recognized to be managed in primary care. P188 Morphometric similarity networks in paediatric migraine without aura: Unravelling the role of gender

M. Valeriani1,2, A. Guarnera3, D. Longo3, A. Napolitano3, G. Baldassari3, G. Pirani3, F. Ursitti1, G. Monte1, G. Sforza1, C. Gandolfo3, L. Papetti1

Objective Migraine causes structural and functional alterations on brain cortex and connectome, yet the underlying mechanism is still unclear. To our knowledge, morphometric similarity mapping (MSM) for studying cerebral connectivity and cortical pattern has never been applied to the study of pediatric migraine without aura. Our study aims to: (a) identify differences in morphometric similarity networks (MSNs) in pediatric patients affected by migraine without aura compared to healthy controls and in subgroups of patients; and (b) correlate these differences in MSNs with patients demographic and clinical characteristics.

Conclusion Differences in MSNs between controls and patients and within subgroups of patients suggest that migraine shapes cerebral connectome and favours neuronal plasticity. Gender is confirmed as a paramount parameter in migraine, supporting the hypothesis of a sex specific phenotype.

P190 My experience with the use of children’s drawings in the differential diagnosis of primary headaches

J. Beranová1

1Hospital Jindřichův Hradec a.s., Neurology, Jindřichův Hradec, Czech Republic

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P190

Objective To examine whether children’s drawings can support the differential diagnosis of primary headaches—especially migraine—in pediatric patients, and to evaluate their usefulness in identifying comorbid psychological traits.

Methods A series of spontaneous drawings were collected from children suffering from primary headaches. Each drawing was qualitatively analyzed with a focus on specific visual motifs, color use, symbolism, and composition. The analysis was conducted in parallel with clinical assessments, allowing comparison between headache type and drawing characteristics.

Results Drawings by children with migraine frequently contained elements that mirror typical migraine symptoms: high-intensity pain, photophobia, phonophobia, unilateral localization, and visual aura. Conclusion Children’s drawings offer a non-invasive, expressive tool that can enrich the diagnostic process in pediatric headache care. They can help distinguish between migraine and tension-type headache and may provide insights into coexisting emotional or behavioral problems. Integrating drawing analysis into clinical practice can support a more nuanced, child-centered approach to headache diagnosis.

P191 Pediatric migraine: A dual burden on cognition and emotion

S. Tarantino1, M. Proietti Checchi1, L. Papetti1, F. Ursitti1, G. Monte1, G. Sforza1, M. Valeriani1,2

1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Developmental Neurology Unit, Rome, Italy; 2University of Rome Tor Vergata, Systems Medicine Department, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P191

Objective Pediatric migraine is often associated with cognitive difficulties and internalizing symptoms, potentially impacting academic and social functioning. This study aimed to examine the associations between migraine frequency, age of onset, and prophylactic treatment use with cognitive and emotional functioning in children and adolescents.

Methods Fifty-two patients (mean age = 12.5 ± 2.6 years; 30 females, 22 males) with migraine were assessed using a comprehensive battery, including verbal memory (Digit Span Forward/Backward, BVN 5-18), verbal fluency (BVN 5-18), attention and executive functions (NEPSY-II: Visual Attention, Inhibition), processing speed (SDMT), intelligence (Raven’s Colored Progressive Matrices), and internalizing symptoms (SAFA-A, SAFA-D). P198 Home-based biofeedback treatment for people with post-traumatic headache: A usability and feasibility study
