Methods This was an iterative mixed-method usability and feasibility study, with one iteration including a 28-day home testing. The outcomes were mHealth App Usability Questionnaire (MAUQ) and Mobile App Rating Scale (MARS) scores, adherence during the home-testing period, and descriptions of adverse events.

Results Twenty-three adults with PTH (median age 52 years, 80% female) were included in the user group, and six clinicians (median age 53 years, 50% female) with a mean of 13 years of PTH experience were included in the clinician group. The usability of the biofeedback app was rated 5.2 (SD 1.0) out of 7 on the MAUQ by the user group. The clinician group rated the app quality at 4.1 (IQR 4.5-4.1) out of 5 on the MARS. The adherence rate among the user group during the 28-day home testing was 84.3% (IQR 28-19). Two adverse events occurred in one participant, who experienced dizziness and headache during and after biofeedback sessions on several occasions. Symptoms resolved spontaneously within two hours.

Conclusion The home-based biofeedback solution is usable, feasible, and safe to use in people with PTH. In this study, we have gathered valuable insights on the necessary adaptations to improve and tailor the solution to people with PTH.

P199 Thiamine could improve migraine characteristics: A randomized double-blind controlled trial

M. Ghods1, M. Togha2, S. Razeghi Jahromi1, E. Jafari2, Z. Salami2

1Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Department of Clinical Nutrition and Dietetics, Faculty of Nutrition and Food Technology, National Nutrition and Food Technology Research Institute, Tehran, Iran; 2Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Headache Department, Iranian Centre of Neurological Research, Neuroscience Institute, Tehran, Iran

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P199

Objective Migraine represents a prevalent neurological disorder that impacts around 14% of people worldwide and is considered the sixth leading cause of disability globally. Vitamin B1 can potentially help prevent migraine due to its cofactor role in energy metabolism enzymes. Therefore, this research aimed to investigate the effects of high-dose thiamine on women experiencing episodic migraines (EM).

Methods This double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial was carried out with 40 women suffering from EM. The participants were allocated into two groups: the B1 group (n = 20) and the placebo group (n = 20). Individuals in the B1 group were administered 990 milligrams of thiamine three times daily, while the placebo group received an equivalent dosage of 990 milligrams of maltodextrin. Headache frequency, duration, and severity were documented using the Headache Diary Questionnaire. The Migraine Disability Assessment Questionnaire (MIDAS) was employed to assess migraine disability. Serum levels of CGRP were evaluated both before and after the intervention.

Results Following a 12-week duration of study, thiamine supplementation yielded a statistically significant reduction in MIDAS scores (P = 0.002), migraine frequency (P < 0.001), and duration (P = 0.001) in comparison to the placebo group. Both groups showed a significant decrease in headache intensity by the study’s conclusion, with the intervention group demonstrating a considerably greater reduction in severity. Serum CGRP levels declined in both groups, although no significant differences were observed either within or between the groups.

Conclusion The findings of this study suggest that high-dose thiamine supplementation may be a beneficial adjunctive treatment for episodic migraines. Additional research with longer intervention durations is needed to confirm these results.

P201 Acupuncture in migraine prevention: High-quality evidence from double-dummy randomized controlled trials and its implications in clinical practice

X. Mu1, M. Nijanth1

1NNI, Singapore General Hospital, Department of Neurology, Singapore, Singapore

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P201

Objective Migraine is a disabling primary headache disorder where preventive drugs are often limited by poor tolerability and adherence. Acupuncture is widely used in migraine treatment, but physician acceptance remains limited due to high sham response rates and persistent concerns regarding methodological heterogeneity, bias, and blinding. Double-dummy randomized controlled trials (RCTs) address this issue and greatly minimize expectation bias and substantially enhance physician confidence in acupuncture for migraine treatment. objective to systematically review double-dummy RCTs comparing acupuncture with pharmacological preventives for migraine, focusing on efficacy, safety, and patient-reported outcomes.

Methods Comprehensive keyword searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library (2000–2024). Eligible studies included adults with episodic or chronic migraine, comparing acupuncture plus placebo versus sham acupuncture plus active medication. Outcomes included migraine frequency, responder rates, disability, safety, and acceptability.

Results Two double-dummy RCTs met inclusion criteria. Wang et al. (2011, n=140) compared acupuncture with flunarizine and found higher ≥50% responder rates (56% vs. 37% at 16 weeks), and greater reductions in migraine days (−4.1 vs. −2.0 at week 16). Liu et al. (2024, n=60) compared acupuncture with topiramate, reporting larger reductions in monthly migraine days (−5.6 vs. -2.8 at 12 weeks), higher ≥50% responder rates (33.3% vs. 6.7%), and fewer adverse events (10% vs. 26.7%).

Conclusion Limited high-quality double-dummy RCTs indicate that acupuncture is an effective and well-tolerated preventive therapy, demonstrating efficacy comparable to or superior to pharmacological treatments with fewer adverse effects. Large-scale, multicentre double-dummy trials remain essential to generate robust evidence to strengthen physicians’ confidence in adopting acupuncture as a viable option for migraine management.

P203 Post-spontaneous intracranial hypotension headache

S. I. Jang1, S. Y. Choi2, M. J. Lee1,3

1Seoul National University Hospital, Neurology, Seoul, South Korea; 2Nanoori Gangnam Hospital, Neurology, Seoul, South Korea; 3Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P203

Objective While spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) is primarily characterized by orthostatic headache, some patients experience headaches after CSF leak has resolved. This study aimed to investigate the characteristics of post-SIH headache.

Methods This prospective study included patients with imaging evidence of SIH at baseline who achieved radiological remission between March 2022 and January 2025. We collected patients’ demographics, disease characteristics, migraine history, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, Pain Catastrophizing Scale scores, and the date of complete remission. Remission was defined as complete resolution of imaging abnormalities. Headache status, phenotype, monthly headache days, and chronicity (defined as ≥15 headache days/month) were evaluated at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months after remission. Logistic regression analyses were performed to identify risk factors for post-SIH headache.

Results A total of 32 patients (mean age 40.7 ± 9.72 years; 71.9% female) were included. The duration from remission to last follow-up was 251.6 days (range, 23.0–735.0 days). Post-SIH headache was reported by 21 patients (65.6%), 14 patients (51.9%), 12 patients (44.4%), and 10 patients (37.0%) at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after remission, with the following phenotypes: tension-type-like in 18 patients (69.2%), migraine-like in 5 patients (19.2%), neuralgic in 3 patients (11.5%). Chronic headache was present in 81.0%, 58.9%, 50.0%, and 26.3% of post-SIH patients at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. No independent association was observed between baseline characteristics and post-SIH headache at 1 month.

Conclusion Post-SIH headache is common after complete resolution of CSF leak. Recognizing this entity would improve patient care and help avoid unnecessary invasive procedures in remitted SIH patients.

P204 Effects of fremanezumab discontinuation on migraine frequency and structural brain alterations: A prospective observational study

Y. Salim1, K. S. Lange1,2, L. Neeb3, B. Raffaelli1,2

1Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Department of Neurology, Headache Center, Berlin, Germany; 2Berlin Institute of Health at Charité (BIH), Clinician Scientist Program, Berlin, Germany; 3Universitätsklinikum Brandenburg an der Havel, Department of Neurology, Brandenburg a. d. Havel, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P204

Objective Monoclonal antibodies targeting the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) pathway are effective preventive treatments for migraine. However, their potential for disease modification and the proportion of patients with sustained benefit after discontinuation remain unclear. This study examined changes in migraine frequency and brain microstructure following the cessation of fremanezumab after 9–12 months of use.

Methods In this prospective study (2022–2025, Headache Center Charité), patients with episodic or chronic migraine discontinued fremanezumab after 9–12 months. MRI (DTI, VBM) and clinical assessments were performed at baseline (T1) and 16 weeks after discontinuation (T2). Age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC) were scanned once. TBSS analyzed fractional anisotropy (FA), axial (AD), and radial diffusivity (RD) using FSL’s randomise (5,000 permutations, TFCE correction). Main outcomes included changes in monthly migraine days (MMD) and DTI parameters.

Results Fifteen patients (47.4 ± 12.2 yrs) and 15 HC (46.0 ± 6.9 yrs) were included. Sustained response (MMD increase <30%) occurred in 46.7%. MMD rose from 5 ± 3 to 8 ± 6 (p = 0.014). No significant FA changes occurred from T1 to T2. RD increased significantly post-discontinuation (20 clusters, max 50 voxels, TFCE p < 0.05), notably in longitudinal fasciculi and cingulum. AD showed bidirectional changes: increases (e.g., splenium, IFOF) and decreases (e.g., brainstem, SLF) (TFCE p < 0.05). Compared to HC, patients at T1 showed higher FA and lower RD in the forceps minor (TFCE p < 0.05).

Conclusion Following fremanezumab discontinuation, nearly half the patients maintained clinical benefit. While FA remained stable, RD and AD changes suggest dynamic white matter adaptation. Baseline forceps minor differences may reflect disease-related remodeling. Final VBM and correlation analyses will be presented at the congress.

P205 Eptinezumab for difficult-to-treat migraine: Who responds and who needs more

F. Genovese1,2, R. Messina1,2, A. Visentini1,2, I. Cetta1,2, E. Ratto1, L. Zanandrea1,2, I. Chinali1, B. Colombo1, M. Filippi1,2,3

1IRCCS San Raffaele, Unit of Neurology, Milan, Italy; 2Vita-Salute San Raffaele University, Neurology research unit, Milan, Italy; 3Vita-Salute San Raffaele University, Neuroimaging research unit, Milan, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P205

Objective Eptinezumab, a monoclonal antibody (mAb) targeting the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), was recently approved for migraine prevention. This study evaluated the rates of responders and super-responders to eptinezumab and assessed clinical predictors of treatment response and dose escalation over 9 months.

Methods Fifty-eight migraine patients were enrolled. Clinical data, including monthly headache (MHD) and migraine days (MMD), acute medication use (pills (AMP) and days (AMD)), intensity (NRS), disability (MIDAS), impact (HIT-6), and allodynia (ASC-12) scores, were collected at baseline and after 3 (M3), 6 (M6), and 9 (M9) months. Adverse events were recorded at all time-points. Responders and super-responders were defined as patients with a ≥50% or ≥75% MMD reduction, respectively. All patients started on 100 mg eptinezumab; dose was increased to 300 mg at M3 or M6 if response was suboptimal.

Results The median baseline clinical values were: MHD: 20, MMD: 16, AMP: 20, AMD: 11, MIDAS: 69, HIT-6: 66, NRS: 8, ASC-12: 7. At M3, 40% were responders (21% super-responders); at M6, 23% (5% super-responders); at M9, 46% (17% super-responders). A significant predictor of non-response to treatment after M3 was prior therapy with mAb (p = 0.0137). Dose escalation occurred in 72% patients at M3 and 87% at M6. Factors associated with dose escalation were higher baseline MHD and MMD (p<0.05) and previous anti-CGRP failure (p<0.04). Only two patients reported mild adverse events.

Conclusion Eptinezumab is effective and well tolerated in difficult-to-treat migraine patients, with sustained benefits up to nine months. Patients with higher baseline migraine frequency and prior exposure to anti-CGRP mAbs are more likely to require dose escalation. Our study suggests that the initial dosage should be tailored to the patient in order to optimize response.

P208 Long term persistence of onabotulinumtoxinA versus calcitonin gene-related peptide monoclonal antibodies in new initiators with chronic migraine

A. Blumenfeld1, J. Ailani2, G. Ahmadyar3, Y. Dong3, J. R. Kim3, I. Shakhmantsir3, P. Gandhi3, S. Nahas4

1The Los Angeles and San Diego Headache Centers, San Diego, CA, USA; 2Georgetown University Hospital, MedStar, Washington, D.C., USA; 3AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA; 4Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, PA, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P208

Objective Traditional oral generic migraine preventive medications show low persistence, impacting clinical and economic outcomes. Initial studies suggest onabotulinumtoxinA(onabotA) for chronic migraine(CM) leads to better persistence than calcitonin gene-related peptide(CGRP) monoclonal antibodies(mAbs) in new initiators, but did not compare persistence long-term (>12 months). This analysis compares real-world long-term persistence in CM patients newly initiating onabotA relative vs. branded CGRP mAbs.

Methods Using Merative Marketscan Commercial and Medicare database, this retrospective observational study included adult patients with CM initiating onabotA or a CGRP mAb (erenumab, fremanezumab, galacanezumab, eptinezumab) who stayed on index treatment 12-24 months. Exclusions included preventive gepant, onabotA, or CGRP mAb use during ≥6-month pre-index period, diagnosis of onabotA non-migraine indications during the study, or patients initiating >1 CGRP mAb or onabotA on index date. Persistence was measured as proportion of patients without treatment gaps (>60 days for fills/administration). Adjusted persistence was calculated via logistic regression adjusting for age, gender, baseline health plan, region, Charlson Comorbidity Index, baseline acute and preventive medication classes, index year, migraine-related comorbidities, and index treatment provider.

Results Of the eligible patients, 5,079 (mean age 43 yrs, 84% female) initiated CGRP mAbs, and 2,223 (mean age 43 yrs, 87% female) initiated onabotA. Adjusted analysis showed significantly higher persistence with onabotA at 12 months (50.3%), vs. CGRP mAb (40.4%; OR: 0.67[95% CI:0.61-0.74]; P<0.001). A significantly higher persistence with onabotA continued at 18 months (38.1% vs. 29.8%; OR: 0.69[95% CI:0.61-0.78]; P<0.001), and 24 months (32.1% vs. 23.0%; OR: 0.63[95% CI:0.54-0.74]; P<0.001).

Conclusion Patients with CM initiating onabotA showed greater persistence at all long-term time points for up to 24 months compared to those initiating CGRP mAb.

P209 Long term persistence of patients with chronic migraine switching to onabotulinumtoxinA or a different calcitonin gene-related peptide monoclonal antibody (CGRP mAb) after initial CGRP mAb treatment

P210 Experience in switching between antibodies against CGRP in a headache unit

M. Polanco1,2, J. Madera1,2, S. Pérez1,2, G. Gárate1,2, M. Muñóz1,2, N. C. Cavada1,2, J. Pascual Gómez1,2, V. González Quintanilla1,2

1Marqués de Valdecilla University Hospital, Neurology, Santander, Spain; 2Marqués de Valdecilla Health Research Institute (IDIVAL), Santander, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P210

Objective The therapeutic strategy of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody switching provides positive results in a variable number of patients. Our aim is to contribute to the elucidation of the potential benefit of switching this treatment and to determine the patient profile that would most benefit from this switch.

Methods We conducted a single-centre, retrospective study in a Headache Unit. Subjects undergoing immediate antiCGRP switch (a gap of less than a month) were included. A descriptive and comparative analysis of demographic variables, comorbidities, headache and migraine days per month (MHD and MMD), monthly analgesic consumption (SM), and medication overuse (MO) in the previous month before the switch and months 3 and 6 after the switch was conducted.

Results Eighty-five patients with a mean age of 52.18 years (87.1% female) were included. 95.3% met chronic migraine criteria, with a mean of 12.83 years of chronification. The improvement was significant and independent of the change in the mechanism of action of the second anti-CGRP. Either patients who had no response to the first antibody or those who had a loss of efficacy, experienced a significant reduction in MMD, MHD and SM at both 3 and 6 months after switching.

Conclusion Monoclonal antibody switching is effective in up to one-third of migraine patients who have failed to a first one. These results are maintained over time and are independent of the switch mechanism and previous experience with other anti-CGRP therapy.

P212 Refractory primary cough headache: More than just a nuisance

A. Costa1, A. Câmara2, S. Moreira1, S. Lopes1, F. Sousa1, S. Varanda1

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Primary cough headache arises moments after intense exercise or Valsalva maneuvers. All patients must perform brain MRI - Arnold-Chiari malformation type 1 is the most common finding.

Methods Case report and literature review.

Results 54-year-old male with a medical history of transient vertical diplopia with mesencephalic captant lesion on brain MRI by the age of 40 years old. He was initially followed for seven years with no other symptoms. When he was 53 years old, he returned to the neurology consult, now reporting severe, pulsating headaches (which lasted for one/two minutes) exclusively triggered by coughing, defecatory effort and Valsalva maneuvers of any kind. Several medications were tried without significant control (indomethacin, acetazolamide, propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate and valproic acid). The patient also underwent lumbar puncture with removal of 30 mL of CSF with no benefit. The patient remained symptomatic which led to the suspension of all medications. He remains with a lack of headache control.

Conclusion Although other primary headaches are usually regarded as benign because of their specific triggers, this case highlights the major impact they can have on a patient’s quality of life.

P214 Atogepant in episodic cluster headache: A case report on efficacy and tolerability

P. Ferreira1, I. Alves1

1Unidade Local de Saúde Entre Douro e Vouga, Neurology, Santa Maria da Feira, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P214

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective To describe the clinical response and tolerability of atogepant in a patient with episodic cluster headache (ECH), in whom standard preventive treatments were ineffective or poorly tolerated.

Methods We report the case of a 37-year-old male with a 5-year history of episodic cluster headache, fulfilling ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria. Previous preventive therapies with high-dose verapamil (240 mg twice daily) and topiramate (50 mg/day) offered limited benefit, with 1-2 bouts of the disease each year. Off-label initiation of atogepant, a selective oral calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor antagonist, was undertaken at a dosage of 60 mg/day during an active cluster period.

Results Treatment with atogepant led to complete suppression of cluster attacks, with therapeutic onset observed within the first 36 h. Remarkably, the patient remained attack-free, despite cessation of treatment.

Conclusion This case suggests that atogepant may represent a promising preventive approach for selected patients with episodic cluster headache, particularly when conventional treatments fail. Although adverse effects limited its use in this case, the rapid and complete response warrant further investigation. Controlled studies are warranted to assess its efficacy, safety and potential role in the management of cluster headache.

P215 Cluster headache impairs quality of life and daily functioning of Portuguese patients

C. Morgado1, S. Gomes1, A. Ferreira1, S. Lopes1, S. Marques1, J. Pinto1, C. Machado1, S. Varanda1, Consórcio Português para o Estudo da Cefaleia em S Cpecs2

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Braga, Portugal; 2CPECS, Braga, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P215

Objective Cluster headache is a rare primary headache disorder known to significantly impair quality of life and daily functioning. To date, no data are available regarding its impact on the Portuguese population. This study aimed at evaluating the quality of life of Portuguese patients diagnosed with cluster headache.

Methods Cross-sectional, multicenter study including participants from 17 specialized headache centers across Portugal. Eligible individuals were aged ≥18 years, with cluster headache diagnosis (ICHD-3 criteria) and with, at least, one cluster episode in the past three years. Socio-demographic and clinical data were collected, and the Portuguese version of the Cluster Headache Quality of Life Questionnaire (CHQ-P) was administered. Results A total of 127 participants were included, 81.1% of whom were male, with a median age of 49 years (IQR 18). Chronic cluster headache was diagnosed in 29.9% of patients. Younger age and chronic cluster headache were identified as predictors of greater impact on mood and interpersonal relationships.

Conclusion Cluster headache is associated with significant impairment in quality of life and daily functioning among Portuguese patients. These findings highlight the need for strategies to prevent or mitigate this burden.

Results We anticipate improvement in migraine-free days and lower scores for ISI and migraine disability scores with this intervention.

Conclusion Should this pilot reveal clinically meaningful improvements in sleep and headache frequency, it would warrant further investigation through a larger, randomized controlled trial.

P220 Refractory morning headaches in a young adult: Clinical relevance of borderline obstructive sleep apnea

M. Henriques1, E. Parreira1

1Hospital Prof Dr Fernando Fonseca, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P220

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Chronic morning headaches in young adults often present a diagnostic challenge, particularly when neuroimaging and standard therapeutic approaches are inconclusive.

Methods We report the case of a 28 year old male who began experiencing daily periorbital headaches at age 16. The pain alternated between eyes, was pulsatile or pressure-like, and predominantly occurred upon awakening, lasting 2–3 h or occasionally the entire day. There was no photophobia, phonophobia, or movement sensitivity, and symptoms improved with physical exercise. He had no known medical history, including hypertension, and was normotensive on examination. He had a history of snoring that resolved after ENT surgery, but without improvement in headache. Brain MRI revealed a non-specific T2 hyperintense lesion in the left cingulate gyrus. In the past, a diagnosis of hypnic headache was considered and empirical treatment with lithium, melatonin, and caffeine was attempted without benefit. Although he denied daytime sleepiness, he reported persistent fatigue.

Results Given the strong circadian pattern and lack of response to treatment, a sleep disorder was suspected. Polysomnography revealed an AHI of 5,9/h and ODI of 6.2/h, consistent with mild obstructive sleep apnea. Though the AHI was only slightly above the normal threshold, and would often be dismissed as clinically insignificant, the alignment between symptoms and sleep-related headache features was striking. CPAP therapy was initiated and resulted in near-complete resolution of symptoms, with only one headache in the following three months.

Conclusion This case highlights the importance of considering even borderline sleep study findings when the clinical picture is suggestive. In young patients with refractory morning headaches and compatible features, low AHI values should not be undervalued, as they may conceal a modifiable cause with significant therapeutic implications.

P222 Participant perspectives on clinical trial experience: Insights from exit interviews from the anti-PACAP antibody Phase 2 HOPE trial for migraine prevention

M. Ashina1, M. Pauline Herman2, I. Florea2, S. Lipson3, M. L. Martin4, J. Sanders5, L. Pickering Boserup2, R. B. Lipton6

1University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark; 3Hope in Pain, Inc, Newport Beach, CA, USA; 4Evidera, Patient Centered Outcomes, Seattle, WA, USA; 5The Migraine Diva, Fredricksburg, VA, USA; 6Montefiore Medical Center and Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, Department of Neurology, New York, NY, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P222

Objective To explore perspectives and experiences of clinical trial participation among people living with migraine who participated in the Phase 2 HOPE trial (NCT05133323) investigating the efficacy and safety of Lu AG09222, an anti-pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (anti-PACAP) monoclonal antibody in development for migraine prevention.

P223 Invisible pain at work: Perceptions, accommodations, and stigma surrounding migraine in the workplace

L. Francisco1, S. Gomes2, S. Moreira2, J. M. Araújo2, S. Varanda2

1Unidade Local de Saúde do Alto Minho, Neurology, Viana do Castelo, Portugal; 2Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Neurology, Braga, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P223

Objective To explore how migraine is perceived and accommodated in the workplace, and to assess the impact of stigma, organizational empathy, and policy on workers living with migraine.

Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 30 adult employees formally diagnosed with migraine. Participants completed a structured questionnaire covering five domains: demographic/professional profile, migraine characteristics, workplace attitudes, organizational policies, and professional/emotional impact. The adapted Stigma Scale for Chronic Illness (SSCI-8) was used to assess both enacted and internalized stigma.

Results Participants (mean age: 41.6) reported 9.3 migraine days/month. Work productivity during attacks was low (mean = 2.0/5). Although 90% felt free to take medication, 63% had felt pressured to keep working, and 60% had hidden their condition. Migraine legitimacy was rated moderately (mean = 3.1/5). While 63% had remote work options, only 30% had additional breaks, and 10% had access to quiet/dark spaces. Just 17% reported training on invisible illnesses. Career impact was significant: 67% felt limited in progression, and 63% had considered changing jobs due to lack of support. Only 23% felt emotionally supported. SSCI-8 scores showed low overt stigma (means 1.2–1.8), but internalized stigma was common: 43% felt ashamed of limitations, and 30% felt responsible for their condition.

Conclusion Migraine significantly affects employees productivity and career development. Despite some accommodations, internalized stigma and lack of emotional support remain widespread. These findings underscore the need for greater awareness, inclusive workplace practices, and targeted training to foster empathy and support.

P224 PGIC vs. MIDAS: PROMs in anti-CGRP migraine mAb therapy

S. Marinho Pinto1, C. Branco1, C. Rodrigues1, H. Lainé2, G. V. Bonifácio1

1ULS Arrábida - Hospital de São Bernardo, Neurology, Setúbal, Portugal; 2Gulbenkian Institute for Molecular Medicine, Digital Technologies, Oeiras, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P224

Objective To evaluate the utility of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) in assessing response to anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy in migraine.

Methods This retrospective, observational study included migraine patients treated with anti-CGRP mAbs at a single centre. Monthly headache days (MHD) and Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS) scores were collected at baseline and quarterly thereafter. The Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC), a 7-point scale reflecting patient-perceived improvement, was recorded quarterly from month 3 to 12. Changes in MHD and MIDAS were expressed as percentages. PGIC was treated as an ordinal variable (1 = very much improved to 7 = very much worsened). Correlations were assessed using Spearman’s coefficient; Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical comparisons.

Results Data was available from 63 patients, totalling 104 MIDAS and 98 PGIC forms. Sixteen patients (25%) filled out MIDAS forms incorrectly at least once, compared to 1 (2%) who incorrectly filled the PGIC form once. Education level was not significantly associated with form errors (p=0.13). All patients who reported a >50% reduction in MHD rated their PGIC as “very much improved” or “improved” (PGIC = 1 or 2). Non-responders (<30% reduction in MHD) rated their status from PGIC 1 to 5, with PGIC 1 or 2 responses increasing from 3 of 7 (43%) to 5 of 7 (71%) by month 9. MIDAS moderately correlated with MHD (rs=0.61, p<0.05), while PGIC showed a weak positive correlation (rs=0.39, p<0.05).

Conclusion MIDAS moderately reflects changes in headache frequency, limiting its added value as a PROM. PGIC correlated poorly with headache frequency, reflecting perceived improvements in severity, duration, or impact of migraine attacks that may better capture the full therapeutic benefit of anti-CGRP mAbs. Findings align with prior data and, given PGIC’s ease of completion, support its inclusion in routine migraine monitoring to enhance individualized care.

P225 Quality of life in migraine: The burden of psychiatric comorbidities

S. Frikha1, M. Messalmani1, O. Selmi1, O. Ben Othman1, H. Derbali1, I. Bedoui1, M. Mansour1, J. Zaouali1

1Military Hospital of Instruction of Tunis, Neurology, Tunis, Tunisia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P225

Objective Migraines are disabling neurological disorders frequently associated with psychiatric comorbidities. These comorbidities may worsen symptoms, hinder treatment response, and negatively impact quality of life (QoL). This study aimed to assess QoL in migraine patients and evaluate how psychiatric comorbidities influence it.

Methods A one-year case-control study (January–December 2022) was conducted at the Military Hospital of Instruction of Tunis. It included 100 migraine patients and 200 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. QoL was measured using the SF-36 questionnaire, which assesses eight domains and provides physical and mental component scores with higher scores indicating better QoL. Psychiatric comorbidities were diagnosed using standardized clinical criteria. Comparisons were made between groups with and without comorbidities.

Results Migraine patients had significantly lower SF-36 scores than controls: physical component (48.7% vs. 82.6%), mental component (42.2% vs. 74.6%), and global score (47.9% vs. 80.3%). Psychiatric comorbidities further worsened outcomes. Migraineurs with depression had a global score of 39% vs. 48% in those without. Those with anxiety disorders scored 42% vs. 49%. Generalized anxiety and panic disorder were associated with the greatest reductions in mental component scores. Migraine patients with psychiatric comorbidities consistently reported lower QoL than both controls and migraineurs without such conditions.

Conclusion Psychiatric comorbidities significantly impair quality of life in migraine sufferers. Early identification and integrated management of these conditions are essential for improving overall outcomes and reducing the burden of migraine.

P226 Measurement properties of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) for assessing physical functioning and quality of life in adults with migraine: A systematic review

A. Rodrigues1,2, E. Tornaci Sönmez1, T. B. N. Nguyen1, O. Giret1, J. Pradela2, J. de Pauw1, D. Bevilaqua-Grossi2, W. de Hertogh1

1University of Antwerp, Rehabilitation Sciences and Physiotherapy, Antwerp, Belgium; 2University of São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P226

Objective To systematically evaluate the measurement properties validity, reliability, and responsiveness of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) used to assess the impact of migraine on patients’ physical functioning and Quality of Life (QOL).

Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Web of Science for studies published in English between 2004 and July 2025. Eligible studies assessed the measurement properties of PROMs evaluating physical functioning and/or QoL in adults with migraine. Independent reviewers performed the studies selection, data extraction, assessed methodological quality, rated measurement properties and synthesized the results according to COSMIN (Consensus-based-Standards for selection of health Measurement Instruments) guidelines.

Results Out of 3,554 articles, 32 met the inclusion criteria, covering 16 distinct PROMs, in which the Migraine Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire Version 2.1 (MSQv2.1), the Headache Impact Test (HIT-6TM), and the Migraine Impact and Disability Assessment Scale (MIDAS) were the most extensively studied instruments. Considering the evaluation of the psychometric properties, most studies focused on aspects of validity (construct, convergent validity) and reliability (test-retest and internal consistency). These PROMS also demonstrated responsiveness, including the establishment of thresholds for clinically significant change. MSQ v2.1 and HIT-6 had a moderate to high level of evidence.

Conclusion The MSQ v2.1, HIT-6TM and MIDAS are the most thoroughly investigated PROMS for assessing physical functioning and QoL in individuals with migraine. Among these, the MSQ v2.1 has the best-established measurement properties with moderate to high level of evidence. Future research should clarify domains coverage and assess the value of combining instruments to provide a comprehensive picture of migraine’s impact.

P227 The effects of allodynia on the pain perception during botulinum toxin treatment for migraine: A cross-sectional study

M. de Oliveira Carvalho1,2, C. Serrão1,2, M. Fortuna Baptista1,2, F. Dourado Sotero1,2, M. I. Pavão Martins1,2

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P227

Objective Migraine patients may develop cutaneous allodynia (CA), characterized by increased pain sensitivity. P229 Insomnia and migraine: Insights from therapeutic response

M. Marques Roque1, M. Costa Taveira1, M. Dias da Costa1, F. Dourado Sotero1,2, M. I. Pavão Martins1,2

1Hospital de Santa Maria, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Centro de Estudos Egas Moniz, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P229

Objective Insomnia frequently coexists with migraine. We aimed to assess whether migraine therapies - monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting CGRP or onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) - lead to insomnia improvement.

Methods We included 67 migraine patients treated with mAbs or Botox. All were assessed before and after treatment using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS). Treatment response was defined as ≥50% reduction in headache frequency. ISI change was compared across treatment types and response status. Linear regressions assessed whether baseline ISI, depressive symptoms, or response status predicted insomnia improvement. A subanalysis focused on patients with clinically significant insomnia (ISI > 7), and an additional analysis was performed based on patients receiving sedative medications as migraine preventives (ex: ADT) or other pathologies.

Results Overall, ISI scores changed minimally after treatment with mAbs (p = 0.298). No significant differences in ISI change were found between responders and non-responders (p = 0.385), nor between treatment types (p=0.148). In multivariable regression, only baseline ISI predicted sleep improvement (B = –0.336, p = 0.004); response status, depression scores (HADS) and sedative medications were not significant. The subgroup with ISI > 7 showed similar results, with no significant treatment effect. Finally, in patients not receiving sedatives, no significant differences in ISI change were observed between treatment types or response status.

Conclusion Insomnia symptoms improved only modestly after migraine treatment and were unrelated to headache response, treatment type or depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that migraine and insomnia may not share a direct mechanistic link, and support the need for separate, targeted management of sleep disturbances in migraine patients.

Objective Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is implicated in migraine pathophysiology and plays a regulatory role in bone metabolism. Concerns have emerged regarding possible osteocatabolic effects of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) used as preventives in migraine patients. We report the 6-month results from an ongoing 24-month prospective study assessing the impact of anti-CGRP mAbs on bone mineral density (BMD), trabecular bone score (TBS), and bone turnover markers in migraine patients.

Methods Migraine patients initiating anti-CGRP mAbs (erenumab, galcanezumab, or fremanezumab) and with no comorbidities or medications affecting bone metabolism, were compared to age- and sex-matched migraine patients with no preventive migraine therapies. BMD was measured at lumbar spine (L1-L4), TBS was calculated using the TBS iNsight® software from lumbar images. Bone metabolism turnover markers included β-CTX and P1NP. Changes from baseline to month 6 were analyzed using non-parametric tests and linear mixed-effects models including time × group interaction.

Results Thirty-eight patients (25 treated, 13 controls; mean age 36.3 ± 9.2 years; 84% female) completed 6-month evaluations. At baseline, BMD, TBS, and bone markers were within normal ranges and comparable. At 6 months, lumbar spine BMD remained stable in both groups (treated +0.02 g/cm², p=0.65; controls –0.01 g/cm², p=0.32). TBS was unchanged in treated patients (–0.001; p=1.000) but increased in controls (+0.052; p=0.026), with a significant time × group interaction (p=0.022). β-CTX and P1NP showed no significant changes or interaction. Treated patients reported a reduction in monthly migraine days (–9.13; p<0.001).

Conclusion Anti-CGRP mAbs treatment was not associated with significant changes in BMD, TBS or bone turnover markers over 6 months in migraine patients.

P232 Circulating CGRP as a diagnostic biomarker in female migraineurs: A single-center case-control study

Q. Huang1, Y. Xu1, Q. Zhang1

1Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, Department of Neurology, Nanjing, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P232

Objective Migraine constitutes the predominant cause of disability-adjusted life years, yet remains diagnostically challenging due to the absence of clinically validated biomarkers. Calcitonin gene-related peptide, recognized as the pathophysiological cornerstone of migraine, mediates cephalic vasodilation and neurogenic inflammation through its release from activated trigeminal ganglion neurons. Despite the therapeutic breakthrough of anti-CGRP therapies, reliable bedside quantification of CGRP levels remains elusive, hindering personalized treatment strategies.

Methods This study enrolled 184 female migraineurs and 85 age-matched controls. Serum CGRP was measured by magnetic bead-based chemiluminescent immunoassay. High-/low-expression subgroups were stratified by predefined CGRP cutoff. Patients receiving CGRP antagonist rimegepant acutely were analyzed.

Results Circulating CGRP was higher in female migraineurs vs. controls. ROC analysis determined 40.00 pg/mL as cutoff for stratification. Patients classified: high-CGRP (n=112) and low-CGRP (n=72). High-CGRP group had higher monthly attack frequency (P=0.013) and more tender points (P=0.026). With rimegepant, 45.0% achieved pain-free at 2 h. Shorter attack duration independently predicted response (P=0.027). Baseline CGRP moderately elevated in responders vs. non-responders, but non-significant.

Conclusion Elevated blood CGRP distinguishes female migraineurs from healthy controls. Baseline CGRP showed no direct association with rimegepant response, but pretreatment levels positively correlated with migraine attack frequency—a feature predicting reduced therapeutic efficacy.

P233 Survey on adherence and tolerability of atogepant used as migraine preventive treatment

D. A. Montisano1, G. Vaghi2,1, A. Parisi3, R. de Icco2,1, B. Agostini2,1, M. Giraudo2,1, C. Tassorelli2,1, L. Grazzi3

1IRCCS Mondino Foundation, Headache Science & Neurorehabilitation Unit, Pavia, Italy; 2University of Pavia, Department of Brain and Behavioral Sciences, Pavia, Italy; 3IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, SSD Headache Center, Milan, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P233

Objective atogepant is a novel anti-calcitonin gene related peptide treatment (CGRP) used in migraine prevention. Our primary aim was to assess its therapeutic adherence, tolerability of the drug, as well as perceived effectiveness when used during a migraine attack.

Methods we conducted a survey involving 51 migraine individuals undergoing atogepant treatment at the Headache Centers of Carlo Besta Neurological Institute in Milan and Mondino Foundation in Pavia. The survey was made on “Microsoft Form” institutional doodle. We investigated therapeutic adherence, treatment tolerability, individuals’ satisfaction, as well as atogepant efficacy despite some missed pills missed, and acute effictiveness during pain.

Results Participants had a mean age of 42y (±8.4), they received treatment for a median of 24 weeks of them 42 out of 51 take atogepant in the morning. Conclusion This study suggests that Erenumab provides an early advantage over Topiramate in reducing triptan utilization among migraine patients, particularly during the first 3 months of treatment.Fig. 1 (abstract P237).Fig. 2 (abstract P237).

P239 Joint impact of headache disorders and depressive symptoms on mild cognitive impairment in older adults: Evidence from a longitudinal cohort in China

J. Fang1, J. Wu1, J. Zheng1, Z. Guo1, H. Yang1

1The First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen University, School of Medicine, Xiamen University, Department of Neurology and Department of Neuroscience, Xiamen, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P239

Objective This study elucidates the intricate interplay between headache disorders, depressive symptoms, and the incidence of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in middle-aged and elderly populations. While prior research has independently examined these factors, their synergistic and mediating effects on cognitive decline remain poorly understood.

Methods This longitudinal study analyzed 2015-2020 CHARLS data from 8,137 middle-aged/elderly participants. Headache was assessed by self-report and ID-Migraine™, depression by CESD-10, and cognition via orientation/memory/calculation/drawing tests. MCI was defined as AACD. Cox models examined: (1) depression/headache-MCI associations; (2) their mediation/joint effects.

Results Baseline analysis showed that individuals reporting headache, migraine, or depressive symptoms had significantly lower cognitive performance. In adjusted models, patients with headache (HR = 1.288, 95% CI: 1.120, 1.481), migraine (HR = 1.274, 95% CI: 1.049, 1.547), and depressive symptoms (HR = 1.357, 95% CI: 1.199, 1.535) demonstrated a substantially higher incidence of MCI. Furthermore, the study indicated that depressive symptoms partially mediated the association between headache and MCI incidence but fully mediated the link between migraine and incident MCI. The joint effects of headache disorders and depressive symptoms were significant among individuals aged ≥60 years.

Conclusion These findings underscore the complex interplay between headache disorders, depression, and cognitive decline, underscoring the need for integrated neurological and psychological healthcare to prevent MCI.

A. Argyriou1, E. Dermitzakis2, G. Xiromerisiou3, M. Chondrogianni4, A. Foska4, P. Soldatos5, E. Mavraki6, D. Rikos7, P. Litsardopoulos1, G. Tsivgoulis4, M. Vikelis8

P246 Cognitive functions comparison between osmophobic and non-osmophobic migraine sufferers

L. Bartole1, A. Granato1, G. Garascia1, T. Lombardo2, L. Pelusi2, T. Cattaruzza2, P. Manganotti1,2

1University of Trieste, Clinical Unit of Neurology, Headache Centre, Department of Medicine, Surgery and Health Sciences, Trieste, Italy; 2University of Trieste, Clinical Unit of Neurology, Centre for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Dementias and Memory and Cognitive Disorders, Department of Medicine, Surgery and Health Sciences, Trieste, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P246

Objective Osmophobia (Osm) is a particular type of odour aversion often associated to migraine. Instead, olfaction deficit has been associated to cognitive impairment. Thus, we inquired whether Osm migraine patients could exhibit a different cognitive profile compared to those without this symptom (NOsm).

Methods We conducted a cross-sectional prospective study involving Osm and NOsm migraine subjects. After excluding conditions potentially affecting olfaction or cognitive functioning, migraine characteristics were collected. Then, cognitive performance was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning (RAVL), the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure (ROCF), the Multiple Features Target Cancellation (MFTC) and the Stroop Colour and Word (SCW) tests. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

Results We enrolled 50 migraine patients with median age of 38.0 (29.0-45.0) years, 27 of whom with Osm. Osm patients reported a median of 5 worsening and 2 causative odours, with cigarette smoke being the most frequently mentioned in both cases (85.2% and 37% of Osm patients, respectively). Osm patients resulted to have a longer migraine history, more frequent pain exacerbation with physical activity and complaint of nausea/vomiting. Cognitive performance did not differ significantly between Osm and NOsm groups in none of the tests. The only significant difference was a slower Stroop Reading Time Score in NOsm patients. Both groups performed below average on cognitive tests compared to the general population, showing that migraine patients, regardless of Osm presence, present with slight cognitive impairment.

Conclusion To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare neuropsychological functions of Osm and NOsm migraine patients. Despite greater clinical severity in Osm patients, no cognitive differences were found. Overall, migraine patients performed slightly below the general population’s expected levels.

1Organon International GmbH, Lucerne, Switzerland; 2Cencora, Madrid, Spain; 3Organon Sweden AB, Stockholm, Sweden; 4Cencora, Bourne End, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P248

Objective Migraine affects 14%-26% of adults in Europe, with a higher prevalence in women than in men. In the absence of a simple diagnostic test for migraine, many people remain undiagnosed and without adequate care despite the availability of a range of effective treatments. This systematic review aims to identify and summarize real-world evidence on treatment patterns for migraine in Europe.

Methods We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and grey literature sources for observational studies published from 2018 to 2024. Eligibility criteria were studies conducted in France, Germany, Spain, Italy, or the United Kingdom (EU5) or Belgium reporting migraine treatment patterns data.

Results From 4,481 records identified by the literature searches, 102 observational studies were included, mostly from Italy (40%) and Spain (30%). Evidence from Italy, Spain, Germany and the UK indicates that more than 20% of patients do not receive any migraine-specific treatment despite meeting migraine diagnostic criteria. In line with clinical guidelines, triptans are the most frequently used acute treatment; however, some evidence from Spain indicates divergence from guideline advice against the use of opioids and ergots as acute treatments. Approximately 25%-40% of patients in the EU5 receive some form of preventive medication, but estimates vary widely and data on specific drug classes are lacking. Adherence to preventive therapy is low; about 75% of patients discontinue treatment within a year, mostly due to adverse events. Despite the higher prevalence of migraine in women, evidence relating to female-specific migraine (e.g. menstrual migraine, migraine during pregnancy/breastfeeding) are sparse.

Conclusion Our findings reveal some disparities between clinical guidelines and clinical practice in diagnosing and managing migraine appropriately. The paucity of data on preventive therapies and female-specific migraine highlights important evidence gaps that should be addressed to improve treatment strategies and patient outcomes.

P250 Prospective, real-world data from the Greek Research Alliance for the Study of headache and Pain (GRASP), on the efficacy and safety of eptinezumab in migraine prophylaxis

E. Dermitzakis1, A. Argyriou2, M. Chondrogianni3, A. Foska3, D. Rikos4, P. Soldatos5, P. Litsardopoulos2, G. Xiromerisiou6, G. Tsivgoulis3, M. Vikelis7

1Headache Clinic, Euromedica General Clinic, Thessaloniki, Greece; 2Agios Andreas General Hospital of Patras, Patras, Greece; 3Attikon University Hospital, Athens, Greece; 4404 Military Hospital, Larissa, Greece; 5Kalamata Headache Clinic, Kalamata, Greece; 6School of Medicine, University of Thessaly, Larissa, Greece; 7Glyfada Headache Clinic, Athens, Greece

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P250

Objective The aim of this real-world prospective study, designed by GRASP, was to determine the efficacy and safety of prophylactic treatment with eptinezumab in patients with high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM) or chronic migraine (CM) who had previously failed at least 3 prophylactic treatments.

Methods After obtaining their informed consent, 100 patients (45 HFEM / 55 CM) who received at least 1 cycle of eptinezumab 100 mg, were studied. Clinical response (at least 50% MHD reduction) was calculated by recording the change in MHD after eptinezumab treatment compared to baseline. The changes in moderate/severe MHD and monthly days with acute medication intake (MAI) after eptinezumab treatment, compared to baseline, were also calculated. Eptinezumab was generally safe and well tolerated.

Conclusion Our prospective results in a real-world setting further support the view that eptinezumab is an effective and safe prophylactic treatment in difficult-to-manage patients with HFEM or CM. The onset of its response is generally rapid.

P252 Blood pressure trends and adverse effects in migraine patients receiving anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies

S. Marinho Pinto1, C. Branco1, C. Rodrigues1, H. Lainé2, G. V. Bonifácio1

1ULS Arrábida - Hospital de São Bernardo, Neurology, Setúbal, Portugal; 2Gulbenkian Institute for Molecular Medicine, Digital Technologies, Oeiras, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P252

Objective To evaluate the safety and side effect profile of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) in a real-world cohort of migraine patients, with particular attention to vascular-related events and blood pressure changes.

Methods This observational, retrospective study included 59 patients treated with anti-CGRP mAbs at a single centre. Data on adverse effects were collected from clinical records. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were recorded at treatment initiation and quarterly thereafter per protocol. Data was analysed using paired t-test, linear mixed-effects model or pairwise comparison to baseline. Adjustments to antihypertensive medications were also documented.

Results Most patients were on anti-CGRP ligand mAbs (n=55, 93%). Side effects were infrequent and mild. Raynaud’s phenomenon was reported in 3 patients (5%), one of whom required permanent treatment discontinuation. Constipation led to mAb switch in 2 patients (3%). There were no significant changes in mean SBP or DBP from baseline to T3 (SBP p=0.77, DBP p=0.98), or during extended treatment (SBP p=0.64, DBP p>0.05 in all pairwise comparisons). Antihypertensive therapy adjustments were needed in 6 patients (10%). Of these, 2 had a prior diagnosis of hypertension; 1 patient continued to experience hypertension after interruption of mAb therapy, while another required only transient dose changes that were quickly reversed. No serious cardiovascular events were reported during the observation period.

Conclusion In this real-world cohort, anti-CGRP mAbs were generally well tolerated. While vascular-related side effects such as Raynaud’s phenomenon and blood pressure fluctuations were observed in a minority of patients, they were often incidental and rarely led to permanent discontinuation. These findings underscore the need for individualized monitoring, especially in patients with pre-existing vascular conditions, but support the overall safety of anti-CGRP mAbs in clinical practice.

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P256

Objective A subset of migraine patients do not respond well to preventive treatments, leading to resistant or refractory migraine, which significantly affects their lives. These patients may be at risk of being misdiagnosed or subjected to unnecessary testing. Methods Participants from the multicenter, prospective REFINE study were classified as RefM, ResM, and NRNRM, according to the proposed European Headache Federation criteria. We assessed the baseline data about diagnosis, including misdiagnosis, clinical and instrumental access in the medical history of those patients.

Results In a cohort of 689 migraine patients (82.7% female, median age 46 [IQR 37.0-54.0]), 51.5% were classified as NRNRM, 37.9% as ResM, and 10.9% as RefM. P260 Migraine and visual snow syndrome: Exploring shared pathways through hallucinogen-induced perceptual disturbances

R. Rodrigues1, M. Roque1, F. Dourado Sotero1,2, M. I. Pavão Martins1,2

1Clínica Universitária de Neurologia, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Centro de Estudos Egas Moniz, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Unidade Local de Saúde Santa Maria, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P260

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Visual Snow Syndrome (VSS) is a condition marked by persistent visual phenomena resembling television static, often accompanied by afterimages, entoptic effects, and nyctalopia. Migraine is the most frequent comorbidity, though the basis for this association remains unclear. VSS pathophysiology points to dysfunction in the salience network and thalamo-cortical visual processing—both similarly affected by certain hallucinogens.

Methods This work is based on two clinical case reports.

Results The first case refers to a 29-year-old male factory worker with episodic migraine without aura developed persistent bright dots, photic flashes, and entoptic phenomena after a single LSD use, lasting six months and more evident in bright environments. Neurological and ophthalmological exams were normal, brain MRI revealed a pineal cyst, with normal EEG and OCT. Treatment with amotrigine 25 mg improved headache but visual symptoms persisted. The second case concerns a 24-year-old female engineering PhD student with chronic migraine with visual aura, hypothyroidism, polycystic ovary syndrome, and ADHD. After a single exposure to MDMA, she reported continuous “visual noise” and afterimages lasting eight months, worsened by screen exposure. Neurological and ophthalmological evaluations were normal. Brain MRI revealed a pineal cyst. She showed no improvement with lamotrigine or gabapentin but responded to valproate 250 mg and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Conclusion Hallucinogens modulate thalamic activity, particularly its inhibitory role in sensory processing, contributing to perceptual disturbances. In migraine, a lowered thalamic threshold may promote visual symptoms, further exacerbated by hallucinogens. These cases suggest overlapping pathophysiological mechanisms between VSS and hallucinogenic effects, highlighting the thalamus as a key structure involved in both conditions.

Results So far, 56 CAS-positive patients are eligible (50 female, 6 male; mean age 40.6). No significant difference in MHD reduction was found across CAPS groups (p = 0.335). A weak but significant correlation was found between CAPS and MHD reduction (r = 0.295, p = 0.029). No significant sex-based difference was observed.

Conclusion liminary data suggest that greater CAPS reduction correlates with greater MHD reduction, indicating stronger treatment response in patients with prominent CAS. Recruitment is ongoing to complete the planned sample and allow full analysis.

P263 Vestibular migraine response to gepant dual therapy – A case report

E. Parreira1

1Hospital Prof Dr Fernando Fonseca, Neurology Department, Amadora, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P263

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Atogepant and rimegepant are new drugs blocking the CGRP receptor for migraine prevention (atogepant and rimegepant) or migraine acute therapy (rimegepant). Their role in vestibular migraine is not yet defined: some evidence suggest efficacy of monoclonal antibody antiCGRP therapies in vestibular migraine (1), CGRP receptors are abundant in vestibular nuclei (2) and in animal models CGRP intervenes in vestibular symptomatology (3). Simultaneous off-label use of more than one gepant is being more frequently reported in real world: patients taking one gepant daily for migraine prevention take another gepant for acute treatment. The safety and efficacy of this combination is not known.

Methods We report a case of vestibular migraine, using both gepants, with a good response to atogepant preventively and to rimegepant acutely. Informed consent was given.

Results Case Report: a 36-year-old female with a 10 year long vestibular migraine and fibromyalgia, previously failed 4 oral preventive treatments. She started rimegepant for migraine prevention with excellent response. Later treatment was switched to atogepant for migraine prevention but maintained rimegepant for acute treatment. With gepants migraine days were reduced from 10 to 15 days/ month to 1-2 per month. She did not experience any side effects. Vertigo disappeared completely after starting atogepant and fibromialgic symptoms were also greatly reduced. She is on atogepant now for 6 months and uses rimegepant as acute treatment whenever she gets a migraine: rimegepant works very fast (less than one hour) and is very effective (pain free in less than 2 h).

Conclusion In this vestibular migraine patient, gepants proved to be very effective in treating both headache and vertigo. The fact that rimegepant continues to be effective as acute medication in a patient already taking 60 mg of atogepant daily for prevention, suggests that there is room for additional CGRP blockade, without, in this case, inducing side-effects.

P264 Greater occipital nerve blocks in episodic cluster headache – Real-world clinical experience

M. Dias da Costa1, M. Olivier2, C. Peiró Vilaplana2,3, S. Díaz Insa2,3

1Unidade Local de Saúde Santa Maria, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Línea de Investigación en Cefaleas, Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria La Fe, Valencia, Spain, Valencia, Spain; 3Unidad de Cefaleas, Neurología, Hospital Universitari i Politècnic La Fe, Valencia, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P264

Objective Real-world experience with greater occipital nerve blocks (GONBs) for the preventive treatment of episodic cluster headache (EHC) is lacking. We aim to describe the clinical experience with GONBs for the preventive treatment of EHC in a Headache Unit of a Spanish hospital.

Methods Retrospective observational study. Adult patients with ECH, according to the ICHD-3, treated with GONBs as a preventive treatment were included. Patients with other concomitant headache types were excluded. Treatment protocol includes a first GONB as soon as bout begins. If no response after 1 week, a second GONB is performed. If bout persists, oral preventive treatment is advocated. Data was retrieved from clinical records from 2015 to 2025. Patients were asked to evaluate their individual perceived benefit after GONBs according to the Patient’s Global Impression of Change (PGIC) score. Descriptive analysis and linear regression models adjusted to cofounders were performed.

Results A total of 51 patients were included [median years of disease of 9.0 (IQR 4.5-17.5)]. Median PGIC score after GONBs was 2.0 (IQR 1-3) with 86.2% of patients scoring ≤3. No patients reported worsening. Median bouts per patient treated with GONBs was 3 (IQR 1-4.5) with a mean total of GONBs per bout of 1.5±0.7. Median days elapsed until the first GONB since bout beginning, per patient, was 9.0 (IQR 4-15). Patients treated with GONB experienced a 59% shorter duration compared to untreated patients, after adjusting for cofounders (p < 0.001). For each day of delay in first GONB, duration of bout increased by 0.7% (p < 0.001). Longer delays (>14 days) after bout begining was associated with higher PGIC scores (p = 0.0205).

Conclusion GONBs are effective as preventive treatment in ECH patients as shown by objective measures and patient related outcomes. Given these results, we advocate that GONBs should be considered mandatory in ECH patients as a preventive or even as a type of abortive treatment.

P265 Efficacy and tolerability of atogepant during the perimenstrual phase of female cycle

R. Nunes Rato1,2, A. L. Neves1,2, C. Sousa1, R. Dias1,2, M. J. Pinto1,2, M. Pinto1, A. Costa1,2

1São João University Hospital, Department of Neurology, Porto, Portugal; 2Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto, Department of Clinical Neurosciences and Mental Health, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P265

Objective This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of atogepant—an oral, small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonist—during the perimenstrual phase.

Methods An ambispective study is currently underway, enrolling consecutive female patients initiating atogepant treatment(60 mg/daily), with preserved menstrual cycles (i.e., not using hormonal suppression), and meeting the ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for menstrually related migraine or pure menstrual migraine. The perimenstrual phase was defined as days −2 to +3 of menstruation. Outcomes assessed include mean number of migraine days, mean migraine intensity, and responder rate (≥50% reduction in migraine frequency) during the perimenstrual phase, evaluated up to three months post-treatment initiation.

Results A total of 24 women of reproductive age (median age 41 years, IQR 36–45), from a single tertiary centre, were included. None met the criteria for pure menstrual migraine. Prior to atogepant initiation, the mean number of perimenstrual migraine days was 4.38 ± 0.21. At follow-up, this had significantly decreased to 1.69 ± 0.50 days (p < 0.001). A ≥50% reduction in perimenstrual migraine days was observed in 58% of patients (n = 14). Approximately 30% of patients no longer required acute treatment during the perimenstrual phase. According to the Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC) scale, 15 patients reported significant improvement specifically during the perimenstrual window. The most frequently reported adverse events were constipation, nausea, and somnolence, however, none of the patients discontinued the medication due to side effects.

Conclusion Preliminary data suggest that atogepant may reduce the burden of menstrually related migraine. The treatment was well tolerated in this cohort. Ongoing data collection will further clarify the impact of hormonal fluctuations on treatment response throughout the menstrual cycle.

Amaducci”, Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Consorziale di Bari, Bari, Italy; 16Azienda Sanitaria Universitaria Integrata di Udine, Dipartimento di Neuroscienze, Udine, Italy; 17Città della Salute e della Scienza di Torino, Department of Neuroscience, Turin, Italy; 18Centro per la diagnosi e terapia delle cefalee, Policlinico Umberto I, Rome, Italy; 19IRCCS Istituto Auxologico, Milan, Italy; 20AOU Alessandria, Allesandria, Italy; 21University of Siena, Siena, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P266

Objective To assess the impact of atogepant in preventing migraine after 24-week of treatment.

Methods Adult patients treated with atogepant 60 mg daily were included. At baseline (T0), after 12 (T3) and 24 weeks (T6) since atogepant first administration, monthly migraine days (MMDs), HIT-6, MIDAS, mTOQ-6, MSQ, ASC-12 and MIBS-4 scores were assessed. The co-primary endpoints were the changes in MMDs and percentage 50%RR responders (i.e. reduction of MMDs≥50%) from T0 to T6.

Results 128 patients (56 [43.8%] with chronic migraine [CM], 115 female [89.9%], age 48.3±13.3) completed the 24-week observation. In the whole group, MMDs reduced from 16.5±8.5 at baseline to 8.0±8.4 at T3 and 8.6±9.2 at T6. Overall, 64.8% of patients were 50%MMDs responders at T3 and 61.7% at T6 (68.1% and 66.7% in the episodic migraine group and 60.7% and 55.4% in the CM group at T3 and at T6, respectively). To note, 81.9% of responders at T3 maintained MMDs 50%RR also at T6, while 24.4% of patients among non-responders at T3 became 50%RR at T6. The 50%RR at T6 was higher in patients who had not previous ineffective anti-CGRP mAbs treatment (63.3% vs. 36.7%, p=0.027) and in those who were not on medication overuse at baseline (55.7% vs. 44.3%, p=0.046). Previous anti-CGRP mAbs failure was the only characteristic associated with the responder status in the multiple regression analysis (p=0.031). From T0 to T6 analgesic use, HIT-6, MIDAS, ASC-12, MIBS-4 and mTOQ-6 scores reduced (p<0.001), and MSQ role-function restriction increased (p<0.01). Changes mainly occurred from T0 to T3, except for MIBS-4 which also decreased from T3 to T6 (p<0.001). Since T3, only 10 subjects (7.8%) dropped out: 6 for lack of effectiveness, of these one also for poor tolerability, and 4 for patients’ decision. Weight reduced of 0.8±3.1 kg (p<0.001) from T0 to T3, while from T3 to T6 remained stable.

Conclusion The multicentric STAR study confirms atogepant effectiveness and tolerability at 24-week follow-up.

P267 OnaBotulinumtoxin-A in chronic migraine patients with short or long disease history and psychiatric comorbidities: Preliminary data from the Italian observational prospective multicentric study BACH study

F. Vernieri1, M. Marcosano1, L. Grazzi2, D. A. Montisano2, R. Ornello3, S. Sacco3, C. Rosignoli3, A. Doretti4, M. Albanese5, G. Viticchi6, N. Brunelli1, L. D’Onofrio1, L. Fofi1, C. Altamura1, P. Pasqualetti7

1Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy; 2IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, Milan, Italy; 3University of L’Aquila, L’Aquila, Italy; 4IRCCS Istituto Auxologico, Milan, Italy; 5University of Rome Tor Vergata, Rome, Italy; 6Marche Polytechnic University, Ancona, Italy; 7Sapienza University of Rome, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P267

Objective To investigate whether the duration of Chronic Migraine (CM) for over or less than 10 years can predict Onabotulinumtoxin-A (OBT-A) effectiveness and to evaluate if patients’ psychopathological profile may influence their outcome.

Methods Consecutive CM patients undergoing OBT-A treatment have been enrolled since January 2024. Evaluation times were at baseline and after 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. We collected Monthly Headache Days (MHDs), number of Monthly Acute Medications (MAMs), HIT-6 and MIDAS scores. Pain intensity was evaluated by NRS. The psychopathological profile was evaluated by BDI-II, BIS-11, STAI-Y, DERS, TAS-20 questionnaires.

In addition, a slight significance (p=0.064) was found for the triple interaction duration x psychiatric comorbidities x time.

Conclusion In this preliminary report OBT-A effectiveness was not affected by disease history or psychiatric comorbidities, except for the latter influencing MIDAS in the short term.

P269 Response to Eptinezumab in a real-world setting – A 24 month experience in a Portuguese hospital

E. Parreira1, M. Saraiva1, S. Machado1

1Hospital Prof Dr Fernando Fonseca, Neurology Department, Amadora, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P269

Objective Eptinezumab, being the only antiCGRP monoclonal antibody for migraine prevention administered intravenously thus, with a more favourable pharmacodynamic profile, has been used, in real world, in particularly challenging patients such as those with chronic migraine, medication overuse headache and previously monoclonal failure. We present the results of the first 24 months of treatment with eptinezumab in our headache centre.

Methods Unicentric retrospective study of all patients treated with Eptinezumab for migraine prevention in our hospital. All patients received 100 mg of Eptinezumab every 12 weeks.

Results 52 patients were included, 6 men and 46 women with a median age of 46 years. Conclusion Eptinezumab efficacy and tolerability was confirmed in this real-world setting. It improved even very difficult migraine patients and reversed analgesic overuse in all patients. After 12 months of therapy improvement continued to be seen, stressing the importance to maintain therapy on the long run.

P270 Use of gepants in the acute treatment and bout modulation of cluster headache: A retrospective case series

M. Saianda Duarte1, G. Diniz Pinho2, R. Gil-Gouveia2

1Hospital Beatriz Ângelo, Neurology Department, Loures, Portugal; 2Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P270

Objective Cluster headache (CH) is a rare but highly disabling primary headache with limited options for acute relief and bout control. Gepants, oral CGRP receptor antagonists approved for migraine, are not indicated for CH. This study evaluated their use in acute and bout-phase management of CH. Notably, no traditional preventive therapies (e.g., verapamil, corticosteroids) were used during the reported bout.

Methods Retrospective case series of six CH patients who used gepants during a recent cluster bout. Data were collected via structured telephone interviews. Outcomes included attack characteristics and Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC). Follow-up extended beyond the bout to assess sustained benefit (mean: 5 months).

Results Six patients (3 men, 3 women; mean age 54.2; mean disease duration 14 years) were included. Five had episodic CH, one chronic CH. Rimegepant 70 mg (every other day, 16–28 days) was used by four patients; two used atogepant 60 mg/day (28 days). Five patients (episodic CH) reported clinical benefit; the chronic CH case did not. Mean time to benefit: 7.2 days. Responders had >50% reduction in daily attack frequency; pain intensity dropped by 5.4/10. Benefit persisted through follow-up. Adverse effects (mild nausea, constipation) occurred in two. PGIC was rated “very much improved” by four, “much improved” by one, and “no benefit” by one.

Conclusion Gepants may represent a promising and well-tolerated therapeutic option for both acute treatment and bout modulation in episodic CH, even in the absence of traditional preventive therapies. Their efficacy in chronic CH remains uncertain. These preliminary findings warrant confirmation in prospective, controlled studies.

P271 Gender differences in clinical features and psychiatric comorbidities among migraine patients: A case-control Tunisian study

O. Ben Othman1, M. Messalmani1, A. Alhajmabrouk1, S. Frikha1, O. Selmi1, H. Derbali1, I. Bedoui1, M. Mansour1, J. Zaouali1

1Military Hospital of Instruction of Tunis, Neurology, Tunis, Tunisia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P271

Objective Migraine is a chronic neurological disorder that can be associated with psychosocial burden.Gender differences in migraine have been reported but insufficiently explored in North African populations.Our study aimed to compare clinical characteristics and psychiatric comorbidities between male and female migraine patients.

Methods We conducted a case-control study including migraine patients diagnosed according to the International Headache Society (IHS) 2018 criteria, and healthy controls.Psychiatric comorbidities were assessed using the MINI DSM-5 structured interview.We used chi-square, Fisher’s exact, and Student’s t-tests for statistical analysis with significance defined as p<0.05.

Results We enrolled 200 healthy controls and 100 migraine patients with mean age of 37 years and a F/M ratio =2.23. Intense migraine attacks were reported by 49% patients. Conclusion Our study revealed a non-significant trend toward a higher prevalence of psychiatric comorbidities among Tunisian women with migraine, highlighting the importance of considering gender in clinical evaluation and follow-up.These findings support the importance of psychiatric screening in migraine management and emphasize the need for larger studies to confirm these associations.

P272 The cognitive dimension of migraine: Adressing a treatable burden

M. Costa Taveira1,2, M. Roque1,2, M. Dias da Costa1,2, F. Dourado Sotero1,2, A. Costa3,4, B. Martins3,4, R. Nunes Rato3,4, M. I. Pavão Martins1,2

1Unidade Local de Saúde Santa Maria, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Centro de Estudos Egas Moniz, Faculty of Medicine, University of Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal; 3Unidade Local de Saúde de São João, E.P.E., Neurology, Porto, Portugal; 4Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade do Porto, Departamento Neurociências, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P272

Objective Cognitive complaints, such as memory and concentration difficulties, are increasingly recognized as part of the clinical spectrum of migraine, rather than merely consequences of comorbid conditions such as depression. We aimed to evaluate whether memory complaints improve with effective preventive treatment for migraine.

Methods We conducted a prospective observational study including 68 patients with migraine initiating preventive treatment with monoclonal antibodies or OnabotulinumtoxinA. Cognitive complaints were assessed using the Memory Complaint Scale (MCS), and depressive symptoms with the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), both at baseline and at 3 months follow-up.
