P273 Four–year real–world efficacy and tolerability of anti–CGRP therapies in a tertiary headache centre in England

M. Garrod1, D. Patel1, J. Lovett1

1University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust, Wessex Neurological Centre, Southampton, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P273

Objective Anti-CGRP therapies show good efficacy and few side effects in clinical trials. We report four years of real-world data from a single tertiary headache centre in England.

Methods Retrospective analysis of adults (≥18 years) treated with anti-CGRPs from April 2021 to July 2025. Changes in monthly migraine days at 12 weeks were calculated from headache diaries, in line with NICE guidelines for the management of migraine. The top 3 discontinuation reasons were identified. Treatment success was defined as meeting NICE criteria and not stopping treatment due to adverse effects or loss of efficacy.

Results A total of 548 treatments were initiated in 415 patients (rimegepant: n=57; atogepant: n=60; erenumab: n=283; fremanezumab: n=136; galcanezumab: n=12). Overall, 52% of treatments were successful. Success rates were: fremanezumab 57.4%, rimegepant 54.4%, atogepant 51.7%, and erenumab 47.7%. Discontinuation occurred in 48% of cases, mostly due to insufficient response at 12 weeks (27.4%), adverse effects (9.1%), and loss of efficacy (7.1%). Insufficient response rates at 12 weeks were highest for rimegepant (38.6%), with similar rates for erenumab (26.5%), fremanezumab (28.7%), and atogepant (21.7%). Discontinuation due to adverse effects was highest with atogepant (23.3%), followed by erenumab (10.6%); rates were <4% for rimegepant and fremanezumab.

Conclusion Real-world efficacy broadly aligns with clinical trial data, though our galcanezumab findings are limited by small sample size. While direct comparisons outside of randomised trials are limited, agents differed in both effectiveness and tolerability. Rimegepant was well tolerated but was associated with the lowest effectiveness at 12 weeks. Atogepant was associated with the most adverse effects, with constipation, dizziness, and “brain fog” reported. Fremanezumab was associated with a higher treatment success rate than erenumab, rimegepant, and atogepant in our cohort.

P274 Recurrent severe headache with a background of functional vomiting and normal brain MRI, in paediatric reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS)

N. R. Loh1

1KKH, Paediatric, Singapore, Singapore

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P274

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective We discuss the learning points in this case of reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) in a 10 year old boy initially diagnosed as migraine.

Methods A 10 year old with several years history of vomiting episodes presented to hospital with vomiting followed by confusion, thunderclap headache and full recovery within 4 h twice a day. These events were stereotypical, starting with nausea, vomiting, confusion followed by severe occipital headaches peaking within 2 min and lasting 1–4 h before fully resolving. He was diagnosed as migraine by the general paediatric team and treated with NSAIDs and paracetamol. Sumatriptan had made his headaches worse.

Physical examination was normal.

Initial CT and MRI of the brain were normal. Two days later, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) revealed characteristic multifocal segmental arterial constriction consistent with RCVS. Subsequent MRA 2months later revealed normalization of his vessels.

Results After the diagnosis of RCVS, he was started on oral Nimodipine and his headaches events reduce in frequency and severity to once a day. At the 3rd day of treatment he stop Nimodipine. His events returned dramatically and Nimodipine was restarted the following day reducing his events and severity of headaches, before finally resolving at day 10.

We include images of the abnormal and normlised MRA.

Conclusion RCVS is a rare condition normally seen in middle age. The pathogenesis is unknown and recurrence is uncommon. Severe cases can lead to stroke due to vasoconstriction. RCVS is easily mistaken for status migranosus. Triptan treatment could potentially worsen this condition due to vasoconstriction as part of its mode of action.

P275 Evaluation of treatment persistence and individual subgroups in German migraine care: A retrospective cohort approach

C. Gaul1, L. Kunk2, J. Noll2, A. Kisser2, M. Hübinger3

1Headache Centre Frankfurt, Frankfurt a. M., Germany; 2Pfizer Pharma GmbH, Berlin, Germany; 3IQVIA Commercial GmbH & Co. OHG, Frankfurt a. M., Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P275

Objective This study aims to assess treatment persistence among individuals receiving either acute or prophylactic pharmacological migraine therapies in Germany.

Methods This retrospective study utilized anonymized pharmacy dispensing data (German IQVIA™ LRx). Adults (≥18 years) with at least one migraine-specific therapy prescription between 05/2022 and 04/2023 were included. Analyses focused on individuals initiated on acute (Triptans, Ditans) and advanced prophylactic migraine therapies (monoclonal antibodies or Gepants). Treatment frequency for acute therapy was calculated by average number of prescriptions within defined time periods after therapy initiation. Treatment persistence for prophylaxis was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis. All therapies were evaluated over 12 and 24 months.

Conclusion Longer-term acute therapy was associated with higher frequency of prescriptions. About 50% of individuals discontinued advanced prophylactic therapies within 12 months. P276 Migraine-related stigma at Erasmus Medical Center: Preliminary findings from a Dutch survey

N. Bruijn1, R. van Lohuizen1, L. Al-Hassany1, A. Maassen van den Brink1

1Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Division of Vascular Medicine and Pharmacology, Department of Internal Medicine, Rotterdam, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P276

Objective Migraine-related stigma is an important yet underrecognized challenge that adversely affects patients’ quality of life, and is linked to job-related disability. As part of the Migraine Friendly Workplace Project, endorsed by the European Migraine and Headache Alliance, we aimed to gain insights into migraine-related stigma in the workplace at Erasmus MC, a university medical center and medical faculty in The Netherlands.

Methods Cross-sectional study using two descriptive and quantitative surveys, launched in May 2025. The surveys were distributed to all employees at Erasmus MC via advertisement on the intranet page. Survey 1 was designed for individuals with migraine, while Survey 2 targeted those without.

Results As of July 2025, Survey 1 received 218 responses. The majority (93%) reported moderate to severe attacks with significant daily impact; 30% must stop working during an attack, while 50% stated this depends on the severity. 37% perceived stigma in the workplace, while 30% were unsure. Conclusion Migraine has substantial impact on daily functioning and work participation, also in a university medical center setting. P278 Preventive migraine care before headache clinical referral: Are we doing it right?

S. Moreira1, A. Costa1, A. Câmara2, J. M. Araújo1, S. Varanda1

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Neurology, Braga, Portugal; 2Hospital Central do Funchal, Neurology, Funchal, Portugal

Objective Early use of preventive migraine therapy in primary care is recommended by current guidelines. However, the adequacy of referrals to tertiary headache clinics remains variable. This study analyzes how the profile and prior management of patients referred from primary care changed over six years in a Portuguese hospital.

Methods Retrospective study of adult migraine patients referred from primary care to a tertiary headache clinic in 2017 and 2023, excluding those with previous neurology follow-up. Variables analyzed included pre-referral preventives, treatments initiated in the clinic, and follow-up duration.

Results A total of 54 eligible patients were included (32 in 2017; 22 in 2023). P279 Switch or maintain: Real-world use of BoNT-A and Anti-CGRP mAbs

T. Morais1,2, L. Fagundes1, C. Fernandes1, I. Costa1, A. Maduro1, B. Rodrigues1, I. Monteiro1, S. Batista1,3, H. Gens1, F. Magalhães1, I. Luzeiro1

1Local Health Unit of Coimbra, Neurology, Coimbra, Portugal; 2Divino Espírito Santo Hospital, Neurology, Ponta Delgada, Portugal; 3University of Coimbra, Faculty of Medicine, Coimbra, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P279

Objective BoNT-A and anti-CGRP mAbs are both recognized as effective disease-specific preventive treatments for chronic migraine. However, real-world data on treatment sequencing between these two approaches remains limited. To evaluate treatment patterns in chronic migraine patients with a prior history or undergoing BoNT-A treatment after initiating mAb therapy.

Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study including chronic migraine patients treated with mAbs at a tertiary hospital center. Patients were followed for 12 months to assess treatment adjustments, including switching from prior BoNT-A to mAb monotherapy versus dual therapy. Clinical and demographic data were analyzed to identify factors influencing treatment strategies.

Results Among the 65 patients included (mean age 46 years; 85% female), 47.7% transitioned from BoNT-A to mAb, while 9.2% received combined treatment. P280 From monotherapy to combination: Use of OnabotulinumtoxinA and anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies in a tertiary Portuguese hospital

P281 Impact of sleep disorders on anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies treatment response in migraine: A cross-sectional study

C. Sottani1, V. Brunetti1,2, F. Cerulli1, G. Avino3, P. Calabresi1,4, C. Vollono1,5

1Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Neuroscience Department, Rome, Italy; 2Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Stroke Unit, Rome, Italy; 3Ospedale Santo Stefano, Neurology Department, Prato, Italy; 4Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Neurology Department, Rome, Italy; 5Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Neurophysiology Department, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P281

P282 Uncommon cause, common symptom: dAVF presenting as migraine-like headache (case report)

R. Boček1, F. Chravát2, M. Šrámek1

1Military University Hospital Prague, Neurology Department, Prague, Czech Republic; 2Military University Hospital Prague, Department of Radiodiagnostics, Prague, Czech Republic

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P282

Objective Dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVFs) are a type of brain high-flow vascular malformation, usually acquired, that can be asymptomatic but can cause serious problems ranging from pulsatile tinnitus, epileptic seizures and headaches to intracranial bleeding.

Methods This case report highlights the need to exclude secondary headaches evem in patients with a primary headache history.

Results A 32-year-old patient presented with an intense throbbing headache in the right occipital region, unresponsive to analgesics, accompanied by photophobia, nausea, vomiting and dizziness. The patient has a medical history of migraine without aura. Neurologic examination and basic blood test were normal. In the emergency department the patient deteriorated to GCS 7 (E1/V1/M5) with psychomotor agitation requiring intubation. Brain CT and CTAg showed a dAVF in the right posterior fossa without active haemorrhage. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Post-extubation, the patient had no focal neurodeficit, a GCS of 15 and headache resolution. Diagnostic DSA (digital subtraction angiography) and MRA demonstrated a dAVF at the tip of the right pyramid, fed by branches of the a. meningea media dextra. Embolization of the dAVF was performed, a follow-up MRA showed that the fistula had been removed from the circulation. The patient had no migraine headaches in the 6-months follow-up.

Conclusion This case meets the ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for Headache attributed to dAVF. The pathogenesis of dAVF related headache is not fully understood. An increase in vascular pulsatility leading to increased irritation of perivascular sensitive nerve endings of the trigeminovascular system is discussed. Subsequent release of neuropeptides from these nerve endings may induce a neurogenic inflammatory response underlying migraine-like headache. Thus, by removing dAVF from the circulation, both headaches and other serious complications can be prevented.

P284 Exploring the short-term impact of the environmental exposome on migraine: Weather and air pollution as potential attack triggers

J. Rosell-Mirmi1, V. J. Gallardo1, A. Alpuente1,2, J. Cloquell1, P. Pozo-Rosich1,2

1Vall d’Hebron Institute of Research (VHIR), Headache and Neurological Pain group, Barcelona, Spain; 2Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Neurology Department, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P284

Objective To analyse the relationship between weather and pollution changes on migraine attack onset, and to develop a prediction model to understand the impact of the environmental exposome in migraine.

Methods This prospective observational study included individuals who used a mobile application to record daily migraine symptoms during one year or more. Environmental exposures were assessed at 96, 72, 48, and 24 h prior to headache onset, for geolocalised weather data and air pollutants concentrations[https://mediambient.gencat.cat/ca/05_ambits_dactuacio/atmosfera/qualitat_de_laire/vols-saber-que-respires/descarrega-de-dades/]. All analyses were conducted in R.

D. de Pinho1, L. de Castro Rocha1, A. C. Mota1, M. Branco1

Methods Characterization of patients presenting with cutaneous/mucosal bleeding within 24 h of a migraine attack, attending Headache consultation of Unidade Local de Saúde de Gaia e Espinho from 1/1 to 18/6 of 2025.

P291 Multimodal assessment of neck musculature in children and adolescents with headache disorders: Palpation, algometry, infrared thermography, and ultrasound

C. Börner-Schröder1,2,3,4, M. Hiendl1,2, L. Horacek1,2, T. Pfeifer1,2, K. Huß1,2, M. Lechner1,2, M. Reichert3,4, S. Schramm3,4, F. Heinen1,2, N. Sollmann3,4,5, M. Bonfert1,2

1LMU Munich, Division of Pediatric Neurology and Developmental Medicine, Department of Pediatrics – Dr.spital, Munich, Germany; 2LMU Munich, Munich, Germany; 3School of Medicine and Health, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Neuroradiology, Munich, Germany; 4TUM Neuroimaging Center, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; 5University Hospital Ulm, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology, Ulm, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P291

Objective Headaches in childhood are frequently associated with complaints in the neck region, which is linked to central pain processing mechanisms by the trigemino-cervical complex. Currently, the muscular component is assessed by clinical examination that do not deliver quantifiable measures. Therefore, pressure pain threshold measurement (algometry), infrared thermography (IRT), and ultrasound are being evaluated as non-invasive, imaging-based, point-of-care tools for diagnosis and follow-up of muscular involvement.

Methods This cross-sectional study involved symptom-oriented history, clinical examination of the neck muscles, algometry, IRT, and ultrasound in healthy children and children with primary headache disorders or post-traumatic headaches (following traumatic brain injury). A longitudinal follow-up was performed at 3 and 6 months for patients.

Results Children with primary headache disorders had lower pressure pain thresholds, indicating higher muscular sensitivity (p=0.010-p=0.249). Greyscale analysis showed significant differences between groups with significantly higher mean grey level values in the headache group (p<0.001). Preliminary descriptive analysis showed higher temperatures in the trapezius muscle area in the headache group compared to controls. This may suggest an inflammatory process in the trapezius muscle.

Conclusion The diagnostic methods of physiotherapy, algometry, IRT, and ultrasound are being evaluated for their utility in objectifying manually assessed muscular findings. In addition, the potential of IRT and ultrasound to differentiate between children with and without headache disorders is being explored.

P292 Headache disorders in youth: A school-based validation of the Italian HARDSHIP questionnaire

A. Onofri1, C. Rosignoli1, V. Trozzi1, R. Ciuffini2, M. D’Ambrosio1, B. Germani1, R. Ornello1, S. Sacco1

1University of L’Aquila, Department of Biotechnological and Applied Clinical Sciences, L’Aquila, Italy; 2University of L’Aquila, Department of Clinical Medicine, Public Health, Life and Environmental Sciences, L’Aquila, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P292

Objective This study aims to validate the Italian version of the Child and Adolescents Headache-Attributed Restriction, Disability, Social Handicap and Impaired Participation (HARDSHIP) questionnaire, a standardized tool for assessing headache prevalence and burden, developed by the Global Campaign Against Headache.

Methods The study was conducted within the REPICEF registry (Registro Epidemiologico delle Cefalee in Età Evolutiva), approved by the Ethics Committee of the Abruzzo Region - Itlay (protocol 035018). Children and adolescents aged 6–17 years from selected schools in L’Aquila were enrolled between February and December 2024. The Italian version of the HARDSHIP questionnaire was developed via TRAPD methodology. Questionnaire-based diagnoses were compared against clinical assessments performed by headache specialists using ICHD-3 criteria. Diagnostic performance was evaluated through sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV-NPV), and Cohen’s kappa.

Results Of 1023 screened students, 858 were included in the cohort; the first 535 (62.4%) were selected for validation analyses. Based on the HARDSHIP questionnaire, the most common diagnoses were migraine in 68 (7.9%), Tension-Type Headache (TTH) in 86 (10.0%), probable Migraine (pMig) in 175 (20.7%), probable Tension-Type Headache (pTTH) in 144 (16.7%), and Undifferentiated Headache (UDH) in 105 (12.2%) children and adolescents. The agreement between questionnaire-based and clinical diagnoses was moderate for pMIG (κ = 0.432) and fair for pTTH (κ = 0.327). Specificity was high for both pMIG and pTTH, while sensitivity remained low.

Conclusion The validated Italian version of the HARDSHIP questionnaire provides a useful instrument for epidemiological research and for the improvement in diagnosis of pediatric headache disorders.

P293 No strings attached: A case of sporadic hemangioblastoma in the spinal cord

I. Ribeiro Sanches1, D. Gomes Antão2, J. Almada Silva1, S. Bernardo1, M. Henriques1, C. Casimiro3, M. Saraiva1, A. Rêgo1

1Hospital Prof Dr Fernando Fonseca, Neurology Department, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Instituto Português de Oncologia de Lisboa Francisco Gentil, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 3Hospital Prof Dr Fernando Fonseca, Neuroradiology Department, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P293

Objective Hemangioblastomas are rare, benign, highly vascularized central nervous system tumors. They occur sporadically (75%), typically as solitary cerebellar lesions, or in association with Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease. In VHL, 50% occur in the spinal cord, 40% in the cerebellum, and 10% in the brainstem. Solitary spinal cord hemangioblastomas are less common and require evaluation to exclude VHL.

Methods Case report.

Results A 39-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of left-sided hemicranial headache radiating to the occiput, worsened by cervical motion. She described painful neck flexion/extension, hoarseness, hypophonia, and progressive numbness in the left upper limb. Neurological exam revealed weakness and hypoesthesia in the C5–C6 dermatome, brisk reflexes, an indifferent plantar response and positive Hoffman’s sign on the left. No bulbar signs were found despite her complaints. Brain CT showed medullary and cervical cord hypodensity with cerebrospinal fluid space effacement. CT angiography identified a vascular saccular lesion at C3–C4. MRI showed an expansile lesion at C3, with edema extending from the medulla to the upper thoracic cord, suggestive of hemangioblastoma (Fig. 1). VHL workup was negative (normal ophthalmologic exam, abdominal imaging, and plasma metanephrines). Angiography excluded arteriovenous malformation. The patient underwent uneventful surgical resection of an intradural lesion with intramedullary and extramedullary components at C3–C4. Findings were consistent with hemangioblastoma. Neurological status was stable at discharge. Histopathological confirmation is pending.

Conclusion Clinical presentation of hemangioblastomas varies by location, driven by mass effect, edema, or hemorrhage. Notably, this disabling spinal cord-related headache pattern is not categorized in the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd Edition.

Disclosure

Informed consent for publication of this case and related details was obtained from the patient.

Fig. 1 (abstract P293).

P294 Posterior circulation stroke or vestibular migraine? Registry-based analysis of predictors in patients presenting with acute dizziness and headache in the emergency department

R. M. Zwergal1, B. Rossmeisl1, R. Strobl2, A. Zwergal1,2

1LMU Munich, Neurology, Munich, Germany; 2LMU Munich, German Center for Vertigo and Balance Disorders, Munich, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P294

Objective In cases of acute dizziness accompanied by headache (HA), distinguishing between posterior circulation vestibular stroke (VS) and vestibular migraine (VM) in the emergency department (ED) proves challenging.

Methods This registry study included 814 patients, who presented to the ED with acute dizziness. Patients were screened for the presence and characteristics of accompanying HA. Demographic and cardiovascular risk factors were systematically collected. The etiology of the dizziness syndrome was classified based on clinical neurological, neuro-otological and imaging findings (cCT/CT-A, MRI) according to current diagnostic guidelines. Using multiple regression models and machine learning (ML, Random Forest), factors were analyzed that can reliably differentiate VS and VM.

Results In the total cohort, 24.1% reported accompanying HA. In this subgroup, VM was the most common diagnosis (30%), followed by VS (25%). The most frequent etiology of VS was vertebral artery dissection (53%). VS lesions regularly involved the PICA territory (74%) and dorsolateral medulla (58%). Abnormalities on CT-A were found in 57% of VS and 0% of VM patients. In a multiple regression model, the following factors were indicative of VM: younger patient age (OR: 0.89), lower diastolic blood pressure (OR: 0.91) and a positive HA history (OR: 10.4). The ML-based calculation of diagnostic probability for VM vs. VS identified age, diastolic blood pressure, HA history, systolic blood pressure, and pulsating HA quality as distinguishing variables, which were integrated into a nomogram based on their diagnostic weight for graphical representation.

Conclusion When acute dizziness and HA occur synchronously, reliable differentiation of benign (VM) and harmful etiologies (VS) is possible based on demographic criteria, HA characteristics, CT-A findings and cardiovascular risk. In VS with HA, dissections are most common, with lesions involving the dorsolateral medulla and PICA territory.

P297 Myofascial headache: A new branch on the headache tree

I. de Greef1, M. Chys1, M. de Sloovere1, K. de Meulemeester1, B. Cagnie1

1Ghent University, Rehabilitation Sciences and Physiotherapy, Ghent, Belgium

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P297

Objective Recently, the International Headache Society postulated a new type of headache, myofascial headache (MFH). It is classified as a subtype of cervicogenic headache (CGH) and aims to resolve the existing overlap between CGH and tension type headache (TTH). In MFH, headache originates from the myofascial structures in the neck, a region that is often affected in TTH as well. This cross-sectional study aims to explore the relationship between the criteria established in the International Classification of Headache Disorders for CGH, TTH and the newly constructed MFH.

Methods 91 participants with regular headache and neck pain completed the Headache Screening Questionnaire to score the criteria for TTH and to identify and exclude migraine. Further, an anamnesis and clinical investigation was performed by an experienced physiotherapist, wherein all criteria of CGH and MFH were investigated. To evaluate the correlation between the criteria, a trivariate Jaccard Similarity Index (JSI) was calculated. Next, a multilabel random forest analysis was performed and a decision tree was constructed.

Results 33 participants were classified as probable or definite TTH, 2 participants as CGH, 6 as MFH, 42 as a combination of TTH and MFH and 5 as a combination of TTH and CGH. 3 participants could not be classified into any category. The duration of TTH episodes and the temporal relation of onset and parallel improvement/deterioration of headache and neck pain in CGH and MFH show high correlations (JSI: 0.69-0.79). The decision tree marks the presence of trigger points as the most defining criterium to discriminate between headaches. Not enough subjects were classified as CGH to include this as an outcome of the tree.

Conclusion 56% of people with TTH also scored positive for MFH. This myofascial componeny is the most defining criterium in differentiating headaches, which justifies the development of the MFH criteria as a specific subtype of headache. More people with CGH are needed to expand the decision tree.Fig. 1 (abstract P297).

.

P298 Development of the EMHA migraine scoring system

P. J. Goadsby1, P. Irimia2, G. M. Terwindt3, D. D. Mitsikostas4, M. Ashina5, A. Maassen van den Brink6, C. Lampl7, R. Gil-Gouveia8, F. Mohammad Amin5, E. Ruiz de la Torre9, D. Hurtado10, C. Fairley11, E. Caronna12, P. Pozo-Rosich12

1King’s College London, London, UK; 2University Clinic of Navarra, Navarra, Spain; 3Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, Netherlands; 4Aeginition Hospital, Athens, Greece; 5Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Copenhagen, Denmark; 6Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Rotterdam, Netherlands; 7Headache Medical Center Linz, Linz, Austria; 8Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal; 9European Migraine & Headache Alliance, Brussels, Belgium; 10Prescient Healthcare Group, Barcelona, Spain; 11Prescient Healthcare Group, London, UK; 12Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P298

Objective The EMHA developed the Migraine Scoring System to enhance patient-clinician communication about migraine burden and reduce stigma, offering a practical tool for patients in clinical and advocacy contexts. Though not intended for diagnosis, it may help track meaningful changes in severity over time (e.g., transitions between episodic and chronic migraine). Development followed key opinion leader workshops and pilot testing in a Spanish patient cohort (n ≈ 300). The final 4-item tool assesses: (1) monthly headache days, (2) effectiveness of acute medication (days with “good response”), (3) pain intensity, and (4) overall attack intensity (categorical scale). This is the first psychometric validation of the tool, as a step toward broader multilingual implementation, with English language validation already conducted with a UK patient cohort (n ≈ 50).

Methods Psychometric evaluation in the Spanish cohort included confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to assess dimensionality and internal consistency using reliability coefficients. Measurement invariance tested whether the scale functioned equivalently across Spanish and English languages. The same methodology is planned for multilingual validation in Danish, Dutch, German, Greek, and Portuguese.

Results CFA supported a unidimensional model with excellent fit (CFI=1.000,TLI=1.001,RMSEA=0.000,SRMR=0.002), with the general factor explaining 74.4% of variance. Internal consistency was acceptable (Cronbach’s α=0.73) and higher when adjusting for item weightings (Omega Total=0.83). Measurement invariance confirmed full equivalence across language, supporting cross-group comparisons.

Conclusion The EMHA Migraine Scoring System is unidimensional, interpretable, and standardized tool with adequate psychometric properties. Ongoing multilingual validation in five European languages will assess its broader applicability, additionally to the already tested Spanish and English languages.

P299 Aura images are not enough to diagnose migraine with aura

N. van Veelen1, E. van Eijk1, I. de Boer1, G. M. Terwindt1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P299

Objective Accurate diagnosis of migraine with aura is crucial. Visual aura images may enhance diagnostic accuracy.

Methods Patients with clinical migraine diagnoses were included. Upon enrolment, participants completed a survey followed by a questionnaire featuring an image depicting visual aura disturbance. The diagnostic accuracy of the iconography alone and the iconography in combination with a questionnaire were compared to clinical diagnoses.

Results A total of 481 migraine patients were included. The visual aura image alone demonstrated a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 65%. When a validated extensive questionnaire was added, the sensitivity decreased to 53%, while the specificity increased to 90%.

Conclusion The visual aura image alone may identify more migraine with aura (MA) cases compared to adding an extensive questionnaire. However, more false positive cases will be identified.Fig. 1 (abstract P299).

P300 Lasmiditan-overuse headache?: Time-series clustering analysis for treatment pattern of lasmiditan for two years from the initial prescription

M. Katsuki1,2,3,4, Y. Yamada5, T. Ichihara5, Y. Matsumori6

1Nagaoka University of Technology, Physical Education and Health Center, Niigata, Japan; 2Dublin City University, School of Human and Health Performance, Dublin, Ireland; 3Dublin City University, Insight Science Foundation Ireland Research Centre, Dublin, Ireland; 4Saitama Medical University, Department of Biostatistics, Saitama, Japan; 5Japan System Techniques Co., Ltd. (JAST), Tokyo, Japan; 6Sendai Headache and Neurology Clinic, Sendai, Japan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P300

Objective Migraine is a highly prevalent neurological disorder and a leading cause of disability worldwide. Although triptans and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are widely used, a substantial proportion of patients show inadequate responses. Lasmiditan, a selective 5-HT1F receptor agonist introduced in Japan in January 2022, represents a novel acute treatment option that lacks vasoconstrictive activity and can be prescribed even in patients with cardiovascular risk. However, little is known about the trend of its long-term real-world use. To characterize two-year lasmiditan prescription patterns using time-series clustering.

Methods Data were extracted from the REZULT database for patients aged ≥15 years diagnosed with migraine (ICD-10 code G43) between January 2022 and December 2024. Prescription claims were analyzed in 90-day intervals for up to 24 months after the initial lasmiditan prescription. Time-series clustering was applied to identify subgroups with distinct trajectories of lasmiditan use.

Results Lasmiditan was prescribed to 21,199 out of 167,461 (12.7%) migraine patients, with a mean age of 33.8 ± 10.3 years, and 76.6% being female. In the first three months, 86.2% were prescribed 50 mg tablets, 12.8% were prescribed 100 mg tablets, and 1.0% received both dosage. About half were also prescribed single analgesics, and 66.7% received triptans, while 33.9% were given prophylactic drugs. The dosages of lasmiditan were gradually tapered down over the two years. The main long-term prescription pattern was a combination of analgesics, triptans, and lasmiditan. Time-series clustering identified three patient groups: Cluster 1 used lasmiditan consistently over time, cluster 2 gradually decreased its usage, and cluster 3 reduced it immediately.

Conclusion According to real-world data, there are three prescription patterns. There might be a possibility of lasmiditan overuse. The appropriate use of lasmiditan should continue to be investigated.

P301 Safety, tolerability and efficacy of atogepant added to onabotulinumtoxina for the preventive treatment of chronic migraine: A phase 3, multicenter, 24-week, open-label study

J. Rothrock1, U. Najib2, J. Ailani3, S. Ashina4, J. Bao5, J. H. Smith5, I. Shakhmantsir5, B. Dabruzzo5, K. Pfleeger5, A. Blumenfeld6

1Inova Neurology, Fairfax, VA, USA; 2Rockefeller Neuroscience Institute, Morgantown, WV, USA; 3MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, Washington, D.C., USA; 4Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA; 5AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA; 6The Los Angeles Headache Center, Los Angeles, CA, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P301

Objective To evaluate the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of adding atogepant to onabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA) for the preventive treatment of chronic migraine (CM).

Methods In this 24-week, Phase 3, open-label, multicenter study (NCT05216263), 75 participants on a stable dose of onabotA (155-200U) received add-on atogepant 60 mg once daily. Primary safety endpoints included treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), and efficacy assessments included changes in mean monthly migraine days (MMDs), and responder rates (RR) (≥50% and ≥75% MMDs) over weeks 1-12 and weeks 13-24.

Results The mean age of study participants was 48 years; 89% were women, and 97% were white. Participants had an established CM diagnosis for 15 (13.27) years (mean (SD)) and had been treated with onabotA for 4 (3.45) years (mean (SD)). In the safety population (n = 75), the incidence of TEAEs was 65.3%. TEAEs occurring in ≥5% of patients were constipation (n=12, 16.0%), nausea (n=10, 13.3%), and urinary tract infection (n=6, 8.0%). Treatment-emergent serious AEs occurred in 2 participants, neither considered treatment-related by the investigators. In the modified intention-to-treat population (n = 72), the change from baseline of 14.34 MMDs was -6.45 MMDs [95% CI: -7.72, -5.19] across weeks 1-4, -6.89 MMDs [95% CI: −8.15, −5.62] across weeks 1-12 and −7.20 MMDs [95% CI: −8.49, -5.91] across weeks 13-24 (least square means). A ≥50% RR was achieved by 54.2% and 61.9% of participants, across weeks 1-12 and weeks 13-24 of combined treatment, respectively. A ≥75% RR was achieved by 30.6% and 38.1% participants, respectively.

Conclusion Combination management with onabotA and atogepant for CM appears to be safe and generally well-tolerated. In this study the addition of atogepant to onabotA resulted in clinically meaningful reductions in migraine days and improvement in responder rates, reflecting the potential benefit of utilizing combination therapy with distinct but complementary mechanisms of action for CM management.

P302 Efficacy and safety of antimigraine therapy with or without fluoxetine for migraine: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2, M. Usman Iqbal1, S. Ali1, M. Mohaimon Kashif1

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P302

Objective To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of fluoxetine addition to antimigraine regimens.

Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, ChongQing VIP Chinese Journals Platform, Cochrane and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to September 2025 for randomized controlled trials comparing fluoxetine addition to antimigraine therapy versus no addition. RevMan v5.4.1 was used for statistical analyses, and dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR) and continuous outcomes as mean differences (MD), with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results Eight trials (N = 610) were included. Compared to control, fluoxetine addition was associated with a significant reduction in attack frequency (MD -0.23, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.13) and attack severity (MD -0.52, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.37). Pooled analysis suggested improved total effective rates (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.58). No significant difference was observed for general cure rates or total adverse event rates between groups.

Conclusion The addition of fluoxetine to standard antimigraine therapy appears to confer modest but clinically meaningful benefits in reducing attack frequency and severity, and in improving overall treatment effectiveness, without a corresponding increase in adverse events. However, evidence for cure rates remains inconclusive. Given the limited number and variable quality of included trials, further large-scale, rigorously designed randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings and to better define the role of fluoxetine in antimigraine regimens.

P303 MIGRA-MS: A case series on chronic migraine and multiple sclerosis

M. d. M. Martínez Salmerón1, I. Andrade Andrade1, T. Garrido Hernández1, L. Andrade Zumarraga1, P. Olea Rodríguez1, B. Garcia Ruiz1, M. Blanco Ruíz1, A. Arjona Padillo1

1Torrecardenas University Hospital, Neurology, Almeria, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P303

Objective To describe the clinical and therapeutic characteristics of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) and chronic migraine, assessing their evolution under conventional and emerging therapeutic strategies.

Methods A retrospective analysis of six adult patients with MS (2017 McDonald criteria), and chronic migraine (ICHD-3 criteria) resistant to conventional therapies. Data collected included sociodemographic variables, headache characteristics, demyelinating disease features, and therapeutic approaches. All patients gave their consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Results Six patients (five women, median age 50 years) with relapsing–remitting MS and psychiatric comorbidities, under adequate relapse control, were included. Prior treatments included interferons and glatiramer acetate; current therapies consisted of ocrelizumab, natalizumab, alemtuzumab, teriflunomide, or dimethyl fumarate. Chronic migraine developed after a mean of 15 years from MS diagnosis, with a median of 27.5 headache days per month (14 severe). All received a median of three classic preventives (amitriptyline in all cases) and onabotulinumtoxinA (PREEMPT, 155 IU) with only one responder; two patients received an extended dose (195 IU) without benefit and later CGRP monoclonal antibodies (galcanezumab, erenumab, eptinezumab) with no response, and atogepant with only transient or partial benefit. No adverse effects were observed. One patient improved after menopause.

Conclusion Migraine is more prevalent in MS patients than in the general population, and their coexistence represents a therapeutic challenge. In this case series of relapsing–remitting MS with chronic resistant migraine, response to onabotulinumtoxinA and anti-CGRP therapies was limited, with no drug interactions or adverse effects observed. An individualized approach and further studies are needed to assess emerging treatments in this subgroup.

P304 Efficacy of greater occipital nerve block in refractory vertex pain

A. Dubey1, S. V2, S. Dubey3

1GMC & Hamidia Hospital, Medicine, Bhopal, India; 2Consultant Neurologist, Guntur, India; 3Consultant Neurologist, Bhopal, India

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P304

Objective Vertex pain syndromes may present as atypical variants of migraine, tension-type headache, or cervicogenic headache. Because the greater occipital nerve (GON) provides overlapping afferents to the trigeminocervical complex, targeted blockade can relieve pain extending to the vertex. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of greater occipital nerve block (GONB) in patients with refractory vertex pain.

Methods Twelve adults (7 women, 5 men; mean age 38 ± 9 years) with chronic vertex pain unresponsive to conventional therapy underwent bilateral GONB using 2 mL of 1% lidocaine + 40 mg triamcinolone per side. Pain intensity (VAS 0–10) and headache frequency were recorded at baseline, 1 week, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks.

Results Mean baseline VAS was 8.1 ± 0.9, which improved to 3.4 ± 1.6 at 1 week, 3.9 ± 1.8 at 4 weeks, and 4.8 ± 2.0 at 8 weeks (p < 0.001). Headache days/month decreased from 22 ± 5 to 10 ± 6 at 4 weeks (p < 0.001). Nine patients (75%) achieved ≥50% pain reduction, with better responses in those with migrainous features. No major adverse events occurred; transient local tenderness in 2 patients resolved spontaneously.

Conclusion GONB provided rapid and sustained relief in most patients with vertex-predominant headache, supporting convergence of occipital and trigeminal pathways as a therapeutic target. It should be considered as an adjunct for refractory vertex pain and atypical migraine variants.

P306 Investigating the neuromuscular mechanisms of repetitive Neuromuscular Magnetic Stimulation (rNMS): A randomized sham-controlled study in healthy adults

C. Börner-Schröder1,2,3,4, L. Horacek1,2, M. Hiendl1,2, A. Höß1,2, M. Reichert3,4, S. Schramm3,4, C. Zimmer3,4, F. Heinen1,2, N. Sollmann3,4,5, M. Bonfert1,2

1LMU Munich, Munich, Germany; 2LMU Munich, Munich, Germany; 3School of Medicine and Health, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Neuroradiology, Munich, Germany; 4TUM Neuroimaging Center, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; 5University Hospital Ulm, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology, Ulm, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P306

Objective Repetitive neuromuscular magnetic stimulation (rNMS) targeting the upper trapezius muscles (UTM) has shown promising results as a non-invasive, non-pharmacological treatment approach for episodic migraine. Its therapeutic effects are presumed to involve modulation of the trigemino-cervical complex. However, the precise neuromuscular and central mechanisms of action remain insufficiently understood. This randomized, sham-controlled, multiparametric diagnostic study aimed to explore the physiological effects and underlying mechanisms of rNMS in healthy individuals.

Methods 70 healthy adults (age 18-35 years) were randomly assigned to receive either active (verum) or sham rNMS. The intervention consisted of 6 sessions over a 2-week period, with bilateral stimulation of the UTM (20 Hz, 7s on/10s off, 15 min per side). The verum group received rNMS using a certified device (Zimmer MedizinSysteme GmbH, Neu-Ulm, Germany), while the sham group was treated with an identical-appearing device that did not emit electromagnetic fields. Assessments were conducted at baseline, post-intervention, and at 3-month follow-up, including physical examination, identification of myofascial trigger points, measurement of pressure pain thresholds (PPT) using algometry, infrared thermography (IRT), and B-mode ultrasound imaging.

Results To determine the neuromuscular effects of rNMS, changes in PPT, thermal distribution (IRT), and sonographic features of the UTM are being analyzed and compared between the verum and sham groups at all timepoints. Data analysis is currently ongoing, and final results will be presented at the conference.

Conclusion This study is expected to provide deeper insights into the physiological mechanisms of rNMS at the level of the UTM. The findings may support the optimization of rNMS treatment protocols and contribute to a better understanding of its application in clinical populations, such as patients with episodic migraine.

P307 Repetitive neuromuscular magnetic stimulation in pediatric headache: Insights from extensive clinical practice

C. Börner-Schröder1,2,3,4, L. Horacek1,2, M. Hiendl1,2, A. Höß1,2, K. Huß1,2, S. Lense1,2, J. Pompignoli1,2, M. Fretz1,2, M. Lechner1,2, S. Schramm3,4, N. Sollmann3,4,5, F. Heinen1,2, M. Bonfert1,2

1LMU Munich, Munich, Germany; 2LMU Munich, Munich, Germany; 3School of Medicine and Health, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Neuroradiology, Munich, Germany; 4TUM Neuroimaging Center, TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; 5University Hospital Ulm, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology, Ulm, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P307

Objective Primary headache disorders are often associated with significant limitations in participation and daily functioning. In addition, myofascial symptoms—particularly in the upper trapezius muscle—frequently occur. Repetitive neuromuscular magnetic stimulation (rNMS) has emerged as a safe and promising intervention targeting both headache symptoms and associated muscle dysfunction via bottom-up neuromodulation of the trigemino-cervical complex. This observational study presents clinical insights and outcomes from the application of rNMS in a large cohort of pediatric patients.

Methods The rNMS treatment protocol consisted of six sessions over three weeks, with each session delivering 30 min of net stimulation time. Pediatric patients receiving care at our headache center underwent a comprehensive evaluation, including headache-specific questionnaires, clinical and physiotherapeutic assessments, pressure algometry of the UTM, and safety monitoring. Feedback from patients and their caregivers regarding treatment experience was also gathered.

Results By the time of the conference, data from 100 completed treatment blocks will be available. Preliminary analysis of 78 blocks showed a significant reduction in headache frequency (p=0.016). Pressure pain thresholds in the UTM increased significantly post-treatment, with these improvements persisting at the three-month follow-up (p<0.001). The intervention was well tolerated, with approximately 80% of patients reporting no adverse events, and adherence was high, with over 85% of sessions completed as scheduled.

Conclusion The high acceptance rate and sustained clinical benefits support rNMS as a promising, non-invasive treatment option for primary headache disorders in pediatric patients. While these initial findings are encouraging, further validation through controlled clinical trials is essential to confirm the efficacy and broaden the understanding of rNMS in this population.

P310 Efficacy of TDCS in chronic migraine

N. Rahman1, M. Togha1, E. Jafari1, A. Biderafsh1

1Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Neurology/Headache, Tehran, Iran

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P310

Objective Chronic migraine (CM) make up the largest proportion of patients referring to specialized headache clinics. Patients with CM, are mostly resistant to medical therapy. Non-pharmaceutical therapies for chronic migraine might provide new opportunities for chronic headache treatment. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), a non-invasive neurostimulation method, is generally considered a safe form of neuromodulation with minimal severe side effects, utilizing constant, low direct current. In this clinical trial, we assessed the efficacy of tDCS in chronic migraine.

Methods to investigate the efficacy of TDCS in the treatment of CM with and without MOH. The anodal stimulation was applied on the right DLPFC and the cathodal stimulation on the occipital cortex. TDCS was applied for 3 consecutive days per week for 2 weeks and then once a week for another 6 weeks. During each session, a current of 2 mA was delivered for 20 min, with a fade-in/fade-out period of 30 s. We assessed the efficacy of this tDCS stimulation protocol based on the mean variation in the number of migraine headache days, the mean headache intensity and the mean headache duration, comparing the baseline pre-interventional period to the 8 week post-interventional period.

Results Of the total 30 CM patients, the co-diagnosis of MOH was found in 56.7% of patients. The data analysis showed significant (p <0.05) reductions in headache frequency until week four (in 70% of cases). The intensity of headache, the number of severe headaches, awakening headache and headache duration were all improved after 6 sessions (week 2). The best response to TDCS was seen in total headache duration and total severe headaches per week. No serious side effect was reported by the patients.

Conclusion With the applied protocols of the present study, tDCS can be used as an effective intervention for the prophylactic and therapeutic treatment of chronic migraine and offers a ray of hope for patients suffering from this debilitating disease.

P311 Occipital nerve stimulation in patients with refractory chronic cluster headache: Long term follow-up

L. Portocarrero-Sánchez1, B. Mansilla-Fernández2, M. Román-de-Aragón2, J. F. Paz-Solís2, J. Díaz de Terán1

1Hospital Universitario La Paz, Headache Unit, Neurology Department, Madrid, Spain; 2Hospital Universitario La Paz, Neurocirugía, Madrid, Spain

Objective To describe the evolution of patients with Refractory Chronic Cluster Headache (RCCH) treated with Occipital Nerve Stimulation (ONS).

Methods A retrospective longitudinal study of patients treated with ONS at a tertiary hospital headache unit. The primary outcome was the change in attacks per week at 3 and 12 months and at the last follow-up. Secondary variables included side effects and complications.

Results Twenty-five patients (52.63% male, mean age 50 ± 8.79 years) were included. Six (24%) showed no response after provisional ONS implantation. The median follow-up was 3.83 years (1.16–16.31 years). Conclusion ONS is an effective therapeutic alternative for RCCH, with long-term effects.Fig. 1 (abstract P311).Fig. 2 (abstract P311).

P314 Preliminary effects of visual and motor cortex tDCS on EEG and clinical outcomes in migraine: A multicenter, double-blind, sham-controlled study

T. Aliyeva1, B. Polat2, S. Avcı3, G. Uzer3, T. Cerrahoglu Sirin4, S. Kılıc1, B. Yulug5, D. Ucak5, S. Kendir3, H. Acar Cakan3, L. Hanoglu1,3

1İstanbul Medipol University Faculty of Medicine, Department of Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey; 2Duzce University Faculty of Medicine, Department of Neurology, Duzce, Turkey; 3Regenerative and Restorative Medicine Research(REMER), Istanbul Medipol University, Department of Neuroscience, Istanbul, Turkey; 4Sisli Hamidiye Etfal Training and Research Hospital, Department of Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey; 5Alanya Alaaddin Keykubat University, Faculty of Medicine, Department of Neurology, Alaniya, Turkey

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P314

Objective Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a non-invasive neuromodulation method for migraine. Evidence on its EEG effects remains limited. We examined clinical and EEG outcomes of a dual-site tDCS protocol targeting the left motor (M1, anodal) and visual cortex (O1, cathodal) in episodic migraine.

Methods In this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 20 patients were enrolled. The active group received 2 mA tDCS for 20 min/day over 3 days; the sham group received identical placement, but stimulation was stopped after 30 s. EEG was recorded at baseline, post-stimulation, and 1-month follow-up. The power spectral density (PSD) was analyzed across the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Clinical assessments included the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Headache Impact Test (HIT-6), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). EEG data were processed using a standardized protocol across centers.

Results Only VAS scores improved significantly in the active group at 1-month follow-up (mean change: 3.7 vs. 1.8; p < 0.05). No significant differences were found for MoCA, BDI, or BAI. At the 1-month follow-up, EEG analysis revealed increased delta power in the left frontal, temporal, and occipital regions (p < 0.05, r = 0.55–0.70), as well as increased alpha power in the central and right parieto-occipital regions. Immediately after stimulation, a transient suppression of alpha activity was observed in frontal-temporal areas. Sustained increases in beta and gamma power were detected in right parieto-occipital regions at 1-month follow-up.

Conclusion Simultaneous tDCS to visual and motor cortices led to pain relief and lasting EEG modulation. Paradoxical increases in alpha, beta, and gamma—contrary to typical interictal patterns—may reflect normalization of cortical excitability. These findings support dual-site tDCS as a promising neuromodulatory strategy.Fig. 1 (abstract P314).Fig. 2 (abstract P314).

P315 Assessment of the effectiveness of sphenopalatine ganglion blockade in the treatment of episodic migraine

S. Kierońska-Siwak1

1University Hospital No 2, Neurosurgery, Functional and Stereotactic Neurosurgery, Bydgoszcz, Poland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P315

Objective The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of sphenopalatine ganglion (SPG) blockade using 4% lidocaine in patients with episodic migraine (EM) who had an inadequate response to conventional pharmacological treatments. The study aimed to assess both the analgesic and preventive effects of repeated SPG blocks on headache intensity, migraine-related disability, and quality of life.

Methods The study included 31 patients (26 women and 4 men) within an age range diagnosed with episodic migraine. Participants were aged 22–55 years, with a median age of 35 years. The SPG block was performed using a soft, needleless Sphenocath applicator (Curonix) with 4% lidocaine. The same procedure was performed in each patient after 6 weeks. Each patient was assessed using three scales: the VAS pain scale, the MIDAS (Migraine Disability Assessment) scale, and the HIT-6 (Headache Impact Test-6). Patients rated their pain in VAS score and impact of headache on daily functioning as measured by the HIT-6 scale before the block, six weeks after the first block, six weeks after the second block, and six months after the second block. Moreover, the impact of migraine on a person’s daily functioning and level of disability was assessed using the MIDAS scale 6 weeks after the second blockade and again 6 months after the second blockade.

Results SPG blockade significantly reduced pain intensity (VAS), migraine-related disability (MIDAS), and headache impact (HIT-6). After two procedures, the number of monthly migraine and headache days decreased by over 60%. The therapeutic effect was sustained at 6-month follow-up.

Conclusion Preliminary results of analyses show that blockade of sphenopalatine ganglion can be an effective method of treating episodic migraine. For patients who suffer from migraine headaches, it may be an alternative or complement to pharmacological treatment.

P317 Primary cough headache – Botulinum toxin protocol treatment with a new indication?

M. Pereira1,2, A. I. Gonçalves1, T. C. Aguiar1

1Hospital Dr. Nélio Mendonça - Centro Hospitalar do Funchal, Serviço Regional de Saúde da Madeira – Portugal, Serviço de Neurologia, Funchal, Portugal; 2Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Instituto de Fisiologia, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P317

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Primary cough headache (PCH) is a rare disorder characterized by sudden-onset, explosive headache triggered by Valsalva maneuvers (e.g., coughing or straining), without underlying intracranial abnormalities. Up to two-thirds of patients may present associated symptoms such as vertigo, nausea, or sleep disturbances. Indomethacin is the first-line treatment, but alternatives like acetazolamide or cerebrospinal fluid drainage have shown benefit in refractory or contraindicated cases.

Methods A 69-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, esophageal hernia, solitary kidney, and menstrual migraine reported a new headache pattern, triggered exclusively by coughing and sneezing. She described sudden, severe headaches, peaking within one minute and lasting less than two hours, without visual changes or jaw claudication. Initial treatment with flunarizine was ineffective. Brain Angio-MRI excluded vascular or structural abnormalities suggesting intracranial hypertension, and fundoscopy was normal. Lab tests including CRP, ESR, and renal function were unremarkable. A diagnosis of PCH was made. Given the solitary kidney, NSAIDs like indomethacin were avoided, and acetazolamide was prescribed, leading to clinical improvement. However, treatment was stopped due to renal impairment.

Results Trials with amitriptyline and propranolol were unsuccessful. A PREEMPT protocol with botulinum toxin was initiated, resulting in a reduction in headache frequency to 15 days/month after the first cycle, and fewer than 5/month after the second, with sustained improvement.

Conclusion Botulinum toxin is a safe and effective therapeutic option for PCH, especially in patients unresponsive to or intolerant of standard pharmacological treatments.

P318 Headache as a secondary manifestation of obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review

W. Gonçalves Horta1, B. Borba de Andrade Couto2, E. Lamprea de Albuquerque2, M. Guedes Almino Pessoa2, T. Gomes Maciel de Lira2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

1Universidade de Pernambuco, Headache clinic from Hospital Oswaldo Cruz, Recife, Brazil; 2Universidade Católica de Pernambuco, Recife, Brazil; 3Faculdade de Medicina de Olinda, Neurology, Paulista, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P318

Objective This study analyzed headache characteristics associated with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and the Impact or therapeutic Interventions, distinguishing morning headache from headache secondary to OsA.

Methods A systematic review was conducted according to the cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. The search included PubMed, Cochrane Library and Lilacs, using descriptors connected to OSA, headache and treatments. Primary studies (clinical trials, cohort studies, observational studies) and systematic reviews were selected. Studies without full text, narrative reviews and those that did not address headache as a primary or secondary outcome were excluded. The analysis followed the PRISMA criteria.

Results A total of 243 studies were identified, including 26 by manual search. After eligibility criteria, 8 were included in the final analysis. The findings indicated that morning headache is the most frequently associated manitestation of OSA, especially in severe cases. Interventions such as the use of CPAP have shown efficacy in reducing the prevalence and severity of headache. The review revealed that headache can be influenced by factors such as sleep fragmentation, daytime sleepiness, and respiratory symptoms.

Conclusion OSA is significantly associated with morning headache. Therapeutic interventions, especially CPAP, appear to be effective in reducing this symptom. However, the methodological heterogeneity of the studies suggests the need for more standardized research to better understand the relationship between OSA and headache. Keywords: Obstructive sleep apnea Secondary headache, CPAP, Systematic review.

P320 Alterations in the expression of histone deacetylases 1 and 6 genes and proteins in migraine patients

M. Fila1, M. Grygiel2, M. Ionov2, J. Krekora3, J. Blasiak4

1Polish Mother’s Memorial Hospital Research Institute, Lodz, Poland; 2University of Lodz, Lodz, Poland; 3Medical University of Lodz, Lodz, Poland; 4Mazovian University in Plock, Faculty of Medicine, Lodz, Poland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P320

Objective The mechanisms of pathogenesis of migraine are poorly understood. Except for a few rare migraine variants, the roles of genetic and epigenetic mechanisms in migraine pathogenesis remain largely unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the expression of histone deacetylases 1 and 6 (HDAC1 and HDAC6) genes, which are enzymes that epigenetically regulate gene expression, in the blood of migraine patients and healthy controls. Both HDCA1 and HDCA6 may facilitate chromatin relaxation, potentially contributing to increased gene expression. Additionally, HDCA6, through the acetylation of non-histone proteins, is involved in cytoskeletal dynamics and protein quality control.

Methods This study included 32 low-frequency episodic migraine patients and 28 controls without headaches. Blood samples were collected during the interictal phase of migraine. The expression of the HDCA1 and HDCA6 genes was determined by real-time qPCR, and the levels of HDCA1 and HDCA6 proteins were assessed using the ELISA test.

Results We observed a decrease in HDCA1 expression in migraine patients compared to controls (p < 0.01). No difference was noted for HDCA6. Similar trends were observed for the HDCA1 and HDCA6 proteins. We observed several correlations between HDCA1 expression and migraine characteristics, including migraine intensity, headache frequency, and the mental state of migraine patients.

Conclusion Migraine patients may be characterized by lower expression of specific genes regulated by HDCA1, which could be further investigated in future research. Overall, our study suggests that epigenetic control may represent an important factor in migraine pathogenesis and, therefore, could be considered in its therapy, with HDCA1 potentially targeted to enhance its expression. However, bioinformatic, experimental, and clinical studies are necessary to clarify how HDCA1 might serve as a therapeutic target in migraine.

P321 Pipeline for DNA methylation analysis using Illumina EPIC Beadchip arrays in complex polygenic diseases

R. Mas de les Valls Cierco1, V. J. Gallardo1, P. Pozo-Rosich1,3

1Vall d’Hebron Institute of Research (VHIR), Headache and Neurological Pain, Barcelona, Spain; 3Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron, Neurology Department, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P321

Objective Genes associated with epigenetic changes in polygenic, complex diseases, such as migraine, tend to be overlooked given their small individual effects and high sample heterogeneity. Moreover, the substantial influence of technical artifacts and the absence of standardized methodologies for EWAS studies further reduce the power to detect potential epigenetic signals. We propose a pipeline for DNA methylation data analysis in migraine, combining two different versions of the Illumina EPIC array.

Methods Data was split into training and test, leveraging the existent split in the two versions of the array and ensuring a proper distribution of cases and controls. After quality control and preprocessing, the M-values were used in four different batch-corrected pipelines. Using feature selection techniques, the most significant CpGs for each methodology were obtained evaluating their outcome predictive ability.

Results Data was collected from 259 samples; training set with 194 individuals (66% cases, 34% controls), and test set with 67 individuals (54% cases, 46% controls). Cell-type composition was estimated and included–along with statistically significant covariates–in the batch-corrected linear models that identified differentially methylated CpGs. Permutation tests were applied to determine the optimal p-value threshold, then combined with random forest-based feature selection. The AUC of each model was compared to identify the best-performing pipeline.

Conclusion The complex methodology described highlights the need for robust and standardised pipelines for methylation data analysis in the context of complex diseases. Such approaches are essential to minimise the false discovery rate and to improve the identification of novel biomarkers.

P323 Polygenic risk score analysis in a portuguese cohort sheds light on migraine genetics

A. Dias1,2,3, K. Pucci1, M. Alves-Ferreira1,4, L. Azevedo1,3, C. Lemos1,3

1ICBAS, UMIB, Porto, Portugal; 2University of Porto, i3S – Instituto de Investigação e Inovação em Saúde, Porto, Portugal; 3ITR—Laboratory for Integrative and Translational Research in Population Health, Porto, Portugal; 4University of Porto, CGPP, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P323

Objective Migraine is a common, polygenic neurovascular disorder whose pathophysiology remains partially understood. This study aimed to develop a polygenic risk score (PRS) based on genome-wide association study (GWAS) data to identify genetic variants associated with migraine and explore their potential relevance in disease mechanisms.

Methods We analyzed GWAS data from a Portuguese cohort of 380 individuals (190 migraine patients and 190 controls) recruited from Centro Hospitalar Universitário de Santo António (CHUdSA) and CGPP-i3S. Quality control and PRS calculation were performed using PLINK software. The PRS was constructed using the clumping + thresholding (C+T) method across multiple p-value thresholds. SNPs were analyzed for association strength, linkage disequilibrium, and known clinical significance.

Results The optimal PRS models were obtained at lower p-value thresholds, reflecting the limited sample size and increased noise at broader thresholds. No previously identified migraine-associated SNPs surpassed genome-wide significance (p < 5 × 10⁻⁸), though several variants of unknown significance (VUS) with strong effect sizes were identified. SNPs such as rs117797734 and rs75485498 showed significant associations and warrant further investigation. While the model shows potential for distinguishing cases from controls, overfitting remains a concern due to sample size limitations.

Conclusion Our findings support the polygenic nature of migraine and underscore the value of PRS in uncovering novel genetic contributors. Though not yet clinically applicable, the PRS framework holds promise for improving migraine pathophysiology. Larger cohorts and in vivo validation are essential for advancing these models toward clinical relevance.

P324 Phenotypic description of a multigenerational family with PRRT2 gene mutation: A case series of six members affected by hemiplegic migraine and paroxysmal events

1Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, Neuroscience, Rome, Italy; 2Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation IRCCS, Neurology, Rome, Italy; 3Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Neurophysiopathology Department, Rome, Italy

Objective Mutations in the PRRT2 gene have been identified as the cause of a spectrum of disorders, including paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia (PKD) and benign familial infantile epilepsy. P325 Familial clustering of visual snow syndrome

L. Weichsel1, N. Slavova1, F. Riederer1, A. Scutelnic1, A. Klein1, S. de Beukelaer1, A. Schaller2, C. Zweier2, C. Schankin1,3

1Inselspital Bern, Neurology, Bern, Switzerland; 2Inselspital Bern, Human Genetics, Bern, Switzerland; 3Bellevue Medical Group, Centre for Migraine and Headache, Zurich, Switzerland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P325

Objective Visual snow syndrome (VSS) is a neurological disorder marked by persistent visual static alongside various visual and non-visual symptoms. Although it substantially impairs quality of life, treatment options are limited. This study describes a family with VSS to characterize phenotypic variability and to examine potential genetic and environmental contributions.

Methods Following a report of familial clustering by an index patient, we conducted detailed clinical assessments of his family. Structured interviews documented age of onset, symptom patterns, triggers, and comorbidities across affected individuals spanning three generations. Written informed consent was obtained from the participating family members.

Results Six family members across three generations were diagnosed with VSS. Eight family members reported visual symptoms not meeting full VSS ICHD-3 criteria. Clinical presentation of VSS varied markedly within the family, i.e. in age of onset (early childhood, n=3; later in life, n=3) and potential triggers. However, visual and non-visual symptom patterns overlapped among first-degree relatives. Visual snow was reported as the most disturbing symptom by all affected individuals. Palinopsia occurred equally in VSS patients and family members with few symptoms. No individual reported progression from isolated visual symptoms to full VSS. Non-visual symptoms included migraine with (n=3) and without aura (n=1), anxiety (n=4), depression (n=1), and tinnitus (n=2).

Conclusion This cluster of family members with VSS and the observed overlap in symptoms support a hereditary component. However, considerable differences in age of onset and symptom patterns among relatives suggest that environmental factors may also influence disease expression in genetically predisposed individuals. Thus, trigger identification and avoidance are as crucial as elucidating the underlying genetic mechanisms.

P327 Behavioural characterisation of a codeine-induced medication overuse headache model in mice: Focus on pain-related behaviour and cognitive impairment

1University of Belgrade - Faculty of Pharmacy, Pharmacology, Belgrade, Serbia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P327

Objective Medication overuse headache (MOH) is a chronic headache disorder caused by the overuse of analgesics in patients with primary headaches. Conclusion Codeine induced cutaneous allodynia and cognitive impairment in mice, with effects comparable to those of sumatriptan. P328 Evolution of nitroglycerin-triggered premonitory symptoms in participants with migraine

G. Sebastianelli1,2, C. Fernandes1,3, P. J. Goadsby1, N. Karsan1

1King’s College London, NIHR King’s Clinical Research Facility, SLaM Biomedical Research Centre and Wolfson SPaRC, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, London, UK; 2Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Medico Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies, Latina, Italy; 3Local Health Unit of Coimbra, Neurology, Coimbra, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P328

Objective While the hypothalamus is reliably shown with functional neuroimaging to be active in the premonitory phase of migraine, other areas including visual, brainstem, and limbic areas may also be seen. To understand how the premonitory phase evolves, the temporal chronology of premonitory symptoms (PS) triggered by nitroglycerin (NTG) was evaluated.

Methods Fifty-three subjects with migraine and a history of spontaneous PS were exposed to NTG infusion (0.5 mcg/kg/min;1° visit, V1). Participants who developed PS and migraine-like headache were invited to be re-exposed to NTG for a maximum of three triggered visits (V2 n=29; V3 n=11). The frequency and chronology of PS were collected for all the visits (n=93). The median time of onset in minutes of each symptom was recorded for all subjects during V1 (n=53).

Results PS were triggered in 92 out of 93 (99%) of visits. The 5 most common PS were: photophobia (77%), fatigue (74%), neck stiffness (63%), difficulty concentrating (62%), and yawning (50%). The premonitory phase started with one PS in 40% (n=37) of the cases, and more than one in the remainder. Neck stiffness (38%), photophobia (38%), and fatigue (33%) were the most common PS occurring as the first symptom across all 93 NTG infusions. In contrast, thirst (14%), food cravings (2%), and yawning (13%) occurred as the first PS in a minority of cases. The median time of onset [IQR] of the most common PS (frequency≥35%) during V1 were: neck stiffness 10 min (6–16), photophobia 11 min (8–20), thirst 19 min (10–81), fatigue 20 min (10–46), difficulty concentrating 20 min (10–34), and yawning 40 min (16–69).

Conclusion Neck stiffness and photophobia are the earliest PS to arise during NTG-triggered migraine attacks. Symptoms that are attributed to the hypothalamus typically begin after. These results may suggest an early dysmodulation of the thalamus, while the hypothalamus could be a later structure involved in the migraine attack, rather than be involved in attack initiation.

P330 Neurophysiological correlates of Anti-CGRP therapy response in chronic migraine: A pilot study using quantitative sensory testing and conditioned pain modulation

A. Costa1,2, S. Moura2, L. Vieira3, M. Gonçalves-Pinho2, P. Abreu1,2, I. Martins4,3

1Hospital Universitário São João, Neurology, Porto, Portugal; 2Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade do Porto, Departamento Neurociências, Porto, Portugal; 3Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto, Porto, Portugal; 4University of Porto, IBMC-I3S, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P330

Objective To explore longitudinal changes in migraine burden, sensory processing, and central pain modulation in women with chronic migraine treated with anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies.

Methods This pilot prospective cohort study enrolled women with chronic migraine under anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy (fremanezumab). Evaluations included: clinical outcomes - migraine days, acute medication use, HIT-6, MIBS-4, CSI, ASC-12, PCS; biomarkers - blood CGRP levels; and neurophysiological testing - quantitative sensory testing (von Frey filaments, pressure algometry) and conditioned pain modulation (CPM) using sequential and simultaneous paradigms.

P332 Regional neurovascular uncoupling as a mechanism for aura initiation and propagation

A. Russo1, F. Esposito2, A. P. de Rosa2, I. Orologio1, F. Trojsi1, L. Tartaglione1, P. Garcia-Polo3, G. Tedeschi1, A. Tessitore1, M. Cirillo2, M. Silvestro1

1University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Headache Centre, Department of Advanced Medical and Surgical Sciences, Naples, Italy; 2University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Advanced MRI Neuroimaging Centre, Department of Advanced Medical and Surgical Sciences, Naples, Italy; 3General Electric Healthcare, Madrid, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P332

Objective While it is well established that the aura phenomenon originates from a hyperexcitable and hyperconnected visual cortex, the mechanisms underlying the brain’s predisposition to initiate cortical spreading depolarization (CSD) in patients with migraine remain debated. Likewise, the neural substrates responsible for the propagation of aura from visual to somatosensory and motor areas—manifesting in complex aura phenotypes—have only been partially elucidated. It is hypothesized that an inadequate vascular supply to meet heightened demand—neurovascular uncoupling—may contribute to aura initiation and propagation.

Methods Forty patients with migraine with aura (21 with simple visual aura and 19 with complex aura), 30 with migraine without aura, and 22 healthy controls (HCs) underwent a 3-Tesla MRI scan. A surrogate estimate of regional neurovascular coupling was obtained for each subject by calculating the correlation coefficient between z-scored ReHo and z-scored cerebral blood flow maps (obtained by multidelay arterial spin labelling).

Results A significantly reduced neurovascular coupling was observed in the primary visual cortex parcels of the large-scale visual network in patients with both simple and complex aura, compared to both patients with migraine without aura and HCs. Additionally, patients with complex aura exhibited reduced neurovascular coupling in the posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus of the default mode network, compared to all other groups.

Conclusion Neurovascular uncoupling in the primary visual cortex may represent a critical link between exposure to trigger factors and the initiation of the aura phenomenon. While physiological vascular oversupply may compensate for resting neurovascular demand, it becomes insufficient when energy requirement increases—such as during trigger exposure—thus facilitating aura onset. Furthermore, impaired neurovascular coupling in the PCC/precuneus may play a key role in facilitating propagation of aura beyond the visual cortex.Fig. 1 (abstract P332).

Y. H. Ling1,2, S. P. Chen2,3, S. J. Wang1,4, L. L. H. Pan1,4

Objective Previous epidemiological studies suggest a bidirectional association between hypertension and migraine. Despite this association, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. .

Conclusion Our findings highlight a link between BP and cortical excitability, which may mediate the clinical association between hypertension and increased migraine susceptibility. P335 Pathophysiology of migraine with aura: A systematic review of current evidence

W. Gonçalves Horta1, A. Beatriz Neves2, C. Ferraz2, I. Mota2, J. Dantas2, L. Nogueria2, P. Eduardo Melo2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

Objective Understand the complex mechanisms involved in the pathophysiological process (PTP) of migraine with aura(MGA), analyzing factors that influence its susceptibility, such as environmental exposure and genetic predisposition, which may contribute to chronification and worsen the condition over time. Methods This work is a systematic Literature review of a quantitative nature. Results From the 3.013 studies identified through the database, after full-text evaluation a total of 6 articles included in the final analysis.

P338 Altered brain structure and function in migraine: Preliminary findings from 5.0T ultra-high-field MRI

H. Han1, J. Lu2, P. Yuan1, X. Zhang2, Q. Zhang1

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P338

Objective Migraine involves complex brain network dysregulation, and ultra-high-field 5T MRI enables enhanced detection of subtle structural and functional alterations. This study aimed to characterize brain abnormalities in migraine using 5T MRI and explore their clinical correlations.

Methods Thirty-three episodic migraine patients and 30 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) underwent 5T MRI, including high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical imaging and resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI). P339 Neurophysiological effects of atogepant in episodic migraine: The ATOM project

R. de Icco1,2, F. Cammarota1,2, V. Grillo1,2, G. Vaghi1,2, M. Corrado1,2, B. Agostini1,2, M. Giraudo1,2, A. Solfrizzi1,2, R. Greco1,2, C. Demartini1,2, A. Zanaboni1,2, M. Francavilla1,2, S. Facchetti1,2, G. Sances1,2, C. Tassorelli1,2

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P339

Objective Our study aims to describe the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying the effect of atogepant in the prevention of high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM). We assessed changes of central sensitization and habituation after three months of atogepant treatment.
