During the interictal phase, we performed a neurophysiological evaluation assessing central sensitization and habituation, by means of the lower limb nociceptive withdrawal reflex (single stimulus threshold–RTh, temporal summation threshold–TST), the nociceptive blink reflex (nBR), and visual evoked potentials (VEPs). PEV evaluation showed a lack of habituation both at T0 and T1 (habituation index: T0: 92.2 ± 22.1 vs. T1 93.2 ± 13.1, p=0.794).

Conclusion Our findings suggest that after a 3-month atogepant treatment there is an improvement in central sensitization mechanisms and a modulation of the habituation pattern.

P343 Can prophylactic single-pulse Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (sTMS) treat motion sensitivity triggered by systemic CGRP or PACAP in a mouse model of vestibular migraine?

A. Luebke1, A. David Pereira2, A. Andreou2,3

1University of Rochester, Rochester, NY, USA; 2Headache Research-Wolfson Centre for Age-Related Diseases (CARD), King’s College London, London, UK; 3Headache Centre, Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P343

Objective In 2022, Lloyd et al. (PMID 35668368) showed that sTMS was an effective treatment of difficult-to-treat migraine causes such as vestibular migraine. Increased motion sensitivity correlates with the severity of vestibular migraine symptoms, and we had previously shown that systemic CGRP and PACAP exacerbate motion-induced nausea in wild-type C57B6/J (WT) mice and olcegepant, a CGRP receptor antagonist, can reverse CGRP’s effect. In this study, we wondered if prophylactic sTMS alone would be effective in reducing motion-induced nausea triggered by systemic CGRP or PACAP.

Methods Eighteen mice were used in these studies (12 F/6 M). As a behavioral surrogate for motion-induced nausea, we performed motion-induced thermoregulation in male and female C57B6/J mice, with mice orbitally rotated for 20 min with head and tail temperatures monitored throughout. Mice were evaluated in these assays following intraperitoneal (IP) injections of (i) vehicle control, (ii) CGRP (0.5 mg/kg in females: 0.1 mg/kg in males), (iii) PACAP (0.15 mg/kg in females: 0.3 mg/kg in males), or iv & v) the same concentration of CGRP (iv) or PACAP (v) in mice that had received two weeks of daily sTMS stimulation. The sTMS parameters were two pulses (~1 ms each) at 1T, delivered over the occipital cortex, mimicking stimulation parameters used in the eNeura SAVI Dual device.

Results Our findings suggest that prophylactic sTMS does reduce motion-induced dizziness/nausea in wild-type C57Bl/6 mice after systemic CGRP or PACAP injection. sTMS reduced motion-induced dizziness to systemic PACAP in both male and female mice, whereas sTMS only partially rescued motion-induced dizziness to systemic CGRP.

Conclusion This study suggests that sTMS may be an effective treatment to reduce motion-induced dizziness/nausea induced by systemic PACAP and, to a lesser extent, systemic CGRP. We would like to acknowledge Ava Thierry for data analysis and grant support from NIH-R01DC017261 (AEL) and The Migraine Trust (APA).

P347 Shared neural signatures of photophobia in migraine and post-traumatic headache: A task-based fMRI study

R. Häckert Christensen1, H. M. Al-Khazali1, A. Melchior1, M. Ashina1, H. Ashina1

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Glostrup, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P347

Objective Persistent post-traumatic headache (PTH) and migraine frequently present with photic hypersensitivity that exacerbates headache symptoms. We sought to determine whether persistent PTH is associated with altered brain responses to visual stimuli and to explore shared neural mechanisms of photophobia with migraine.

Methods This cross-sectional functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study included 80 adults with persistent PTH, 261 with migraine, and 143 healthy controls (HCs). All participants underwent visual stimulation using a flickering checkerboard during a 3T fMRI session. Blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) responses were examined using whole-brain and region-of-interest (ROI) analyses. All analyses were adjusted for age and sex.

Results Whole-brain analysis revealed no significant BOLD differences across the full persistent PTH, migraine, and HC groups. However, participants with persistent PTH who experienced photophobia during the scan (n = 41) showed greater activation in the anterior and mid-cingulate cortex compared with HCs (PFWE = 0.010). ROI analyses identified greater activation in the anterior cingulate, mid-cingulate, and insular cortices in both photophobic participants with persistent PTH and ictal participants with migraine, relative to HCs (all P < 0.05). No significant differences were found between photophobic participants with persistent PTH and ictal participants with migraine.

Conclusion Photophobia in persistent PTH is associated with greater activation in cortical regions implicated in pain processing. These patterns parallel those observed during migraine attacks, indicating shared neural mechanisms between the two headache disorders.

P348 Shaken and stirred: CGRP stability endorses pragmatic clinical and research sampling

F. Frank1, M. Eller1, S. Maier1, L. Janisch1, S. Labrecque1, K. Kaltseis1, K. Meßlinger2, M. Reindl1, G. Broessner1

1Medical University of Innsbruck, Neurology, Innsbruck, Austria; 2Friedrich-Alexander University of Erlangen-Nürnberg, Institute for Physiology and Pathophysiology, Erlangen, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P348

Objective Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a pivotal peptide in the pathophysiology and therapy of migraine. Pharmacological and clinical research increasingly focuses on the effects of inhibiting the CGRP pathway. Striking inter-individual differences fuel the question of biological CGRP variability or the influence of analytical pitfalls. We analyzed the stability of CGRP in human plasma and provide evidence-based recommendations for sample preprocessing.

Methods In this analytical measurement study, blood samples from 40 healthy volunteers were collected and processed at predefined time points (6–180 min) under varying conditions (immediate and delayed centrifugation). CGRP concentrations were quantified using a validated sandwich ELISA. Statistical analyses included repeated measures ANOVA (adjusted for age and sex) and paired t-tests.

Results Median CGRP values showed a slight numerical increase over time, with a tendency for higher levels in females. However, repeated measures ANOVA revealed no significant effect of processing delay on CGRP concentrations (P = 0·326). The interaction between time and sex was significant (partial eta squared = 0·069, P = 0·040), but subgroup analyses did not yield significant within-subject effects. Immediate versus delayed centrifugation (30 and 60 min) did not significantly affect CGRP levels.

Conclusion CGRP in human plasma is stable across a range of delayed processing and centrifugation protocols. Technical artifacts contribute minimally to interindividual variability, supporting the feasibility of multicenter studies and routine clinical sampling for CGRP biomarker research.Fig. 1 (abstract P348).Fig. 2 (abstract P348).

P349 Ion channel plasticity in trigeminal neurons following acute and chronic infraorbital nerve injury

A. R. Abreu1,2, B. Szwarc1, A. Bernardo1, A. Chegão1, A. Bastos1, P. Lima1,2

1Sea4Us - Biotecnologia e Recursos Marinhos, Lisbon, Portugal; 2NOVA Medical School, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P349

Objective The trigeminal system is responsible for transmitting pain signals in the craniofacial region. Primary headache disorders are characterised by dysfunction and sensitization of these neurons, leading to amplified and sustained pain symptoms. This study examined the electrophysiological properties of trigeminal neurons, following acute and chronic infraorbital nerve (ION) injury, in order to understand how peripheral nerve damage may contribute to changes in trigeminal excitability.

Methods Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were conducted on trigeminal ganglion neurons isolated from female Wistar rats subjected to acute or chronic ION injury, alongside naive controls. Results Acute ION injury led to heightened neuronal activity, evidenced by increased sodium currents and increased spontaneous activity. In contrast, chronic injury resulted in reduced sodium and potassium currents and diminished excitability, indicating a distinct neurophysiological phenotype.

Conclusion These findings suggest that acute peripheral trigeminal insult induces hyperexcitability, while chronic injury leads to a transition toward a more stable but maladaptive state. P350 Occipital headache unveiling cerebral venous sinus thrombosis: A hypothesis linking sleep deprivation, elevated creatine kinase, and neuroinflammation

1Emergency Hospital “Prof.Dr.N.Oblu”, Neurology, Iasi, Romania; 2Univeristy of Medicine and Pharmacy “Grigore T.Popa”, Iasi, Romania

Objective This case aims to analyze the potential pathophysiological interplay between acute sleep deprivation, elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, and the emergence of headache as a clinical manifestation of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST). P352 Presentation and treatment determinants in cerebrospinal fluid hypotension syndrome: A case series

G. Diniz Pinho1, I. Brás Marques1

1Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P352

Objective Cerebrospinal fluid hypotension (CSFH) is typically caused by spontaneous/traumatic spinal dural tears or subarachnoid-venous system communications. They may heal naturally or require medical therapy. We intended to characterize phenotypes and therapy response factors in a CSFH population.

Methods Case series - patients admitted in our center between 2018 and 2025.

Results 13 patients (12 female, mean age 46 years) were included. 38,5% reported cervical/thoracic trauma (car, sport accidents; massage). 12 had orthostatic headache, 6 had nausea/vomiting, 3 had diplopia (2 horizontal, 1 combined horizontal-vertical - the latter being the only case without headache), 3 had tinnitus and 3 had either vertigo, ear fullness or reduction of sound perception. Conclusion Our series demonstrates some classic signatures of CSFH. Limited sample size/imaging need be addressed for future more conclusive research.

P354 Network-level brain connectivity alterations in an animal model of migraine and the effects of olcegepant treatment

R. Greco1, G. Castellazzi1, M. Francavilla1,2, C. Demartini1, S. Facchetti1,2, D. Martinelli1, C. Tassorelli1,2

1IRCCS Mondino Foundation, Pavia, Italy; 2University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P354

Objective Migraine is a neurological disorder involving disrupted brain connectivity during attacks. While CGRP-targeted therapies are clinically effective, their impact on brain networks is unclear. We previously showed that nitroglycerin (NTG) induces thalamic and subcortical connectivity changes in male rats, mimicking migraine-like network disruption. Here, we examine how CGRP receptor antagonism affects brain connectivity in this NTG-based model.

Methods Seven rats received NTG followed by vehicle (NTG + vehicle), and 8 received NTG followed by olcegepant (NTG + OLC) one hour and 30 min later. Resting-state fMRI was acquired two hours post-NTG under isoflurane anaesthesia. Resting-state fMRI was acquired two hours post-NTG under isoflurane anaesthesia. Data were pre-processed and parcellated into 232 regions of interest (ROIs) using the SIGMA atlas. Functional connectivity matrices were computed via Spearman correlations between ROI time series. Graph-theoretical measures, nodal degree, clustering coefficient (CC) and global efficiency, were derived using the Brain Connectivity Toolbox in MATLAB. Key regions of the rat pain matrix were selected for their role in nociception and migraine-related dysfunction.

Results Compared to NTG + vehicle, NTG + OLC rats exhibited reduced nodal degree in the left striatum, bilateral cingulate, and insular cortices, indicating decreased hub centrality. Conclusion Olcegepant significantly modulated connectivity within the pain matrix towards greater efficiency and reduced hubness in regions such as the thalamus, insula, and cingulate cortex, to restore migraine-related impairments in connectivity.

P359 Prevalence and characteristics of Visual Snow symptoms in migraine: A cohort study in patients with and without aura

N. van Veelen1, K. Kaushik1, N. Pelzer1, I. de Boer1, G. M. Terwindt1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P359

Objective Visual symptoms are common in migraine, yet their prevalence and relation to migraine subtype and aura frequency remain insufficiently characterized. We assessed the prevalence and features of visual symptoms, focusing on visual static and other symptoms associated with Visual Snow Syndrome (VSS), in migraine with aura (MA) and without aura (MO).

Methods A cross-sectional survey in the Leiden Migraine Cohort, a web- and clinic-based sample, captured migraine characteristics and visual phenomena, including visual static, palinopsia, afterimages, photophobia, nyctalopia, and entoptic phenomena. Outcomes included prevalence, episodic versus continuous course, and intensity of visual static, with logistic regression and correlation analyses assessing subgroup differences and relationships with aura frequency.

Results Among 441 participants (34% MA, 66% MO), visual static was reported by 24%, predominantly as episodic phenomenon (92%). Aura frequency correlated positively with visual static intensity (r = 0.33, p < 0.001), but overall prevalence of visual static did not differ between MA and MO (24% vs. 24%; OR 1.0, 95% CI [0.6–1.5]). Other visual symptoms were common: palinopsia/afterimages (32%), afterimages of light sources (32%), entoptic phenomena (22%), self-light of the eye (32%), interictal photophobia (68%), and nyctalopia (25%). The point prevalence of VSS was 2.0% (95% CI [0.7–3.3]).

Conclusion Episodic visual static is common in migraine, and its intensity increases with aura frequency. While up to one-third of participants report episodic VSS-like symptoms, continuous visual snow and full VSS are rare.

P362 Artificial intelligence for stroke risk and care in migraineurs: A scoping review

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P362

Objective To map and synthesize existing evidence on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for predicting stroke risk, incidence, and timing in patients with migraine.

Methods We conducted a scoping review. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and grey literature were searched from inception to August 2025. Eligible studies applied AI or machine learning or deep learning to migraine populations to assess stroke risk, incidence, or in managing acute stroke care in migraineurs.

Results Nine studies met inclusion criteria. Three large cohort studies used AI enhanced electrocardiography (AIECG) and found migraine with aura to have higher risk of atrial fibrillation and consequent vascular outcomes, especially stroke, compared to migraine without aura (P<0.001). Conclusion AI methods show promise in identifying migraine patients at elevated risk of atrial fibrillation and stroke and in supporting acute stroke care. Current evidence, however, is heterogeneous and exploratory. Future research should prioritize large-scale, prospective multicentric validations to assess the reliability, generalizability, and clinical utility of these approaches.

P366 Toward predictive migraine care: Development of a 24-hour risk model from daily patient diaries

N. van Veelen1, S. van der Griend2, M. Vinkenoog2, I. de Boer1, G. M. Terwindt3

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Leiden University Medical Center, Public health, Leiden, Netherlands; 3Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P366

Objective Predicting migraine attacks creates opportunities for early intervention and may help individuals with migraine maintain control over their daily lives. The aim of this study was to develop and internally validate a model to predict 24-hour attack risk in patients with episodic migraine.

Methods In this cohort study, individuals with episodic migraine completed a validated e-diary for at least 3 and up to 12 months, recording headache characteristics, triggers, and lifestyle factors (e.g., sleep, exercise, stress) on a daily basis. A generalized linear mixed-effect model with 23 literature-based predictors was first used to forecast whether a new attack would occur within 24 h based on factors from the previous 24 h. The final model was then derived from the significant predictors of this initial model together with 60 additional candidate predictors, which were subjected to LASSO variable selection. LASSO is a regression-based statistical method that performs both variable selection and regularization to improve model prediction and interpretability.

Results A total of 88,921 diary entries, including 9,820 migraine onset events, were collected from 348 participants with migraine. The initial model showed moderate discrimination (AUC= 0.63) and good calibration (intercept=0.29,slope=1.15). Risk-increasing factors were natural menses, sleep-deprivation, stress, and intense physical activity; lower risk was linked to a recent attack, skipping meals, and reduced stress. In the final model (AUC=0.62, Intercept=0,slope=1), variable selection added pain coping, well-being, and severe hangover as predictive factors.

Conclusion Diary-based factors allow moderate prediction of 24-hour migraine risk, and future use of advanced AI models may improve accuracy by capturing more complex patterns.

However, its external validation in other cohorts abroad has not been performed. Therefore, we validated its utility using an Italian cohort.

Methods We previously developed an AI-based headache diagnosis model in Japan (PMID: 37596885) using a headache questionnaire at the initial consultation based on a retrospective investigation of 6058 patients diagnosed by a headache specialist. The model was a 5-class classification model. As for the diagnostic performance, sensitivity and specificity were both 84.2%. Using the AI-based headache diagnosis model, we tested its utility using the Italian cohort consisting of 411 medical students with headache disorders with 17 variables of headache characteristics. The prediction was migraine or non-migraine headache disorders, and the ground truth was based on the neurologists’ diagnosis.

Results Of the 411 medical students with headache disorders, 245 (59.6%) had migraine, and others had non-migraine headache disorders. The sensitivity was 91.8% and the specificity was 62.3%.

Conclusion AI developed using the Japanese cohort had different performance for the Italian cohort. Given the model’s limitations based on the data from a single clinic in Japan and the skewed cohort of Italian medical students, our results suggested that an AI-based diagnosis model should be developed depending on the clinical settings in each country.

P377 Assessing the effectiveness of personalized migraine treatment – A 22-year N-of-1 study

M. Saianda Duarte1, R. Gil-Gouveia2

1Hospital Beatriz Ângelo, Neurology Department, Loures, Portugal; 2Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P377

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Migraine exhibits significant clinical variability, both between individuals and within the same patient over time. This variability reflects genetic, environmental, and pharmacological factors, influencing attack frequency, duration, intensity, phenotype, and therapeutic response. We aimed to analyze this variability in a single patient treated with multiple preventive drugs in monotherapy over 22 years.

Methods This retrospective analysis examined prospectively collected data from a 65-year-old man with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder and a long history of migraine without aura, evolving into chronic migraine with triptan overuse. Continuous daily headache calendars from 2002 to 2024 recorded headache days and zolmitriptan use. P380 Temporal fluctuations of premonitory symptoms in vestibular migraine

M. D. Villar-Martínez1, A. Abdalla1, U. Ashraf1, C. Belo1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P380

Objective To investigate the temporal dynamics of symptom fluctuations around acute dizziness exacerbations in vestibular migraine (VM), we conducted a time-locked analysis centered on dizziness spikes.

Methods We analysed 1-month prospective diary data from the NitroVest mechanistic study at King’s College London. Symptoms were scored by participants on a 1–10 scale. Participants with dizziness reporting on ≥5 distinct days were included. Dizziness spikes were defined as a ≥2-point increase compared to prior day. Per spike, a 7-day window (day −3 to +3) was constructed, and symptom scores were aligned to the spike and averaged across events and participants. Linear mixed-effects models assessed the effect of day-relative-to-spike on symptom scores, with participant ID as a random intercept. Analyses were conducted in R (v4.5.0) & RStudio (24.12.0).

Results Twenty-two participants. Headache, movement sensitivity, photophobia, and osmophobia significantly increased during the spike. Headache and osmophobia followed a biphasic W-shaped pattern, while movement sensitivity and photophobia remained elevated post-spike. These latter symptoms, along with osmophobia, dropped below average one day before the spike. Phonophobia and nausea showed a biphasic sine-like pattern peaking post-spike, though not significantly. Among non-canonical symptoms, fatigue and tinnitus dropped pre-spike and peaked on day 0. Pallor rose with the spike and persisted for a day, while micturition decreased during and polyuria increased after the spike. Subjective happiness declined in the 3 days pre-spike and remained low post-spike.

Conclusion Symptom dynamics around dizziness spikes in VM point to central autonomic and sensory dysregulation. Pre-spike sensory improvement may reflect false recovery before decompensation. Changes in pallor, urinary function, and mood suggest hypothalamic or brainstem involvement, likely monoaminergic. These findings support a premonitory phase in VM and may offer a window for early intervention.

P382 Comparative efficacy and safety of prednisolone versus conservative management in treating post-dural puncture headache: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P382

Objective This review aims to compare the efficacy and safety of prednisolone versus conservative management in treating post-dural puncture headache (PDPH).

Methods PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to September 4, 2025 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing prednisolone to conservative management in treating PDPH. Data analyses were performed using RevMan v5.4.1. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR) and continuous outcomes as mean differences (MD), with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Primary outcome was reduction in pain Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores post-treatment from baseline. Secondary outcomes were need for epidural blood patch (EBP), adverse event rate and diclofenac consumption.

Results Three studies were included, comprising 183 patients (64.8% female, mean ages 28.5 ± 4.3 to 47.33 ± 10.44 years). Prednisolone use was associated with significantly greater reductions in VAS scores at Day 1 (MD -0.67, 95% CI -1.02 to -0.32), Day 3 (MD -2.18, 95% CI -3.59 to -0.77) and Day 4 (MD -3.74, 95% CI -4.06 to -3.42) post-treatment. However, non-significant differences were seen at 12 h and Day 2 post-treatment. Adverse event rates were lower with prednisolone use (RR 0.3, 95% CI 0.18-0.51), and also mean diclofenac consumption (MD -3.48, 95% CI -3.85 to -3.1). However, no significant differences were observed for EBP need.

Conclusion Prednisolone demonstrated greater short-term pain relief, lower adverse event rates, and reduced analgesic use compared to conservative management for PDPH, though no difference was observed in epidural blood patch requirements. These findings suggest potential benefit, but confirmation in larger, high-quality trials is required for confident integration into clinical practice.

P384 Efficacy and safety of almotriptan for treatment of menstrual migraine: A systematic review

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2, F. Amin1

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P384

Objective This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of almotriptan for treating menstrual migraine.

Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to August 21, 2025. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating effectiveness of almotriptan in treating menstrual migraine.

Results Three randomized controlled trials involving 469 women with menstrual migraine were included (mean ages 36.2 to 37 years). In a large trial (n=255), almotriptan 12.5 mg and zolmitriptan 2.5 mg were compared and both demonstrated comparable efficacy. At 2 h pain relief rates were similar (67.9% versus 68.6%), with no significant differences in recurrence, rescue medication use, or adverse events. Another placebo-controlled crossover trial (n=147) found almotriptan significantly more effective than placebo, with higher rates of 2-hour pain freedom (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.28-2.57) and sustained pain freedom up to 24 h (36.1% versus 17.2%). Rescue medication use was reduced (39.3% versus 59.8%), while recurrence rates and adverse events were similar. In a third trial (n=67) comparing almotriptan and frovatriptan, both achieved comparable rates of 2-hour pain relief (41% versus 36%) and pain freedom (29% versus 19%), but recurrence was lower with frovatriptan at 24 and 48 h. Across studies, almotriptan was well tolerated, with adverse events generally mild and similar to comparator drugs or placebo.

Conclusion Almotriptan is effective and well tolerated for the acute treatment of menstrual migraine, showing superiority over placebo and comparable efficacy to other triptans. Frovatriptan may reduce recurrence more effectively, but larger, dedicated trials are needed to confirm these findings.

P385 Traumatic experiences and their implications for core clinical features of nociplastic pain conditions

S. Bottiroli1,2, M. Cangelosi1, M. Cavicchioli3, M. Mesce3, A. Torelli3, A. Benfante4, A. Romeo4, F. Nimbi5, L. Castelli4, N. Ghiotto2, G. Sances2, R. de Icco1,2, C. Tassorelli1,2, F. Galli3

P386 Chronic cluster headache coexisting with primary headache associated with sexual activity: A case report

V. Grozeva1

1Private Headache Practice, Sofia, Bulgaria

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P386

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Chronic Cluster headache is defined as attacks occurring for one year or longer without remission, or with remission periods lasting less than 3 months. The attacks are of severe, unilateral pain, lasting 15–180 min and occurring from once every other day to eight times a day. The pain is associated with ipsilateral conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhoea, forehead and facial sweating, miosis, ptosis and/or eyelid oedema, and/or with restlessness or agitation. Primary headache associated with sexual activity is headache precipitated by sexual activity, starting as a dull bilateral ache as sexual excitement increases and suddenly becoming intense at orgasm. Both headaches are more prevalent in males than in females. However, their co-existance has rarely been reported.

Methods To describe a clinical case of two co-existing primary headaches in one and the same patient.

Results A 38-year-old man, with long-standing (>20 years) de novo chronic cluster headache presenting with severe, strictly right-sided occipital, orbital and temporal pain, intensity of VAS=10, with accompanying conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, and restlessness; lasting from 5 min to 3 h, with a frequency of 2 to 3 attackes per 24 h, mostly appearing at night. The patient has never had remissions longer than 1.5 months. Five years after the onset of his chronic cluster headache, attacks with the same characteristics, but shorter in duration (around 30 min only) started to appear during sexual intercourse, just before or at orgasm.

Conclusion There is some limited clinical evidence describing that sexual activity may trigger cluster headaches attacks in some patients. However, in this particular case there is no temporal relation between the onset of both headache types, suggesting two distinct co-existing headache types in the same individual. Further research is needed to look for possible common pathophysiological mechanisms between these two primary headache disorders.

P387 Comparative analysis of efficacy between sumatriptan and naratriptan in the abortive treatment of migraine

Objective Migraine often improves during pregnancy, but close monitoring remains important to protect maternal and fetal health. Non-drug approaches and nerve blocks are preferred. If medication is needed, risks should be weighed and discussed. β-blockers are used during pregnancy but may cause intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), particularly non-selective agents like propranolol. β1-selective blockers carry a lower risk. Propranolol should be discontinued late in pregnancy due to potential neonatal effects. Fetal growth and neonatal health should be closely monitored.

Methods Clinical case description.

Results A healthy 30-year-old woman with migraine without aura since age 20, previously on propranolol 40 mg/day for prophylaxis and sertraline 50 mg/day, had propranolol continued during the preconception period - following a risk-benefit discussion - due to frequent migraine attacks. At 21 weeks of an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy, the fetus was growing along the 50th percentile, and the patient reported a reduction in migraine frequency. In this context, a gradual taper of propranolol to 20 mg/day was initiated. However, at 27 weeks, while still on 20 mg/day, routine ultrasound revealed severe intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), with fetal growth falling to below the 1st percentile. Propranolol was discontinued immediately. A follow-up scan 15 days later showed recovery to the 10th percentile. Delivery occurred at 33 weeks and 5 days, with the infant weighing at the 15th percentile and reaching the 50th percentile by one month of age, remaining healthy with appropriate growth. Neonatal monitoring included regular growth and heart rate assessments.

Conclusion Preconception counseling is vital to provide safe treatment for headache disorders during pregnancy. This case highlights the need for individualized treatment planning. In cases using non-selective agents like propranolol, fetal risks - particularly IUGR - must be considered and monitored carefully.

P389 Refractory chronic cluster headache: A new therapeutic option

T. Andrade Martins1, J. M. Oliveira1, L. Pereira1, M. Rodrigues1

1Hospital Garcia de Orta, ULSAS, Neurology, Almada, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P389

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Cluster headache is the most common of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias. The prevalence of refractory chronic cluster headache is unknown, and in the face of failure of preventive therapies, alternative options are urgently needed.

Methods A 54-year-old woman with hypertension began, at age 46, experiencing very intense (10/10) stabbing facial pain that started in the left nostril and radiated retro-ocularly and to the ipsilateral forehead, a few hours after sleep onset, accompanied by ipsilateral ocular autonomic signs and agitation, lasting between 1 and 2 h. Secondary causes, as well as comorbid migraine, were excluded. Acute therapy with oral zolmitriptan 5 mg, subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg, and oxygen were used, with moderate effect. Preventive treatment included prednisolone and occipital nerve block during exacerbations, and verapamil, both as monotherapy and in combination with topiramate and lithium in various regimens. Nevertheless, a profile of therapeutic resistance persisted, with rare pain-free periods. The addition of botulinum toxin, following the PREEMPT protocol, yielded only a partial response. In the presence of up to six episodes per day, invasive neuromodulation was considered when, in January 2025, off-label use of atogepant administered once daily at a dose of 60 mg was proposed.

Results The patient responded with approximately a 90% reduction in headaches to date (no more than one per week), experiencing anorexia and constipation as adverse effects, symptoms considered tolerable relative to the functional gain and pain relief.

Conclusion Treating refractory chronic cluster headache is challenging, as it is highly disabling for the patient. Although other therapies targeting CGRP have not shown clear benefit in clinical trials, especially in chronic forms, atogepant may offer a promising alternative.

P390 Efficacy of oral and non-oral migraine prophylactic treatment on self-reported subjective sleep quality in migraine patients with sleep problems: A review and meta-analysis

R. van Oosterhout1, L. Kanis2, N. Wiendels1, J. Reijngoudt3

1Zaans Medisch Centrum, Neurology, Zaandam, Netherlands; 2Canisius Wilhelmina Hospital, Nijmegen, Netherlands; 3Fontys Hogeschool, Mens en Gezondheid, Eindhoven, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P390

Objective To investigate the effects of oral and non-oral migraine prophylaxis on subjective sleep quality in migraine patients with sleep problems. Possibly, prophylactic treatment of migraine aiming at a reduction of migraine attack frequency can also positively affect the quality of sleep for patients with migraine with sleep problems.

Methods PubMed, Cochrane, Embase and CINAHL databases were searched in March 2022 for studies evaluating prophylactic treatment of migraine and the impact on perceived sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index or Insomnia Severity Index). A systematic review using the McMaster Tool and a random-effects meta-analysis (effect size Cohen’s d) were conducted.

Results Seven studies were identified, including 989 participants, of which 844/989 (85.3%) female, with a mean (SD) age of 41.3 (12.1) years. In 6/7 (85.7%) studies, monthly migraine days improved (p < 0.002). Five out of six (83.3%) studies presented a relevant improvement in quality of sleep (p < 0.05), and one study reported a clinically meaningful improvement in the treatment group (Insomnia Severity Index change >7, in >50% of participants). The meta-analysis showed a large effect size of 1.09 (95% confidence interval 0.57-1.62; overall p < 0.001; Cochran’s Q < 0.0001) for migraine prophylaxis on improving sleep quality.

Conclusion In conclusion, prophylactic migraine treatment improves sleep quality in patients with migraine and sleep problems, as measured with self-reported questionnaires Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Insomnia Severity Index. Unfortunately, some included studies used prophylactic treatment that is not in current (international) guidelines. The evidence for this improvement in quality of sleep is strong, and seems a generic effect of migraine prophylaxis.Fig. 1 (abstract P390).Fig. 2 (abstract P390).

P393 Efficacy and safety of valproate versus topiramate in migraine prophylaxis: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, B. Sabir2, S. Noman Qayyum3, A. Amir2, M. Shamikh Shahid1, A. Wasti4, M. Qadri5

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Rawalpindi Medical University, Rawalpindi, Pakistan; 3Bacha Khan Medical College, Mardan, Pakistan; 4Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan; 5Jinnah Sindh Medical University, Karachi, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P393

Objective This study aims to compare the efficacy and safety of Valproate and Topiramate, which are two drugs used for migraine prophylaxis.

Methods We systematically searched the PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane, and ClinicalTrials.gov databases from inception to June 12, 2025. Relevant controlled vocabulary terms and keywords were used. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing valproate to topiramate for migraine prophylaxis in adults. Meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager v5.4.1. Continuous and dichotomous outcomes were presented as mean differences (MD) and risk-ratios (RR) respectively, with 95% continuous intervals (CI). Inter-study heterogeneity was evaluated with I2 statistics. Outcomes evaluated were frequency of migraine, severity of migraine, duration of migraine attack, MIDAS score, responder rate, and adverse events (nausea, paresthesia, memory disturbance, tremors, diarrhea, weight loss, and hair loss).

Results A total of seven RCTs were included, comprising 1003 participants in total. Topiramate significantly reduced migraine frequency compared to valproate (MD 0.25, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.43). No significant differences were observed in migraine severity, duration, MIDAS score, or responder rate. For adverse events, incidence of hair loss was significantly higher with valproate (RR 4.82, 95% CI 1.91 to 12.14), while weight loss was more frequent with topiramate (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.60). No significant differences were observed in other adverse events.

Conclusion Topiramate and valproate demonstrated comparable efficacy in migraine prophylaxis, though topiramate was associated with greater reduction in migraine frequency. Safety profiles differed, with more hair loss reported with valproate and more weight loss with topiramate.Fig. 1 (abstract P393).

P394 Examination of perceived barriers to physical activity participation according to functional status in individuals with migraine: A pilot study

H. Altay1, Ş. Toprak Çelenay2

1Mardin Artuklu University, Health Sciences, Mardin, Turkey; 2Ankara Yildirim Beyazit University, Health Sciences, Ankara, Turkey

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P394

Objective This study aimed to examine perceived barriers to physical activity according to functional status in individuals with migraine.

Methods Forty-six migraine patients (median age: 26.78±10.55 years) participated. Functional disability was assessed via the Migraine Disability Assessment Scale (MIDAS). Participants were classified as low-disability (LD, n=22) or high-disability (HD, n=24). Pain intensity, physical activity level, and perceived barriers were evaluated with the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ-7), and Self-Perceived Barriers for Physical Activity Scale (SPB-PAS), respectively.

Results The study results showed that the HD group had significantly higher scores in terms of body image/physical-social anxiety (p=0.047) and pain intensity (VAS) (p=0.002), compared to the LD group. Conclusion Individuals with HD migraine perceived greater barriers related to body image and physical-social anxiety, and reported higher pain intensity. However, physical activity levels were not significantly influenced by disability status. These findings highlight that factors influencing participation in physical activity are not limited to functional impairments, but also encompass psychosocial elements, pain perception, and individual coping strategies. It is important to consider these multidimensional barriers. Personalizing patient education and self-management strategies accordingly can enhance the effectiveness of interventions supporting behavioral change.

P402 Cost-effectiveness of adding mindfulness to standard care for chronic migraine with medication overuse

D. A. Montisano1, A. Raggi2, D. D’Amico1, E. Guastafierro2, E. Ciusani3, A. Parisi1, A. Erbetta4, G. de Michelis4, D. Fedeli4, A. Nigri4, L. Grazzi1

1IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, SSD Headache Center, Milan, Italy; 2IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, SC Neurologia Salute Pubblica e Disabilità, Milan, Italy; 3IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, Laboratorio Analisi, Milan, Italy; 4IRCCS Foundation “Carlo Besta” Neurological Institute, Neuroradiology Unit, Milan, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P402

Objective Chronic Migraine with Medication Overuse Headache (CM-MOH) leads to significant healthcare and productivity costs. A recent study showed that adding a mindfulness-based program to treatment as usual (TaU+MIND) improved outcomes compared to TaU alone. This study evaluates the cost-effectiveness of this combined approach.

Methods Patients with CM-MOH completed a cost-assessment protocol covering the three months prior to treatment, including direct healthcare, non-medical, and indirect costs. Repeated measures analysis compared cost reductions between groups, and independent-sample t-tests assessed differences in cost changes post-treatment.

Results 154 patients completed the 12-month follow-up. In the TaU group, costs dropped from €2620 (95% CI: €2146–3094) to €1603 (95% CI: €1182–2023). In the TaU + MIND group, costs fell from €2978 (95% CI: €2293–3656) to €752 (95% CI: €539–965). The interaction analysis showed a significant group*time effect (F = 2.953,149; p = 0.035) with a moderate effect size (partial η² = 0.056). The largest part of cost reduction was due to indirect cost (i.e. related to reduction in productivity) which in the TaU+MIND group fell from €2,487 (95% CI: €1,902-3,071) to €573 (95% CI: €215–930), the same figures being €2,148 (95% CI: € 1,563-2,732) and € 1,419 (95%CI: €1061-1,777) respectively in the TaU group. The average annual cost saving was €2582 in favor of the TaU + MIND group—well above the €57 reimbursement per patient for mindfulness sessions by the Lombardia Region Health System.

Conclusion Adding six weekly group mindfulness sessions to standard care is a cost-effective strategy for managing CM-MOH.

P403 Cost-effectiveness and resource allocation in migraine management: Real-world economic burden in lebanon

N. Mourad1,2,3,4, S. Younes1,2,4, J. Dahham2,5, P. Salameh2,6,7,8, P. M. Preux4

1Lebanese International University, Bekaa, Lebanon; 2INSPECT-LB, Beirut, Lebanon; 3IVPN-Network, Fujairah, United Arab Emirates; 4Inserm U1094, IRD UMR270, Univ. Limoges, CHU Limoges, EpiMaCT - Michel Dumas, OmegaHealth, Limoges, France; 5Maastricht University, Department of Health Services Research, Maastricht, Netherlands; 6Lebanese American University, School of Medicine, Beirut, Lebanon; 7Lebanese University, Faculty of Pharmacy, Hadath, Lebanon; 8University of Nicosia Medical School, Department of Primary Care and Population Health, Nicosia, Cyprus

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P403

Objective To quantify the economic burden of migraine in Lebanon and assess implications for cost-effectiveness and resource allocation.

Methods A cross-sectional study of 337 adults (≥18 years) with migraine receiving treatment ≥6 months was conducted. Data included sociodemographics, insurance coverage, direct out-of-pocket (OOP) costs (hospitalizations, day cases, neurology consultations, diagnostic tests, nursing/home help, transportation), indirect costs (sick leave, income loss, work impairment), and household income. Costs were collected over 3 months, winsorized at the 99th percentile, and annualized.

Results Mean age was 32.8 years; 78.0% were female, 36.2% uninsured, and 61.7% employed. Over 3 months, 13.7% reported hospital admission, 16.6% a day case, 26.7% a neurology visit, and 27.6% diagnostic testing. Mean OOP cost was $217.8 (median $40; IQR $0–260), equivalent to ~$872 annually, with investigations ($79.1), admissions ($42.5), and consultations ($37.0) as main drivers. Productivity loss was notable: 32.3% reported sick leave (mean 2.8 days/quarter; median 1), and 14.5% reported wage loss, averaging $19.5/month overall, rising to $134 (median $74) among those affected. Work impairment averaged 3.7/10. Combined economic burden was ~$245 per quarter (~$980 annually). Vulnerability was high: 77.8% earned <$1,500/month and 11.6% <$500/month.

Conclusion Migraine care imposes a substantial burden (~$1,000/patient/year), disproportionately affecting uninsured and low-income groups. Current approaches are unsustainable. Resource allocation should prioritize preventive therapies, streamlined diagnostics, subsidies for essential services, and workplace interventions to reduce productivity loss, supported by economic evaluation frameworks to optimize outcomes under constrained resources.

P404 The “Chronic Headache Project” of the Veneto region: A new opportunity to bring hidden cases to light and optimize patient management through a network-based organizational strategy and continuous training

F. Boscain1, E. Pesce1, F. Danesin2, S. Marangoni3, M. Saiani3, S. Favaretto4, I. Toldo5, M. Navaro6, E. Mampreso1

1Euganea Health Unit, Headache Center, Padua, Italy; 2Euganea Health Unit, Innovation & Development, Padua, Italy; 3Berica Health Unit, Neurology, Vicenza, Italy; 4Neuroscience Department, Headache Center, Padua, Italy; 5Child Neurology & Neurophysiology Unit, Headache Center, Padua, Italy; 6Veneto Region, Health Management & Programming, Venezia, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P404

Objective The Veneto Region recognized chronic primary headache as a widespread and disabling condition with a significant socio-economic burden. A regional pilot project called the “Chronic Headache Project” was developed thanks to funds made available following the approval of Italian law 81/2020, with the aim of improving care and management of adult and pediatric patients suffering from chronic primary headache.

Methods Approximately €922,000 were allocated by the Ministry of Health over a two-year period (2023–2024). The funds were designated for the following initiatives: 1) mapping of third-level Headache Centers and assessment of their quality; 2) developing alternative follow-up and treatment methods through telemedicine; 3) multiprofessional training involving neurologists and other specialist physicians, general practitioners, pediatricians, nurses and pharmacists; 4) standardization of patient management by Headache Centers; 5) development of a multidisciplinary care model involving neuroscience-trained nurses (“case managers”), pain therapists, gynecologists, dietitians/nutritionists, and psychologists; 6) organization of awareness events for the general public, including schools; 7) creation of a validated digital population screening tool (app); 8) involvement of patients” associations; 9) information campaigns.

Results Results will be measured using the following indicators: number of individuals participating in the population screening, number of dedicated prescriptions for chronic headache, waiting times, number of telemedicine services provided, number of trained nurse case managers, number of training courses organized and number of their participants.

Conclusion The “Chronic Headache Project” aims to improve the care and management of adult and pediatric chronic primary headache patients. The project was supported by ministerial funding, based on a specific Italian national law — an initiative that is unique in Europe.

P405 Evaluating a rapid-access headache pathway for trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias: A service-based review

P. Amarasena1, L. B. Alves1, M. Njohjam1, W. A. Wan Sulaiman1, M. D. Villar-Martínez1, N. Karsan1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, Headache Group, Institute of Psychiatry Psychology and Neuroscience, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P405

Objective Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs) are a group of primary headache disorders often requiring urgent specialist input due to their severity and impact. To address this, a dedicated rapid-access headache service was implemented to provide timely assessment, advice, and treatment. This evaluation assesses the effectiveness and outcomes of this service model.

Methods A retrospective review was conducted of 419 consecutive consultations for 190 patients seen in the rapid-access TAC service between February 19, 2018, and July 29, 2024. Data were extracted from clinic letters and summarized using percentages or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR).

Results The median patient age was 49 years (IQR: 38–58), with 67% being male. The majority of referrals occurred in March (11.5%) and November (9.8%), with 19% representing new patients. The distance to patients’ home ranged from 1 to 423 Km (median 32, IQR: 8 - 103). Most cases were diagnosed with cluster headache (79%), followed by other primary headaches (20%) and secondary headaches (1%). Among TAC patients, the median duration of the headache bout at the time of review was 3 weeks (IQR: 1–8). Interventions included treatment adjustments (51%), greater occipital nerve (GON) injections (13%), a combination of both (24%), or advice only (11%). Clinical benefit was reported in 62% of patients following intervention.

Conclusion A dedicated rapid-access TAC headache service is a clinically effective model for managing patients with primary headache disorders, particularly cluster headache. This approach facilitates timely, targeted treatment and reduces reliance on emergency care services.

P406 Early efficacy of fremanezumab in children and adolescents with episodic migraine

A. D. Hershey1, C. L. Szperka2, P. Barbanti3,4, P. Pozo-Rosich5, P. Bittigau6, T. Li7, S. E. Collins8, J. Bryson9, Y. Kessler7, Y. Carmeli Schwartz7, H. Akcicek10, X. Ning9

The ≥50% MMD RRs were numerically higher for fremanezumab versus placebo at Month 1 (41.5% vs. 23.4%), Month 2 (49.6% vs. 30.6%) and Month 3 (53.7% vs. 37.8%).

P407 OnabotulinumtoxinA in the management of refractory migraines in adolescents: A prospective clinical study

M. Morozova1, I. Abu-Arafeh1

1Royal Hospital for Children, Neurology, Glasgow, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P407

Objective Migraine is a common and disabling neurological condition in adolescents, particularly when it becomes chronic or refractory to standard treatments. OnabotulinumtoxinA (BOTOX®) has proven efficacy in adults with chronic migraine, but data in the paediatric population are limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of Botulinum toxin in adolescents with treatment-resistant migraine.

Methods This prospective study included all patients who received BOTOX treatment between 2018 and 2025 at our tertiary paediatric headache clinic. Diagnoses were made according to the ICHD-3. BOTOX was administered following the PREEMPT injection protocol (155 units). Treatment response was evaluated 6–12 weeks post-injection. A “good response” was defined as a sustained reduction in headache frequency and/or severity for more than four weeks, “partial response” as transient improvement lasting less than four weeks, and “no response” as no meaningful clinical improvement. Tolerability and adverse effects were also recorded.

Results Thirty-seven patients aged 13–17 years (mean 15 years), 84% female, underwent 70 treatment sessions (1–4 per patient, mean 1.9). The majority (97%) were diagnosed with chronic migraine, one patient had high-frequency episodic migraine. All had failed standard preventive treatments, with an average of 5 medications tried per patient. Of 65 evaluable sessions, 35 (54%) resulted in a good response, 7 (11%) in a partial response, and 23 (33%) showed no response. Adverse effects were reported in 16 sessions (23%), most commonly procedural anxiety and pain. No serious complications were observed.

Conclusion Botulinum toxin appears to be a safe, well-tolerated, and effective treatment for adolescents with refractory migraine. Over half of treatment sessions provided sustained symptomatic relief. These findings support the inclusion of OnabotulinumtoxinA as a therapeutic option within a multidisciplinary approach to paediatric migraine management.

P409 Suggestions for managing adolescents with unspecified headaches

H. Kawasaki1, B. Fekede1, S. Yamasaki1, S. Nakaoka1, R. Sakai1

1Hiroshima University, Hiroshima, Japan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P409

Objective Headaches among adolescent children often lead to school absenteeism. Headaches among adolescent children can be difficult to pinpoint physical causes, which may cause difficulties for parents. This study aims to clarify the characteristics associated with headaches in junior high school students to facilitate support strategies when no clear cause is evident.

Methods This study is a secondary analysis of a survey administered to junior high school students aged 12 to 13 years. A total of 98 students who completed the online Lifestyle Attitudes, blood pressure measurements, and the Japanese version of the Abbreviated Impulsiveness Scale (JABIS), with all data available, were included in the analysis. The university’s ethics committee approved the study and the principal of the affiliated junior high school issued an information notice to parents. As children are often unable to clarify a headache, morning discomfort was considered equivalent to a headache. Students were divided into two groups: those who felt uncomfortable and those who did not, and were compared.

Results Thirty-five individuals felt uncomfortable upon arrival at the school. No significant differences were observed in average sleep duration, blood pressure, or Attentional Impulsiveness. Statistically significant differences were identified between the two groups in Nonplanning Impulsiveness (p=0.043) and Motor Impulsiveness (p=0.073). It is important to note that JABIS had a higher average score for Nonplanning Impulsiveness compared to university students at the time of the scale’s development.

Conclusion In Japan, when students experience headaches, they are frequently provided with general lifestyle advice that lacks specific directives. Our research suggests that offering targeted guidance on planning school life could help reduce stress-related headaches among Japanese adolescents, who are obligated to handle large amounts of information and multitask daily basis.

P410 Diagnostic accuracy of the timed up and go test in children and adolescents with migraine

V. Leonel1, C. F. Pinheiro-Araújo1, A. Rodrigues1, N. da Silva1, F. Dach2, D. Bevilaqua-Grossi1

1University of São Paulo, Health Sciences, Ribeirão Preto, Brazil; 2University of São Paulo, Neuroscience and Behavioral Sciences, Ribeirão Preto, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P410

Objective Altered balance and gait have been observed in adults with migraine, often reflected in longer Timed Up and Go (TUG) test times. This study aimed to assess whether the TUG test can distinguish children and adolescents with migraine from healthy controls.

Methods A total of 102 participants aged 6 to 16 years were included, comprising 51 children with migraine and 51 age-matched healthy controls. Demographic data were collected from all participants, and clinical data from the migraine group. All participants performed the TUG test three times, with a one-minute interval between trials; the shortest time was used for analysis.

Results Children with migraine had significantly longer TUG times (mean ± SD 6.76 ± 0.9 s) than controls (5.37 ± 0.5 s; p < 0.001). The ROC analysis demonstrated good discriminatory ability (AUC = 0.787; 95% CI: 0.694–0.880), with an optimal cutoff of 5.96 s. At this threshold, sensitivity was 82.4% and specificity 76.5% (Table 1).

P411 Idiopathic intracranial hypertension in children and adolescents: A retrospective study in a third level center

G. Sforza1, C. Dargenio2, L. Papetti1, F. Ursitti1, G. Monte1, A. Borrelli1, S. Tarantino1, M. Proietti Checchi1, M. Valeriani1,3

1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Rome, Italy; 2G. Tatarella’ Hospital, Unit of Pediatrics-Neonatology-Cystic Fibrosis, Cerignola, Italy; 3Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P411

Objective This retrospective study analyzes clinical presentation, radiological findings, and outcomes of pediatric idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), a rare disorder marked by elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) without intracranial pathology.

Methods We reviewed 68 pediatric cases (36 females, 32 males) referred between January 2007 and March 2024. Patients were stratified into <8 years (prepubertal) and ≥8 years (pubertal/postpubertal) due to different anthropometric and clinical profiles.

Results Symptoms varied by age and sex. Headache dominated in pubertal patients (80.9%), especially females (87%), while prepubertal males more often had diplopia (11.4%) and fewer headaches. Diplopia with sixth nerve palsy was the second most common sign (29.4%), followed by nausea/vomiting (23.5%), visual obscurations or loss (19.5%), photophobia/phonophobia (17.6%), vertigo (11.7%), and neck pain (4.4%). Mean CSF opening pressure was 40.5 cmH₂O (SD 13.6), higher in pubertal patients (42.6 vs. 33.4 cmH₂O) and in those with headache plus diplopia (54.9 cmH₂O, P<0.01). Papilledema was almost universal; 7.4% were asymptomatic, detected via screening. MRI abnormalities were present in 79.6% of 54 imaged patients: perioptic sheath distension (70%), empty sella (37.2%), tortuous optic nerves (16.3%), and transverse sinus stenosis (4.6%). Visual evoked potentials were often abnormal with cranial nerve involvement, while electroretinograms were normal. Acetazolamide was the main therapy, lasting on average 5.4 months. Treatment usually continued for about one month beyond fundus normalization.

Conclusion Pediatric IIH shows distinct patterns: prepubertal males frequently present with diplopia without headache, while pubertal females more often exhibit headache and obesity. Early recognition and treatment are essential to prevent visual damage.

P412 Stigma and healthcare transition for headache disorders: A mixed-methods survey of young adults in three countries

R. deMayo1,2,3, E. O. Wakefield1,3, C. Delgaudio2, A. Anuar2, K. Hinderer1,4,2

1University of Connecticut School of Medicine, Farmington, CT, USA; 2Connecticut Children’s Research Institute, Hartford, CT, USA; 3Connecticut Children’s, Hartford, CT, USA; 4University of Connecticut School of Nursing, Farmington, CT, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P412

Objective Headache disorders are a leading source of care-sensitive disability worldwide. The transition from adolescent to adult healthcare is an important juncture for effective management. This study examined associations between stigma and headache care continuity for emerging adults.

Methods A convergent mixed-methods design was used in this online observational survey of young adults aged 18–25 from the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada. Of 784 individuals screened, 309 reported recurring headache, and 260 (84.1%) completed measures including the Headache Impact Test, Migraine-Related Stigma questionnaire, and open-ended items on transition care, supplying over 1000 free text comments. Logistic regression examined factors associated with a source of headache care; narrative thematic analysis explored manifestations of stigma in care trajectories.

Results Respondents (median age 23 [22-24], 67.3% female; 67.7% non-White, 58.1% migraine) had a median of 7 [5-12] monthly headache days, with 73.1% experiencing substantial-to-severe functional impact. Overall, 31.5% lacked a headache provider. Nearly half (45.4%) reported their pain had been doubted or dismissed by healthcare professionals. In multivariable modeling, transition services (aOR 2.17, 95% CI 1.71–2.84), transition skills (aOR 1.38, 95% CI 1.12–1.71), and perceived headache burden minimization by others (aOR 1.12, 95% CI 1.01–1.25) were associated with having a headache provider (pseudo R²=0.30). Yet early qualitative analysis indicates stigma’s harmful role in transition: eroding therapeutic relationships, delaying care-seeking, prompting provider switching, and diminishing confidence in treatment when headache is delegitimized as a neurologic condition.

Conclusion Many individuals with functionally impactful headache fail to establish adult care. Pervasive stigma undermines care continuity. P413 Specialist transition headache clinic from an UK perspective: From children to young adults

D. Y. Wei1,2, J. Mortimer3, K. Crumpler3, P. J. Goadsby2, P. Prabhakar3

1King’s College Hospital, Neurology, London, UK; 2King’s College London, Wolfson SPaRC, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, London, UK; 3Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, Department of Neurology, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P413

Objective The transition from paediatric to adult care for young people with headache disorders can often be fragmented. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence set out a quality standard identifying this as a high-priority area for quality improvement. We established a dedicated transition headache clinic to support young adults moving from the Headache Team at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) to the adult service within King’s Health Partners (KHP).

Methods We developed a joint clinic with GOSH Specialist Headache Nurses and adult headache specialists to facilitate a smooth transition for young adults with complex headache disorders. The process begins as they approach their 17th birthday, a period that coincides with significant academic pressures in the UK. The GOSH team initiates this, and cases are discussed in a multidisciplinary meeting. During the appointment, parents are asked to step out for the history and examination, encouraging the young person to become accustomed to the adult clinic setting and advocate for themselves.

Results Thirty-eight patients were seen in the KHP Transition headache clinic, 13 continued their adult care in King’s College Hospital, 24 in Guy’s and St Thomas’ Hospital. The main diagnosis was migraine (n= 37), of which 27% had aura. The most common preventive treatments tried were pizotifen, propranolol and amitriptyline. In this cohort, 92% received unilateral GON (greater occipital nerve) injections. For those who turned 18 years old, four patients started on gepants, seven patients started on CGRP mAbs, and two patients were initiated on botulinum toxin type A by PREEMPT.

Conclusion A structured transition headache clinic can successfully bridge the gap and provide continuity of care during a pivotal time in the young adult’s lives, both academically and developmentally. As more patients access novel treatments in adulthood, continued follow-up will be crucial to assess long-term outcomes.

P414 Effectiveness and tolerability of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies for the prevention of migraine in pediatric patients in real world

E. Caronna1, J. Rusell-Mirmi1, V. J. Gallardo1, E. Gines1, L. Gomez-Dabo1, A. Alpuente1, M. Torres-Ferrús1, P. Pozo-Rosich1

1Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P414

Objective To analyze the effectiveness and tolerability of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (anti-CGRP mAbs) in pediatric patients with resistant migraine in a real-world setting.

Methods Prospective observational study including patients under 18 years with resistant migraine (≥3 prior preventive treatment failures), treated with anti-CGRP mAbs under compassionate use. Demographic data, efficacy variables (monthly headache days – MHD; monthly migraine days – MMD), and adverse events were collected. Response to anti-CGRP mAbs was defined as a ≥50% reduction in MHD. Effectiveness and tolerability were analyzed at 3 months (M3).

Results Of the 15 patients included, 10 had reached M3: median age 15 [14, 16] years, 7 females (70.0%), 7 with chronic migraine (70.0%), and 3 with high-frequency episodic migraine. Types of mAbs: erenumab 140 mg (50.0%), fremanezumab 125 mg (30.0%), galcanezumab 120 mg (20.0%). Mean baseline frequency: 19.1 ± 6.9 MHD, 16.0 ± 6.8 MMD. At 3 months, 50.0% were responders, with a mean reduction in MHD of −8.5 ± 6.7 (p=0.03) and in MMD of −9.2 ± 5.6 (p=0.03). No adverse events or treatment discontinuations were reported during the first 3 months.

Conclusion Anti-CGRP mAbs in adolescents with resistant migraine in real world are well tolerated, with effectiveness similar to that observed in the adult population during the first 3 months of treatment. Our data support the use of anti-CGRP mAbs as a therapeutic option in the pediatric population.

P415 The associations of neck discomfort in children and adolescents with chronic migraine

N. Karsan1,2, D. Moreno Ajona1, P. Prabhakar2, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, London, UK; 2Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P415

Objective We have previously presented data on the premonitory manifestations of neck discomfort, vertigo and allodynia in migraine, and suggested that these may share neurobiological central sensitisation mechanisms. We aimed to study the associations of neck discomfort in our paediatric chronic migraine patients.

Methods Chronic migraine patients seen within the Children’s Headache Clinic at Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children from January 2022-February 2023 were identified (n=76). Extended phenotypic data was collected from the first clinic consultation letter and analysed (IBM SPSS v 31). Migraine symptoms were coded as dichotomous variables (present/absent). Descriptive statistics were used to summarise patient demographics (Table 1). The co-associations of neck discomfort were analysed using Cohen’s kappa. A binomial logistic regression model with logit link function was used to identify variables of interest that may be associated with neck discomfort: vertigo, age, aura, allodynia, sex and monthly headache days.

Results Patients were aged 5-17 years (median 14, IQR 12-15), and 75% were female. Aura was reported by 37%. The median number of monthly headache days was 30 (IQR 26-30). Neck discomfort was reported by 32%. The percentage agreement between the reporting of allodynia and neck discomfort was 71%, with fair agreement (kappa 0.26, P=0.02), and between vertigo and neck discomfort was 58%, with fair agreement (kappa 0.23, P=0.01). The presence of allodynia was significantly associated with neck discomfort (OR 4, 95% CI 1-17, P=0.04). There were no other variables of significance (for vertigo; OR 3.3, 95% CI 0.9-12, P=0.07), Table 2.

Conclusion Neck discomfort and allodynia may be mediated via shared thalamic and brainstem sensitisation mechanisms, even in the absence of migraine headache during the premonitory phase. P416 A structured pediatric headache registry: Enhancing documentation, patient outcomes, and research capacity in Canada

E. Lin1, N. Lee1, N. Wills2, M. Lagman2

1Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, London, Canada; 2London Health Sciences Centre, London, Canada

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P416

Objective Despite the high prevalence and disease burden of pediatric headaches, diagnosis and management practices remain variable, in part due to inconsistent clinical documentation and inadequate longitudinal data. This study will establish a registry that generates real-time standardized clinic notes for pediatric patients (<18 years) with primary headache disorders. We will evaluate how structured documentation potentially shortens visit duration, improves note completeness, and enhances clinician and patient satisfaction.

Methods This prospective observational study will begin recruitment in June 2026, with an anticipated sample size of 350-450 patients from the Comprehensive Pediatric Headache Centre in London, Ontario. Data collection includes headache and medical history, neurological examination findings, comorbidity screening, laboratory investigations, and brain imaging results per standard of care, as well as patient-reported headache diaries and response to treatment. Patient and caregiver satisfaction will be evaluated through surveys and summarized descriptively.

Conclusion Through standardized notes and longitudinal data collection, this registry aims to improve the workflow and quality of routine care and establish a foundation for future pediatric headache research.

P417 Childhood migraine chronification: Is there a role for prophylactic treatment?

G. Monte1, F. Ursitti1, G. Sforza1, S. Tarantino1, M. Proietti Checchi1, A. Borrelli1, L. Papetti1, M. Valeriani1

1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Developmental Neurology Unit, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P417

Objective Chronic migraine (CM) is a very debilitating condition and the transformation to CM typically occurs over months. We investigated the effect of prophylactic therapy on childhood migraine chronification and predictive factors of chronification.

Methods We included 165 pediatric patients with migraine evaluated at Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital from May 2021 to May 2023. All had headache frequency > 4 per month (i.e. “high frequency”), anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-9) screening, no ongoing preventive treatment at baseline visit (T0). Demographic and clinical data were recorded at T0. Headache frequency, the use of attack and prophylactic treatment were recorded at follow-up T1 (approximately 4 months) and T2 (approximately 12 months). The sample was divided in two groups based on exposure or not to prophylaxis in order to compare the chronification frequency. Subsequently, we divided our cohort in two groups based on progression or not to CM to identify features associated to chronification using multivariate logistic regression analysis.

Results Chronification frequency was significantly lower in the treated group: 14% vs. 88.9% (Odds-Ratio 0.023, 95% CI 0.0079-0.052, p<0.001), suggesting a protective role of prophylaxis against migraine chronification. At multivariate logistic regression analysis, we found that the independent variables significantly associated to progression to CM were excessive use of analgesics (p = 0.001) and psychiatric comorbidities (p = 0.005), while it was confirmed the protective role of preventive treatment (p < 0.0001).

Conclusion Clinicians should consider pharmacological treatment in children with increasing headache frequency to prevent CM. Objective Headache is a common and debilitating condition that places a significant burden on the healthcare system. It can negatively affect psychological and social well-being. P419 Migraine in men – Differences in phenotype and treatment patterns: Results from the migraine in Poland cross-sectional national survey

M. Waliszewska-Prosół1, K. Marschollek1, S. Budrewicz1, M. Nowaczewska2, M. Straburzyński3

1Wroclaw Medical University, Neurology, Wroclaw, Poland; 2Ludwik Rydygier Collegium Medicum in Bydgoszcz, Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Bydgoszcz, Department of Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, and Laryngological Oncology, Bydgoszcz, Poland; 3University of Warmia and Mazury, Family Medicine and Infectious Diseases, Olsztyn, Poland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P419

Objective The “Migraine in Poland” study is a large-scale nationwide cross-sectional online survey that assessed symptomatology, consulting, diagnosis, treatment, and burden of migraine in Poland. The purpose of this analysis is to define migraine phenotype and patterns of care for Polish men.

Methods The questionnaire evaluated healthcare system utilization, headache features, history of diagnosis, comorbidities, burden, as well as the use of acute or preventive treatment. The survey included questions that allowed for diagnosis according to the ICHD-3.

Results 3225 individuals aged 13 to 80 (mean age 38.9) responded to the survey (87.1% were women). Conclusion Our study confirms the existence of significant gender differences in the course of migraine, both in terms of clinical characteristics of the disease and patterns related to health behaviors and access to medical care.

P420 Men in the headache clinic: Characterization and sex comparison

N. Sjöholm1, F. Dourado Sotero1,2, M. I. Pavão Martins1

1Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Centro de Estudos Egas Moniz, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Hospital de Santa Maria (Unidade Local de Saúde Santa Maria), Serviço de Neurologia, Departamento de Neurociências e Saúde Mental, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P420

Objective Headaches are more prevalent in women, leading to underrepresentation of men in related studies. This study aimed to characterize male headache patients and explore sex differences.

Methods This retrospective observational study was conducted at headache consultations of both a public and a private hospital. Clinical data from medical records were entered into a uniform, sex-stratified database, including sociodemographics, ICHD-3 diagnosis, neuroimaging, family history and treatment.

Results Out of 700 patients, 112 were men (16.0%), comprising 12.2% of the public and 26.3% of the private hospital samples (p<0.001). Conclusion These results highlight sex differences among headache clinic patients, particularly regarding type of diagnoses, likelihood of having secondary headaches and prescribed treatment. P421 Sex-related disparities in migraine diagnosis and treatment: Insights from a tertiary headache center

C. Angerhöfer1, C. L. Höhne1, L. H. Overeem1, M. Ulrich1, M. P. Fitzek1, K. S. Lange1, Y. Salim1, U. Reuter1, B. Raffaelli1

1Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Neurology, Berlin, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P421

Objective Migraine is a prevalent and disabling neurological disorder that is often underdiagnosed and undertreated, especially in early care. Sex-related factors may contribute to this gap. This study examines sex differences in migraine diagnosis and management before and after presentation at a tertiary headache center and explores whether disparities are linked to clinical presentation.

Methods In this retrospective, cross-sectional study conducted at the tertiary headache center of Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, we included patients diagnosed with migraine between December 2015 and January 2023. We examined sex-related differences in prior diagnoses, clinical presentation, and treatment strategies, both before and after tertiary center evaluation.

Results Among 1,168 migraine patients, men were significantly less likely than women to have received an accurate migraine diagnosis prior to presentation at the tertiary center (54.3% vs. 71.6%, p < 0.01, OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.36 - 0.81). The diagnosis at our headache center was made in 99.6% of cases according to the ICHD-3 criteria. In men, the clinical presentation of migraine attacks did not differ between those correctly diagnosed and those missed at prior care. In contrast, women with prior accurate diagnoses reported significantly more migraine-associated symptoms and subjective trigger factors than women with missed diagnoses or men (p < 0.01). No sex differences were found in drug treatment for acute and preventive care, neither prior to nor after presentation at our center.

Conclusion Men with migraine are substantially less likely than women to receive a correct diagnosis in routine care. Higher diagnostic accuracy in women appears to be driven by more recognizable symptom patterns, whereas underdiagnosis in men may stem from limited awareness of less canonical clinical presentations. Enhancing early detection calls for sex-sensitive clinical training and increased recognition of the diverse manifestations of migraine.

P424 Long-term effectiveness of monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP in migraine patients

V. Pallarés Santos1, C. Morales Hernández1, A. E. Bartolomé Yumar1, I. N. Owrang Calvo1, M. Millet Oval1, A. González Pérez1, M. Solé Sabater1, E. Cubas Regulo1, S. del Águila Romero1, P. I. Dupuy Oria1, S. Fregel Frías1, C. Madrid Pérez1

1Hospital Universitario de Canarias, Neurology, Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P424

Objective Monoclonal antibodies are a new therapeutic strategy for episodic and chronic migraine prophylaxis. Their target is the calcitonin gene-related neuropeptide, which is a strong vasodilator for meningeal arteries and arterioles by activating endothelial adenylyl cyclase, which seems to be involved in the beginning of inflammation and headache. However, long-term effectiveness of these drugs are still scarce. We aim to evaluate the effectiveness of 3 anti-CGRP subcutaneous monoclonal treatments (erenumab, galcanezumab and fremanezumab) over 2 to 3 years.

Methods Observational, retrospective study involving 334 patients. The collected variables before treatment, and after 6, 12, 24 and 36 months, were the following: days of migraine and headache, and punctuation in HIT-6 and MIDAS scores. P425 Improvement in headache frequency does not alter pain sensitivity in chronic migraine treated with flunarizine

L. L. H. Pan1, Y. H. Ling2,3,4, S. J. Wang1,2,3

1National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Brain Research Center, Taipei, Taiwan; 2Taipei Veterans General Hospital, Department of Neurology, Neurological Institute, Taipei, Taiwan; 3National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, School of Medicine, College of Medicine, Taipei, Taiwan; 4National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Institute of Clinical Medicine, Taipei, Taiwan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P425

Objective Pain sensitivity has been previously found to be related to headache frequency and treatment outcomes. In this study, we are particularly interested in whether improvement in headache alters pain sensitivity.

Methods We included patients with chronic migraine who were responders of three-month flunarizine. Migraine Disability Assessment Scale (MIDAS) and Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (YBOCS) were used to assess disability and analgesic obsession. Treatment responders were defined as a ≧50% reduction in headache frequency in the third month compared to baseline.
