P427 Treatment pattern and reasons for discontinuing preventive treatment in cluster headache: A prospective cohort study

A. S. Petersen1, M. L. K. Søborg1, S. B. Laursen1, R. H. Jensen1,2, N. Lund1

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Glostrup, Denmark; 2University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Faculty of Health and Medical Sciences, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P427

Objective Pharmacological prevention of cluster headache aims to reduce the frequency and intensity of attacks, but its long-term effectiveness and tolerance remains uncertain. The aim of this study was twofold: first, to quantify the discontinuation rates of prophylactic therapeutics due to adverse effects; and second, we assessed the proportion of verapamil responders who maintained its prophylactic effectiveness at follow-up.

Methods In total, 596 patients with cluster headache fulfilling the ICHD-criteria (the baseline cohort) completed a semi-structured interview between 2017 and 2023. Of these, 430 were re-interviewed after a median time of 4.6 years, forming the follow-up cohort.

Results Of the baseline cohort, 457 patients (77%) had taken preventive medicine. Among these, 123 (27%) had discontinued treatment due to adverse effects. The discontinuation rate first-line treatment verapamil was 18%. Proportionally, the second-line treatments with lithium or topiramate were discontinued due to intolerance in nearly half of the patients. The odds of discontinuing lithium or topiramate therapy were four times higher than for verapamil (p<0.0001). In the follow-up cohort, only 33%, i.e. 143 patients received prophylactic medicine at the time of the second interview. Of the initial 131 verapamil responders, 77 patients continued the use of verapamil, and 54 patients had discontinued due to remission. At the time of the second interview, 91 patients were treated with verapamil and 55% of them were 50% responders. Adverse effects were the cause for discontinuation of verapamil in 17% between the first and second interview.

Conclusion Effective therapeutic prevention of cluster headache is hindered by intolerance and insufficient efficacy of the preventatives. Verapamil remains effective over time for a subgroup of initial responders, but our findings underscore the need for more tolerable and effective prophylactic medicine in the treatment of cluster headache.

This study aims to describe the characteristics and post-discontinuation outcomes of patients who stopped anti-CGRP mAb therapy for migraine.

Methods Unicentric, retrospective, observational study of migraine patients who discontinued anti-CGRP mAbs. Collected data included treatment duration, monthly headache days (MHD) before starting therapy and at discontinuation, reasons for stopping, and timing of treatment reintroduction.

Results We analysed 12 patients (83% female, mean age 48 years, mean MHD 10.5±8.0), two of whom discontinued treatment twice, totalling 14 treatment cycles. Reasons for discontinuation included sustained efficacy (n=10), pregnancy planning, unplanned pregnancy, Raynaud’s phenomenon, and switch to oral anti-CGRP. Mean treatment duration at discontinuation was 20 months, while mean MHD was 5.3±7.6. Among the 10 patients who discontinued due to sustained efficacy, 7 restarted treatment: 4 within 3 months, 1 within 6 months, and 2 after 6 months. All patients who did not restart had <2 MHD at discontinuation (mean: 0.9±0.8), compared to only 1 of the 7 who did restart (mean: 7.0±10.4). Patients who did not restart had no other oral preventives at discontinuation. Upon reintroduction, response was comparable to the initial cycle (average MHD at 3 months: 9.0±11.9 vs. 9.2±11.8).

Conclusion Most discontinuations occurred due to sustained efficacy. However, many patients resumed treatment, reflecting a need for continued preventive therapy in a significant subset of migraneurs. Those who did not restart had excellent migraine control at the time of discontinuation. Importantly, treatment interruption did not impair response upon reinitiation in our cohort. These findings underscore the need for personalized treatment strategies and close follow-up in migraine management.

P430 Chronology of response to Anti-CGRP mAbs in migraine: The CRONOS-CGRP study

A. Jaimes Sanchez1, J. Rodriguez Vico1, A. L. Nystrom Hernández1, O. Pajares1, A. Gómez1, J. Porta Etessam1

1Fundacion Jimenez Diaz, Madrid, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P430

Objective To characterize the temporal dynamics of response to anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) using survival analysis over a 12-month period, and to identify the optimal time to switch therapy in non-responders and clinical predictors of response.

Methods We conducted a single-center prospective cohort study including 462 patients with episodic or chronic migraine treated with erenumab, galcanezumab, or fremanezumab between February 2021 and November 2024. The baseline period was defined as the month preceding treatment initiation. Response was defined as a ≥50% reduction in monthly headache days (MHDs). Cumulative and instantaneous probabilities of response were estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves. A subgroup analysis compared anti-CGRP mAb-naïve patients with those who switched due to lack or loss of effectiveness, in order to evaluate the optimal switching time. Cox regression was used to identify predictors of response.

Results Median baseline MHDs was 18.5 (IQR 12.3–30.0); 76.6% had chronic migraine. Among 301(72.0%) responders, 252(83.7%) achieved response within the first 3 months. Cumulative probability of response plateaued at 72.0% by month 10. Instantaneous hazard peaked in month 1 (36.1%) and dropped below 10% after month 3. Naïve patients showed higher cumulative response (78.7%) and earlier hazard peaks than switchers (49.9%). A crossover in hazard curves suggested month 4 as the earliest point where switching offered a higher probability of response than continuing the initial mAb. In multivariable analysis, male sex was linked to a 32% lower response likelihood. Each additional headache day and prior preventive reduced response odds by 3.1% and 4.7%, respectively. Unilateral pain and photophobia increased the probability of early response by 30.6% and 63.9%.

Conclusion The probability of response to anti-CGRP mAbs is highest within the first 3 months. Switching may be most beneficial around month 4 in non-responders. Baseline clinical features may help predict early response.Fig. 1 (abstract P430).Fig. 2 (abstract P430).Fig. 3 (abstract P430).

P431 Predictors of response to antiCGRP monoclonal antibodies in real-world: Czech Migraine Registry (ReMig)

A. Bártková1, T. Nežádal2, I. Niedermayerová3, B. Turková4, P. Polidar1, L. Klečka5

1Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry Palacký University Olomouc, Neurology, Olomouc, Czech Republic; 2Military University Hospital Prague, Neurology Department, Prague, Czech Republic; 3University Hospital Brno, Neurology, Brno, Czech Republic; 4Value Outcomes, Prague, Czech Republic; 5Municipal Hospital of Ostrava, Neurology, Ostrava, Czech Republic

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P431

Objective To identify predictors of treatment response to anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) in patients enrolled in the Czech Registry of Migraine Patients on Biological Treatment (ReMig).

Methods This was a prospective, multicenter study utilizing data from the ReMig database, aimed at evaluating the impact of clinical and sociodemographic factors on the efficacy of all 4 mAbs. Patients were classified as responders (R) if they experienced a ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days (MMD), and as non-responders (NR) if the reduction was <50%. Logistic regression analysis was used. Data collection spanned from January 2021 to July 2024.

Results A total of 3285 patients (87.4% female) were analysed. Of these, 2422 (73.7%) were classified as R and 863 (26.3%) as NR. Female patients had a 29% lower likelihood of treatment failure. No significant differences were observed in terms of age, age at diagnosis, or disease duration. Patients with chronic migraine had a 40.1% higher risk of NR. Previously failed prophylactic treatments did not differ significantly between groups (mean 2.2; median 2.0). Medication overuse headache (MOH) did not negatively impact treatment outcomes (R: 34.9%; NR: 36.8%, p=0.423). Response to triptans was associated with a 27% lower risk of treatment failure. Higher education was significantly more prevalent among R (p=0.004). Part-time employment or disability pension status was associated with a 54.6% and 51.5% risk of NR respectively. No comorbidities, psychiatric included (p=0.693), significantly influenced treatment outcomes. However, each unit increase in body mass index (BMI) was associated with a 1.9% increase in the risk of treatment failure.

Conclusion Chronic migraine, poor response to triptans, higher BMI, lower educational attainment, and male sex may be associated with reduced efficacy of anti-CGRP mAb therapy. In contrast, disease duration, prior prophylactic treatment failures, MOH, and comorbidities did not significantly impact treatment response in this cohort.

P432 Retrospective evaluation of safety and tolerability of fremanezumab in patients with vascular risk factors

S. Broadhurst1, C. Monk1, J. Winstanley1, M. Ghadiri-Sani1

1Walton Centre NHS Trust, Liverpool, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P432

Objective The objective of this retrospective evaluation was to assess the safety and tolerability of fremanezumab (Ajovy) in patients with cerebrovascular risk factors.

Methods We currently have over 2000 patients on Ajovy at the Walton Centre NHS Trust. We retrospectively reviewed the notes for 1000 patients from November 2020 until October 2023, identifying any patients with potential cerebrovascular risk factors, in particular, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, previous strokes and cerebral bleeds.

Results We analysed the notes of 986 patients as we were unable to access the notes for 14/1000 patients who were managed in Welsh satellite clinics. Majority of the patients we reviewed were young female patients (F: M 800 187) with no cerebrovascular risk factors. 178 (18%) of the evaluated patients had at least one identifiable vascular risk factor. 97 (54.5%) of these patients remain on Ajovy. P433 Atogepant for vestibular migraine: Preliminary clinical experience in two patients

G. Sousa1, A. L. Neves1, A. Costa1

1Unidade Local de Saúde de São João, E.P.E., Neurology Department, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P433

Objective Vestibular migraine (VM) is the second most common cause of recurrent vertigo. It shares migraine pathophysiology but presents with episodic vertigo, dizziness, and balance disturbances. Treatment is often extrapolated from general migraine prevention strategies. The role of gepants (CGRP receptor antagonists) in VM remains unclear despite their proven efficacy in classic migraine. The objective is to describe clinical outcomes in two patients with VM treated preventively with atogepant, providing initial evidence to support its potential role in VM management.

Methods Two patients (one male, one female; aged 35 and 44 years) with neurologist-andENT-confirmed VM were assessed using validated instruments, including the Headache Impact Test (HIT-6) and Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC). Results Both patients showed marked clinical improvement in migraine attack intensity and frequency after one month of daily atogepant. Conclusion Atogepant showed promising efficacy in reducing migraine burden and vestibular symptoms in these VM cases. P434 People with migraine and two years treatment with anti-CGRP therapies. First results from the prospective national registry “Hercules”

D. D. Mitsikostas1, C. Deligianni1,2, E. Giannouli3, E. Kouremenos4, I. Spanou4, T. Constantinidis5, T. Sagona6, E. Chroni6, Z. Tsouris7, E. Dardiotis7, C. Tsironis8, S. Konitsiotis8

1National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, First Neurology, Athens, Greece; 2Athens naval Hospital, Neurology, Athens, Greece; 3Athens Medical Center, Headache Clinic, Athens, Greece; 4251 Generel Hospital of Air Forces, Neurology, Athens, Greece; 5Neurology Clinic, Corinth, Greece; 6Patras University Hospital, Neurology, Patras, Greece; 7University of Thessaly, Neurology, Larissa, Greece; 8University of Ioannina, Neurology, Ioannina, Greece

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P434

Objective Novel agents targeting the CGRP pathway constitute a novel mechanism-based treatment for migraine that has revolutionized the therapeutic landscape. Our aim was to document their long-term efficacy and safety outcomes in Hellas.

Methods The “HERCULES” is a patient-centered, national, multicenter, longitudinal, prospective, observational, non-interventional study supported by the Hellenic Headache Society.

Results So far, 322 subjects with migraine and prior failure to at least 3 repurposed anti-migraine prophylactic treatments attending 7 headache centers in Greece have been recorded, of whom 141 (43.7%) completed the 2-year treatment with anti-CGRP agents [17/141 (12%) subjects with erenumab; 18/141 (12.7%) with galcanezumab; and 106/141 (75.2%) with fremanezumab] while 51/322 (15.8%) participants discontinued treatment [fremanezumab 26/322 (8%); galcanezumab 17/322 (5.3%); 7/322 (2.2%) erenumab; eptinezumab 1/322 (0.3%)], due to failure [40/322 (12.4%)], adverse events (AE) [9/322 (2.8%)], or complete remission of migraine [2/51 (0.6%)]. P437 Local cutaneous complications of CGRP monoclonal antibodies: A case series

M. d. M. Martínez Salmerón1, E. Cabrera García1, J. A. García Gálvez1, L. Andrade Zumarraga1, P. Olea Rodríguez1, A. Arjona Padillo1

1Torrecardenas University Hospital, Neurology, Almeria, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P437

Objective To characterize the frequency, clinical features, management, and implications of local cutaneous adverse reactions associated with subcutaneous anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies in resistant migraine patients.

Methods Retrospective case series of resistant migraine patients followed at a headache outpatient clinic between November 2023-June 2025. All received subcutaneous anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies and developed mild to moderate injection-site reactions. Demographic, clinical data, treatment response, management were collected from records and analyzed descriptively. Patients gave their consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Results Nine women treated with subcutaneous anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies developed mild/moderate local cutaneous reactions (mainly erythema, induration, edema, and pruritus) representing 5% of all treated patients (n=190; fremanezumab 88, galcanezumab 75, erenumab 27). Reactions appeared after first dose in five patients and between the second and fifth in four. Mean age was 45.9 years (SD 3.2), and six (66.7%) had a history of allergy. Seven cases occurred with fremanezumab (8% of those exposed). Two continued therapy with supportive measures (local cooling, topical corticosteroid cream, pre/post-injection antihistamines, and rotation of injection site to abdominal area), while five required switching due to persistent reactions with or without lack of efficacy: two to atogepant, one to erenumab then eptinezumab, and one directly to eptinezumab; one discontinued. Of the remaining, one switched from galcanezumab to erenumab and one from erenumab to eptinezumab, both with good tolerability.

Conclusion Local cutaneous reactions to subcutaneous anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies occurred in nearly 5% of patients and were generally mild. Supportive measures allowed continuation in some cases, but most required switching to another monoclonal antibody or a gepant. Monitoring and proactive management are essential to minimize treatment discontinuation.

P440 Impact of CGRP monoclonal antibodies on the most bothersome non-pain symptom in migraine: A service evaluation

P. Amarasena1, A. Gimson1, F. Greenwood1, S. Maniataki1, U. Ashraf1, M. D. Villar-Martínez1, N. Karsan1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, Headache Group, Institute of Psychiatry Psychology and Neuroscience, London, UK

Objective Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide have been in use as migraine preventives for five years. We conducted a service evaluation to assess their efficacy and the impact on the most bothersome non-pain symptom (MBS).

P441 CGRP monoclonal antibodies in migraine: Do premonitory symptoms persist without headache? – A service evaluation

P. Amarasena1, A. Gimson1, F. Greenwood1, G. Sebastianelli1, S. Maniataki1, U. Ashraf1, M. D. Villar-Martínez1, D. Moreno Ajona1, N. Karsan1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, Headache Group, Institute of Psychiatry Psychology and Neuroscience, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P441

Objective Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) have been in use for migraine prevention for five years. We conducted a service evaluation focusing on efficacy and the effect of CGRP-mAbs on premonitory symptoms (PreS).

Methods Patients currently receiving mAbs at King’s College Hospital, London completed a questionnaire, including data on PreS. Clinical data were extracted from patient records. Data were summarised as percentages or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). Associations between categorical variables were assessed using Pearson Chi-Square tests.

Results Patients (n=223) responded (median age 48, IQR 35–57; 82% female), with diagnoses of chronic migraine (n=138, 62%), episodic migraine (n=65, 29%), and new daily persistent headache with migraine phenotype (n=20, 9%). Overall, 188 patients (84%) recognised PreS, with a median of 6 symptoms (IQR 2–9). Most common PreS were fatigue (67%), neck stiffness (58%) and brain fog (58%). Symptoms which were more frequent in the premonitory phase than in the headache phase were yawning (76% vs. 61%), food cravings (57% vs. 50%) and euphoria (56% vs. 13%). Although present in the premonitory phase, all other symptoms were more frequent during headache. Build-up of PreS that did not evolve into headache was reported by 114 (53%), which included 54% (n=104) of patients with >30% improvement in headache and 38% (n=10) of those with <30% improvement. Median number of PreS in this group was 5 (IQR 3–7). Brain fog (60%), fatigue (54%), and neck stiffness (51%) were most common and the duration of PreS was 1–24 h in most (67%). The type of mAb did not have a significant association with the occurrence of PreS without headache (χ² = 0.71, df=2, P = 0.70).

Conclusion Premonitory symptoms are recognised by a significant majority of migraine patients. Over half of those responding to mAbs continue to experience premonitory symptoms without headache, supporting a central mechanism in migraine pathophysiology.

P442 Superiority of candesartan over topiramate in the treatment of migraine: A comparative cohort study

A. Oosterlee1, B. van der Arend1, N. van Veelen1, I. de Boer1, A. de Groot1, B. Geuns1, E. van Zwet1, N. Pelzer1, G. M. Terwindt1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Neurology, Leiden, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P442

Objective To compare the tolerability and effectiveness of candesartan versus topiramate using real-world data.

Methods In this longitudinal cohort study at the Leiden Headache Center, data were collected via a validated E-diary. The 28 days before treatment served as baseline. The primary endpoint was medication discontinuation within 6 months. Secondary endpoints included ≥50% response rate, and changes in monthly migraine days (MMD), headache days (MHD), acute medication days (MAMD), and HIT-6 score. Patients received a propensity score based on baseline MHD, MMD, HADS, and prior preventive treatment failures. Discontinuation was assessed via Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression, adjusting for propensity score. Secondary outcomes were analyzed using adjusted regressions. Sensitivity analyses with optimal matching were also included.

Results 661 patients were included. Discontinuation was lower for candesartan (29.7%) vs. topiramate (67.3%; HR 2.5 [95% CI: 1.9–3.3], p<0.001). Candesartan also showed a higher ≥50% response rate (47% vs. 29%; OR 0.6 [95% CI: 0.4–0.8], p=0.004) and greater reduction in MHD (-1.1 days [95% CI: -2.2 to -0.01], p=0.04). No significant differences were seen in MMD, MAMD, or HIT-6 after adjustment. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the results.

Conclusion Candesartan appears better tolerated and more effective than topiramate. These findings suggest a need to revise treatment guidelines to avoid exposing patients to less tolerable and less effective therapies.

P443 Satisfaction rates and self-reported adverse events of antiCGRP therapies for migraine prevention – Focus on patient perspectives

E. Parreira1, S. Machado1, M. Saraiva1, J. Dionísio1

1Hospital Prof Dr Fernando Fonseca, Neurology Department, Amadora, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P443

Objective Anti-CGRP therapies are an important breakthrough in migraine prevention because of increased efficacy, specific mechanism of action and better tolerability that renders patient adhesion to these treatments much higher. Real world data showed more side effects than in clinical trials but nevertheless these drugs are well tolerated. We present the results of a study on self -reported efficacy and adverse effects of a large sample of patients on anti-CGRP therapies.

Methods Single-center observational study assessing the self-reported efficacy and adverse effects of anti-CGRP therapies via online surveys, over the past 12 months.

Results 277 online questionnaires were fulfilled by 142 patients, 91% women, mean age 48.8 years. 4% of questionnaires corresponded to patients on Atogepant, 9.3% on Erenumab, 24.4% on Eptinezumab, 29% on Galcanezumab and 32% on Fremanezumab. Duration of treatment ranged from 1 to 48 months.22,1% stated that were “much better” (7 in the Patient Global Impression of Change scale - PGIC) and 35.3% were “better with a real and useful difference” scoring 6 in PGIC. 55.9% reported one or more adverse events caused by the medication. P446 A preliminary study on the effects of vestibular migraine, Ménière’s disease and comorbidities on emotional status and cognitive function

P452 Response of migraine aura to CGRP-mAbs

L. Gufler1, G. Broessner1, K. Zebenholzer2, C. Wöber2, S. M. Tesar3, F. Riederer4

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P452

Objective Phase 3 studies have shown that monoclonal antibodies targeting calcitonin gene-related peptide or its receptor (anti-CGRP mAbs) are effective in both migraine without aura (MwoA) and migraine with aura (MwA). However, the occurrence and clinical course of migraine aura have rarely been assessed as outcomes. Anecdotal and cohort studies suggest that aura may improve with CGRP-based treatments, although de novo aura has also been reported. It remains unclear why the cortical phenomenon of migraine aura should respond to peripherally acting treatment. Results Out of 417 patients, 117 patients fulfilled criteria for MWA. At baseline (n=107), median aura frequency was 4 days/month (IQR 5), duration 30 min (IQR 45), and intensity 8 (IQR 4, NRS). Conclusion Preliminary data suggests anti-CGRP mAbs may reduce aura frequency and duration, while intensity remains unchanged.

P453 Measuring what matters: Emotional well-being and the impact of headache-free days

G. Fiorentini1,2, S. Ardis3, M. Abanese4, M. Padroni5, P. Barbanti1,2, S. Bonassi2, A. Porreca2, C. Aurilia1, G. Egeo1, F. Frediani6, A. Lerario7, S. Massari8, S. Cevoli9, V. Drago10, F. Giambattistelli11, M. G. Saracco12, M. L. Bartolozzi13, L. Giani14, M. C. Tonini15

1IRCCS San Raffaele, Rome, Italy; 2San Raffaele University, Rome, Italy; 3Gruppo Italiano Felicità e Salute Positiva, Rome, Italy; 4University of Rome Tor Vergata, Rome, Italy; 5Sant’Anna University Hospital, Ferrara, Italy; 6San Carlo Borromeo Hospital, ASST Santi Paolo e Carlo, Milan, Italy; 7Fondazione IRCCS Ca’ Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Milan, Italy; 8ASST Melegnano Martesana, Milan, Italy; 9IRCCS Istituto delle Scienze Neurologiche, Bologna, Italy; 10UOSD Neurologia ASP, Siracusa, Italy; 11Casa di Cura Figlie di San Camillo, Cremona, Italy; 12CDC - Centro Diagnostico Cernaia, Asti, Italy; 13UOC Neurologia, ASL Toscana centro, Empoli, Italy; 14ICS Maugeri, Milan, Italy; 15Clinica San Carlo - Paderno Dugnano, Milan, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P453

Objective This study assess subjective emotional well-being in patients with episodic migraine (EM) or chronic migraine (CM), by evaluating positive and negative emotions experienced on the last day with migraine and on the last day without migraine.

Methods A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted across 13 Italian headache centers. Adults with EM or CM were enrolled and demographic and clinical variables were collected. All patients completed validated questionnaires assessing, on a 10 point Likert Scale, the Emotional Well-Being (EWB), calculated as the sum of positive affects (PA) and negative affects (NA) experienced on their most recent day with and without migraine. Disability was measured with MIDAS and its correlation with EWB explored.

Results A total of 436 patients were enrolled (F/M: 378/58; mean age: 44.5±13.5; EM/CM: 342/94; mean disease duration: 23.5±14.9 years; mean migraine frequency: 9.9±7.5); Of these, 55.5% were married or cohabiting; 49.5% held a university degree. PA was significantly higher on migraine-free days (p<0.001), while NA was significantly higher during migraine days (p<0.001), indicating reduced EWB in presence of migraine. Moreover, subjects with EM reported higher EWB values compared with those with CM (3.7±1.5 vs. 3.2±1.9, p<0.005) on a migraine day, but no differences emerged between EM and CM on migraine-free days. MIDAS correlate with lower PA score (p<0.001), higher NA (p<0.001) and reduced EWB (p<0.001) on migraine days, but not on migraine-free days, suggesting that disability does not influence positive emotions when patients are free of headache.

Conclusion CM is associated with significantly reduced EWB compared to EM. While migraine disability, as measured by MIDAS, predicts EWB during migraine days, it does not capture positive affects and EWB on headache-free days. These findings underscore the importance of integrating subjective well-being into migraine assessment to better address patients’ quality of life beyond pain and disability.

P454 When aura does not always mean migraine: Visual aura from intracranial internal carotid artery aneurysms

M. Chondrogianni1, E. M. Dimitriadou1, K. Foska1, A. Akrivaki1, G. Magoufis1, G. Papagiannopoulou1, A. Theodorou1, E. Bakola1, L. Palaiodimou1, A. Safouris1, G. Tsivgoulis1

1Attikon University Hospital, 2nd Neurological Department of NKUA, Athens, Greece

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P454

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective We present a rare case of migraine-like visual aura without headache, triggered by two large left intracranial internal carotid artery (ICA) aneurysms. Endovascular repair of these aneurysms led to ischemic strokes in the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory, likely via a functional posterior communicating artery (PComA). To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of headache-free visual aura precipitated by intracranial ICA aneurysms.

Methods A 46-year-old woman experienced stereotypical right visual field auras for 18 months. MRI revealed four intracranial aneurysms: two in the left ICA, one in the right ICA, and one small basilar artery aneurysm. Following endovascular repair of the left ICA aneurysms, she developed multiple PCA strokes, attributed to embolic events through a functional PComA.

Results -.

Conclusion Cortical spreading depression (CSD), a self-propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarization, underlies migraine aura. Cerebral microembolism, arising from hemodynamic changes or microthrombi in unruptured aneurysms, can trigger CSD. In this patient, a functional PComA likely facilitated thromboembolic transmission before and after intervention, causing recurrent visual auras and occipital ischemic injury. This case illustrates that visual aura without headache does not always indicate migraine and may reflect underlying vascular pathology. Migraine-like aura associated with ICA aneurysms highlights the importance of considering secondary causes in atypical presentations. These findings support the role of cerebral microembolism in initiating CSD via a functional PComA, mimicking migraine aura. Prompt recognition and management of aneurysmal disease are essential to prevent ischemic complications.

Objective Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is an orphan chronic condition with severe facial pain attacks and significant unmet need. Conclusion The new TnED® has demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity to serve as a clinical outcome assessment for TN, with paroxysm severity being highly correlated with other validated instruments.

P457 Anxiety, depression and premonitory mood disturbance in vestibular migraine

P459 Side-shifting pattern of hemicrania continua: A rare variant

A. Dubey1, S. Dubey2, P. Naveen.3

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Hemicrania Continua (HC) presents as unilateral headache associated with autonomic features. Prompt clinical diagnosis leads to early effective management of this entity. We present an interesting case of HC which mimicked migraine.

Methods Single-patient case report with retrospective review of the clinical course, headache pattern, neurological examination, brain imaging, prior migraine treatments, and standardized indomethacin test (dose-escalation with withdrawal–rechallenge). Safety monitoring included renal and gastrointestinal profiles.

Results A 42-year-old man had 2 to 3 years history of continuous daily headache that alternated between hemicrania over days–weeks. Methods Clinical evaluation-neuroimaging-treatment.

Results 1st case: A 57-year-old man, was presented with severe orthostatic headache accompanied by dizziness, nausea, tinnitus and horizontal diplopia (right abducens nerve palsy). Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) was initially performed and revealed pachymeningitis with gadolinium-enhancement and spinal-cord MRI revealed a subdural hygroma at the A6-level, suggestive of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak (Fig. 1). Conservative management(intravenous fluids-oral caffeine-analgesics) was administered, followed by epidural blood patch, which resulted in resolution of symptoms. 2nd case: A 37-year-old male underwent suboccipital craniectomy for Chiari I malformation. Fifteen days postoperatively, he developed othrostatic headache, nausea and dizziness. Brain MRI demonstrated a supine CSF leak and hydromyelia of cervical spinal cord (Fig. 2). The patient was treated with conservative treatment with improvement of symptoms over the following month. 3rd case: A 49-year-old male precented with orthostatic headache, nausea and dizziness. Brain MRI demonstrated sinus venous enlargement and dura enhancement, while MRI of the spinal axis did not reveal any evidence of CSF leak (Fig. 3). Conservative management failed to achieve clinical improvement; epidural blood patch was performed leading to resolution of symptoms.

Conclusion Although intracranial hypotension can be diagnosed clinically and supported by its characteristic MRI findings, determining the underlying etiology may be challenging and necessitates comprehensive imaging of the entire spinal axis. In many cases conservative management proves insufficient and treatment with epidural blood patch is required.

P462 Efficacy of eptinezumab during a migraine attack: Preliminary data from an Italian multicenter real-world experience (the BEFREE study)

L. Fofi1, C. Altamura1, M. Marcosano1, A. Doretti2, F. Pistoia3, A. Granato4, S. Guerzoni5, M. Trimboli6, L. Grazzi7, D. A. Montisano7, G. Avino8, G. Sebastianelli9, C. Fasano10, E. M. Piella11, N. Brunelli1, L. F. Iannone5,12, F. Vernieri1

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P462

Objective In the RELIEF study, eptinezumab significantly shortened time to headache pain freedom and to absence of most bothersome symptom when administered during a migraine attack, 0.5–1 h following the start of infusion. The aim of this study was to observe the possible resolution of a migraine attack during eptinezumab infusion in a real-world setting, particularly exploring the first 30 min.

Methods This is an ongoing multicenter Italian observational prospective study. Patients with episodic (EM) and chronic migraine (CM) receiving eptinezumab 100 mg or 300 mg during a migraine attack were enrolled. Eptinezumab was administered within 1–12 h of onset of the qualifying migraine. Migraine features were recorded at different timepoints after infusion start: 10 min (T10), 20 min (T20), 30 min (T30), 1 h, 1.5 h, 2.5 h, 3 h, 3.5 h, and from 4 h to 48 h.

Results We enrolled 31 patients, mainly female (87%) with a mean age of 43.1+2.7 yrs; 68% had CM and 62% MO. The NRS score (baseline 6.2+1.9) progressively reduced at different timepoints, with the lowest value after 12 h after the infusion (2.9+3.7). In the first 30 min of the infusion, NRS score significantly varied from T0 to T10 (p=0.011) and from 10 to 20 min (p=0.004). Photophobia was significantly lower at T10 (p=0.025) and at T20 (p=0.08) compared to baseline. The presence of phonophobia was significantly lower comparing baseline to T20 (p=0.005) and T30 (p=0.005). Osmophobia was also significant comparing baseline to T30 (p=0.046). Pain freedom was reported by 6.5% of patients at T10, 20% T20, 13.3% T30, 16.7% 1 h, 19% 2 h, 58% 12 h, 35.3% 24 h and 31.3% 48 h. The achievement of pain freedom from T10 to T20 and from 4 h to 12 h was significant (p=0.046).

Conclusion During the first 30 min of the infusion, eptinezumab demonstrated to induce a rapid resolution of migraine pain intensity and associated symptoms, suggesting a peripheral site of pharmacological action for CGRP blockade.

P464 Prevalence of migraine and its neurological burden in Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis of community-based studies

H. Atwan1, M. Gamal1, O. Rageh2, M. Nada3

1Assiut University, Faculty of Medicine, Assiut, Egypt; 2Faculty of Medicine, Tanta University, Tanta, Egypt; 3Faculty of Medicine, Cairo University, Neurology Department, Cairo, Egypt

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P464

Objective Migraine is a disabling neurological disorder and a leading cause of years lived with disability. In Africa, community-based data on migraine remain limited. This review aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of migraine and summarize its neurological burden across African populations.

Methods We systematically searched three major databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus) in June 2025 for community-based studies reporting migraine prevalence in African countries.

Results We included 49 studies with 113,022 participants from 14 African countries. Ethiopia (23.4%), Egypt (17.0%), and Nigeria (14.9%) were most represented. Most studies were urban-based; the largest samples came from the general population (59.8%) and students (12.0%). Sex distribution was nearly equal (50.5% female). Participants were mostly aged 20–40 years. Reported migraine prevalence ranged from 3.4% to 53.4%, with most studies between 5 and 17.3%. Some reported prevalence per 100,000, ranging from 6,400 to 50,600. Incidence was rarely assessed. Female predominance was common, with sex ratios often between 0.7 and 1.2:1 (M: F), though some studies showed male dominance. The ICHD criteria were most used for diagnosis, followed by the HARDSHIP and MIDAS tools. Tension-type headache and probable migraine were frequently reported. Common risk factors included female sex, family history, stress, poor sleep, menstruation, noise, sunlight, and dietary triggers.

Conclusion Migraine prevalence in Africa shows wide variability, but consistent links to sex, psychosocial, and environmental factors. Greater awareness and targeted strategies are needed to address its burden across diverse African settings.

P466 Headache characteristics of patients diagnosed with Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) in a UK District general hospital

R. Pearce1, A. Verdiyeva1, A. Riaz1, K. Chinthapalli1

1Wexham Park Hospital, Slough, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P466

Objective To assess headache characteristics in GCA as per the 2020 European Headache Federation recommendations for neurologists managing GCA.

Methods We conducted retrospective data collection of initial presentation of 78 patients with GCA between 2018 and 2025 at Frimley Health NHS Trust. We analysed headache characteristics and additional GCA features documented in clinical notes.

Results 72% of the patients were female with a median age of onset 74 years (range 54-91 years). 81% of patients presented with a headache and 57 patients had a location documented. P467 A prospective real-world analysis of atogepant in refractory migraine patients

A. Andreou1,2, A. Nawaci1, B. Hill2, M. Murphy2, R. Kilner2, J. Briscoe2, G. Lambru2

1King’s College London, Headache Research - Wolfson SPaRC, London, UK; 2Guy’s And St Thomas NHS Foundation, Headache Centre, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P467

Objective The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness, tolerability, and impact of atogepant in a real-world population of patients with medically refractory episodic and chronic migraine.

Methods This prospective, single-centre audit included adults with episodic or chronic migraine who were refractory to ≥3 classes of preventive therapies and initiated on daily oral atogepant for 3 months.

Results Of 153 patients treated, 78 (M/F: 14/64; mean age 48.3±1.6 years) who submitted 3-month headache diaries were included in the analysis. Patients had failed a mean of 8.3±0.3 preventive treatments prior to atogepant; 38% (N=30) had failed to respond or tolerate a CGRP monoclonal antibody (mAb). At 3 months, monthly migraine days were reduced by 8.7 days (P=0.001), and monthly headache days by 7.5 days (P<0.001). Mean HIT-6 scores dropped by 6.0 points (from 69.0±0.4 to 63.0±0.8, P<0.001). Atogepant achieved ≥50% reduction in migraine days in 63% of patients. Among those who previously failed a CGRP mAb, 70% (N=21) had ≥30% reduction in monthly migraine days. Patients reported a mean 54±3% benefit on the global impression of change scale. Adverse events were reported in 49% over 3 months. The most common were constipation (19%), decreased appetite/weight loss (13%), nausea/vomiting (12%), fatigue (12%), and dizziness (5%), all considered mild.

Conclusion Atogepant appears to be an effective and well-tolerated treatment for patients who are refractory to other preventive therapies, including those who failed to respond or tolerate previously a CGRP mAbs. These real-world findings support atogepant’s utility in complex clinical populations.

P468 Eptinezumab for migraine prevention: Initial experience from a Portuguese tertiary hospital

S. Moreira1, A. Costa1, A. Câmara2, S. Gomes1, L. Francisco1, S. Varanda1

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Neurology, Braga, Portugal; 2Hospital Central do Funchal, Neurology, Funchal, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P468

Objective Eptinezumab was recently approved in our hospital, with the first patient receiving treatment in August 2024. Given the limited European real-world data available, we aimed to describe the clinical profile of patients who initiated eptinezumab in our hospital.

Methods Retrospective descriptive study of adult patients who initiated eptinezumab for migraine prevention in our tertiary headache clinic between August 2024 and May 2025. Demographic, clinical, and treatment-related data were retrieved from medical records.

Results Eighteen patients initiated eptinezumab. Overall, 72% were female, and the mean age was 43.3 years (range: 20–63). Migraine was chronic in 10 patients (56%) and episodic in 8 (44%).

All patients had previously tried more than two oral preventive treatments (range: 3 to over 10). Prior anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody use was documented in 14 patients (78%), all of whom had previously received galcanezumab. Among them, 4 were also treated with fremanezumab, and 1 of these had additionally received erenumab. In total, 4 patients had been exposed to more than one monoclonal antibody (range: 1 to 3). Four patients (22%) started eptinezumab as their first anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody. At the time of analysis, 17 patients were under active treatment: 10 (59%) were receiving eptinezumab with oral preventives (of whom 2 [12%] also received botulinum toxin); 1 (6%) was treated with botulinum toxin only; and 4 (24%) were on monotherapy. No patient was using another monoclonal antibody concurrently. One patient discontinued eptinezumab due to lack of efficacy and resumed fremanezumab.

Conclusion Eptinezumab offers distinct advantages. Nonetheless, in this cohort, it was not frequently selected as a first-line option, being primarily used in patients with highly refractory migraine. Treatment adherence was high and further data are needed to assess long-term effectiveness and better define its role in clinical practice.

P471 The burden of high-frequency episodic migraine and chronic migraine in the population-based PopHEAD study

H. Engstrand1, M. Argren1, J. A. Zwart1, E. A. Tronvik2, B. Winsvold1

1Oslo University Hospital, Department of Research and Innovation, Division of Clinical Neuroscience, Oslo, Norway; 2Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Norwegian Centre for Headache Research (NorHead), Trondheim, Norway

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P471

Objective Is there any difference between the disease burden and quality of life among individuals with high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM) and chronic migraine (CM)?

Methods PopHEAD is a population-based cross-sectional study in the Norwegian county of Vestfold and Telemark. 28,753 participants (18-70 years) were invited to fill in an electronic questionnaire. The questionnaire was a modified version of the HARDSHIP-questionnaire. HFEM was classified according to newly proposed criteria, and CM according to ICHD-3. Using linear regression for continuous variables and logistic regression for binary outcomes, we compared measures of disease burden and quality of life between participants classified with HFEM and CM. The analysis was conducted first with adjustment for age and sex, then with additional adjustment for monthly migraine days.

Results Of 8,265 participants 225 had HFEM and 349 had CM. Compared to the HFEM group, the CM group had more monthly migraine days (17.9 vs. 9.7, p < 0.001) and headache days (20.8 vs. 9.9, p < 0.001). In analyses adjusted for age and sex, the CM group reported greater disease burden across nearly all measures, including work and social impairment, and had a lower quality of life (p < 0.01). With additional adjustment for monthly migraine days, no significant differences in disease burden were found between the two groups, except from days missed from household work (p = 0.03).

Conclusion The higher disease burden observed in CM compared to HFEM was fully explained by the higher number of monthly migraine days in the CM group. This finding suggests that monthly migraine days, not monthly headache days, are the primary driver of burden and should form the basis for future revisions to the ICHD criteria.

P473 Real-world effectiveness of eptinezumab in participants in whom ≥1 prior anti-cgrp preventive treatment had failed: Results for the first 75 participants in an ongoing prospective study

A. Starling1, S. Regnier2, S. Soni-Brahmbhatt2, S. F. Awad3, S. W. Grossman2,4, D. F. Eisenberg2, D. Fiore2, M. Townshend5, S. Sharma2, E. Estemalik6

1Mayo Clinic Arizona, Scottsdale, AZ, USA; 2Lundbeck, Deerfield, IL, USA; 3H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark; 4Lundbeck LLC, Deerfield, IL, USA; 5ZS Associates, Evanston, IL, USA; 6Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, OH, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P473

Objective To assess the real-world effectiveness of eptinezumab for preventive treatment of migraine in participants in whom ≥1 preventive calcitonin gene-related peptide antagonist (anti-CGRP) had previously failed.

Methods INFUSE was an observational, prospective study with 190 participants potentially recruited from ≥100 United States infusion centers. P479 The role of unavoidable triggers in the chronification of migraine among teachers

I. Azizova1, R. Hasanov2

1Neurology Clinic “New Medical Technologies”, Baku, Azerbaijan; 2Azerbaijan State Advanced Training Institute for Doctors named after A.Aliyev, Baku, Azerbaijan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P479

Objective Teachers and academic staff are one of the most common groups of people whose occupations have been observed in specialized neurological clinic. Their profession is accompanied by significant mental and emotional stress, long hours in front of the screen, lack of proper rest, and a low possibility of avoiding the already known migraine triggers. This research was conducted to assess the clinical features and work-related factors that lead to chronic migraine and medication overuse headache (MOH) in teachers.

Methods We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of 502 patients who visited our headache clinic from January 1 to October 5, 2025. Out of these, 480 (95.6%) were diagnosed with migraine according to ICHD-3 criteria, and 440 (88%) were chronic migraine patients with medication overuse. A subgroup of 152 patients (30.3%) were teachers or lecturers. The study analyzed demographics, headache type, medication use, and trigger exposure.

Results Majority of the teachers suffered from chronic migraine with medication overuse. The main triggers were found to be sleep deprivation, prolonged screen time, emotional stress, noise exposure, irregular meals, and physical inactivity. Most of them knew their triggers; however, they mentioned that they could not manage them because of too much work, preparing lessons, giving after-school tutoring, and domestic chores that went on late into the night.

Conclusion Teachers are an occupational group at great risk for their episodic migraine to progress to chronic migraine and for them to develop a medication overuse headache. The fact that they are constantly exposed to certain professional stressors which they cannot avoid, makes it very difficult for them to control their triggers and as a result, they suffer from headaches more frequently. An educational program and changes in the work environment would not only have a positive effect on the proper management of migraine but would also improve the general health of this population.

P480 The long-term effectiveness and tolerability of rimegepant administered as needed in the acute treatment of migraine among chinese adults in a real-world study

W. Kang1,2, P. Huang1,2

1Ruijin Hospital Affiliated Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China; 2Ruijin-Hainan hospital Shanghai Affiliated Jiao Tong University School of Medicine (Hainan Boao Research Hospotal), Boao, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P480

Objective This analysis aimed to describe patterns in monthly migraine days (MMDs) and monthly tablet utilization, as well as tolerability in patients treated as needed (PRN) with rimegepant over 12 months (4 weeks as a month).

Patients were eligible for inclusion in this analysis if, during follow-up months with non-missing data, at least 50% of those months satisfied the following criterion: the number of days on which rimegepant was used was equal to or greater than 50% of the MMDs. Those who treated with CGRP monoclonal antibodies or abotulinumtoxinA during the 12-month follow-up were excluded from this analysis. MMDs and monthly tablet utilization were calculated and described over 12 months.

Results 79 patients were included in the analysis. Patients were predominantly female (n=55, 69.6%) with a mean (SD) age of 41.9 (11.4) years. The overall mean (SD) MMDs were 10.9 (8.1) at baseline and decreased to 3.4 (4.0) by month 12 (Fig. 1). Additionally, the median (Q1, Q3) number of rimegepant tablets administered per month declined from 5.0 (2.0, 9.0) at month 1 to 2.0 (0, 3.0) by month 12 (Fig. 1). To exclude the effects of other analgesics, the usage of acute and preventive medications was also analyzed. Overall, the percentages of patients using any acute medications (from 91.1% at baseline to 29.6% at month 12) or preventive medications (from 20.3% at baseline to 3.7% at month 12) were both decreased from baseline over the 12 months, respectively. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 20 (25.3%) patients.

Conclusion Both MMDs and monthly tablet utilization showed a trend of reduction during one-year of follow-up for the acute treatment of migraine attacks with rimegepant on a PRN basis. Rimegepant also demonstrated a favorable safety profile and was well-tolerated.Fig. 1 (abstract P480).

P481 Prevalence of migraine in fibromyalgia patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, M. Azaan Khan1, F. Gul Awan1, M. Azfar1, M. Muddassar1, J. Ajmal1

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P481

Objective This review aims to estimate the prevalence of migraine in fibromyalgia patients.

Methods PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science and grey literature were searched from inception to September 2025 for studies reporting prevalence of migraine in fibromyalgia patients. Analyses were conducted using R software, version 5.4.1. Prevalences were pooled as proportions, and stabilized through Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformations. Random-effects model was used for pooling. Prevalences were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

Results Twelve studies were included. A total of 55,879 participants were analyzed. Pooled migraine prevalence in fibromyalgia patients was 36% (95% CI 24% to 49%). Subgroup analysis by country revealed marked variations, with country-wise prevalences ranging from 3% to 59%. Subgrouping by continent also revealed major differences in migraine burden (Asia: 15%, Europe: 41%, North America: 41%, Oceania: 59%, South America: 26%). One study reported data for migraine prevalence in both sexes and noted a two-fold higher burden of migraine in female fibromyalgia patients than in males.

Conclusion This is the first meta-analysis to estimate migraine burden in fibromyalgia patients, demonstrating variations in migraine burden across regions and biologic sexes. Almost 2 in 5 fibromyalgia patients experienced migraine, highlighting significant burden and calling for adequate migraine care in this vulnerable population.Fig. 1 (abstract P481).Fig. 2 (abstract P481).Fig. 3 (abstract P481).

P483 What is the consistency of response to rimegepant at a group level in the acute treatment of migraine in UK adult patients? Protocol for a real-world, patient-centred study

G. O’Neil1, L. Abraham2, R. Pawinski1, K. Nakajima3, E. Bagshaw4, A. Fellows4, S. Llewellyn4, G. Lambru5

1Pfizer, Ltd., Tadworth, UK; 2Pfizer R&D UK Ltd., Tadworth, UK; 3Pfizer, Inc., New York, NY, USA; 4Vitaccess Ltd, London, UK; 5Guy’s and St. Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P483

Conclusion CORRELATE-UK will assess real-world effectiveness of rimegepant for acute migraine treatment across multiple attacks over 12 weeks in a UK population, including in those on preventive therapy and with chronic migraine.Fig. 1 (abstract P483).

P486 Migraine epidemiology in Taiwan: Age-specific burden and impact of the COVID-19 pandemic

H. W. Jao1, C. H. Tang1, D. Shen1, S. A. Lin1, I. C. Tai1, H. W. Chou1, Y. H. Chang1

1School of Health Care Administration, College of Management, Taipei Medical University, Taipei, Taiwan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P486

Objective This study evaluates migraine prevalence and local epidemiology in individuals aged ≥6 in Taiwan, addressing limited data in early age and COVID-19’s impact on health-seeking behavior.

Methods This cohort study used population-based claims data from the Taiwan National Health Insurance Research Database, covering 99.9% of the population. Individuals aged ≥6 years from 2018 to 2023 were identified as having migraine if they met any of the following criteria: ≥2 outpatient visits or ≥1 inpatient visit with a migraine diagnosis; treatment with ergot alkaloids for headache; or use of migraine-specific medications, including triptans or CGRP monoclonal antibody (mAb). Chronic migraine (CM) was defined by ICD-10 code G43.7X, or CGRP mAb use, or high-dose onabotulinumtoxin A; others were classified as episodic migraine (EM). The COVID-19 period was defined as 2021–2022, with its impact assessed using a validation approach based on Meniere’s disease. Cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, obesity, smoking) were identified using ATC codes.

Results A total of 1,010,125 patients were identified as having migraine. Annual prevalence increased from 1,013.2 to 1,188.9 per 100,000 between 2018 and 2023. The overall prevalence during 2018–2023 was 4,223.9 per 100,000. Prevalence was 678.7 per 100,000 for ages 6–12 and 2,648.6 per 100,000 for ages 13–17. No apparent changes in health-seeking behavior were observed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Among all patients, 23.1% had at least one cardiovascular risk factor. EM accounted for 88.2% of all patients, with the highest prevalence in the 30–40 age group; CM accounted for 11.8% of all patients, peaking in the 40–50 age group.

Conclusion Migraine prevalence in Taiwan has increased in recent years, especially after COVID-19, with a noticeable concern on individuals aged 6–18, while health-seeking behaviors remained unchanged during the pandemic.

P487 Migraine treatment outcomes with rimegepant in rimegepant-naive patients: A real-world, multi-center, prospective, observational study

Y. Ran1, Q. Zhao2, H. Su1, S. Zhang1,3, Z. He1, Y. Liu4, Z. Dong1, S. Yu1

11st Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital, Department of Neurology, Beijing, China; 2Pfizer, Inc., Chengdu, China; 3The First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, Chongqing, China; 4Pfizer, Inc., Beijing, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P487

Objective This analysis aimed to explore the real-world effectiveness and tolerability of rimegepant for acute migraine therapy in rimegepant-naive patients defined as those who had never used Rimegepant before joining the study.

Methods A single arm, multicenter, prospective, observational registry (NCT06439628) aimed to recruit 3,000 adults who were prescribed rimegepant for acute treatment of migraine across 70 sites in China. Treatment history was collected at baseline. Patient-reported outcomes, including 1.Most severe pain after taking rimegepant, 2.Time to onset time of meaningful pain relief (MPR), 3. Time to onset for meaningful relief from associated symptoms (MRA), and 4. Patient satisfaction with pain relief and return to normal function (RNF), were collected via a remote digital platform (encouraged within 48 h of treatment). Follow-up is planned for 12 months. This report focused on outcomes in rimegepant-naive subgroup at 3 months.

Results A total of 2,141 participants were included in this subgroup analysis. The majority (81.4%) were female, with a mean (SD) age of 38.5 (10.7) years, and the mean (SD) monthly migraine days in the past three months was 7.0 (7.5). P488 Changes in acute treatment effectiveness in migraine patients switching from standard of care to rimegepant: Findings from a real-world study

Y. Ran1, Q. Zhao2, H. Su1, S. Zhang1,3, Z. He1, Y. Liu4, Z. Dong1, S. Yu1

11st Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital, Department of Neurology, Beijing, China; 2Pfizer, Inc., Chengdu, China; 3The First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, Chongqing, China; 4Pfizer, Inc., Beijing, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P488

Objective This analysis aimed to explore acute treatment effectiveness changes among rimegepant-naive migraine patients switching from standard of care (SOC) to rimegepant.

Methods A single-arm, multicenter, prospective, observational registry (NCT06439628) aimed to recruit 3,000 adults prescribed rimegepant for acute migraine treatment at 70 Chinese sites. Patient-reported outcomes, including 1.worst pain after rimegepant, 2. Time to meaningful pain relief (MPR), 3. Time to meaningful relief from associated symptoms (MRA), and 4. Satisfaction with pain relief and return to normal function (RNF), were collected via a digital platform (encouraged within 48 h of treatment). Follow-up is for 12 months. P489 Efficacy of rimegepant in treating acute vertigo attacks in vestibular migraine: A retrospective open-label study

D. Bing1

1Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology., Department of Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, Wuhan, China

Objective To test the efficacy of Rimegepant (RIM) in treating acute vertigo attacks in patients with vestibular migraine (VM) or probable vestibular migraine (pVM).

P490 Efficacy, safety, and tolerability of atogepant in migraine patients from the UAE

T. Alsaadi1, R. Suliman1, M. Aljaafari1, G. Alsabbagh1, Y. El Rifai1, K. Hamoulila1

1American Center for Psychiatry and Neurology, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P490

Objective Atogepant is a novel oral calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonist approved for migraine prevention, but evidence from the MENA region remains limited. We evaluated its efficacy and safety in chronic and episodic migraine patients in the United Arab Emirates.

Methods This is a retrospective study of patients aged ≥18 years with chronic or episodic migraine who received atogepant for at least six months. Clinical data were extracted from medical records at the American Center for Psychiatry and Neurology, Abu Dhabi. Baseline Monthly Migraine Days (MMD) were compared with a minimum follow-up documented MMD every two months. Safety was evaluated via descriptive analysis of reported adverse events.

Results 86 patients were identified who were prescribed atogepant60 met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed. 23 (38%) had chronic migraine, whereas 37 (62%) were diagnosed with episodic migraine. The majority were female (85%) and Emirati nationals (70%). Out of 60, 6 patients completed 6 months, between 6-9-8 months 6 more patients completed treatment. By 12 months, 19 patients while the remaining 29 remained on treatment for over 12 months where 2 patients continued atogepant for 23 months. P491 Risk of hypertension with Atogepant use in migraine patients in the UAE

T. Alsaadi1, R. Suliman1, M. Aljaafari1, G. Alsabbagh1, B. Pagdato1, K. Hamoulila1

1American Center for Psychiatry and Neurology, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P491

Objective Atogepant is an oral CGRP receptor antagonist used for migraine prevention. Previous studies have demonstrated potential risk of hypertension among some CGRP antagonist users (mAbs). However, it is not known if that risk would also apply for gepants users. This study evaluated the effect of atogepant on systolic and diastolic blood pressure in migraine patients in the UAE.

Methods A retrospective study included adults ≥18 years with chronic or episodic migraine who received atogepant for at least 6 months. Data were extracted from medical records at the American Center for Psychiatry and Neurology, Abu Dhabi. We included only patients with recorded systolic and diastolic blood pressure at baseline and at least once every three months at their follow up vitits. We excluded patients with prior use of mAbs in the past 6 months prior to initiating treatment. Paired t-tests were used to assess changes from baseline.

Results 86 patients were identified and 70 participants met the inclusion criteria; 82.9% were female, and 6% had a prior history of hypertension prior to initiating treatment. Mean systolic blood pressure changed slightly from 121.7 ± 11.4 mmHg at baseline to 120.1 ± 12.2 mmHg at 6 months, while mean diastolic blood pressure changed from 79.0 ± 8.2 mmHg at baseline to 78.5 ± 7.8 mmHg at 6 months. Changes at three and twelve months were similarly minimal. Paired t-tests showed no statistically significant differences in systolic or diastolic blood pressure at any follow-up visit (p > 0.05).

Conclusion Atogepant use in migraine patients was not associated with any significant changes in systolic or diastolic blood pressure, indicating no apparent risk of hypertension in this population.

P492 Autonomic nervous system function in exercise intolerant patients with post traumatic headache

M. I. Sandboe1, J. Stensheim1, C. I. Sørgjerd1, T. Sand1, P. Moe Omland1, T. Skandsen1

1NTNU, Department of Neuromedicine and Movement Science, Trondheim, Norway

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P492

Objective To investigate if exercise intolerance in patients with post traumatic headache (PTH) was characterized by abnormal autonomic nervous system (ANS) function.

Methods Participants 18-60 years from the Trondheim Post Concussion Symptom (PCS) study with PTH and exercise intolerance, n =19, and controls matched on age and sex, n=24, were included. Participants with PTH had conducted orthostatic tilt test, deep breathing and Valsalva maneuver to measure function of the ANS, and Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test to assess exercise intolerance. ANS function in controls was also tested with orthostatic tilt test, deep breathing and Valsalva maneuver.

Results Participants with PTH and exercise intolerance did not exhibit statistically significant differences on measurements of the ANS compared to healthy controls. There were trends towards longer Valsalva recovery time for systolic blood pressure (1.8 vs. 1.4 s, p=0.065) in the PTH group. ANS assessments revealed that one patient demonstrated findings characteristic of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

Conclusion Although group differences in ANS measurements between participants with PTH and controls did not reach statistical significance, observable trends suggest possibly altered sympathetic function (i.e. prolonged Valsalva recovery time). However, we found no trends towards parasympathetic dysfunction. Future studies with larger samples are needed to investigate if ANS function may be causally related to some symptoms in exercise intolerant PTH patients.

G. Fiorentini1,2, G. Egeo1, C. Aurilia1, P. Torelli3, F. Pistoia4, S. Strumia5, P. Scatena6, S. Rinalduzzi6, A. Salerno7, F. Frediani8, A. Galli8, M. Autunno9, S. Messina10, A. 1IRCCS San Raffaele, Rome, Italy; 2San Raffaele University, Rome, Italy; 3University of Parma, Parma, Italy; 4University of L’Aquila, L’Aquila, Italy; 5G.B. Morgagni L. Pierantoni Hospital, Forlì, Italy; 6San Camillo de Lellis, General District Hospital, Rieti, Italy; 7San Giovanni Addolorata Hospital, Rome, Italy; 8San Carlo Borromeo Hospital, ASST Santi Paolo e Carlo, Milan, Italy; 9University of Messina, Messina, Italy; 10Istituto Auxologico Italiano, IRCCS, Milan, Italy; 11San Camillo-Forlanini Hospital, Rome, Italy; 12Antonio Cardarelli Hospital, Naples, Italy; 13Francesco Spaziani Hospital, Frosinone, Italy; 14University Hospital Tor Vergata, Rome, Italy; 15University of Palermo, Palermo, Italy; 16A.O.U.
