The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P493

Objective To evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of atogepant 60 mg over 24 weeks in patients with high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM; 8–14 days/month) or chronic migraine (CM), with a focus on responder (≥50% reduction) and super-responder (≥75% reduction) rates.

Methods GIANT II is a prospective, multicenter (n=16), real-world study within the Italian Migraine Registry (I-GRAINE). Consecutive adults with HFEM or CM who had failed ≥3 prior preventive treatments (AIFA criteria) received atogepant 60 mg/day for >24 months. Co-primary endpoints: responders and super-responder rates at weeks 21–24 vs. baseline. Secondary endpoints: change in monthly migraine days (MMD for HFEM) or monthly headache days (MHD for CM), 100% response rate, acute medication intake (MAI), pain intensity (NRS), disability (HIT-6, MIDAS), interictal burden (MIBS-4), and treatment satisfaction (PGIC). Adverse events were collected.

Results A total of 233 patients received ≥1 dose (safety population), 156 completed ≥24 weeks (effectiveness population). Overall, 39% had previously failed anti-CGRP mAbs. At week 24, 76.9% were responders, 45.5% super-responders, and 5.1% achieved 100% response (HFEM: 89.1%, 45.3%, 9.4%; CM: 68.5%, 45.3%, 2.2%). Mean changes from baseline (all p<0.001) were: MMD –10.0, MHD – 10.2, MAI – 12.1, NRS –3.1, HIT-6 –15.8, MIDAS –66.6, MIBS-4 -4.60. PGIC documented high satisfaction (much/very much improved: 88%). Among prior mAb non-responders, response rates were 70.7% (≥50%), 39.7% (≥75%), and 1.7% (100%), with consistent improvements across all endpoints. Adverse events occurred in 12.4% (mainly constipation and nausea); 2.1% discontinued.

Conclusion Atogepant showed marked 6-month effectiveness in highly refractory patients, with three-quarters achieving response, nearly half super-response, and ~5% absolute response. Notably, most prior anti-CGRP mAb non-responders benefited (~71% responders; ~40% super-responders). The treatment was well tolerated and safe.

P494 Switching patterns of CGRP monoclonal antibodies in migraine: A service evaluation

A. Gimson1, P. Amarasena1, F. Greenwood1, S. Maniataki1, U. Ashraf1, M. D. Villar-Martínez1, D. Moreno Ajona1, N. Karsan1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, Headache Group, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P494

Objective Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting calcitonin gene-related peptide have been used for migraine prevention for five years. We evaluated switching patterns in patients receiving mAbs.

Methods Efficacy data of patients receiving mAbs at King’s College Hospital, London were collected from patient records as part of a service evaluation. Data were summarised as percentages or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). Associations between categorical variables were assessed using Pearson Chi-Square tests. Response was defined as >30% improvement.

Results In 223 patients (median age 48 years, IQR 35–57; 82% female), diagnoses included chronic migraine (62%), episodic migraine (29%), and new daily persistent headache with migraine phenotype (9%). Most (n=179, 80%) received one mAb; 36 (16%) received two, 8 (4%) received three. The first used mAb was discontinued by 53 (23.8%): 21 (9.4%) for lack of response, 21 (9.4%) for loss of efficacy, and 11 (4.9%) for AEs. Cause of discontinuation was not associated with the type of mAb (χ² = 4.94, df = 2, P = 0.09). Median treatment duration before losing efficacy was 123 weeks (IQR 92–165). Constipation (4, 36%) and skin reactions (3, 27%) were the most common AEs leading to discontinuation. Efficacy data was unavailable for 4 out of 44 patients who received a second mAb due to short follow-up. Treatment was effective in 26 (65%), while 9 (22.5%) discontinued for lack of response, 3 (7.5%) for loss of efficacy, and 2 (5%) for AEs. A third mAb was used in 8 patients and was effective in 6 (75%), with 2 losing efficacy. Of 13 patients who stopped the first mAb for non-response, 6 (46.2%) responded to the second. Among 19 who stopped due to loss of efficacy, 12 (63.2%) had ongoing benefit, and 2 (10.5%) lost efficacy.

Conclusion Lack of response or loss of efficacy were the commonest causes for first mAb discontinuation. A notable proportion of initial non-responders benefited from switching to an alternative mAb.

P495 Does Fibromyalgia improve with CGRP targeting therapy?

U. Ashraf1, P. Amarasena1, A. Gimson1, F. Greenwood1, S. Maniataki1, N. Karsan1, M. D. Villar-Martínez1, P. J. Goadsby1,2

1King’s College London, Headache, London, UK; 2King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Thuwal, Saudi Arabia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P495

Objective Previous data has shown that certain migraine co-morbidities, such as vertigo and mood disturbance, can improve with the use of CGRP monoclonal antibodies (CGRP mAbs), independent of headache improvement. Fibromyalgia has been reported as a common co-morbidity of migraine, however, there is a paucity of data exploring the effect of CGRP mAbs on symptoms.

Methods A retrospective service evaluation was performed using clinic letters from the King’s College Hospital Tertiary headache service from January 2019-September 2025. Patients fulfilling International Classification of Headache Disorders-3 criteria for migraine who had received CGRP mAbs for at least 3 months, and who reported a diagnosis of fibromyalgia were included. Data on age, sex, specific CGRP mAb, patient-reported improvement in fibromyalgia symptoms and improvement in monthly headache days (MHD) were collected. A responder to CGRP mAb was defined as having at least 30% reduction in MHD from baseline at 3 months. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistical Software (v 29).

Results In total, 43 patients were identified, 38 (88%) women and 5 (12%) men. The median age was 47 years (IQR 36-53). The most commonly used CGRP monoclonal antibody was fremanezumab (63%), followed by erenumab (30%) and galcanezumab (7%).

Improvement of fibromyalgia symptoms were reported by 12% (5/43), no improvement in 65% (28/43,) and worsening in 19% (8/43). There was no statistically significant difference in fibromyalgia symptom improvement between responders and non-responders (12% vs. 25%, P = 0.20), and between fremanezumab, erenumab and galcanezumab use respectively (4% vs. 23% vs. 33%, P = 0.16).

Conclusion Our study showed that a minority of patients with migraine and fibromyalgia will experience improvement in their fibromyalgia symptoms with CGRP mAbs. This may suggest the underlying biology of fibromyalgia in patients with migraine is largely driven by mechanisms other than CGRP.

P496 Reasons for discontinuing triptans among current users of rimegepant for the acute treatment of migraine in the CONFIDENCE study

K. Hygge Blakeman1, A. Urani2, G. Lambru3, R. B. Lipton4, P. J. Goadsby5,6, P. Pozo-Rosich7, T. J. Schwedt8, K. M. Fanning9, F. Dai10, L. Abraham11

1Pfizer AB, Stockholm, Sweden; 2Aptar Digital Health, Paris, France; 3The Headache and Facial Pain Service, Guy’s and St. Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK; 4Montefiore Medical Center and Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, New York, NY, USA; 5King’s College Hospital, NIHR King’s Clinical Research Facility, London, UK; 6King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Thuwal, Saudi Arabia; 7Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona, Headache and Neurological Pain Research Group, Barcelona, Spain; 8Mayo Clinic, Department of Neurology, Scottsdale, AZ, USA; 9MIST Research, Wilmington, NC, USA; 10Pfizer, Inc., New York, NY, USA; 11Pfizer R&D UK Ltd., Tadworth, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P496

Objective CONFIDENCE was a prospective observational study conducted via the Migraine Buddy” app to evaluate the real-world use of rimegepant for the acute treatment of migraine. Data from the CONFIDENCE study was used to better understand the reasons participants had previously discontinued ≥1 triptans.

Methods The study enrolled US adults with 3–14 headache days in the prior 30 days and plans to use rimegepant in the subsequent 30 days. At enrolment, participants reported the number of triptans previously used and discontinued (lapsed), and the reasons behind these lapses (all that applied from 9 items).

Results Among the 416 participants in the CONFIDENCE study, 46 (11%) had no lapsed triptans, 132 (32%) had 1, 134 (32%) had 2, and 104 (25%) had ≥3. 103/370 (28%) participants with ≥1 lapsed triptan currently used another triptan. Among participants with responses, the most common reasons for prior triptan lapses were insufficient headache pain reduction (66%), side effects (50%), not working as well as it used to (28%), and not working quickly enough (28%). Insufficient pain reduction (59% of those with 1 lapsed triptan, 65% with 2, 77% with ≥3; linear by linear association p=0.004), not working as well as it used to (23%, 28%, 36%; p=0.033), and not working quickly enough (20%, 34%, 32%; p=0.034) were reasons generally reported by higher proportions of participants with higher numbers of lapsed triptans. Similar proportions of participants who had lapsed 1, 2, or ≥3 triptans reported side effects (45%, 54%, and 49%; p=0.481).

Conclusion Insufficient pain reduction, side effects, not working as well as it used to, and not working quickly enough were common reasons for triptan lapse. Side effects were reported by ~50% of participants, irrespective of how many triptans had lapsed. The three other most common reasons were more frequently reported in participants with more lapsed triptans. NCT06467370.

P497 Cycles in cluster headache – A prospective study with smart phone app

L. Jabbarian1, D. Ramanagoudra1, F. Riederer1,2, L. Weichsel1,2, C. Schankin1,2

1My Clusters, Founder, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Insel Gruppe AG Neurologische Klinik, Neurology, Bern, Switzerland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P497

Objective Cluster headache (CH) is the most severe primary headache condition, leading to significant suffering and burden. CH is the prototype of a cyclic disorder, with circadian and circannual rhythmicity. Epidemiological data suggest a seasonal pattern in CH occurrence, with peaks around equinoxes, but different patterns have been described with a possible influence of latitude. Most epidemiologic studies on seasonal occurrence were retrospective. Studying cycles in CH such as circadian, circannual or multidien cycles provides further insight in the chronobiologic basis of the disorder. Aim of the study is to further characterize cycles in cluster headache in multinational cohorts distributed over the globe, using a smart phone app to prospectively register attacks.

Methods MyClusters is a live app on the Apple and Google stores where users explicitly consent to sharing data for research. The App was launched on patients’ initiative. All data is anonymized and aggregated in full compliance with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) regulations, ensuring both valuable research insights and absolute patient privacy.

Results Currently as of 26/09/2025 there are 1241 users of the MyClusters app (Fig. 1). 60% agreed to share their user data in anonymized form. This cohort includes 584 men (mean age 42.11±12.91) and 472 women (mean age 41.44+13.66). The mean disease duration is 9.9 years. 374 have episodic cluster headache and 647 chronic.

Conclusion We suggest that studying temporal dynamics with a smart phone app can yield important information on the chronobiology of the disease. Integrating patients’ organizations in App and study design will ensure user friendliness and adherence.

P498 Development of the Sinus Headache Screener (SHS) for identification of non-rhinogenic facial pressure/pain

D. Jang1, H. J. Lee2, F. Godley III3, T. Collins2, R. Abi Hachem1, B. Goldstein1, T. Coles2

1Duke University, Otolaryngology, Durham, NC, USA; 2Duke University, Durham, NC, USA; 3University Otolaryngology, Providence, RI, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P498

Objective Patients presenting with sinus headaches often have non-rhinogenic facial pain/pressure (NRFP). However, these patients are frequently misdiagnosed with sinusitis, leading to inappropriate antibiotic utilization and unnecessary surgical procedures. We introduce the Sinus Headache Screener (SHS), which was developed for the purpose of differentiating NRFP from sinusitis.

Methods A question bank consisting of 89 items was developed through a qualitative interview process of 26 patients with midfacial pain or pressure. The question bank was then administered to a larger cohort of patients and a backward variable selection logistic model was utilized to identify the items that could best differentiate CRS from NRFP. The diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) or NRFP was assigned based on imaging criteria. The predictive performance of the SHS was evaluated with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).

Results Of the 251 patients enrolled, 114 had CRS, and 137 had NRFP. Mean (SD) age was 50 (16), and 69.3% (n=174) were women. Eight items pertaining to symptom chronicity, triggers (weather changes, exercise), associated symptoms (motion sickness, loss of ability to smell, twitching on face, ear pain) and nasal mucus quality were selected and assigned a score. Using a total score of 1 or greater to identify NRFP, the eight-item SHS had a sensitivity of 0.79 and specificity of 0.64, and positive/negative predictive values of 0.72/0.73. The AUROC was 0.822 (95% confidence interval 0.796, 0.902).

Conclusion The SHS can serve as an effective screening tool for differentiating CRS from NRFP. Given the high incidence of NRFP in the general population, the SHS could significantly improve healthcare efficiency and cost.

P499 Cluster headache in the emergency department

M. Ravelo León1, D. S. Gómez de la Torre Morales1, B. Rodríguez García1, J. S. Rodríguez Carrillo1, J. A. Aguilera Aguilera1, M. Luz Esteve1, I. Díaz Díaz1, S. Borja Andrés1, L. López Mesonero1, Á. Criado Antón1

1Hospital Universitario de Salamanca, Neurology, Salamanca, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P499

Objective To analyse the treatment received and subsequent follow-up of patients diagnosed with cluster headache in the emergency department of a fourth level hospital.

Methods We retrospectively reviewed 101 episodes with coding compatible with cluster headache, corresponding to 73 patients from July 2021 to May 2025.

Results 71.2% were men compared to 28.8% women, with a mean age of 42.2 years (SD 12.97). Most patients were not urgently evaluated by Neurology (87.1%) and a high percentage were not discharged to outpatient clinics (40.6%), while 9.9% were evaluated in outpatient clinics with an alternative diagnostic impression. In relation to the treatment received in the emergency department, the most used was the combination of NSAIDs plus oxygen therapy in 21.8% of cases, followed by triptans plus oxygen therapy in 16.8% and isolated NSAIDs in 15.8%, followed by other more infrequent combinations. Anesthetic block was performed in 6.0%. As for preventive treatment at discharge, no preventive treatment was initiated in 59.4%. In the remaining patients, the most used options were corticosteroids (12.9%), corticosteroids and verapamil (11.9%) and verapamil (6.9%). The months with the most episodes were July, January and December with 13.9%, 11.9% and 10.9% of visits respectively, and those with the least were June and October with 4% and 5% respectively.

Conclusion Most cases do not receive urgent care by Neurology, which results in worse therapeutic regimens, less use of preventive drugs at discharge and lack of subsequent follow-up.

P500 Validation of MIGRAGILE: A self-administered screening tool for the early detection of disabling migraine in primary care

M. T. Marco Galindo1, M. d. l. N. Fabregat Fabra1, V. Obach Baurier1, A. Grajea1, S. Fernández Fernández1

1Hospital Clinic Barcelona, Neurology, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P500

Objective To develop and validate a self-administered screening tool (MIGRAGILE) for the early identification of disabling migraine, specifically high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM) and chronic migraine (CM), in primary care.

Methods MIGRAGILE was developed through a systematic literature review, application of ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria, and expert consensus using the Delphi method. Psychometric validation followed COSMIN guidelines, assessing sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve (AUC), test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC), and interrater reliability (Fleiss’ Kappa). The tool was evaluated in a primary care population with headache, using neurologist-confirmed diagnosis as the gold standard.

Results MIGRAGILE showed a sensitivity of 93.7%, specificity of 94.0%, and an AUC of 0.938. Test-retest reliability had an ICC of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.85–0.93), and interrater reliability was substantial (Fleiss’ Kappa = 0.81). Compared to tools such as ID-Migraine™, CATI, and Structured Migraine Interview, MIGRAGILE demonstrated higher diagnostic performance and better suitability for digital self-administration.

Conclusion MIGRAGILE is a valid, reliable, and clinically useful self-administered screening tool for early detection of disabling migraine in primary care. Its integration into nurse-led care models may improve diagnostic timeliness and therapeutic outcomes. Further research should explore its broader implementation.

P501 Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias following unilateral dorsolateral medullary infarction: A case series

S. H. Lee1, J. M. Kim1

1Chonnam National University Hospital, Chonnam National University Medical School, Neurology, Gwangju, South Korea

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P501

Objective Secondary trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs) have predominantly been associated with posterior fossa abnormalities, such as tumors and vascular malformations. However, TACs following brainstem ischemic lesions have rarely been reported. We aimed to determine the clinical characteristics and anatomical substrates for TACs after unilateral dorsolateral medullary infarction.

Methods We identified four patients (3 men; mean age=58.2) who developed TACs after unilateral dorsolateral medullary infarction, fulfilling the diagnostic criteria of the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3). All patients underwent detailed neurological examinations and neuroimaging including diffusion-weighted MRI and MRA. Headache characteristics and cranial autonomic symptoms were analyzed.

Results All patients exhibited stabbing or electric shock-like pain in the ipsilateral periorbital, hemifacial, and temporal regions. Headaches developed weeks after the infarction with brief attacks lasting 1–2 min, occurring 1–5 times per day. Lacrimation (100%) and conjunctival injection (75%) were common autonomic features. Three patients (75%) met criteria for short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache with conjunctival injection and tearing (SUNCT) and one with short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache with autonomic symptoms (SUNA). Notably, each patient exhibited at least one focal neurological deficit (e.g., nystagmus, sensory disturbance), which preceded or accompanied headache onset. Neuroimaging consistently revealed involvement of the trigeminal spinal tract and nucleus, as well as the adjacent spinothalamic tract.

Conclusion In these cases, headache characteristics were more consistent with SUNCT or SUNA than with typical cluster headache. The presence of focal neurological signs in all patients highlights the importance of careful neurological examination in identifying secondary causes of TACs. All patients provided informed consent for publication in an open access journal.

P502 Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia triggered by a viral upper respiratory tract infection

J. M. A. Oliveira1, T. Martins1, M. Rodrigues1, L. Pereira1

1Hospital Garcia de Orta, ULSAS, Serviço Neurologia, Almada, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P502

Objective The trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs) are a group of primary headache disorders characterized by unilateral pain and ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms. Secondary causes must always be excluded, especially in case of rare triggers.

Methods A 32-year-old male, (consenting to have his data published), with previous history of migraine without aura, presents with pharyngeal discomfort, rhinorrhea, dry cough, and low fever, managed symptomatically. By the third day of illness, he develops severe, stabbing pain in the right maxilla irradiating to the ipsilateral occipitotemporal region along with ipsilateral ptosis, lacrimation and conjunctival injection. The episodes last 6–7 s individually, and repeat for 1–2 h at a time, usually thrice daily at fixed hours, with a possible fourth episode during the night. After four days the episodes remitted, alongside resolution of the infectious symptoms. He had similar headaches since his teens, always associated with upper respiratory tract infections, but without autonomic features. He never experienced an episode without an infectious prodrome.

Results Neurological examination was normal. Cranioencephalic MRI showed no abnormality correlating with the cephalalgia. There was only mild past response to paracetamol and no acute response to zolmitriptan. A presumptive diagnosis of secondary SUNCT was made. He is currently managed with a short term prophylactic course of prednisolone 60 mg starting on the first day of a viral upper respiratory tract infection and has since experienced no further episodes.

Conclusion This case highlights a unique presentation of upper respiratory tract infection as a rare TCA mimic/trigger. Secondary cephalalgias are uncommon, but there are cases described associated with tumors, rhinosinusitis. Management is challenging in the absence of definitive guidelines, and in this case patient preference for a short-acting treatment was taken into account.

P504 Factors contributing to inaccurate migraine diagnosis in a tertiary hospital setting in southern Thailand

K. Suwanlaong1, S. Sittisomwong1, D. Dutsadeethammo1

1Songkhla Hospital / Prince Naradhiwas University, Medicine, Songkhla, Thailand

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P504

Objective Migraine is a prevalent and disabling neurological disorder. Accurate and timely diagnosis is crucial for effective treatment. However, misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis is common and leads to suboptimal care and worsened clinical outcomes. This study aims to identify demographic and clinical factors associated with the inappropriate initial diagnosis of migraine among patients attending the Neurology and Headache Clinics at Songkhla Hospital.

Methods A prospective cross-sectional study was conducted from April 2024 to April 2025. Patients ≥18 years with a migraine diagnosis confirmed by two neurologists were enrolled and divided into two groups: those appropriately diagnosed at first consultation and those with prior misdiagnosis. Demographic data, clinical features, treatment history, and the initial diagnosing physician were recorded. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of inappropriate diagnosis.

Results Among 90 patients (mean age 44.4 years; 85% female), 44% had an inappropriate diagnosis. Inappropriately diagnosed patients were more likely to be male (p=0.051), present with bilateral pain (38.5% vs. 19.6%), and report headache worsening with outdoor activities (p=0.019). They were also more likely to have seen non-neurologists initially (only 5.2% saw neurologists vs. 31.4% in the appropriate group, p<0.001). Multivariable analysis revealed that male sex (mOR 14.07, p=0.011), bilateral headache (mOR 3.86, p=0.021), symptom duration >5 months (mOR 3.96, p=0.030), and medication-overuse headache (mOR 3.21, p=0.043) were independently associated with misdiagnosis.

Conclusion Recognizing factors associated with inaccurate migraine diagnosis can guide better screening, referral, and education for primary care providers. This may lead to earlier, more accurate diagnoses and improved patient outcomes.Fig. 1 (abstract P504).

P505 Thunderclap headache as an isolated manifestation of vertebral artery dissection

J. Almeida Ferreira1, T. Geraldes1, M. Rodrigues1, L. Pereira1

1Hospital Garcia de Orta, ULSAS, Neurology, Almada, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P505

Objective Headache red flags are crucial in emergency settings, allowing the identification of etiologies that require specific approaches. These include age over 50 years, explosive onset, positional headache, focal neurological deficits, headache waking the patient from sleep or headache with characteristics different from the patient’s usual pattern.

Methods Patient consent to publish details in an open access journal.

Results A 51-year-old man with no significant personal medical history was admitted in the Emergency Department with sudden onset, throbbing, left occipital headache, with maximum intensity of 8/10 from the start, unresponsive to paracetamol and only temporarily relieved by ibuprofen, for the last 15 days. The neurological exam was normal. Due to a new headache, sudden onset, and refractory nature investigation was carried out. A cerebral CT and an angio-CT revealed a fusiform aneurysm of the V4 segment of the left vertebral artery, with no evidence of hemorrhage. The case was discussed with Neurosurgery and Neuroradiology, and a decision of conservative treatment approach was made. A follow-up MRI with Angio-MRI revised the diagnosis to a pseudoaneurysm caused by dissection of the left vertebral artery. No focal signs or parenchymal vascular lesions were observed. There was no history of trauma, cervical manipulation or any predisposing activity/position. On the 9-month follow-up Angio-MRI, a significant reduction in the aneurysm size was observed. The headache progressively resolved and no new episodes occurred.

Conclusion The initial diagnosis at the emergency department of a secondary headache due to an unruptured vascular malformation was revised during follow-up to acute headache attributed to vertebral artery dissection. We emphasize the importance of clinical and imaging re-evaluation of patients with explosive headaches, which enables definitive etiological diagnosis and, consequently, more appropriate preventive treatment.

P506 Intracranial hypertension without visual disturbance in seronegative viral meningitis

K. Chang1

1Uijeongbu Eulji University Hospital, Neurology, Seoul, South Korea

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P506

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Intracranial hypertension(IH) may be observed in patients with meningitis, but this is most often due to bacterial, fungal or tuberculous causes rather than viruses. IH secondary to viral infection (IHSVI) is a rare manifestation of viral meningitis. In known cases of IHSVI, specific viruses such as HIV, enterovirus, VZV and HHV-6 have commonly been detected in patients presenting with visual disturbance. We present a patient of IH with seronegative viral meningitis, but without visual disturbance.

Methods Case.

Results A 20-year-old woman (BMI 21.2 kg/m²) was hospitalized with persistent headache, fever, and nausea for three weeks, with no visual disturbance. A neurological examination revealed bilateral papilledema, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study showed an opening pressure of 36cmH₂O, WBC 33/μL (with 98% lymphocytes), RBC 0, protein 25.5(15–45 mg/dL), glucose 51(45–75 mg/dL). CSF showed negative for CMV, HSV, VZV, enterovirus, VDRL, cryptococcal antigen, bacterial and fungal cultures. Her brain MRI revealed no other cause of elevated intracranial pressure or leptomeningeal enhancement. She was initially started on IV mannitol six times daily and dexamethasone four times daily, which were tapered off when her symptoms disappeared and also started on acetazolamide 500 mg twice daily. CSF study performed two weeks later showed an opening pressure of 19.5cmH₂O, WBC 3 cells/μL, RBC 0, protein 40.8 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL. She was discharged from the hospital and discontinued acetazolamide without experiencing any symptoms at her first outpatient follow-up.

Conclusion This case shows that severe elevations in intracranial pressure can occur in seronegative viral meningitis without visual disturbance.

P507 Acute confusional migraine in adults – A case report

M. Pereira1,2, A. I. Gonçalves1, A. Fernandes1, T. C. Aguiar1

1Hospital Dr. Nélio Mendonça - Centro Hospitalar do Funchal, Serviço Regional de Saúde da Madeira – Portugal, Serviço de Neurologia, Funchal, Portugal; 2Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Instituto de Fisiologia, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P507

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Acute confusional migraine is characterized by transient impairment of higher cortical functions and behavioral changes, with or without altered consciousness. Episodes last around 6 h, resolve fully within 24 h, and are followed or accompanied by migraine. Its prevalence is low, and adult-onset is particularly rare. There are no recognized diagnostic criteria; diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, migraine history, and exclusion of other causes.

Methods A 68-year-old man with hypertension and episodic migraine with visual aura presented to the emergency department with behavioral changes lasting 2 h, preceded by a visual disturbance identical to his usual aura. During observation, he developed prosopagnosia toward relatives and severe hetero-aggressiveness. Diazepam, haloperidol, and chlorpromazine were administered, but agitation persisted. Brain CT with angiography and lab tests were unremarkable. Due to acute behavioral change and isolated fever (38.4 °C), infectious encephalitis was suspected. Lumbar puncture was performed, and empiric antibiotics plus acyclovir were started but discontinued within hours after normal CSF and negative viral PCR. The patient remained afebrile; hyperthermia was attributed to neuroleptics.

Results Brain MRI and EEG showed no significant findings. Symptoms resolved within 24 h. After recovery, the patient reported that the episode had been preceded by his usual visual aura and migraine.

Conclusion Although self-limiting, no abortive treatment is available; however, valproic acid and topiramate may be used to treat and prevent recurrences. The absence of formal criteria and the diagnosis being one of exclusion hinder clinical recognition.

P508 Diagnostic challenges of secondary headache due to arteriovenous fistula in a patient with neurofibromatosis type 1

O. Tsurkalenko1,2, Y. Cherednichenko3, L. Dziak1, V. Suk1, M. Reiff2, S. Beyenburg2

1Dnipro Medical University, Dnipro, Ukraine; 2Center Hospitalier de Luxembourg, Strassen, Luxembourg; 3Mechnikov Dnipropetrovsk Regional Clinical Hospital, Dnipro, Ukraine

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P508

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective To highlight the diagnostic complexity of secondary headache due to rare vascular pathology in a patient with Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1), initially misdiagnosed as migraine.

Methods We present a rare clinical case of a patient with NF1 who developed a new-onset, migraine-like headache, ultimately diagnosed as a secondary headache due to an underlying craniovertebral arteriovenous fistula (AVF).

Results A 52-year-old female with a longstanding history of NF1 presented with new-onset episodes of left-sided pulsatile hemicranial headaches, associated with photophobia and phonophobia but unresponsive to analgesics or triptans. Over the course of one year, headache frequency progressively increased, reaching 23 days per month. Migraine was preliminary diagnosed by family doctor. Three days prior to a scheduled neurologic consultation, she developed transient right-sided weakness and speech problems. Similar transient episodes subsequently occurred daily. Neurological examination was unremarkable, except for numerous cutaneous neurofibromas and café-au-lait spots (Fig. 1); a pulsatile mass was palpable in the left posterolateral cervical region. Endovascular embolization was performed using a balloon-assisted technique with Onyx and detachable coils, achieving complete AVF occlusion (Fig. 3). Post-procedure, the patient reported complete resolution of headache and transient neurological symptoms.

Conclusion New-onset headaches may mimic primary headache disorders but can signal serious secondary causes like AVF. Prompt imaging and referral are essential to prevent complications and ensure timely, effective treatment.Fig. 1 (abstract P508).Fig. 2 (abstract P508).Fig. 3 (abstract P508).

P509 When the face twitches: An atypical neurological presentation of spontaneous intracranial hypotension

S. Gomes1, S. Moreira1, S. Marques2, J. Louro Cruz3, S. Varanda1, A. R. Silva1

1Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Neurology, Braga, Portugal; 2ULS do Tâmega e Sousa, Neurology, Penafiel, Portugal; 3Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Anaesthesiology, Braga, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P509

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Hemifacial spasm has been reported as a manifestation of spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH). Downward traction of the VII cranial nerve and venous congestion near the nerve root may represent the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Treatment with an epidural blood patch may lead to symptomatic improvement and enhance the response to botulinum toxin.

Methods Case presentation with literature review.

Results A 45-year-old man presented with right hemifacial spasm occurring multiple times per hour throughout the day and persistent during sleep. Further anamnesis revealed a new-onset, moderate-intensity occipital non-positional headache, triggered by Valsalva maneuvers and resolving spontaneously within a few minutes. He also experienced right-sided tinnitus and subjective memory impairment. MRI revealed pachymeningeal enhancement, engorgement of the venous sinuses, pituitary enlargement, and brain sagging. There was no evidence of a dural arteriovenous fistula, neurovascular contact or parenchymal lesions. He was initially treated with clonazepam without improvement, followed by botulinum toxin type A injections, which resulted in a partial reduction of the spasms. Due to partial response, the patient underwent a lumbar epidural blood patch with 22 mL of autologous blood, which led to an improvement in the frequency of the spasms.

Conclusion This case underscores the importance of integrating focal neurological deficits with headache syndromes, including rare manifestations of SIH. Considering the long-term complications of venous congestion, an alternative treatment was proposed for both headache and hemifacial spasm.

P515 A novel liquid biopsy for patient triage

E. Gray1, J. Cameron1, H. Butler1, G. Antoniou1, D. Eustace1, A. Lazarus1, D. Palmer1, A. Sala1, A. Lishman1, M. Baker1

1Dxcover Limited, Glasgow, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P515

Objective Early brain tumour signs can be subtle and mistaken for conditions including migraine, fatigue and stress. Resulting diagnostic delays impact brain cancer patient quality of life and survival. Positive predictive value (PPV) of symptom-based suspected brain cancer referral guidelines, for the presence of “symptoms related to the central nervous system” is 2.9%, but such well-differentiated symptoms are rare. The PPV for symptoms such as headache is only 0.09%.

The Dxcover® Brain liquid biopsy is a rapid multiomic test that detects brain tumours in serum. Infrared spectroscopy produces a molecular signature, and an algorithm predicts presence or absence of cancer.

Objective

To introduce a rapid liquid biopsy to triage patients with non-specific symptoms of brain cancer.

Methods EMBRACE is a prospective multicentre clinical validation study with 7 UK & European sites. Diagnostic performance (sensitivity & specificity) for the detection of malignant tumours was estimated across all patients, and for an intended-use population subgroup presenting with relatively non-specific and non-urgent symptoms including headache.

Results Over 2500 patients participated, of which the intended use population was 1338. Among intended-use patients, 42% presented with headache as primary symptom, and test sensitivity was 86% (95%CI:80-90%) at 44% (95%CI:41-47%) specificity. Negative predictive value (NPV) is predicted to range from 99.0% to 99.8% in symptomatic populations with disease prevalence between 0.5% and 3%. Corresponding PPVs ranged from 0.8% to 4.5%.

Conclusion Early and expeditious diagnosis is crucial to reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with brain cancer. This simple, non-invasive test would support clinical decision-making and facilitate patient triage to rapid imaging. Diagnosis when tumours are smaller is asssociated with reduced morbidity, reduced healthcare resource utilisation, and a mortality benefit (data under review).

P516 Red flags in headache attributed to infection: A diagnostic aid based on SNNOOP10 and ICHD-3 classification

M. Kozák1, V. Bencs2

1University of Debrecen, Department of Infectology, Debrecen, Hungary; 2University of Debrecen, Department of Neurology, Debrecen, Hungary

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P516

Objective Infection-related headaches are common but often under-recognized, particularly when clinical features are subtle or atypical. Our aim was to develop a structured diagnostic aid that integrates the SNNOOP10 red flag system with the ICHD-3 classification to improve early detection of infectious causes of headache.

Methods We performed a structured comparative analysis of the SNNOOP10 red flag symptoms and the corresponding infection-related categories in the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3). For each SNNOOP10 item, we identified the most relevant ICHD-3 diagnostic subtype and its potential infectious etiologies based on expert consensus and literature review. These relationships were summarized in a correlation table intended as a practical tool for use in emergency and inpatient neurology settings.

Results The analysis demonstrated a strong alignment between SNNOOP10 components and ICHD-3 infection-related categories. For instance, systemic fever was linked to meningitis or encephalitis, altered mental status to brain abscess or viral encephalitis, and immunosuppression to opportunistic infections such as cryptococcosis. The resulting table visually maps SNNOOP10 symptoms to relevant infectious mechanisms and ICHD-3 subtypes, supporting rapid and focused diagnostic reasoning.

Conclusion An infection-adapted interpretation of SNNOOP10, when combined with ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria, may enhance early recognition of infection-associated headaches. This integrated framework offers a practical clinical support tool to aid urgent triage and improve diagnostic accuracy in settings where timely identification of CNS infections is critical.

P518 Benign episodic unilateral mydriasis and headache: More than meets the eye

U. Ashraf1,2, N. Karsan3,1,2, P. J. Goadsby4,1,2

1King’s College London, NIHR King’s Clinical Research Facility, SLaM Biomedical Research Centre, London, UK; 2King’s College London, Wolfson Sensory, Pain and Regeneration Centre, London, UK; 3University Hospital Lewisham, Department of Neurology, London, UK; 4King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Thuwal, Saudi Arabia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P518

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Benign episodic unilateral mydriasis (BEUM) is a rare and incompletely understood entity that has previously been associated with migraine. Associations with other headache phenotypes have not been reported.

Methods We present two cases of BEUM associated with differing headache phenotypes.

Results A 47-year-old man presented to our service with approximately 30-40 episodes a day of unilateral right eye pupillary dilation, associated with blurring of right eye vision resolving in 2–3 min and 2-4/10 severity throbbing pain in the right occiput that lasted between 3 and 10 min. P519 Migrainous infarction: A systematic review and critical reappraisal

E. Schou1, A. Harriott2, C. Ayata2, A. Hougaard1

1Copenhagen University Hospital, Department of Neurology, Herlev, Denmark; 2Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P519

Objective Migrainous infarction - ischemic stroke occurring during migraine with aura - is a rare stroke etiology, typically affecting young women. The mechanism by which aura might cause infarction remains uncertain, while emerging evidence suggests the reverse relation: cerebral ischemia may trigger spreading depolarization, perceived as migraine aura. We systematically reviewed reported cases to assess whether clinical or imaging data support migraine aura as a cause of infarction.

Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched without date or language restrictions for ischemic strokes attributed to migraine with aura. Two reviewers extracted clinical, neuroimaging, and etiological data, evaluating fulfillment of migrainous infarction criteria and evidence supporting aura-induced ischemia.

Results Among 2,762 screened records, 156 cases (102 women, mean age 35.5 years) published between 1883 and 2024 in nine languages were identified. One hundred twenty-three patients had prior migraine with aura, but in 85 cases the presenting symptoms differed from previous auras. Neuroimaging confirmed ischemic stroke in 128 patients, yet none showed patterns suggestive of spreading depolarization–induced infarction, such as lesions spanning adjacent vascular territories. Only 33 cases underwent a basic etiologic work-up; none received a guideline-recommended evaluation including echocardiography, ≥48-h cardiac monitoring, vascular imaging, and antiphospholipid screening.

Conclusion We did not identify cases clearly demonstrating cerebral infarction caused by migraine aura. Co-occurring migraine with aura and cerebral infarction may be better explained by ischemia-induced spreading depolarization. A diagnosis of migrainous infarction may lead to insufficient diagnostic evaluation to rule out alternative stroke etiologies.

P520 Clinical characteristics and treatment outcomes in resistant and refractory migraine: Application of the European Headache Federation (EHF) 2020 criteria in a UK tertiary headache cohort

E. James1, D. Folami1, M. Randall1, S. Fairclough1, L. Idrovo1

1Leeds Teaching Hospital NHS, Neurology, Headache Service, Leeds, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P520

Objective To characterise resistant and refractory migraine patients according to EHF 2020 criteria in a tertiary UK headache service and to compare demographics, phenotype, and treatment outcomes.

Methods Consecutive migraine patients referred to Leeds Headache Service between 2019 and 2024 were included. Demographics, disease duration, baseline headache/migraine frequency, and treatment outcomes (oral, BTX-A, and CGRPmab) Classification as resistant(rM)or refractory(RM) according to EHF2020 criteria.Data was analysed using ‘base r’ and the ‘mgcv’ packages. A logistic regression model was formulated to ascertain predictors of refractoriness.

Migraine Aura present in 53%, with >1 aura subtype more common in resistant patients. (p=0.02, OR 0.16) Higher BMI +depression showed a trend to respond less to first line antiCGRP. P521 Headache characteristics in patients with epilepsy – An observational study

M. Rathinasabapathi1,2, A. Tiwari2,3, M. Kumar2, N. Kumar2,4, P. K. Panda2, Y. Bahurupi2, R. Kumar2

1Pondicherry Institute of Medical sciences, Neurology, Pondicherry, India; 2AIIMS Rishikesh, Neurology, Rishikesh, India; 3AIIMS Gorakhpur, Neurology, Gorakhpur, India; 4AIIMS BibiNagar, Neurology, BIbinagar, India

Objective Headache and epilepsy are two closely related disorders, with the relation between the two disorders still a matter of debate. P523 The role of a double-blind, placebo-controlled intramuscular indomethacin test (IndoTest) for the diagnosis of indomethacin-sensitive headache in an outpatient setting: A prospective cohort study

S. Maniataki1, F. Greenwood1, P. Amarasena1,2, N. Karsan1,2, U. Ashraf1,2, A. Gimson1,2, M. D. Villar-Martínez1,2, D. Moreno Ajona1,2, D. Y. Wei1,2, P. J. Goadsby1,2

1King’s College Hospital, Neurology, London, UK; 2King’s College London, Wolfson SPaRC, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P523

Objective Accurate diagnosis of indomethacin-sensitive headache is vital and can save patients from a frustrating journey of trying unhelpful treatments. The simplest way is an oral indomethacin trial; however, for many patients with comorbidities, this can be a relative contraindication and therefore not done. In these cases, an observed double-blind, placebo-controlled intramuscular (IM) indomethacin test (IndoTest) is recommended.

Methods We collected a prospective cohort (2024-2025) of adults who underwent an outpatient IndoTest at King’s College Hospital London as part of a service evaluation. Reasons for referral, headache phenotype with test response, and final diagnosis, alongside patient characteristics were recorded.

Results Thirty patients were screened and contacted; two did not attend, and six did not proceed with the IndoTest due to medical issues present upon review of day one of the IndoTest. The average age was 50 years old (range 31-69), 77% women. The reason for the referral was possible hemicrania continua (80%), paroxysmal hemicrania (17%) and primary cough headache (3%). The majority of patients had a relative contraindication to the oral test, and 11 patients had tried the oral trial already, 45% reaching the maximum daily dose of 225 mg. There were 6 patients (27%) who had a positive IndoTest, 5 hemicrania continua and 1 primary stabbing headache. Two had tried indomethacin orally, one reached the maximum dose with an unclear response and caused low mood. The rest had relative contraindications to an oral test. Following the IndoTest, melatonin (n = 3), greater occipital nerve injections (n = 3), and non-invasive vagal nerve stimulator (n = 3) were initiated.

Conclusion The double-blind, placebo-controlled IndoTest is a useful tool, especially for those who are not able to tolerate the oral test. In the absence of this, patients may be incorrectly managed.

P524 Phenotypic features of menstrually-related migraine without aura

H. Cetinalp1,2, H. Al-Mashat1,2, E. Gozalov1,2, S. Younis1,2, F. M. Amin1,2

1Danish Headache Center, Rigshospitalet, Neurology, Rigshospitalet, Glostrup, Denmark; 2Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Glostrup, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P524

Objective Menstrually-related migraine (MRM) is often reported as a severe subtype of migraine. However, International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD)-3 does not provide specific criteria for MRM based on clinical phenotype. Aim of this study was to characterize clinical phenotype in women experiencing MRM.

Methods A semi-structured interview (SSI) was used to characterize the clinical phenotype in women screened for a separate study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06470958). These women were required to report at hospital during ongoing migraine attacks without aura in relation to their menstrual period. Women who arrived at hospital during ongoing attacks were also clinically phenotyped during these attacks.

Results A total of 32 women with MRM were interviewed, whereof 18 completed a questionnaire during ongoing attacks. Mean age was 30.7 years (SD 5.4). Mean disease duration was 11.3 years (SD: 6.6). In total group, 59.4 reported unilateral pain, 84.4% throbbing quality, 100% moderate/severe pain, 96.9% experienced aggravation by routine physical activity, 90.6% reported nausea, 93.8% photophobia and 78.1% phonophobia. Importantly, less than 50% of the patients experienced unilateral pain and nausea during MRM attacks. These findings highlights the need for a comprehensive characterization of MRM phenotype in a large-scale MRM population to improve diagnosis of this subtype of migraine in the ICHD.

P525 Underestimated headache frequency in healthy control volunteers

C. Domingos Belo1, M. D. Villar-Martínez1, A. Abdalla1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College Hospital, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P525

Objective Reliable identification of “healthy controls” (HC) is important in migraine research. Volunteers who consider themselves “headache-free” may underestimate headache (HA) frequency and have unrecognised migraine, complicating control selection. We explored discrepancies between self-perceived and objective HA frequency and characterised migraine-related features and history.

Methods Pre-screening data from 56 volunteers (aged 18–52) registering as HC for our migraine studies were analysed. HC was defined as <4 HA/year and no migraine characteristics per ICHD-3. Participants reported HA occurrence via an open-ended question, a categorical scale (frequently, sometimes, rarely, very rarely, never) and a quantitative scale (daily, <3/week, <3/month, <3/year, <1/year, never had). Associated symptoms per ICHD-3: photophobia, phonophobia, motion sensitivity, nausea, vomiting), and other medical or family history were recorded. Verbal descriptions were categorised, and descriptive analyses explored mismatches between perceived and reported frequency.

Results Although all participants self-identified as headache-free, 31/56 did not meet preliminary HC criteria. Self-perception often underestimated frequency: 15/31 reported ≥2–3 HA/month, of which 11/15 selected “rare” or “very rare”; 27/31 reported migraine characteristics, and 19/27 had ≥2 features. Most frequent qualitative descriptions were “occasional HA”, “due to dehydration”, or “sleep deprivation”.

Conclusion Discrepancies between self-perceived and reported phenotype were common: 55% of volunteers identifying as “headache-free” did not meet HC criteria. Many reported migraine-like features per ICHD-3, suggesting possible undiagnosed migraine. These findings open the discussion of how HC should be defined in migraine studies and highlight the need for structured screening to ensure valid HC selection.

P526 Challenging the criteria: A case of unclassifiable trigeminal autonomic-like headache

E. Cruz Alves1, P. Lopes Ferreira1, I. Alves1

1Unidade Local de Saúde Entre Douro e Vouga, Neurology, Santa Maria da Feira, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P526

Objective To discuss the diagnostic challenges of headaches with prominent autonomic features that don’t meet criteria for any defined trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia.

Methods Clinical case report.

Results A 52-year-old woman with a history of right-sided hemicranial headache associated with the menstrual cycle, resolved after surgical menopause. No regular medication or relevant family history. Conclusion Despite the atypical pain duration, the presence of prominent autonomic signs and the partial response to Verapamil favours a diagnosis within the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia spectrum, highlighting the diagnostic complexity of these entities.

P527 CSF hypotension headache and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS)

D. Siquenique1, M. Henriques1, R. Gonçalo Pinheiro1, P. Neves1, J. Peres1, E. Parreira1

1ULS Amadora Sintra, Neurology, Amadora, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P527

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Can orthostatic headache following spinal anaesthesia be explained solely by CSF hypotension, or might it reflect overlap with autonomic disorders such as POTS?

Methods Clinical observation of a 65-year-old male with post-spinal anaesthesia orthostatic headache.

Results A 65-year-old male developed headache 2 days after spinal anaesthesia. The headache was 6/10 in the pain scale, had photophobia and phonophobia, worsened with orthostatism and was partially relieved by oral painkillers. At that time he was treated only with oral analgesics. Two months later the headache got worse, (8/10 in the pain scale) and with inability to tolerate standing. A Neuraxis MRI did not document signs of CSF hypotension (Bern Score = 0), intracranial bleeding or cerebral venous thrombosis. A lumbar puncture in the left lateral decubitus position revealed opening pressure of 5cmCSF. The CSF analysis was normal. After treatment with painkillers, caffeine and two epidural blood patches there was a modest improvement of the headache. An occipital nerve block was successful in reducing the headache to 2/10. Nevertheless, the patient began to complain of unspecific symptoms upon assuming the upright position. These symptoms included light-headedness, malaise, and palpitation. A heart rate increase of 29 bpm was noted in orthostatic position, without orthostatic hypotension. A tilt table test confirmed the diagnosis of POTS. The patient began propranolol that resolved his complaints.

Conclusion This case shows the clinical overlap between CSF hypotension manifestations and POTS. Orthostatic headache, although typical of CSF hypotension, can occur in POTS due to autonomic mechanisms still to be ascertained. The persistence of symptoms with orthostatism should motivate the exclusion of complications and additional investigation of other etiologies that are associated with orthostatic headaches. The association between these two conditions requires further investigation as a causality is yet to be established with certainty.

P528 Tension headache treatment using local mechanical vibration targeting temporalis and occipitalis muscles – A non-invasive method

M. Ameer1,2, G. Alfuhigi2, F. Alruwaili2, S. Alruwaili2

Objective Tension headaches are the most common type of headache and thought to be caused by stress in daily life. So, this study uses a non-invasive vibration technique to target the precranial muscles’ myofascial trigger points, which can reduce pain.

Methods A randomized control trial was conducted. Conclusion Patients with tension headaches who received vibration therapy employing 150 Hz frequency ranges experienced improvements in their NPRS and disability. Mechanical Vibration therapy may therefore be a useful strategy for relieving tension headache discomfort.

P532 High lung doses of Aerosolized Acetylsalicylic Acid (ASA) feasible with new customized mesh nebulizer device: The ASCOT™ inhaler

M. Frey1, T. Kolb1, A. Fischer2, K. Sommerer3, K. Nocker4

1Activoris Medizintechnik GmbH, Development, Gauting, Germany; 2Activoris Medizintechnik GmbH, Headquarters, Gemünden, Germany; 3Actarmo Medical GmbH, Gauting, Germany; 4AspiAir GmbH, Gemünden, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P532

Objective To assess the optimum drug concentration and device parameters for high alveolar deposition and acceptable treatment time of ASA. Commercially available mesh nebulizers generate inappropriate particle sizes for deep lung delivery of ASA, or even produce no aerosol at all, calling for a customized high-performance nebulizer. Dose requirements (up to 1,000 mg ASA) and human factor aspects are a challenge for migraine treatments. Nebulizer design must consider these requirements.

Methods Initial bench tests indicated individual mesh and electronic parameters for different ASA concentrations. Particle size by laser diffraction, total output rate (TOR) were used as criteria for optimization of hard- and software parameters. Drug stability post nebulization and Delivered Dose ex mouthpiece (DD) was confirmed externally (Actarmo Medical, Munich). Following the optimization cycles, in-vitro aerosol characterization studies were done. Data were used to calculate lung dose and treatment time using the ICRP model.

Results Particle size for LASAG (µm) were at 4.6 ± 0.45 (1 g/5 ml), and 4.0 ± 0.25 (2 g/5 ml). TOR (ml/min) was at 1.25 ± 0.45 (1 g/5 ml), and 0.9 ± 0.25 (2 g/5 ml), corresponding to a TOR of 2.25 ± 0.65 with NaCL. Given a 1:1 ratio of inhalation/exhalation (4 s/4sec), treatment times were estimated to be between 10 and 12 min for one vial (500 mg ASA). DD (mg ASA) was at 400 ± 25. The optimized setup was used in a PK-study with 16 healthy subjects, confirming the expected high deep lung deposition. Bioavailability of ASA was at 62% of the previously measured DD.

Conclusion The PK-study indicates that the ASCOT™ Inhaler delivers therapeutically relevant doses of ASA to the lung in healthy subjects. Measured bioavailability confirmed bench tests and model calculations. Results will be included in further device optimizations.

P534 The efficacy of gepants in the prophylactic management of migraine: A systematic review

W. Gonçalves Horta1, L. Raulino de Souza Moreira2, A. Vitor Vasconcelos Maciel2, E. Barros Teti2, G. Batista dos Santos Porto2, L. Antonio Lima Santos2, T. Diniz Amorim Simões2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

1Universidade de Pernambuco, Headache clinic from Hospital Oswaldo Cruz, Recife, Brazil; 2Universidade Católica de Pernambuco, Recife, Brazil; 3Faculdade de Medicina de Olinda, Neurology, Paulista, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P534

Objective To evaluate the efficacy of Gepants in the prophylactic management of migraine, focusing on the reduction of attack frequency in adult patients.

Methods This systematic review was conducted in accordance with Cochrane and PRISMA guidelines, with protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251017211). PubMed and BVS were searched through March 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating rimegepant or atogepant for migraine prevention. Included studies enrolled adults with migraine onset before age 50 and 4–14 migraine days per month.

Results Six RCTs were analyzed. The primary outcome was the reduction in monthly migraine days compared to placebo. Rimegepant 75 mg taken every other day reduced migraine days by 0.8 (95% CI: -1.5 to -0.2; p = 0.0099). Conclusion Gepants represent a safe and effective oral option for migraine prevention, with significant reductions in attack frequency and improved patient-reported outcomes. Their favorable safety profile and ease of use make them a valuable alternative to existing therapies. Further long-term, head-to-head studies are needed to confirm their sustained efficacy and comparative effectiveness.

P535 Is there an association between the effectiveness of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies in migraine and injection site reactions?

M. Millet Oval1, C. Morales Hernández1, E. Torrent Paz1, A. E. Bartolomé Yumar1, I. N. Owrang Calvo1, V. Pallarés Santos1, E. Rodríguez García1, O. Cruz Cordobés1, A. González Pérez1, E. Cubas Regulo1, M. Solé Sabater1, S. del Águila Romero1, P. I. Dupuy Oria1, Y. Miranda Bacallado2, J. A. Rojo Aladro1

1University Hospital Complex of the Canary Islands, Neurology, La Laguna, Spain; 2Hospital Doctor Negrín, Neurology, Las Palmas de Gran Canarias, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P535

Objective Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) that target the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) pathway are an effective prophylactic treatment for migraine. However, their subcutaneous administration can cause local injection site reactions (ISRs), such as erythema, induration or pain. It has been hypothesized that these reactions could alter the absorption and, consequently, the clinical effectiveness of these protein-based drugs. This study aimed to determine the frequency of ISRs and to investigate whether their presence is associated with treatment efficacy.

Methods We conducted a retrospective, observational study of 334 patients treated with subcutaneous anti-CGRP mAbs at our center between 2021 and 2024. The cohort included patients receiving erenumab (24.8%), galcanezumab (27.8%) and fremanezumab (47.4%). Clinical effectiveness was assessed by comparing changes in the number of migraine and headache days, medication overuse status, and scores on the MIDAS and HIT-6 questionnaires between patients who experienced ISRs.

Results Injection site reactions were reported in 29.5% of the 334 patients. The most common injection site was the abdomen (47.3%), followed by multiple sites (29.3%), the leg (18.5%), and the arm (5%). Despite the high incidence of local reactions, no statistically significant differences were found in any of the measured efficacy outcomes when comparing patients with and without ISRs.

Conclusion Local reactions at the injection site are a common occurrence, affecting nearly one-third of patients on subcutaneous anti-CGRP mAb therapy for migraine. However, our findings suggest that the presence of these reactions does not compromise the clinical efficacy of the treatment. While ISRs may cause patient discomfort, they do not appear to influence therapeutic outcomes.

P536 Efficacy of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions in the prophylaxis cluster headache: A systematic review

W. Gonçalves Horta1, A. Almeida Cavalcante de Melo2, A. Lívia Almeida de Araújo2, G. Nunes Lima2, M. Antonia Souza Bezerra de Carvalho2, M. Gomes da Silva2, M. Guerra Arruda2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

1Universidade de Pernambuco, Headache clinic from Hospital Oswaldo Cruz, Recife, Brazil; 2Universidade Católica de Pernambuco, Recife, Brazil; 3Faculdade de Medicina de Olinda, Neurology, Paulista, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P536

Objective This systematic review evaluates the efficacy and safety of prophylactic treatments for cluster headache (CH). The main question is which preventive therapies effectively reduce attack frequency, intensity, and duration, and their safety profiles. Objectives include assessing pharmacological treatments like galcanezumab, verapamil, lithium, and non-pharmacological options such as non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation (nVNS).

Methods Following Cochrane and PRISMA guidelines, the protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251012089) and published on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.15105877). Included were English-language RCTs and observational studies on adults with frequent or refractory CH undergoing prophylaxis. Exclusions were studies with ineligible designs, pediatric subjects, or lacking relevant outcomes. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central from February 2025 onward, plus backward snowballing. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed bias using Cochrane’s RoB-I tool.

Results From 1,029 articles, 16 met criteria, including RCTs and observational studies with adults experiencing frequent or refractory CH. Galcanezumab showed significant reductions in attack frequency, with ~79% achieving ≥50% reduction by week three. Verapamil and lithium also reduced attacks, differing in onset and side effects. nVNS effectively lowered attack frequency and intensity and reduced abortive medication use. Most studies had moderate risk of bias. Quality of life improved notably with nVNS.

Conclusion Both pharmacological and non-pharmacological prophylaxis effectively manage CH. Galcanezumab and nVNS have the strongest evidence for reducing attack frequency and severity. More long-term, large-scale studies are needed to confirm findings and tailor treatments.

P537 Comparative effectiveness: Amitriptyline and toxin botulinum in tension type headache

W. Gonçalves Horta1, D. Vasconcelos Ferraz de Carvalho2, E. Fernando Viana da Silva2, F. Cintra Uchoa Campelo Costa2, G. Victor Xavier Pacheco2, R. Lopes Falcão Souto2, V. Souza Brandão2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

Objective The study aimed to compare the efficacy of two antidepressant drugs in the treatment of tension headache: amitriptyline and botulinum toxin, based on recent evidence, especially between 2010 and 2025.

Methods Data was searched in the available literature, covering evidence on both the intensity of TTE attacks and their reduction.

Results Amitriptyline is effective in reducing the frequency, duration and intensity of TTC crises. On the other hand, botulinum toxin proved to be an effective alternative for patients who do not respond to or tolerate tricyclic antidepressants.

Conclusion Amitriptyline remains the first-line drug in the treatment of most people. However, botulinum toxin is an important alternative for cases that do not respond to the conventional approach.

P538 Performance analysis of galcanezumab in the prophylaxis of cluster headache: A systematic review of clinical trials

W. Gonçalves Horta1, J. Souza2, L. Lins2, M. Lopes2, M. Isabel Andrade Lima2, M. Isabel Lencastre2, V. Lima2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P538

Objective To assess the quality, safety and effectiveness of Galcanezumab as a preventive and abortive therapy for Cluster Headache.

Methods Searches for clinical trials were conducted in the PubMed® database. Six randomized studies, published between 2019 and 2022, which analyzed the impact of the monoclonal antibody Galcanezumab in cluster headache were included. Effectiveness was the primary outcome, the secondary outcomes were safety and side effects.

Results Galcanezumab has shown effectiveness in preventing cluster headache, with 63,4% to 81% of patients reporting significant improvement in the frequentness of episodes. Conclusion The use of immunotherapy represents great advance in the studies on treating cluster headaches. In the long term, however, additional studies, with a larger number of subjects, will be necessary to consolidate the findings and rectify the biases of the therapeutic approach.

P539 Botulinum toxin as a preventive therapy for tension type headache: A systematic review

W. Gonçalves Horta1, L. de Aquino Arruda Lima2, L. Gama Vilar2, M. Pereira Guirra2, P. Inácio de Oliveira Souza2, R. Jordan Gomes De Oliveira Paulino2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

P540 Reporting of lack of efficacy of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies in migraine patients treated with other concomitant monoclonal antibodies: A VigiBase disproportionality analysis

C. Zecca1,2, R. Noseda3, F. Bedussi3, C. Gobbi1,2,4, A. Ceschi2,3,5

1Neurocenter of Southern Switzerland, Ente Ospedaliero Cantonale, Department of Neurology, Lugano, Switzerland; 2Università della Svizzera Italiana, Faculty of Biomedical Sciences, Lugano, Switzerland; 3Institute of Pharmacological Sciences of Southern Switzerland, Ente Ospedaliero Cantonale, Lugano, Switzerland; 4University Hospital Basel, Department of Neurology, Basel, Switzerland; 5Clinical Trial Unit, Ente Ospedaliero Cantonale, Lugano, Switzerland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P540

Objective Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) pathway are effective preventive treatments for migraine. The impact of concurrent use of other mAbs for different indications on the efficacy of anti-CGRP mAbs remains unclear. This study evaluated reports of lack of efficacy of anti-CGRP mAbs in patients concomitantly treated with other mAbs using VigiBase, the global pharmacovigilance database.

Methods Reports listing erenumab, galcanezumab, fremanezumab, or eptinezumab as suspected or interacting drugs and collected in VigiBase up to March 9th, 2025 were included and classified as cases (reporting lack of efficacy) or non-cases (reporting other adverse drug reactions). Disproportionality analysis was performed and adjusted reporting odds ratios (aRORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) estimated via multivariable logistic regression. A signal of disproportionate reporting was defined as aROR with 95% CI lower bound >1.

Results The study included 20,866 cases and 76,538 non-cases. Non-health professionals were the most frequent reporters, more so among cases (68.1% vs. 58.7%, P<0.0001). Female patients were less represented in cases than non-cases (65.2% vs. 76.4%, P<0.0001), as were young adults (16.2% vs. 22.8%, P<0.0001). Co-reporting of other mAbs for non-migraine indications was uncommon (0.6% cases vs. 1.1% non-cases) and not associated with increased odds of reporting lack of efficacy of anti-CGRP mAb treatment (aROR 0.601; 95% CI lower bound <1).

Conclusion The concomitant use of other mAbs in patients receiving anti-CGRP mAbs for migraine is not associated with increased reporting of lack of efficacy in VigiBase. These findings offer preliminary reassurance regarding the real-world effectiveness of anti-CGRP mAbs when administered in combinations with mAbs for other indications.

P541 Pharmacokinetics and safety of Lu AG09222, an anti-PACAP monoclonal antibody in development for migraine prevention

M. Ashina1,2, J. Areberg3, P. Eriksen3, S. Larsen3, J. Buch Østergaard3, O. M. Lemming3, T. Krogh-Meibom3, I. Florea3, C. Granhall3

1Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Copenhagen, Denmark; 3H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P541

Objective To investigate the pharmacokinetics (PK) and safety of Lu AG09222 using data from three phase 1 clinical trials. Lu AG09222 is a humanised monoclonal antibody targeting pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) that is in development for migraine prevention.

Methods Data were included from a (1) first-in-human single ascending dose trial in healthy participants, including a cohort with co-administered sumatriptan (Lu AG09222 n=68; placebo n=28); (2) single-dose trial in healthy Caucasian, Chinese, and Japanese participants (Lu AG09222 n=40; placebo n=12); and (3) multiple-dose trial in participants with symptomatic allergic rhinitis (Lu AG09222 n=20; placebo n=10). Assessments included intravenous (IV) doses ranging from 1 mg to 750 mg and subcutaneous (SC) doses of 100 mg and 600 mg.

Results Overall, 128 and 50 participants received Lu AG09222 and placebo, respectively. Half-life was ~15 days (IV) and ~15–17 days (SC). Bioavailability after SC administration was ~80%. Maximum serum concentration and area under the curve increased in a dose-proportionate manner in participants receiving single IV doses from 1 mg to 750 mg. After multiple SC doses, exposure increased proportionally between 100 mg and 600 mg. There were no PK differences by sex, and PK was comparable in Caucasian, Japanese, and Chinese cohorts. Co-administration with sumatriptan did not result in PK interactions. Most treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild; the most common TEAEs were injection site reactions (SC) and headache (both IV and SC). One serious AE, perniosis of moderate severity, occurred in a participant 112 days after receiving a single IV dose of 750 mg Lu AG09222 co-administered with sumatriptan.

Conclusion Lu AG09222 exhibited a consistent PK profile across dosing regimens, route of administration and race/ethnicity. Across these trials, no safety concerns were identified, and Lu AG09222 was generally well-tolerated.

P542 Discontinuation of anti-calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) monoclonal Antibodies (mAbs) in migraine patients after 12 months of good response: Are there any predictors of restarting mAbs need? Real-world cohort of 103 patients

A. Grajea1, X. Cifuentes1, S. Fernández Fernández1, V. Obach-Irimia1, N. Pola2, A. Rizo2, M. Á. Sosa1, M. T. Marco Galindo1, M. d. l. N. Fabregat Fabra1, V. Obach Baurier1

1Hospital Clinic, Neurology, Barcelona, Spain; 2Hospital Clinic, Pharmacy, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P542

Objective To assess whether specific demographic or clinical factors in migraine patients with good response to mAbs for at least 12 months are associated with the likelihood of retreatment after discontinuation of antiCGRP mAbs.

Methods Retrospective observational cohort study at a tertiary Headache Unit. We included consecutive patients with high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM) or chronic migraine (CM) treated with anti-CGRP mAbs for ≥12 months, who discontinued due to a sustained good response, defined as ≥50% reduction in baseline monthly headache days (MHD) or ≤4 MHD. Data collected included age, sex, MHD at discontinuation, treatment duration, use of concomitant botulinum toxin, and presence other chronic pain conditions. Follow-up included MHD and HIT-6 scores every 3 months. Patients provided informed consent; study approved by local Ethics Committee (HCB/2021/1327). Variables associated with mAbs reinitiation were analyzed using multivariate logistic regression (SPSS v20).

Results We included 103 patients (mean age 49.0±13.7 years; 86.4% female); 60 had HFEM and 43 CM. They received fremanezumab (n=77) or galcanezumab (n=26) for a median of 25.9 months (IQR 15.6–39.7). Concomitant botulinum toxin was used in 40.8%. mAbs was reinitiated in 46 patients (44.7%) after a median of 91 days (IQR 67.3–126.2). No clinical or demographic variable was significantly associated with reinitiation.

Conclusion In this real-world cohort, nearly half of the patients who discontinued anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies after a sustained good response eventually required resuming treatment. No clinical or demographic predictors were identified, supporting individualized decisions and close follow-up.

P543 Population pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of Lu AG09222, an anti-PACAP monoclonal antibody in development for migraine prevention

J. Areberg1, H. Ashina2, J. Bahl1, I. Florea1, T. Krogh-Meibom1, C. Granhall1

1H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P543

Objective To characterise the population pharmacokinetics (popPK) of Lu AG09222, a humanised anti-pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) monoclonal antibody in development for migraine prevention, and to explore its pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) in terms of PACAP binding (target engagement).

Methods Data were pooled from five clinical trials: four phase 1 trials in healthy individuals and one phase 2 trial in participants with migraine. These included both intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) routes of administration, with single and multiple dosing regimens. Concentrations of Lu AG09222:PACAP complexes in serum (reflecting target engagement) were used as input variables for popPK and PK/PD analyses, which were performed using nonlinear mixed-effects modelling. The interaction between Lu AG09222 and PACAP was characterised through the full target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD) model. Serum disposition of unbound Lu AG09222 was described using a two-compartment model with first-order absorption (for SC administration) and elimination.

Results Dose- and time-dependent increases in Lu AG09222:PACAP-complex concentrations were observed, reaching approximately 50 picomolar at the highest tested dose of 750 mg IV. A clear relationship between the PK profile of Lu AG09222 and its PD effect on PACAP binding was noted for both IV and SC administration. TMDD-based model simulations showed that doses above 100 mg resulted in sustained PACAP inhibition exceeding 90% for several weeks, with modelling indicating up to 8 weeks at higher doses for both IV and SC administration.

Conclusion Both popPK analysis and TMDD-based model simulations of Lu AG09222 demonstrated prolonged, high-level PACAP inhibition after IV and SC administration. These results support the potential of Lu AG09222 for sustained PACAP binding and inhibition in migraine prevention.

P545 Failure of CGRP inhibition as a treatment for complex regional pain syndrome

M. Marques Roque1, R. Rodrigues1, F. Dourado Sotero1,2, M. I. Pavão Martins1,2

1Hospital de Santa Maria, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Centro de Estudos Egas Moniz, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P545

Objective Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a potent vasodilator and pain modulator involved in migraine pathophysiology and possibly in complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS). Both conditions have been associated with elevated CGRP levels, raising interest in targeting this peptide therapeutically.

Methods We report a 51-year-old woman with chronic, treatment-resistant migraine and a 2-year history of CRPS following Achilles tendon rupture.

The patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Results Preventive migraine therapies, including oral drugs and botulinum toxin, were ineffective. She was started on galcanezumab (anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody), resulting in a rapid and sustained reduction in migraine frequency (from 16 to 4 days/month) and severity, with significant improvement in quality of life. Rimegepant (a CGRP receptor antagonist) was also effective for acute attacks. However, despite this response, CRPS-related pain and autonomic symptoms remained unchanged, with scales of pain dimension (PGIC and PNVRS) revealing severe pain persistence and lack of perceived change in CPRS-related symptoms despite six months of anti-CGRP therapy.

Conclusion This case highlights a clinical dissociation between two CGRP-associated conditions. Despite a marked improvement in migraine with anti-CGRP therapies, chronic CRPS did not respond to the same treatment. This may suggest that, in the chronic phase of CRPS, the pathophysiological mechanisms may not predominantly depend on CGRP, reflecting differences in pain pathophysiology in the chronic stage. While migraine predominantly involves CGRP-mediated trigeminovascular pathways, CRPS may involve more complex and multifactorial mechanisms, including central sensitization, neurogenic inflammation, and autonomic dysfunction. This example underscores the importance of a differentiated approach to chronic pain conditions, even in the presence of shared biomarkers.
