P549 Efficacy, safety, and tolerability of atogepant for the acute treatment of migraine: Results from the ECLIPSE trial

A. van Dycke1, E. Brand-Schieber2, R. Ornello3, M. J. Lee4,5, H. Guo2, L. Luo2, T. Takeshima6, D. Holle-Lee7, C. Tassorelli8,9, E. Cohen2, L. Barcomb2, K. Nagy2

1General Hospital Sint-Jan Bruges, Department of Neurology, Brugge, Belgium; 2AbbVie, North Chicago, IL, USA; 3University of L’Aquila, Department of Biotechnological and Applied Clinical Sciences, L’Aquila, Italy; 4Seoul National University Hospital, Department of Neurology, Seoul, South Korea; 5Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea; 6Tominaga Hospital, Headache Center and Department of Neurology, Osaka, Japan; 7University of Essen, Department of Neurology, West German Headache and Vertigo Center Essen, Essen, Germany; 8University of Pavia, Department of Brain and Behavioral Sciences, Pavia, Italy; 9IRCCS C. Mondino Foundation, Headache Science & Neurorehabilitation Centre, Pavia, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P549

Objective Evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of atogepant 60 mg compared with placebo for the acute treatment of a single migraine attack.

Methods ECLIPSE was a randomized, double-blind (DB), placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of atogepant for the acute treatment of migraine. Subjects were randomized to 4 DB treatment sequences to treat 4 qualifying migraine attacks with moderate or severe headache with atogepant or placebo. The first attack (1:1 placebo to atogepant allocation) was the single attack used for the primary and 16 secondary efficacy endpoints. The primary endpoint was pain freedom at 2 h postdose (2 h). Two of the key secondary endpoints were absence of the most bothersome symptom (MBS) and pain relief at 2 h. The multiple-attack design was to evaluate consistency of effect. After treating 4 qualifying DB migraine attacks within 16 weeks, subjects entered an open-label (OL) period up to week 24. Efficacy was assessed after all main study subjects completed the DB period; safety was assessed for DB and available OL data.

Results Atogepant (N=602) was superior (P<0.0001) to placebo (N=612) when percent responders were compared for pain freedom (atogepant=24.3%; placebo=13.1%; OR:2.36[1.76,3.15]), MBS freedom (atogepant=43.7%; placebo=32.7%; OR:1.77[1.41,2.24]), and pain relief (atogepant=72.1%; placebo=54.4%; OR:2.35[1.85,2.98]) at 2 h. There were no treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) with incidence ≥2%, and one serious AE (SAE) occurred after placebo treatment for the first attack. No SAEs were considered related to atogepant or occurred in >1 subject in the DB period. No new safety signals were identified.

Conclusion Atogepant was efficacious, safe, and well tolerated for the acute treatment of migraine.

P551 Preclinical platforms for headache therapeutics: PACAP-38 and Capsaicin Vasodilation models in rodents

A. Asuni1, S. Goineau-Brissieux2, S. Djemmali2, F. Tantot2, P. Guillaume2

1H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2Porsolt, Le Genest-Saint-Isle, France

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P551

Objective Migraine is a complex neurovascular disorder involving vasodilation, neuroimmune activation, and nociceptive signaling. PACAP-38 and capsaicin are key mediators implicated in migraine pathophysiology through distinct mechanisms; PACAP-38 via signaling through its receptors and mast cell activation, and capsaicin via TRPV1 receptor-mediated neurogenic inflammation. This study aimed to establish and validate two complementary in vivo models of dermal vasodilation in anesthetized rats to support mechanistic profiling and therapeutic screening of headache-relevant targets.

Methods In the PACAP model, male Sprague-Dawley rats received intravenous DPBS 24 h prior to intradermal PACAP-38 (1 nmol or 10 pmol/site) or PBS vehicle. In the capsaicin model, male Wistar rats received topical capsaicin (1 mg/site) or ethanol: acetone vehicle applied on the ears (1 - 2 mg/site), abdomen, or back. Vasodilation was monitored using laser speckle contrast imaging (Moor FLPI2) at baseline and at intervals up to 60 min (PACAP) or 30 min (capsaicin).

Results PACAP-38 at 1 nmol/site administered at the lower abdomen level induced a robust increase in dermal blood flow (~50%), sustained over 60 min. No effect was observed at the lower dose (10 pmol/site) or when administered at the dorsal lower back level, indicating a dose- and site-dependent response. The capsaicin effect in the ear was dose-dependent, with the 2 mg/site dose producing a peak increase of ~83% at 15–17.5 min, compared to ~48% with the 1 mg/site dose. In the abdomen, capsaicin elicited a peak increase of ~43–48% between 10 and 20 min, with consistent significance across time points. In the back, the response was moderate (~37–41%), peaking around 15–20 min. Responses were consistent across anatomical sites and time points, validating the model’s robustness for mechanistic profiling.

Conclusion These models offer a translational platform for dissecting migraine-relevant mechanisms and validating therapeutic hypotheses.

P552 Candesartan exerts an antinociceptive effect in trigeminal pain model and reduces serotonin content in the brainstem

A. Lasica1, Z. Bugarin1, K. Nastić1, U. Pecikoza1, N. Jasnić2, R. Stepanović-Petrović1, M. Tomić1

1University of Belgrade - Faculty of Pharmacy, Department of Pharmacology, Belgrade, Serbia; 2University of Belgrade - Faculty of Biology, Department of Physiology and Biochemistry, Belgrade, Serbia

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P552

Objective Candesartan, an AT1 angiotensin receptor antagonist, primarily a cardiovascular drug, has also been used for migraine prophylaxis. While its clinical benefit in migraine prevention has been proven, the mechanism of this effect is still unknown. Considering that some migraine prophylactics target serotonergic and/or noradrenergic transmission and that the projections from serotonergic/noradrenergic brainstem nuclei can modulate trigeminal nociception, we tested the effect of candesartan in a trigeminal pain model and its propensity to affect the content of these monoamines in the brainstem.

Methods The antinociceptive effect of candesartan was investigated in the orofacial formalin test (OFT) in mice, after acute and five-day repeated oral administration. Its effect on motor ability was assessed by rotarod test. Serotonin and noradrenaline concentrations in brainstem homogenates were determined by HPLC with electrochemical detection.

Results Candesartan significantly and dose-dependently reduced the duration nociceptive behavior in the first and second phase of the OFT, after both acute (0.5-7 mg/kg) and prolonged administration (0.5-4 mg/kg; Fig. 1). The highest acutely administered dose (7 mg/kg) did not affect rotarod performance (Fig. 2). Repeated administration of candesartan (4 mg/kg/day) significantly reduced serotonin concentrations in the brainstem, while the concentrations of noradrenaline remained unaffected (Fig. 3).

P554 Dual inhibition of FAAH and TRPV1 receptors counteracts nitroglycerin-induced migraine-like symptoms only in male rats

1IRCCS Mondino Foundation, Pavia, Italy; 2University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P554

Objective Anandamide (AEA), an endogenous cannabinoid, plays a key role in migraine pain via CB receptors and TRPV1. P555 Calcitonin gene-related peptide induces headache exacerbations in people with idiopathic intracranial hypertension

A. Yiangou1, T. P. Do2, M. Thaller1, J. L. Mitchell1, M. Byrne3, G. Tsermoulas3, L. J. Hill1, S. P. Mollan1, S. J. E. Lucas1, M. Ashina2, A. J. Sinclair1

Objective Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), known for its role in migraine pathogenesis, may also underlie headache generation in idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), which commonly presents with migraine-like features.

P557 Eye movement patterns reflect vertigo sensations in vestibular migraine

M. D. Villar-Martínez1, A. Bronstein2,3, F. Greenwood1, S. Maniataki1, P. Castro-Abarca3, F. Puledda1,2, D. Kaski3, D. Moreno Ajona1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, London, UK; 2Imperial College London, London, UK; 3University College London, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P557

Objective Vertigo in vestibular migraine (VM) is often difficult to describe yet may provide mechanistic clues. We examined the relationship between subjective vertigo sensations and eye movement patterns to explore oculo-perceptual dynamics in VM.

Methods Fifteen participants with VM (diagnosed per Bárány Society and ICHD-3 criteria) and ten healthy participants (HP) underwent neuro-otological testing, including 3D video-oculography (VOG) in primary gaze, with and without visual fixation (20 s per condition). P558 Preserved reaction time but increased cognitive errors after nitroglycerin in vestibular migraine: A brain fog phenotype?

M. D. Villar-Martínez1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P558

Objective Patients with migraine often report “brain fog”, a subjective cognitive dysfunction that lacks objective characterization. Nitroglycerin (NTG) infusion, a validated human migraine model, may reveal subtle cognitive changes during interictal or early migraine states. We used a sustained attention to response task (SART) to assess error rate and reaction time before and after NTG administration in vestibular migraine patients.

Methods Seven participants with vestibular migraine completed a computerized SART task before and after i.v. NTG (0.5 mcg/Kg) as part of the NitroVest study at King’s College London. P559 Hyperprolactinemia and migraine-like headache: A case report and literature review

B. M. Santos Carvalho1,2, A. Costa1,2,3

1Hospital São João, Department of Neurology, Vila do Conde, Portugal; 2University of Porto, Clinical Neurosciences and Mental Health Department, Porto, Portugal; 3Hospital CUF, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P559

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Prolactin (PRL), a pituitary hormone, has been increasingly implicated in migraine pathophysiology. Clinical and experimental studies suggest that hyperprolactinemia may contribute to headache—particularly in women—through sensitization of trigeminal nociceptors and interaction with CGRP pathways. Headache may be independent of tumor mass effect and respond to dopamine agonists.

Methods We present a case of migraine-like headache in a young woman with hyperprolactinemia due to a prolactinoma, highlighting pathophysiology and treatment.The patient provided informed consent for journal publication.

Results A 23-year-old female pharmacist initially presented to gynecology with headaches as the primary complaint. Routine labs revealed elevated prolactin. Brain MRI showed an indeterminate pituitary lesion. She was treated with bromocriptine for three months, achieving complete headache resolution. Symptoms recurred several months after discontinuation, prompting endocrinology follow-up. Repeat MRI showed a pituitary microadenoma, and cabergoline was reinitiated, with significant headache improvement. Three months before reassessment, the cabergoline dose was halved per endocrinologist recommendation. Headaches then recurred—mainly during periovulatory and perimenstrual phases. Prolactin levels slightly increased. Headaches were severe, holocranial, migrainous with nausea, and resistant to analgesics. Neurological exam was unremarkable. Pituitary hormones like PRL and hypothalamic peptides such as oxytocin may underlie sex differences in migraine.Endocrine evaluation is advised in refractory or atypical headache cases.

P563 Beyond symptom: Exploring the analgesic properties of vomiting in migraine patients

A. Munafò1, A. Burgalassi1, G. Vigani1, L. F. Iannone2, F. de Cesaris1, A. Chiarugi3

1University of Florence, Headache Center and Clinical Pharmacology Unit, Careggi University Hospital, Florence, Italy. Section of Clinical Pharmacology and Oncology, Department of Health Sciences, University of Florence, Florence, Italy, Florence, Italy; 2University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, Modena, Italy; 3Section of Clinical Pharmacology and Oncology, Department of Health Sciences, University of Florence, Florence, Italy, Florence, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P563

Objective To characterize the prevalence, temporal kinetics, and extent of vomiting-induced migraine pain relief (VIMPR).

Methods We conducted an explorative, cross-sectional, questionnaire-based study on migraine patients referring to our headache center. We assessed vomiting frequency, number of episodes, pain intensity on numerical rating scales (0-10) for attacks with and without vomiting, temporal relationship between vomiting and VIMPR, pain recurrence patterns, as well as vomiting induction behaviors.

Results Among 106 migraine patients, 82 (77.4%) reported vomiting during attacks. Attacks with vomiting were significantly more painful than those without (median 9.0 vs. 7.0, p<0.001). VIMPR occurred in 45 patients (54.9%), with 12 (14.6%) experiencing complete attack cessation while 33 (40.2%) only temporary reduction. The rapid onset of VIMPR suggests activation of endogenous antinociceptive mechanisms rather than coincidental attack resolution. The learned behavior of voluntary vomiting induction further supports the genuine neurobiological basis of VIMPR. Overall, findings highlight vomiting as a potential activator of migraine pain–terminating circuits, and underscore the need for further studies to elucidate the underlying neurological mechanisms.

P564 Arterial spin labeling evaluation of cerebral perfusion during spontaneous attacks of migraine without aura – A 3-Tesla MRI Study

H. Al-Mashat1,2, A. Yakubova1,2, U. Lindberg1,2, S. Younis1,2, F. M. Amin1,2

1Danish Headache Center, Rigshospitalet, Neurology, Rigshospitalet, Glostrup, Denmark; 2Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Department of Neurology, Glostrup, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P564

Objective Migraine is a complex disorder that involves both peripheral and central components of the trigeminovascular pain pathway. However, the interaction between these peripheral and central structures of this system is unknown. During migraine attacks, dilation of meningeal and cerebral arteries on the pain side has been suggested to reflect peripheral activation of the trigeminovascular system. A key question is whether changes in cerebral blood flow (CBF) may reflect increased neuronal activation on pain side during migraine attacks, potentially serving as a surrogate marker for underlying central mechanisms.

Methods Migraine patients without aura were MRI scanned during spontaneous attacks and on a separate, attack-free day, using arterial spin labeling at 3T.

Results Twenty-one patients were scanned during a migraine attack, and 17 of them were also scanned on an attack-free day. Among these, 13 patients were scanned during unilateral attacks. The CBF increased on pain side during these unilateral attacks, compared to attack-free days (7%, p= 0.038). This increase in CBF was positively correlated with pain intensity (p=0.038). The CBF remained unchanged between attack day and attack-free day in patients with bilateral attacks (p=0.154).

Conclusion The CBF was increased on pain side during spontaneous attacks of migraine without aura. This increase was positively correlated with pain intensity. Our findings suggest lateralized changes in neuronal activity during migraine attacks, supporting the previously observed lateralized vasodilation towards the pain side. Further studies are needed to clarify the sequential activation of peripheral and central mechanisms during migraine attacks.

P565 The association between vertigo and neck discomfort in chronic migraine

D. Moreno Ajona1, N. Karsan1, P. J. Goadsby1

1King’s College London, Headache Group, NIHR King’s Clinical Research Facility & SLaM Biomedical Research Centre, and Wolfson SPaRC, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, London, UK

P566 Altered functional connectivity between the middle cingulate cortex and occipital cortex in migraine: A REFORM study

R. Messina1,2,3, R. H. Christensen3, H. Ashina3, A. Sankar3, C. Gollion3,4, H. M. Al-Khazali3, M. Filippi1,2, M. Ashina3

Objective Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has advanced our understanding of migraine neurobiology. P571 Auditory processing deficits in migraine: CGRP drives excitotoxic cochlear injury via ZBP1-Mediated PANoptosis

W. Xu1, S. Zhang1

1Wuhan Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Department of Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, Wuhan, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P571

Objective While sensory processing abnormalities—affecting visual, somatosensory, and proprioceptive systems—are well-documented in migraine, the auditory domain remains largely unexplored, particularly regarding peripheral mechanisms. This study aims to elucidate how migraine induces peripheral auditory damage and the role of CGRP in the inner ear, which may contribute to the precise subtyping of migraine and inform targeted auditory-protective therapies.

Methods A mouse model of chronic migraine was established with injections of NTG. The expression of CGRP in the cochlea was measured. Auditory brainstem response (ABR) was used to evaluate hearing function. The target differentially expressed pathway was validated and manipulated in both HEI-OC1 cells and the inner ear.

Results Mice developed hind paw mechanical and hot plate hyperalgesia after NTG injections. The CGRP and its receptor expression was upregulated, especially in outer hair cells(OHCs).The migraine mouse model exhibited higher ABR thresholds, longer wave I latency and hair cell injury, all of which could be reversed by Rimegepant.We found that ZBP1 and its related PANoptosis and inflammation pathway were significantly upregulated in the cochlea.Blockade of ZBP1 and its downstream signaling could rescue migraine-related hair cell injury both in vivo and in vitro.

Conclusion We extend the pathophysiology relevance of migraine and auditory dysfunction, demonstrate that migraine causes functional and structural damage to the OHCs(the cochlear amplifiers)-rather than to spiral ganglion neurons, challenging the previous common presumed injury site. We identified CGRP-mediated excitotoxicity as the direct driver of this damage, beyond classic vascular permeability mechanisms.These findings refine the mechanistic model of migraine-related auditory dysfunction and provide a phenotypic basis for further subtyping of cochlear migraine, paving the way for mechanism-driven auditory protection strategies.Fig. 1 (abstract P571).Fig. 2 (abstract P571).Fig. 3 (abstract P571).

P572 Sleep macro- and microstructure in migraine and cluster headache: A systematic review of objective assessments

V. Munday1, E. Watson1, P. Holland1, I. Rosenzweig2

1King’s College London, Wolfson Sensory, Pain and Regeneration Centre, London, UK; 2King’s College London, Neuroimaging, London, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P572

Objective Sleep disturbances are commonly reported in primary headache, yet the neurophysiological basis remains poorly defined. While subjective reports of sleep disruption are well established, there is no consensus on the objective alterations in sleep architecture which may occur in headache.

Methods We conducted a systematic review across 4 databases (Embase, Medline, PubMed and APA PsycInfo) to identify studies assessing objective sleep parameters via polysomnography or actigraphy in individuals with migraine or cluster headache, including relevant preclinical models. Sleep macrostructure and microstructure were evaluated across different ages and headache attack phases.

Results Thirty-one studies met the inclusion criteria, with significant heterogeneity resulting in varied findings. Among paediatric migraine, evidence indicates a significant reduction in total sleep time and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, in addition to elevated wake after sleep onset. In adult migraine, findings were more variable, though several studies indicate an increase in sleep fragmentation, although such measures are under-reported. Though limited, microstructural analysis including cyclic alternating pattern and sleep spindles revealed alterations compared to controls, though a consistent pattern of changes is not yet apparent across studies. Notably, a small number of studies report reduced arousability the night preceding headache headache onset, compared to headache-free periods, suggesting headache-phase specific changes in sleep architecture.

Conclusion Objective evidence supports disrupted sleep architecture in headache disorders, particularly in relation to fragmentation and microstructure. These changes may reflect shared pathophysiological mechanisms involving brainstem and hypothalamic arousal networks. Greater methodological consistency, patient stratification and detailed reporting of headache phase are essential to establish whether a reproducible sleep phenotype exists in migraine and cluster headache.

P573 Increased susceptibility to cortical spreading depolarization in mouse models of migraine and depression

O. Gliga1, V. J. Gallardo1, P. Pozo-Rosich2,1, M. Vila Pueyo1

1Headache and Neurological Pain Research Group, Vall d’Hebron Research Institute, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain; 2Headache Unit, Neurology Department, Vall d’Hebron University Hospital, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P573

Objective Migraine often coexists with depression, increasing the overall disease burden. Cortical spreading depolarization (CSD), the physiological correlate of migraine aura, can be measured in preclinical mouse models. This study aims to assess CSD susceptibility in mouse models of migraine, depression, and, a novel combined model of both conditions, in order to better understand their relationship.

Methods C57BL/6J 8-week-old female and male mice were randomly assigned to four groups: (1) Control, (2) Migraine, (3) Depression, and (4) Migraine+Depression. The Migraine group received 5 nitroglycerin injections (10 mg/kg) administered every other day for 9 days. The Depression group underwent a 21-day chronic unpredictable mild stress protocol. The Migraine+Depression group was exposed to both protocols. KCl-induced CSDs were recorded in anesthetised mice 24 h after completion of the protocols. The number of CSDs were quantified, and data were analysed using Poisson models in R, with results expressed as incidence rate ratios (IRRs), representing the relative change in CSD counts between groups.

Results Poisson models revealed that female mice in the Migraine (IRR=1.45; p=0.001), Depression (IRR=1.75; p<0.001), and Migraine+Depression groups (IRR=1.90; p<0.001) showed significantly higher CSDs counts compared with Controls. By contrast, no significant differences were detected among male groups.

Conclusion These findings suggest that depression alone and the combination of migraine and depression markedly increase CSD susceptibility in females mice, to a level comparable with that observed in the migraine model. In contrast, no significant effects were detected in males, underscoring a sex-specific influence on CSD susceptibility. Taken together, these results provide experimental evidence for a comorbid interaction between migraine and depression, particularly in females.

P576 Sensory certainty and placebo effect in migraine: The role of interoceptive awareness

M. Agostinho1,2,3, L. Viveiros2, C. Calado2, R. Treister3, R. Gil-Gouveia4,5, R. Canaipa1,2

1Universidade Católica Portuguesa, Centre for Interdisciplinary Research in Health, Lisbon, Portugal; 2Universidade Católica Portuguesa, Faculty of Health Sciences and Nursing, Lisbon, Portugal; 3University of Haifa, The Cheryl Spencer Department of Nursing, Faculty of Social Welfare and Health Sciences, Haifa, Israel; 4Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal; 5Católica Medical School, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P576

Objective The Bayesian Brain Hypothesis (BBH) proposes that pain perception results from the interaction between certainty in priors (e.g. conditioning) and sensory signals [1]. Migraine may emerge from an increased reliance on prior experiences, contributing to its chronification. We aimed to assess the certainty of sensory signals, the placebo effect, and their associations with clinical characteristics using the Focused Analgesia Selection Test (FAST) and an experimental placebo paradigm.

Methods This abstract reports preliminary data from an ongoing study including episodic migraine patients (MG) and healthy controls (H). Participants attended two sessions: (1) clinical assessment and (2) completion of the FAST and a conditioning + verbal suggestion paradigm. Primary outcomes included FASTR2, FASTICC, expectations (E1–E3), conditioning strength (CondSTR), placebo effect (PlacEff), years with symptoms (YS), and the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA).

Results To date, 27 MG and 19 H have been enrolled. PlacEff did not differ between groups (p = 0.403). In MG, ICC correlated negatively with PlacEff (FASTR2: rs = –0.447, p = 0.019; FASTICC: rs = –0.375, p = 0.054), suggesting that greater sensory certainty is associated with a lower placebo effect. In H, higher MAIA “Not Distracting” scores showed a trend towards moderating the FASTICC–PlacEff relationship (p = 0.056), which was not observed in MG (p = 0.175).

Conclusion These preliminary results suggest that migraine patients with greater sensory certainty (higher FAST outcomes) may exhibit lower placebo effects. The MAIA findings indicate that higher interoceptive awareness in healthy individuals may help preserve flexibility between sensory input and expectation—a mechanism that seems less effective in migraine and may relate to its persistence.

References

1. Friston K. et al., Brain 2010; 133: 252–267.

2. Colloca L. et al., Pain 2023; 164: 1032–1042.

P578 Distinct inflammatory profiles across migraine clinical states: A systematic review and meta-analysis

E. Stuchfield-Denby1, B. Pereira2, D. Bouvier3, R. Dallel1, X. Moisset1

1Université Clermont Auvergne, NEURO-DOL, Clermont-Ferrand, France; 2CHU Clermont-Ferrand, Department of Clinical Research and Innovation, Clermont-Ferrand, France; 3Université Clermont Auvergne, iGred, Clermont-Ferrand, France

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P578

Objective Although several meta-analyses have emphasised the role of inflammation in migraine, none have accounted for the diversity of its clinical manifestations. This review and meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and reliable assessment of cytokine levels in migraine.

Methods Original studies on cytokine levels in migraine were included through a systematic search on PubMed, Embase and Cochrane on July 4–5, 2024. Non-inclusion criteria covered studies on hemiplegic migraine, controls with tension-type headache, and unclear cytokine identification. Studies involving less than 10 participants per group or lacking accessible numeral data were not included.

Results Fifty-seven studies were included in the narrative review and/or meta-analysis. In episodic migraine patients versus controls, blood levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6, Standardized Mean Difference [SMD] 0.37 [95% CI, 0.10; 0.63], P=0.008, I²=71.8%, nine articles), transforming growth factor β (TGF- β, SMD 0.64 [95% CI, 0.44; 0.84], P=0.000, I²=0.0%, two articles) and C-X-C motif ligand 8 (CXCL-8, narrative review, three articles) were elevated. Levels of IL-6 (narrative review, three articles; SMD 1.40 [95% CI, 0.95; 1.86], P=0.000, I²=0.0%, two articles) and adiponectin (ADP, SMD 0.59 [95% CI, 0.19; 0.99], P=0.003, I²=36.0%, three articles) were elevated in chronic versus episodic migraine. Levels of interleukin-1β (IL-1β, SMD 0.43 [95% CI, 0.10; 0.75], P=0.010, I²=0.0%, two articles), interleukin-10 (IL-10, narrative review, two studies) and salivary levels of IL-6 (narrative review, two articles) were elevated in ictal versus interictal migraine.

Conclusion This study highlights the association of distinct cytokine profiles with migraine disease (IL-6, TGF-β, CXCL-8), migraine attacks (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10) and migraine chronification (IL-6, ADP). Differences in inflammatory profiles across migraine clinical states have significant implications for understanding disease mechanisms, progression, and potential therapeutic interventions.

P579 Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide-38 (PACAP-38)-mediated mast cell degranulation: Targeting immune interactions

A. Asuni1, D. Silke Malling Damlund1, L. Rørbæk Olsen1, J. Juhl Weisser1, M. Tollenaere-Larsen1, C. Ratner1

1H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P579

Objective PACAP-38 is involved in vasodilation, nociceptive signalling, and immune interactions. Previous studies suggest that PACAP-38 influences mast cell activity, particularly in meningeal tissues, where mast cell-derived mediators contribute to inflammatory processes. This study aimed to establish an in vitro PACAP-mediated mast cell degranulation (MCD) model to investigate the effects of PACAP-38 on histamine release and assess the inhibitory potential of a PACAP-targeting antibody.

Methods Rat peritoneal mast cells were incubated with increasing concentrations of PACAP-38 (0.005 to 30 µM) for a two-hour stimulation period. Histamine release was quantified using an enzyme immunoassay, with Compound 48/80 (a selective mast cell activator) serving as a positive control. To evaluate inhibition, mast cells were pre-treated with either an anti-PACAP antibody or control human IgG (hIgG) at concentrations of 0.01–30 µM prior to PACAP-38 exposure. Cromoglycate, a mast cell stabilizer, was included as a reference inhibitor.

Results PACAP-38 induced a robust concentration-dependent histamine release, confirming its role in mast cell activation. Anti-PACAP significantly inhibited PACAP-38-mediated histamine release, with up to 151% relative inhibition. Cromoglycate efficiently inhibited histamine release induced by PACAP-38, and hIgG exhibited no inhibitory effect, verifying its function as a negative control.

Conclusion Our findings provide further evidence that PACAP-38 plays a role in MCD and immune interactions. The MCD model offers a platform to assess molecular modulators of mast cell responses. The observed inhibition of histamine release by anti-PACAP suggests opportunities for further investigation, particularly in understanding the broader implications of PACAP-driven immune processes. Future studies will be necessary to define how PACAP-targeted approaches may contribute to the regulation of inflammatory pathways and potentially MCD in the context of pain pathophysiology.

P580 When headaches speak first: Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia as an early clue to autoimmune encephalitis – A case report

F. Moghadas1, E. Jafari2, B. Rezaeian2, M. Togha2

1Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Neurology/Headache, Kerman, Iran; 2Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Neurology/Headache, Tehran, Iran

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P580

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC) syndromes, although rare in the spectrum of headache disorders, are of great importance to recognize, because they can be debilitating and may be linked to potentially serious underlying causes. We present a patient with a TAC-like headache, where the diagnostic workup revealed a new secondary cause for TAC syndromes.

Methods A 62-year-old male patient has been referred with a complaint of experiencing a new-onset headache located in the left orbitofrontal region. Each episode lasted 15 min and was repeated 3 to 4 times a day with mild continuous pain between episodes. Severe pain was associated with psychomotor agitation and ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms. Brain and vascular imaging showed mild pachymeningeal enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid pressure and analysis were normal except for a high protein level. Further investigation for a secondary cause revealed a positive result for serum anti-N-methyl D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antibody. The headaches were resolved after 5 days of intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone.

Results There are various etiologies for secondary TACs. Most of them are structural lesions, especially in the sella turcica region, and vascular disorders such as dissection or aneurysm. To our knowledge, this is the first case of TAC associated with autoimmune encephalitis antibodies that responded significantly to corticosteroids.

Conclusion This patient, along with cases of Neuromyelitis Optica-Spectrum Disorder (NMO-SD) with TAC presentation, highlights the role of autoimmunity in TAC syndromes.

P581 The role of microglia in migraine pathophysiology: Emerging mechanisms and translational potential

C. Xie1

1Clinical Medical College & The Affiliated Hospital of Chengdu University, Neurology, Chengdu, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P581

Objective To review current findings on microglial involvement in migraine pathophysiology, with an emphasis on molecular signaling pathways, sex-specific responses, and therapeutic implications.

Methods We conducted a literature review of preclinical and clinical studies (2018–2025) investigating microglial function in migraine models, focusing on inflammatory mediators, neuron–glia interactions, and genetic or pharmacological manipulation of microglial activity.

Results Experimental studies demonstrate that microglial activation in key migraine-related brain regions (e.g., trigeminal nucleus caudalis, thalamus, cortex) precedes or accompanies headache-like behavior in animal models. Activated microglia release pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α) and promote neuronal sensitization via purinergic (P2 × 4, P2 × 7), TLR4, and cGAS-STING pathways. Notably, sex-dependent differences in microglial responses have been observed, potentially contributing to the female predominance in migraine prevalence. Emerging data also suggest that CGRP and microglial signaling may intersect to exacerbate pain pathways.

Conclusion Microglia are not passive bystanders but active modulators of migraine pathophysiology. Targeting microglial signaling offers a novel therapeutic avenue and may help refine current treatments by accounting for neuroimmune mechanisms. Further studies are needed to delineate the temporal dynamics and regional specificity of microglial responses in migraine.

P582 Migraine as a differential diagnosis for cadasil in young individuals

W. Gonçalves Horta1, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto2, M. de Souza Horta3, S. de Sousa Costa Gonçalves2, N. Carvalho Figueredo4, L. Cahú da Silva Falcão4

1Universidade de Pernambuco, Headache clinic from Hospital Oswaldo Cruz, Recife, Brazil; 2Faculdade de Medicina de Olinda, Neurology, Paulista, Brazil; 3Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), Neurosurgery, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; 4Universidade Católica de Pernambuco, Recife, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P582

Objective To identify migraine as an initial symptom of CADASIL.

Methods Assess migraine in patients with CADASIL.

Results The proportion of migraine in patients with CADASIL is five times higher than in the general population. The first symptoms usually occur before the age of 20, with the average age of onset being 30 years. In women, symptoms appear earlier than in men. Migraine often precedes other symptoms by many years and MRI scans may still appear normal, leading to delays and diagnostic errors. The relationship between migraine and CADASIL may be explained by the identification of genetic abnormalities occurring on chromosome 19, the same chromosome involved in familial hemiplegic migraine. A characteristic feature of migraine in CADASIL is the presence of aura symptoms, with visual symptoms being the most prevalent, followed by sensory, aphasic, motor symptoms. Some individuals present with atypical aura. A possible mechanism for the increased prevalence of aura in CADASIL patients is an increased susceptibility to cortical spreading depression. The triggering factors of migraine with aura are similar to those in the general population.

Conclusion Migraine, especially when accompanied by aura symptoms, may be an initial symptom of CADASIL and should be considered as a differential diagnosis, particularly in younger individuals.

P583 Pathophysiological mechanisms in infectious headache

V. Bencs1, M. Kozák2

1University of Debrecen, Department of Neurology, Debrecen, Hungary; 2University of Debrecen, Department of Infectology, Debrecen, Hungary

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P583

Objective Headache is a frequent manifestation of both systemic and central nervous system (CNS) infections, yet its underlying pathophysiology remains underrecognized and poorly characterized in clinical neurology. This abstract aims to summarize key mechanistic pathways linking infection and headache, emphasizing their diagnostic and therapeutic relevance.

Methods We conducted a targeted literature review using PubMed and Scopus databases to identify recent studies addressing the mechanisms of infection-associated headache. Articles discussing intracranial and systemic infectious processes, meningeal nociception, cytokine-mediated inflammation, and post-infectious neuroimmune changes were included. Conceptual synthesis was aligned with the ICHD-3 framework to ensure clinical relevance.

Results Infectious headache develops through overlapping mechanisms, including meningeal irritation, activation of the trigeminovascular system, intracranial pressure changes, and systemic inflammation. Post-infectious cases may reflect sustained neuroimmune activation even after pathogen clearance.

Conclusion Infectious headache is not a uniform entity but results from distinct and overlapping pathophysiological mechanisms. Recognizing these pathways may improve classification, enhance clinical suspicion in atypical cases, and support the development of mechanism-based treatment strategies. Integrating immune and structural insights into routine diagnostic frameworks may refine the management of infection-related headaches in both acute and post-infectious settings.

P584 Altered cytokine receptor expression in cluster headache patients

J. Lloyd1, C. Ran1, K. Wellfelt1, A. Steinberg2,3, A. Sundholm1,2, A. Carmine Belin1

1Karolinska Institutet, Department of Neuroscience, Stockholm, Sweden; 2Karolinska University Hospital, Department of Neurology, Stockholm, Sweden; 3Karolinska Institutet, Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Stockholm, Sweden

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P584

Objective To investigate cytokine receptor expression in cluster headache (CH).

Methods RNA was purified from collected blood samples from 16x CH participants and 16x control participants. RNA was also purified from fibroblast cultures from 11x CH participants and 9x control participants. RNA was converted to cDNA to perform RTqPCR on a QuantStudio 5 instrument using SYBR green. Primers for 7x cytokine receptor genes (CCR3 and CCR5 (cytokines: CCL8, CCL11, CCL13), CXCR3 (cytokines: CXCL10, CXCL11), MET (cytokine: HGF), TNFRSF10c (cytokine: TNFSF10), TNFRSF25 (cytokine: TNFSF12) and OSMR (cytokine: OSM)) were obtained from Invitrogen. RNA expression was normalized to housekeeping gene TBP. Group averages were analysed using welch t-test in R-studios.

Results In blood samples, a significant increase was seen in RNA expression of TNFRSF10c (P<0.05) and TNFRSF25 (P<0.05) in CH group vs. healthy controls, no difference was seen in RNA expression of CCR3, CCR5, CXCR3, or MET genes. In fibroblast culture supernatant, RNA expression was significantly increased in CXCR3 (P>0.05) and TNFRSF10c (P<0,05) and significantly decreased in OSM (P<0.01) in CH group vs. healthy controls. No difference was seen in expression of MET or TNFRSF25 genes.

Conclusion There is altered expression of receptors for cytokines in both blood and fibroblast samples from participants with cluster headache. This is in line with the previous distinct alterations in cytokine expression seen in Swedish1 and Danish2 patients with cluster headache.

2 Lund, N.L.T., Westgate, C.S.J., Søborg, M.L.K., Snoer, A.H., Jensen, R.H., Hansen, T.F. and Petersen, A.S., 2025. Distinct Alterations of Inflammatory Biomarkers in Cluster Headache: A Case Control Study. Annals of Neurology.

P585 Isolated trigeminal sensory neuropathy in a patient with mixed connective tissue disease: A diagnostic challenge

T. Ascensão Pinheiro1, J. Martins2, V. Salgado3, S. Machado1

1Amadora-Sintra Hospital, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal; 2CUF Sintra Hospital, Neurophysiology, Lisbon, Portugal; 3CUF Sintra Hospital, Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P585

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective Trigeminal neuropathy is a rare condition with a broad differential diagnosis, including autoimmune, infectious, structural and neoplastic causes. Diagnostic evaluation may be complex, particularly in patients with systemic inflammatory conditions.

Methods We present the case of a 46-year-old Caucasian male from Greece, residing in Portugal, with mixed connective tissue disease (Raynaud’s phenomenon, sacroiliitis, pulmonary hypertension), a clipped left occipital artery aneurysm, atrial flutter and resected dorsal melanoma. He developed progressive numbness on the left side of the face from June 2024, starting centrally and spreading centrifugally. He denied sicca symptoms. Chronic medication included gabapentin 100 mg three times daily, prednisolone 10 mg, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg, aspirin 150 mg, pentoxifylline 400 mg, nifedipine 20 mg, furosemide, tadalafil and ambrisentan. He was not on anticoagulants and had no known drug allergies.

Results Neurological examination revealed isolated tactile hypoesthesia of the left hemiface.Brain MRI was unremarkable.Electromyography showed a severe sensory lesion of the left trigeminal nerve and abnormal blink reflex, without motor involvement. CSF was normal, with negative microbiology, no oligoclonal bands/neoplastic cells. Immunological studies showed high-titre ANA (1:1280) and strong anti-RNP, anti-SSA(Ro), and anti-Ro52 positivity in serum and CSF. Antineuronal antibodies were negative.

A diagnosis of isolated trigeminal sensory neuropathy was made, likely autoimmune. The patient was referred to rheumatology to escalate immunosuppression.

Conclusion This case highlights the importance of considering autoimmune mechanisms in isolated trigeminal neuropathies, especially in patients with systemic connective tissue disease. EMG may assist in detecting trigeminal dysfunction, and intrathecal autoantibodies, even without structural lesions, support an immune-mediated process and underscore the value of CSF analysis in atypical neurological presentations.

P586 Migraine and allergy – Two faces of the same hypersensitivity?

I. Rosciszewska -Zukowska1, M. Rachel2

1University of Rzeszow, Poland; Provincial Clinical Hospital No. 2 St. Jadwiga the Queen in Rzeszów, Neurology, Rzeszow, Poland; 2University of Rzeszow, Poland; Provincial Clinical Hospital No. 2 St. Jadwiga the Queen in Rzeszów, Allergology, Rzeszow, Poland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P586

Objective The link between migraines and allergies is unclear, with experts divided on the relationship. New tests like the ALEX² test can measure IgE levels for over 295 allergens, but some migraine patients with allergy histories still get negative results. This suggests there may be other types of allergies not related to IgE. The ALEX² study investigates the prevalence of allergies in migraine patients with known allergies.

Methods Analysis of a group of 47 patients (36 women, 11 men; mean age 35.6 ± 9.4 years) diagnosed with migraine (ICHD-3 criteria) and a history of allergies (seasonal symptoms, urticaria, asthma, allergic rhinitis). All patients underwent the ALEX² test (MacroArray Diagnostics, Austria). Assessed: ALEX² test result (positive vs. negative); Type of allergic symptoms from the history; Impact of migraine on quality of life (MIDAS); Serum total IgE concentration.

Results In a study of 47 patients with allergies and migraines, the ALEX² test revealed that 28 patients (59.6%) had no allergies. Among those testing negative for allergies: - 60.7% reported seasonal symptoms like sneezing and nasal itching. - 28.5% experienced skin symptoms such as hives. - 10.8% had allergic asthma. - 21.4% had elevated total IgE levels (greater than 100 IU/ml). There was no significant difference in migraine frequency or mean MIDAS scores between patients with positive and negative ALEX² results. Antihistamine treatment did not notably affect migraine outcomes.

Conclusion Many patients with allergies and migraines do not show sensitization on the ALEX² test. This suggests that allergy-like symptoms may stem from non-IgE-mediated mechanisms, such as hypersensitivity or autonomic hyperresponsiveness. Additionally, the lack of correlation between ALEX² scores and migraine severity implies that other factors, like neurogenic inflammation, may be more influential. More research is needed to understand the role of non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity in these patients.

P587 Foreign body granuloma: An endovascular cerebral aneurysm treatment complication

B. Pflantzer1,2, D. Orion1,2, G. Yaniv3,4

1Sheba Medical Center, Neurology, Ramat Gan, Israel; 2Tel Aviv University, Department of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Tel Aviv, Israel; 3Sheba Medical Center, Diagnostic Imaging, Ramat Gan, Israel; 4Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Tel Aviv University, Department of Imaging, Tel Aviv, Israel

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P587

Objective Foreign body granuloma (FBG) is a rare complication after endovascular treatment of unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs), thought to result from embolization of hydrophilic polymer coatings and subsequent granulomatous inflammation. Presentation and imaging can mimic infection, vasculitis, or embolic stroke.

Methods Retrospective case series of three women who developed new neurological symptoms after endovascular UIA treatment. We reviewed clinical course, MRI features, devices used, management, and outcomes.

Results Ages were 53–72 years. Symptom onset ranged from hours to weeks post-procedure and included headache, transient focal deficits, hemiparesis, and encephalopathy. MRI showed multiple enhancing parenchymal lesions with or without leptomeningeal enhancement with edema and SWI microbleeds, without diffusion restriction or infectious/vasculitic markers. Patients received high-dose corticosteroids with taper and showed marked clinical and radiological improvement. All three cases involved the use of PHENOM PLUS catheter.

Conclusion FBG should be considered when unexplained neurological symptoms and enhancing brain lesions arise after endovascular UIA therapy. Early recognition enables corticosteroid treatment, which was associated with improvement in our steroid-treated patients; delayed recognition may preclude immunotherapy. The repeated presence of the PHENOM PLUS catheter across all cases raises concern for a potential role in this complication. Systematic reporting and device-level investigations are needed to define incidence, risk factors, and optimal management.Fig. 1 (abstract P587).Fig. 2 (abstract P587).Fig. 3 (abstract P587).

P591 CGRP, VIP and PACAP plasmatic levels in migraine patients before and after anti-CGRP(R) monoclonal antibodies prophylaxis

A. Bellotti1, D. Chiasserini1, G. Tringali2, P. Navarra2, A. Megaro1, V. Teti1, E. Cresta1, I. Corbelli1, D. Fruttini1, P. Calabresi2,3, L. Parnetti1, P. Sarchielli1

1University of Perugia, Perugia, Italy; 2Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Rome, Italy; 3Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P591

Objective CGRP, VIP, and PACAP are key mediators in migraine pathophysiology. Anti-CGRP(R) mAbs have recently emerged as the first targeted, effective prophylactic therapy. This study aimed to evaluate plasma levels of these neuropeptides pre- and post-anti-CGRP(R) mAb treatment, assessing changes and potential predictors of response.

Methods From Feb 2022 to Feb 2023, we enrolled 56 migraineurs who began prophylaxis with erenumab (n=26), galcanezumab (n=16), or fremanezumab (n=14). Responders were defined as those achieving ≥50% MMDs reduction at 6 months. Blood was collected at T0, T1 (3 mo), T2 (6 mo), and T3 (12 mo). CGRP, VIP, and PACAP plasma levels were assessed via RIA and ELISA.

Results Overall, 80.3% (45/56) responded to anti-CGRP(R) mAbs, with a significant reduction in all clinical variables (MIDAS, HIT-6, ASC, MMDs) from T0 to T3 (Fig. 1). In the erenumab group, CGRP levels showed no significant change, though responders exhibited a decreasing trend from T0 to T2 compared to non-responders. Galcanezumab induced a significant CGRP reduction by T1 (p < 0.01). Fremanezumab led to a rapid CGRP rise >3000 pg/ml, likely assay interference. VIP and PACAP levels remained stable in plasma from T0 to T3, with no significant differences between responders and non-responders (Fig. 2).

Conclusion Anti-CGRP(R) mAbs are very effective migraine prophylactic agents. Galcanezumab significantly reduced plasma CGRP by 3 months, with near-undetectable levels at 6 months, consistent with its CGRP-binding mechanism and prior studies. In contrast, erenumab did not affect significantly CGRP plasmatic levels, potentially due to its different binding site on the CGRP receptor. VIP and PACAP levels remained unaffected by treatment. Further studies are needed to clarify their interplay with CGRP in migraine pathogenesis.Fig. 1 (abstract P591).Fig. 2 (abstract P591).

1IRCCS Istituto delle scienze neurologiche di Bologna, Bologna, Italy; 2Alma Mater Studiorum Bologna, Bologna, Italy; 3Alma Mater Studiorum Bologna, DIBINEM - Department of Biomdical and Neuromotor Sciences, Bologna, Italy

P595 Plasma with added protease inhibitors improves alpha and beta-CGRP measurement as compared to serum: Towards a reliable biomarker for chronic migraine

L. de La Guerra-Sasián1, G. Gárate1, J. Madera1, S. Pérez-Pereda1, V. González Quintanilla1, J. Pascual Gómez1, M. Muñóz1

1Marqués de Valdecilla Health Research Institute (IDIVAL), Cefaleas y otras enfermedades neurológicas no degenerativas, Santander, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P595

Objective CGRP, mainly a-CGRP, is central in migraine pathophysiology, whereas β-CGRP is more prevalent in the gut. Although CGRP is both a therapeutic target and potential biomarker, measurement inconsistencies limit its reliability. CGRP degrades rapidly, and studies suggest adding protease inhibitors (PI) to improve accuracy. This study aims to explore factors influencing CGRP levels as a biomarker.

Methods Chronic migraine patients (n=145) were recruited in our Headache Unit. Blood samples were collected at baseline, 6, and 12 months post-treatment. Plasma was processed with and without PI and stored at -70º. CGRP isoforms were measured with specific ELISAs. Statistical tests were made for level changes and group differences (significance p<0.05).

Results PI-added plasma correlated with standard plasma (rs=0.9310, p<0.0001), but showed higher a-CGRP levels (median=21.26; PI-median=38.29, p<0.0001). For β-CGRP, correlation was smaller (rs=0.8390, p<0.0001), with no significant difference between samples. No correlation was found between a- and β-CGRP (rs=0.05405, p=0.5662). Conclusion PI improved a-CGRP detection in plasma, supporting its use for a more accurate quantification. The lack of correlation between isoforms suggests independent regulation. a-CGRP levels decreased with treatment and correlated negatively with age, highlighting its role as a biomarker. b-CGRP stability and higher detection in plasma suggest it as the preferred biofluid for its measurement. These results call for implementation of PI-plasma samples in future research.

P597 Longitudinal EEG assessment of cortical responsivity before migraine attacks: A study of visual chirp responses

A. Oosterlee1, T. van den Hoek1, J. Duijvelshoff2, N. Pelzer1, E. van Zwet1, E. Tolner1, M. van de Ruit2, G. M. Terwindt1

1Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, Netherlands; 2Delft University of Technology, Delft, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P597

Objective Migraine attacks are unpredictable, often disrupting daily life. Previous research suggested that EEG responses to visual chirp stimulation (VEP-EEG) may help detect changes in cortical responsivity during the preictal phase. This study aims to further investigate that hypothesis.

Methods In this longitudinal, non-interventional study, participants with episodic migraine completed a validated e-headache diary for at least one month. The preictal phase was defined as the 48 h before an attack. Each participant underwent several EEG recordings in response to 10–40 Hz visual chirp stimulation on separate days at our hospital, continuing until a migraine attack occurred. Changes from baseline in EEG spectral power were compared between interictal and preictal phases across individual stimulation frequencies (10–40 Hz), including driving, harmonic, and overall responses.

Results Of the 31 patients who participated, 17 had at least one interictal and one preictal measurement which met the criteria for inclusion in the analysis. The mean participant age was 52 ± 15 years; 82% were female, 77% had migraine without aura, and baseline monthly migraine days (MMD) averaged 3.7 ± 2.3. Additionally, 65% of participants were not using prophylactic medication. We observed high variability in EEG responses to chirp stimulation, both between patients and between interictal and preictal measurements. No significant differences were found in EEG spectral power across the individual stimulation frequencies between interictal and preictal recordings for the driving, harmonic, or overall chirp responses (p = 0.92, p = 0.69, and p = 0.68, respectively).

Conclusion This study did not replicate previous findings of preictal changes in cortical responsivity in migraine. We recommend increasing the sample size and number of recording days, potentially by adapting the protocol to a home-based setup.

P604 Tear fluid calcitonin gene-related peptide is elevated during spontaneous migraine attacks – Results from a pilot study

K. Kamm1, A. Brandi-Dohrn1, A. Straube1, R. Ruscheweyh1

1LMU Munich, Department of Neurology, Munich, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P604

Objective Recurrent headache attacks characterize the primary headache disorder migraine. The neuropeptide calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) plays a major role in its pathophysiology as it was shown that the peptide is elevated in interictal and ictal migraine patients. The detection of CGRP has been confirmed in tear fluid in interictal migraine patients and during experimentally induced migraine attacks. The aim of the present study was to investigate CGRP during spontaneous migraine attacks.

Methods Episodic migraine (EM) patients were studied at two separate study days. At study day 1, patients were interviewed regarding their migraine history and tear fluid was sampled from both eyes (baseline). At study day 2, patients were asked to come to the study center, as soon as they experienced a migraine attack. After arrival, headache characteristics as well as tear fluid was obtained every hour. Patients were allowed to take their usual abortive medication (AM) as needed.

Results 14 female migraine patients (28.4 9.3 years) were included. Patients arrived at the headache center 4.2 2.9 h after migraine onset. The first tear fluid sampling was before intake of abortive medication. Tear fluid CGRP levels were significantly higher during the migraine attack compared to baseline and after resolution of headache (baseline: 1.89 ± 1.68 ng/ml, headache: 2.34 ± 2.20 ng/ml, post headache: 1.23 ± 0.80 ng/ml; Friedman χ2[2] = 11. 286, p = 0.004). Rise of tear fluid CGRP levels was significantly dependent on the timepoint of sampling. Conclusion Tear fluid CGRP significantly rises during spontaneous migraine attacks with a higher rise at the beginning of the attack. This might be one reason for better efficacy if abortive medication is taken early.

P605 Neuroimaging biomarkers for differentiating migraine and multiple sclerosis: A systematic literature review

J. Wołos1,2, O. Grodzka1,2, P. Sochań1, J. Kochanowski1, I. Domitrz1

1Medical University of Warsaw, Department of Neurology, Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry, Warsaw, Poland; 2Medical University of Warsaw, Doctoral School, Warsaw, Poland

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P605

Objective Migraine and multiple sclerosis (MS) are neurological diseases sharing demographic characteristics, since they most commonly affect young women. Moreover, white matter hyperintensities (WMHs) may appear on the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of patients with migraine and can be mistaken for non-active lesions of MS aetiology. Since clinical overlap sometimes occurs, diagnostic difficulties may arise. Therefore, a novel neuroimaging biomarker could become a valuable aid in differentiation between these two conditions.

Methods This systematic review aimed to provide an overview of the currently investigated MRI assessment methods and imaging markers as potential novel tools in migraine and MS differentiation. PubMed (MEDLINE), EMBASE and Web of Science databases were searches in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews (PRISMA) guidelines.

Results Among 685 records screened, we identified 22 studies eligible for inclusion. Central vein sign (CVS) positivity of lesions was significantly higher in MS patients compared to migraineurs. Volumetric markers were also able to distinguish between MS and migraine, with MS individuals having decreased thalamic and increased choroid plexus volume. Significant differences were also found in terms of lesion number and localization. Although the research covering this subject is limited, available studies provide promising results.

Conclusion Studies suggest novel MRI approaches can become helpful tools in migraine and MS differential diagnosis, with CVS emerging as a particularly valuable neuroimaging biomarker.

P607 Efficacy and safety of prophylactic cycloxygenase inhibitor usage to prevent headache during religious fasting: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P607

Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors in preventing headache during religious fasting through a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.

Methods A search was conducted on PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), European Union (EU) Clinical Trials Register, and ClinicalTrials.gov till June, 2025 to retrieve randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating COX inhibitor usage to prevent headache associated with religious fasting (e.g., Ramadan, Yom Kippur). Meta-analysis was performed using RStudio v2025.05.1+513. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. Outcomes were headache incidence during fasting, headache severity, and incidence of adverse events.

Results Three RCTs were included in this study. Two reported on Ramadan fast, and one reported on Yom Kippur fast. A total of 556 participants (51.1% male) were involved, with mean ages ranging from 32±10 to 41.9±10.4 years. However, no significant differences were observed on Days 1, 4, 5, or 6 (P > 0.05). Headache severity was lower in intervention groups across the studies; however, meta-analysis was not feasible due to substantial variation in format of reporting data. Safety outcomes were similarly not pooled due to inconsistent reporting; Nonetheless, all included trials reported comparable rates of adverse events between intervention and control groups.

Conclusion Prophylactic COX inhibitors may reduce fasting-related headache during fasts on Days 2 and 3, without increasing adverse events. Though severity data were not pooled, individual trials showed benefit. Further trials with standardized outcomes are needed to confirm effectiveness and safety.Fig. 1 (abstract P607).Fig. 2 (abstract P607).

P609 Comparative efficacy and safety of venlafaxine versus amitriptyline for migraine prophylaxis: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P609

Objective To compare the efficacy and safety of venlafaxine to amitriptyline in the prophylactic treatment of migraine.

Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL), International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to June 25, 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing venlafaxine to amitriptyline for migraine prevention. All statistical analyses were done using Review Manager, version 5.4.1. Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MD), or standardized mean differences (SMD) where scales differed. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR). 95% Confidence intervals (CI) were used. I2 statistics was used for inter-study heterogeneity. Efficacy outcomes included reduction, from baseline, in migraine frequency, migraine severity and migraine duration. Safety outcomes were incidence of adverse events.

Results A total of 3 RCTs were included, comprising a total of 232 participants (65.5% being female). Mean age varied from 32.5 ± 7.5 years to 39.7 ± 12.7 years. Pooled analyses showed that venlafaxine usage resulted in statistically significant reduction in headache frequency during treatment, compared to amitriptyline (MD -0.39, 95% CI [-0.68 to -0.11], P = 0.006, I2 = 0%). No significant differences were observed between groups in migraine severity or duration. The incidence of adverse events, including blurred vision, dry mouth, and constipation, was comparable between the two treatments.

Conclusion Venlafaxine demonstrated superior efficacy in reducing migraine frequency compared to amitriptyline, while both treatments demonstrated comparable efficacy in reducing migraine severity and duration. Safety profiles were similar, suggesting venlafaxine may be a clinically appropriate alternative for migraine prophylaxis. Further trials are needed to confirm these findings.Fig. 1 (abstract P609).Fig. 2 (abstract P609).Fig. 3 (abstract P609).

P610 Comparative efficacy and safety of topiramate versus flunarizine in migraine prophylaxis: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P610

Objective To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of two drugs, topiramate and flunarizine, in preventing migraine.

Methods Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and trial registries. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing topiramate and flunarizine were included. Continuous outcomes were pooled as change from baseline to adjust for baseline imbalances. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan v5.4.1.

Results A total of 6 RCTs were included, with a total of 410 migraine patients (68.5% being female). Participants’ mean ages varied from 30.7±10.8 to 43.2±13.9 years. The flunarizine group had significantly lower mean headache days at 8 weeks, compared to the topiramate group (Mean Difference (MD) 2.34 days, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) [0.88-3.79], P = 0.002, I2 = 0%). No significant between-group differences were observed for other efficacy endpoints (pain intensity (VAS), attack frequency, responder rate (≥50% reduction), SOS (abortive) medication use, or mean migraine days). For incidences of overall or individual adverse events, no statistically significant differences were found, except for paresthesia which had significantly higher incidence in the topiramate group (Risk Ratio (RR) 8.62, 95% CI [1.58-46.89], P = 0.013, I2 = 0%).

Conclusion Both topiramate and flunarizine generally demonstrated comparable efficacy in migraine prophylaxis, but flunarizine usage was associated with greater reduction in mean headache days at 8 weeks. Safety profiles were broadly similar, except that the topiramate group demonstrated higher incidences of paresthesia. Future RCTs should include larger sample sizes and use standardized reporting frameworks, including a core outcome set, to ensure consistency across studies and allow for more definitive and generalizable conclusions.Fig. 1 (abstract P610).Fig. 2 (abstract P610).Fig. 3 (abstract P610).

P611 Prophylactic efficacy and safety of intravenous aminophylline compared to intravenous normal saline for post-dural puncture headache in cesarean section patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Saes2, S. ur Rahman2, R. Hotak2, A. Wasti3, S. Noman Qayyum2

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Bacha Khan Medical College, Mardan, Pakistan; 3Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P611

Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of intravenous (IV) aminophylline versus IV normal saline (as comparator) in preventing post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) in people undergoing cesarean section.

Methods We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and clinical trial registries till June, 2025 for randomized controlled studies comparing IV aminophylline to IV normal saline in cesarean patients. Statistical analyses were performed in Review Manager (RevMan), version 5.4.1.

Results Nine studies (N = 1029) were included. Six were conducted in Iran; others were from China, Egypt, and Iraq. Participant mean ages ranged from 24.0±3.9 to 30.5±4.9 years. Aminophylline significantly reduced PDPH incidence at 48 h (2 days) postoperatively (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.61, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) [0.39 to 0.95]), but no significant differences were found at other time points. No consistent effect was seen on severity or intensity, and AE data remain inconclusive. These findings are hoped to inform PDPH protocols regarding low-cost alternatives to techniques such as epidural blood patches. Further high-quality, adequately powered trials with standardized outcome definitions and AE monitoring are needed, however, for more definitive conclusions.Fig. 1 (abstract P611).Fig. 2 (abstract P611).Fig. 3 (abstract P611).

P612 Prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy and safety of oral pregabalin for post-dural puncture headache (PDPH): A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2, M. Atif Bashir1, A. Ehtisham1, M. Ali1

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P612

Objective To evaluate efficacy and safety of oral pregabalin in preventing and treating postdural puncture headache (PDPH).

Methods Searches were run on PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane and clinical trial registries till June, 2025. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing oral pregabalin to conservative therapy or placebo (control) were included, with no language restrictions. RevMan v5.4.1 was used for all statistical analyses.

Results 7 RCTs (N=1004) were included; 4 evaluated prophylactic use and 3 evaluated therapeutic use for PDPH. Prophylactically, pregabalin significantly reduced PDPH incidence versus control (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.47, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) [0.32-0.70]). It also reduced time to modified Bromage motor scale grade 3 (Mean Difference [MD] -3.18 min, 95% CI [-4.93 to -1.42]) and prolonged time to rescue analgesia (MD 45.15 min, 95% CI [4.06-86.25]). No significant differences were seen regarding PDPH onset, time to two-segment regression or incidence of postoperative nausea/vomiting (PONV). Therapeutically, pregabalin significantly reduced headache intensity at 24 h (MD -1.76, 95% CI [-3.48 to -0.03]), 48 h (MD -1.74, 95% CI [-2.26 to -1.21]), and 72 h (MD -1.68, 95% CI [-2.25 to -1.11]). It also lowered modified Lybecker headache severity scores at 48 h (MD -0.57, 95% CI [-0.84 to -0.31]). Safety data, though could not be pooled due to reporting heterogeneity, showed no significant increase in adverse effects.

Conclusion Oral pregabalin shows promise as both a prophylactic and therapeutic option for PDPH, with considerable reductions in PDPH incidence, intensity, and severity, without increased adverse events. Whilst current evidence supports its perioperative use, future research must directly compare pregabalin with established pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic strategies. In settings where therapies like epidural blood patches are impractical or delayed, pregabalin may offer a safer, non-invasive window for intervention.Fig. 1 (abstract P612).Fig. 2 (abstract P612).Fig. 3 (abstract P612).

P613 Discontinuation of oral migraine preventives during anti-CGRP therapy: A retrospective cohort study

L. Fagundes1, T. Morais2,1, C. Fernandes1, I. Costa1, A. Maduro1, B. Rodrigues1, I. Monteiro1, S. Batista1,3, H. Gens1, F. Magalhães1, I. Luzeiro1

1Local Health Unit of Coimbra, Neurology, Coimbra, Portugal; 2Espírito Santo Hospital, Neurology, Azores, Portugal; 3University of Coimbra, Faculty of Medicine, Coimbra, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P613

Objective CGRP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) have revolutionized migraine prevention. European guidelines recommend maintaining oral preventive medications during the initial treatment period with mAbs, followed by reassessment for potential tapering after 3 months. However, real-world evidence on the feasibility of this approach remains scarce. The aim of this study was to evaluate the proportion of migraine patients who were able to reduce or discontinue oral preventive medications within one year of initiating monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy.

Methods This retrospective cohort study included migraine patients treated with mAbs at a tertiary hospital center. Oral preventive medication use was monitored for 12 months. The primary endpoint was the rate of successful reduction or discontinuation of oral preventives. Secondary analyses explored patient characteristics linked to these outcomes.

Results At baseline, each patient was, on average, under 1.4 oral preventive medications. Among 82 patients (mean age 45 years; 87% female), 56.7% reduced or discontinued oral therapies within one year. By the end of the follow-up period, there was a significant decrease in the use of oral preventive medications (χ²(2) = 23.01, p < 0.001) and 34.1% had successfully discontinued all oral medications. The proportion of patients with ≤15 headache days per month increased from 30.5% at baseline to 80.5% at 12 months (χ²(1) = 39.02, p < 0.001). Patient with more than 15 headache days per month at baseline was significantly associated with a lower likelihood of reducing oral preventives at 12 months (OR = 0.33; 95% CI = 0.12–0.96; p = 0.042).

Conclusion This study provides real-world evidence supporting the safety and feasibility of reducing or discontinuing oral preventive medications in mAb-responsive migraine patients. Higher baseline migraine frequency was linked to a lower likelihood of discontinuation of oral preventives, possibly reflecting greater disease burden or treatment resistance.

P615 Therapeutic challenges in a rare trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia

M. T. Rego1, C. Rocha Oliveira1, A. L. Pires1, P. Ferreira1, I. Alves1, J. M. Roriz1

1Unidade Local de Saúde Entre Douro e Vouga, Santa Maria da Feira, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P615

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective To discuss therapeutic challenges associated with a probable SUNCT. It’s a rare entity with pathophysiological mechanisms that remain incompletely understood and for which evidence regarding effective treatment strategies is limited. Clinical management therefore requires an individualized, multidisciplinary approach, given the high rate of refractoriness and significant functional impact.

Methods Clinical case report.

Results A 39-year-old man, with no relevant past medical history, presented with continuous left-sided hemicranial headache, accompanied by dozens to hundreds of daily paroxysms of excruciating, shock-like pain lasting from seconds to a few minutes. He also had persistent ipsilateral autonomic signs/symptoms (ptosis, conjunctival injection and tearing), which began several months prior to the onset of the headache. Brain and orbital MRI revealed no structural abnormalities, nor evidence of neurovascular contact. Immunological work-up showed persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies and HLA-B51 positivity, prompting referral to Rheumatology. A probable diagnosis of SUNCT was considered. Multiple preventive treatments were trialed without sustained benefit. A sphenopalatine ganglion block was also attempted with no lasting improvement. A discrete improvement was noted with intravenous eptinezumab 300 mg every 12 weeks, in combination with duloxetine, gabapentin, topiramate and tapentadol. He makes excessive use of fast-acting tramadol and ibuprofen to alleviate acute pain. He was referred to Neurosurgery and awaits therapeutic decision. Despite optimized pharmacological management, he continues to experience countless debilitating episodes with severe impact on functionality and mental health.

Conclusion SUNCT remains a therapeutic challenge due to its rarity, limited evidence base, and frequent refractoriness. This reinforces the need for further research and therapeutic innovation.

P616 Efficacy and safety of single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation for migraine: A systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2, F. Amin1

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P616

Objective This review aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (sTMS) for migraine.

Methods We searched PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, Embase, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to August 28, 2025. We included studies evaluating the use of sTMS for migraine. Meta-analysis was performed using R/RStudio v2025.05.1+513. Continuous and dichotomous outcomes were pooled as means and proportions respectively, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). I2-statistics were used to evaluate inter-study heterogeneity. Outcomes evaluated were patient-reported pain relief, change in HIT-6 scores, change in mean headache days, and adverse events (overall and individual [paresthesia, scalp discomfort, headache directly caused by intervention]).

Results Four studies were included, comprising 557 participants (78.8% female, mean ages 39 to 49 years). Pooled analysis revealed the participant-reported pain relief rate to be 66% (95% CI 57%-75%). Mean reduction in HIT-6 scores at 3 months, from baseline, was -4.71 (95% CI -6.87 to -2.55) and mean reduction in headache days was -3.6 days (95% CI -4.91 to -2.28) at 3-months follow-up. Overall adverse event rate was 19% (95% CI 11%-29%), and individual adverse event rates were 1% for paresthesia, 2% for scalp discomfort, and 2% for headache.

Conclusion Single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation demonstrates meaningful efficacy in reducing migraine burden with a favorable safety profile. However, high-quality trials against standard-of-care interventions are needed to further clarify its role in migraine.Fig. 1 (abstract P616).Fig. 2 (abstract P616).

P617 Comparative efficacy and safety of proximal versus distal greater occipital nerve block in managing headache disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P617

Objective This review aims to compare the efficacy and safety of proximal versus distal greater occipital nerve blocks (GONB) in managing headache disorders.

Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to September 9, 2025. Eligible studies were randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing proximal GONB to distal GONB for managing headache disorders in adults. Statistical analyses were performed in Review Manager v5.4.1. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk-ratios (RR) and continuous outcomes as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity was assessed using I2-statistics. Primary outcomes were block success rate and reduction in Numeric Rating Scale (NRS-11) score. Secondary outcomes were analgesic requirement and adverse event rate.

Results Three RCTs were included in this review, consisting of a total of 270 patients (61.9% female). Mean participant ages varied from 29 ± 3.4 to 49.50 ± 12.53 years. Proximal GONB use was associated with significantly higher block success rates (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.13-1.72, I2 = 28%) and significantly greater reductions in Numeric Rating Scale (NRS-11) scores at 24 h post-block (MD -0.26, 95% CI -0.46 to -0.06). Proximal GONB use also resulted in significantly fewer analgesic requirements (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.98). No significant differences were seen for overall adverse event rates. Heterogeneity was absent for all outcomes (I2 = 0%) other than block success rate.

Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrates that proximal greater occipital nerve block provides superior clinical benefit compared to distal block in adults with headache disorders, with higher success rates and greater short-term pain relief, without increasing adverse events. Further high-quality trials with longer follow-ups are needed to confirm benefits.Fig. 1 (abstract P617).

P624 “Cefaleias em rede”: A pilot project to improve headache management in health care
