The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P624

Objective Headache, especially migraine, is a leading cause of disability worldwide and places a significant burden on secondary care, often due to avoidable referrals. With appropriate support, up to 90% of headache cases can be effectively managed in Primary Health Care (PHC). In our center, approximately 8% of referrals from PHC are for headache, with an average wait time of nine months for a first neurology consult. A survey among local PHC physicians revealed major gaps in diagnosis and both acute and preventive treatment. Our goal is to empower family physicians to accurately diagnose and manage headache disorders, while optimizing referrals in line with published criteria.

Methods Starting in 2025, over 100 family medicine residents and physicians will receive training in headache care, focusing on red flags, differential diagnosis, treatment strategies for common primary headaches, and referral guidelines. Each of five participating PHC centers will have a designated liaison family doctor serving as the main contact with the hospital’s Headache Clinic. For referrals that can be managed in PHC with specialist input, a group consultation model will be implemented. Conclusion The “Cefaleias em Rede” pilot project offers a scalable model to strengthen headache care within PHC. By equipping family doctors with targeted training and establishing structured collaboration with headache specialists, we aim to reduce unnecessary referrals, shorten wait times, and improve patient outcomes. P625 Multidisciplinary management of headaches in a Brazilian tertiary hospital

F. Sambini1, A. Rodrigues1, C. Ferreira Pinheiro-Araújo1, F. Dach2, D. Bevilaqua-Grossi1

1Univertisy of São Paulo, Health Sciences, Ribeirão Preto, Brazil; 2Univertisy of São Paulo, Neurology, Ribeirão Preto, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P625

Objective To describe how multidisciplinary management of headaches happens in a Brazilian tertiary hospital.

Methods Medical records from the Headache and Craniofacial Pain outpatient Clinic (HCPC) were analyzed from July to December 2024.

Results In the period of 6 months 595 individuals were treated by neurologists at the headache outpatient clinic. Of these, 56 were referred to physiotherapy. All individuals with headache were diagnosed using the third edition of the International Classification of Headache Disorders. The fig. 1 shows the treatment plan for patients with headache and orofacial pain in a Brazilian tertiary hospital. After being referred to the outpatient clinic, these patients undergo a complete evaluation of the cervical spine, including the presence of trigger points, strength and cervical ROM, in addition to specific tests, such as the CCFT and FRT. In addition, evaluation of mandibular ROM and postural assessment are also included. Regarding the treatment of individuals with headache, the initial phase includes education in pain neuroscience, diaphragmatic breathing associated with cervical traction and mobilization, and release of trigger points. A second phase includes active stretching of the cervical spine and strengthening exercises for the deep flexors and cervical extensors, and cervical resistance training. In a more advanced phase, scapular strengthening exercises are included. Patients usually undergo treatment for 8 or 12 weeks, after which they are re-evaluated. At this point, there are 2 possible stages: discharge or redefinition of therapeutic goals.

Conclusion The public and free tertiary hospital in Ribeirão Preto has a multidisciplinary team that works together for the benefit of the patient, according to their demandsFig. 1 (abstract P625)..

P629 MIGRAGILE: A self-administered tool for early detection of disabling migraine at primary care setting

V. Obach Baurier1, M. T. Marco Galindo2, S. Mamani3, G. Morera Vila-Real4, C. Vazquez Veloso5, A. Picas Jufresa6, Z. Herreras7, M. d. l. Á. Sosa2, A. Grajea2, S. Fernández Fernández2, M. d. l. N. Fabregat Fabra2

1Hospital Clinic, Headache Unit, Neurology Department, Barcelona, Spain; 2Hospital Clinic, Headache Unit, Barcelona, Spain; 3CAP BORRELL, AISBE, Barcelona, Spain; 4CAP SARRIA, AISBE, Barcelona, Spain; 5CAP LES HORTES, AISBE, Barcelona, Spain; 6CAP ROGER, AISBE, Barcelona, Spain; 7CAP BORRELL, OFICINA TECNICA AISBE, Barcelona, Spain

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P629

Objective Migraine is a common and disabling neurological disorder frequently underdiagnosed, causing delays in treatment and increased burden on patients and healthcare systems.

Aim: To evaluate a self-administered screening tool (MIGRAGILE) for early identification of disabling migraine, specifically High Frequency Episodic Migraine (HFEM) and Chronic Migraine (CM), at primary care setting.

Methods We designed MIGRAGILE e-survey with 15 questions, self-completed by patients with headache. It allowed to characterize (1) migraine diagnosis, (2) degree of headache disability, (3) acute and preventive treatment prescribed, and (4) need to be assessed by general neurologist or more specialized headache neurologist. In a routine medical appointment, the General Practitioner provided the MIGRAGILE e-survey and recommended patients with headache to fill in the QR code survey in RedCap platform. Headache Nurse reviewed the surveys sent twice per week. Our reference population is 540.000 inhabitants distributed in 20 Primary care centers.

Results From July 2023 to July 2025, 332 patients completed the survey. After the learning curve, an average of 22 patients are presently evaluated every month. False Positive (n=9) and False negative (n=1) for migraine diagnose resulted in a Sensibility, Specificity, Positive Predicting Value and Negative Predicting Value of 99.7%, 75.7%, 96.9% and 96.5%, respectively. Headache diagnosis distribution was: (1) Low Frequency episodic migraine 50.2%, (2) HFEM and CM 37.1% 4) Medication overuse headache 2.4% and 5) Other non-migraine headaches 10.3%. Headache nurse evaluated and sent 33.1% of patient to online educational migraine program and 30.7% to priority visits at the Headache Unit.

Conclusion In our center, MIGRAGILE is a clinically useful self-administered screening tool for early detection of disabling migraine in primary care, integrated into headache nurse activity.

P632 Intracranial incidental findings on brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) in a pediatric population with primary headache: Our experience and management

F. Ursitti1, F. Tripodi2, L. Papetti1, G. Sforza1, G. Monte1, A. Borrelli1, S. Tarantino1, M. Proietti Checchi1, M. Valeriani1,3,4

1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Developmental Neurology, Rome, Italy; 2Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Rome, Italy; 3University of Rome Tor Vergata, Rome, Italy; 4Translational Pain Neuroscience and Precision Medicine, CNAP, Department of Health Science and Technology, Aalborg, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P632

Objective Headache is frequent symptom in children, which often leads to execution of neuroradiological examinations and to finding of incidentalomas. In fact, headache is often attributed to primary headache, neurological disorder common in developmental age. Recent widespread access to neuroradiological examinations has led to increase in number of incidental brain lesions in children with headache.

Methods We reported retrospective study (28 patients under 18 years) with primary headache and incidental findings of suspected low-grade lesion at brain MRI. Data were collected on age, sex, headache characteristics. Patients were treated conservatively with neuroimaging surveillance of suspected low-grade lesion. Lesions were divided in supratentorial (thalamic) and infratentorial (cerebellar). The first follow-up MRI was performed after 6 months and follow-up were carried out every 12 to 18 months.

Results Patients included 13 females (46%) and 15 males (54%): 67.8% presented migraine without aura, 25% tensive headache, 14.3% migraine with aura, 7% both tensive headache and migraine without aura. In following period: 7% was stable at 84 months, 17.8% at 72 months, 21.5% at 60 months, 46.5% at 48 months, 64.3% at 36 months, 96.5% at 24 months. 96.5% of the patients showed radiological stability during the whole follow-up period. No significant radiological changes were found during follow-up in 27 of 28 patients.

Conclusion With increasing detail of imaging techniques, there has been an increase in number of incidentally brain lesions in children with primary headache, leading to a management dilemma for neurologists. Incidentally low-grade lesions are not related to headache. This study reports data on long-term clinical and radiological follow-up period in patients with primary headache and occasional low-grade lesion findings during headache assessment, showing stability over time and safety of conservative management.

P633 Unveiling the hidden burden of migraine in Cape Verde: Clinical characterisation and impact assessment from a real-world care setting

D. D. J. Vaz1, F. Dourado Sotero1, M. I. Pavão Martins1

1Faculty of Medicine, University of Lisbon, Department of Neurology, Lisbon, Portugal

Objective This study aims to provide aclinical and demographic characterization of a cohort of migraine patients in Cape Verde, assessing ictal, interictal, and quality of life impact.

Methods Adults diagnosed with migraine according to ICHD-3 criteria, followed at the Neurology outpatient clinic of a central hospital in Cape Verde, were included. P636 Comorbid migraine and epilepsy in a UK neurology tertiary service: Clinical characteristics, treatment outcomes, and prognosis

D. Sunar1, A. Bennett1, S. Fairclough2, M. Maguire2, L. Idrovo1

1Leeds Teaching Hospital NHS, Neurology, Headache Service, Leeds, UK; 2Leeds Teaching Hospital NHS, Neurology, Epilepsy Clinic, Leeds, UK

Objective To describe the demographics, clinical phenotype and treatment outcomes of patients with comorbid migraine and epilepsy referred to a tertiary UK Neuroscience centre.

P637 The real pain of abuse: Not all bruises are visible

J. Almeida Ferreira1, T. Geraldes1, M. Rodrigues1, L. Pereira1

1Hospital Garcia de Orta, ULSAS, Neurology, Almada, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P637

Objective One of the diagnostic challenges in headaches is to dissect the symptoms in patients with depressive disorders, requiring careful clinical evaluation to differentiate overlapping diseases and guide appropriate management.

Methods Patient consent to publish details in an open access journal.

Results A 48-year-old woman, with a medical history of hypertension, fibromyalgia and depression, was referred to neurology consult for episodes of right, stabbing, intense (10/10), frontal headache, lasting 5 min, recurring up to 2-3 times daily, associated with ipsilateral tearing, ptosis and miosis, and refractory to acute treatment. The hypothesis of short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic symptoms (SUNA) was considered, but there was no response to either lamotrigine nor topiramate at therapeutic doses. MRI was normal. Later, the characteristics of headache changed. It became right-sided hemicrania, pressure-type, constant, less intense (4/10, with paroxysmal worsening (intensity 10/10, lasting 5–10 min, with ipsilateral ptosis, conjunctival erythema, and tearing), 2-3 times per day. The hypothesis of hemicrania continua was considered, but again there was no response to indomethacin. When cognitive and depressive symptoms arose, psychiatry consultation was requested, where the circumstance of domestic violence was identified. One of the final diagnosis of this patient was headache attributed to psychiatric disorder, and non-pharmacologic treatment was proposed.

Conclusion Currently, there are no established guidelines for the diagnosis or treatment of headache attributed to psychiatric disorder. Nonetheless, it is of supreme importance to systematically inquire about prior or ongoing physical, emotional, and/or sexual abuse. Emphasis is on the complex diagnostic process, the critical role of a multidisciplinary approach, and the consideration of the patients’ emotional and social dimensions.

P638 The impact of migraine with aura on cardiovascular risk in women: A systematic review

W. Gonçalves Horta1, A. José Bezerra Jovino Marques2, A. Sofia De Moura Nóbrega Barroso2, J. Nascimento Maciel2, K. Ferraz2, L. Leite Carvalho2, M. Luiza Almeida Braga Camargo2, D. Rodrigues Lemos Neto3

1Universidade de Pernambuco, Headache clinic from Hospital Oswaldo Cruz, Recife, Brazil; 2Universidade Católica de Pernambuco, Recife, Brazil; 3Faculdade de Medicina de Olinda, Neurology, Paulista, Brazil

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P638

Objective This systematic review aims to evaluate the association between migraine with aura and cardiovascular risk in women. It focuses on identifying key cardiovascular outcomes linked to migraine with aura, analyzing the impact of additional risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, and hormonal contraceptive use, and comparing cardiovascular event incidence between women with and without migraine with aura.

Methods A systematic search was performed in PubMed, LILACS, and SciELO databases using the terms “Migraine,” “Aura,” “Cardiovascular Risk,” and “Woman” combined with the Boolean operator AND. Studies published from 2015 to 2025 in English or Portuguese involving women with migraine with aura who developed cardiovascular diseases were included. After screening 137 articles by title, abstract, and full text, nine studies met the eligibility criteria. The selected studies were appraised according to evidence levels from meta-analyses (Level I) to cross-sectional studies (Level V).

Results The evidence consistently indicates that migraine with aura increases the risk of major cardiovascular events, especially myocardial infarction and stroke, in women. Prospective cohorts and meta-analyses provided the strongest support. Additional factors such as smoking, hypertension, and oral contraceptive use further increase this risk. Migraine with aura is considered an independent cardiovascular risk factor and may improve risk prediction models. Associations with vascular dysfunction and higher risk of cervical artery dissection were also reported, emphasizing the need for clinical vigilance.

Conclusion Migraine with aura is strongly associated with increased cardiovascular risk in women, acting as both an independent risk factor and marker of vascular vulnerability. Clinical management should address modifiable risk factors to prevent adverse outcomes. Further research is essential to clarify causality and optimize personalized prevention and treatment strategies.

P639 Sex differences in clinical presentation and diagnostic delay in cluster headache

L. Portocarrero-Sánchez1, J. Díaz de Terán1

1Hospital Universitario La Paz, Headache Unit, Neurology Department, Madrid, Spain

Objective Studies suggest sex-based differences in cluster headache (CH). We analyzed clinical variability by sex, focusing on age of onset, diagnostic delay, trigeminal-autonomic symptoms (TAS), and remission periods.

P640 Migraine burden in postmenopausal women and the need for prophylactic treatment

C. A. Diaz Garza1, E. G. Gama Reyes1, A. Leyva-Rendon1, J. A. Galnares Olade1

1National Institute of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Headache Clinic, Mexico City, Mexico

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P640

Objective To assess the need to continue preventive treatment for migraine in women after the onset of menopause.

Methods We performed a retrospective chart review of female patients with a longstanding diagnosis of migraine according to ICHD-3 criteria. Patients aged 50 or older, who had received a clinical diagnosis of menopause between 2024 and 2025, were included. Menopause was established clinically. Patients with secondary headaches were excluded. Data were obtained from a specialized Headache Clinic in Mexico City. Treatment continuation reflected a clinical decision during follow-up.

Results Fifty-nine patients were included. Median age was 57 years (IQR 52–59). A first-degree relative with migraine was reported in 15%. The most common comorbidities were hypertension (13%) and depression (7%). Tension-type headache was present in 10%. 12% had a history of mild traumatic brain injury, without a clear relationship to migraine diagnosis or worsening. Alternating hemicranial pain was reported in 44%, side-locked pain in 25%, and frontal predominance in 16%. Median pain intensity during attacks was 7/10 (IQR 4–8.75), and median monthly migraine days were 2 (IQR 1–8). 79% of patients continued using preventive treatment after menopause. The most prescribed agents were amitriptyline (37%), topiramate (27%), and propranolol (10%). Acute treatment was not used in 44% of cases. The most common acute medications were zolmitriptan (10%), paracetamol (8.6%), and ketorolac (8.6%). Twenty patients used two prophylactics; 22% reported intolerance to at least one drug. 4% had medication-overuse headache, and 5% had contraindications to triptans.

Conclusion Our findings highlight the persistent burden of migraine after menopause and support the ongoing need for prophylaxis in a majority of patients. This may challenge assumptions of reduced treatment need post-menopause and suggests a specific phenotype of late-life persistent migraine.

M. Noory1, J. Worm1, A. S. S. Andersen1, N. Noory1, T. B. Heinskou2, L. Bendtsen1, D. M. Kristensen3, C. S. J. Westgate1,4, S. Maarbjerg5

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P641

Objective To investigate the potential role of sex hormones in women with trigeminal neuralgia by exploring associations with major hormonal life events, hormone-related medications, and comorbidities that may influence hormone levels.

Methods In this cross-sectional case-control study, women with trigeminal neuralgia aged ≤ 60 years were consecutively included and interviewed using a semi-structured questionnaire covering pain characteristics, hormonal life events, hormone-related treatments, and relevant comorbidities. P642 Is sexual dysfunction the forgotten burden of migraine? A systematic review and meta-analysis

A. Ç. Atalar1, Ş. O. Dörtkol1, E. Ekizoğlu2, B. Baykan3

1Istanbul Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation Training and Research Hospital, Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey; 2Istanbul University Istanbul Faculty of Medicine, Department of Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey; 3EMAR Medical Center, Neurology, Istanbul, Turkey

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P642

Objective Migraine is a significant cause of disability affecting social functioning including sexual life. Despite this, data on the presence and extent of sexual problems in individuals with migraine remain surprisingly limited. This study aims to review and analyse existing evidence on the prevalence, subtypes, and predictors of sexual dysfunction (SD) in patients with migraine.

Methods An extensive literature search was conducted in Pubmed, Cochrane and Google Scholar, from 1987 July to October 2023. The study was registered in PROSPERO (No: CRD42024562356). After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, the retrieved references were imported into the Rayyan platform, and the abstracts were screened blindly. Following the blind screening phase, the researchers held a consensus meeting to resolve conflicts. Full texts of the eligible studies were reviewed after quality assessment using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.

Results Among the 21 studies, 18(85.7%) were cross-sectional, while 3(14.3%) were prospective in design. The majority of included studies focused exclusively on female participants (n=17); three included only males, and one included both sexes. The most frequent subtype of SD was reduced sexual desire (79.35±7.99%), followed by arousal, lubrication, orgasm and satisfaction issues.

Conclusion SD is a highly prevalent but an underestimated problem in patients with migraine. Given the substantial impact of this condition on patients’ quality of life, rigorous screening and precise diagnosis of SD in individuals with migraine are essential to inform and optimize targeted therapeutic strategies.

P643 Sex-related clinical differences in cluster headache

N. Imai1, A. Iwasaki1, A. Moriya1, E. Kitamura2

1Japanese Red Cross Shizuoka Hospital, Shizuoka-Shi, Japan; 2Kitasato University, Sagamihara, Japan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P643

Objective Cluster headache (CH) is classically male-predominant. Recent cohorts suggest women may experience earlier onset, more chronic disease, and fewer alcohol-related attacks. We examined if comparable sex differences exist in a Japanese CH cohort.

Methods We retrospectively reviewed 237 consecutive patients diagnosed with CH at Shizuoka Red Cross Hospital (ICHD-3; men=167, women=70). Variables included age at onset, family history, migraine comorbidity, HIT-6, VAS, headache varacteristics, and potential triggers (bathing, alcohol, smoking). Groups were compared using chi-square or Mann–Whitney U tests.

Results Women tended to develop CH earlier (median 23.5 vs. 29 years; p=0.079). Relative to men, women more often had bouts <1 month or chronic CH (p<0.001), year-round/multiple annual bouts (p=0.014), and longer individual attacks (≥4 h vs. 1–2 h; p=0.011). Positive family history (p=0.031), migraine comorbidity (p<0.001), phonophobia (p=0.006), and vomiting (p=0.004) were also more frequent in women. Conclusion Japanese women with CH display earlier onset, greater chronicity, longer attacks, and stronger migraine features. Men remain more strongly associated with alcohol/tobacco triggers. Recognising these sex-specific patterns may facilitate earlier diagnosis and personalised management of CH across diverse populations.

P644 Gender differences in dependence level and behaviours in patients with Medication-Overuse Headache (MOH)

E. Lebedeva1, I. Kniazeva1, D. Gilev2, J. Olesen3

1the Ural State Medical University, International Headache Center, Yekaterinburg, Russian Federation; 2the Ural Federal University named after the First President of Russia B.N. Yeltsin, Economics, Yekaterinburg, Russian Federation; 3Copenhagen University Hospital - Rigshospitalet, Danish Headache Center, Copenhagen, Denmark

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P644

Objective Dependence behaviours сan differ between females and males with medication overuse headache (MOH) and can influence the higher prevalence of MOH in females. This prospective study aimed to characterise gender differences in dependence behaviours in MOH by using the Leeds Dependence Questionnaire (LDQ), and other dependencies, including smoking and alcohol abuse.

Methods In total, 344 consecutive patients were recruited and professionally face-to-face interviewed, including 171 patients with MOH (mean age 43.3 years, 81.9% women, migraine 64.9%, tension-type headache 35.1%) and 173 patients without MOH (mean age 41.4 years, 74.6% women, migraine 57.8%, tension-type headache 42.2%).

Results The presence of dependence by LDQ was significantly more often detected in patients with MOH (95.3%) than without MOH (69.4%) (p<0.001; OR 9.0; 95% CI 4.1-19.6). This can’t explain the higher prevalence of MOH in females and stresses the necessity of further studies.

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P645

Objective Clinical trial data suggest a decreased efficacy of CGRPr oral inhibitors – i.e., gepants – for acute migraine treatment in males compared with females. We aimed at assessing sex differences in the response to rimegepant for acute migraine treament in a real-world setting.

Methods We included patients with either episodic or chronic migraine who treated at least one migraine attack with rimegepant according to clinical indications from June 2023 to April 2025. Conclusion We found a higher effectiveness of rimegepant for the acute treatment of migraine in females compared with males. Nevertheless, the drug was effective in both sexes. P646 Preventive treatment of migraine in males: The role of monoclonal antibodies

C. Marques1, R. Nunes Rato2, R. Dias2,3, M. Pinto2, A. Costa2,3

1Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto, Porto, Portugal; 2Unidade Local de Saúde de São João, E.P.E., Neurology Department, Porto, Portugal; 3Clinical Neuroscience and Mental Health Department, Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto, Porto, Portugal

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P646

Objective Anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody (aCGRP) trials for migraine have mostly included women, with limited data on the response of men, in both clinical trials and real-world settings. This study aimed to evaluate and compare the clinical response to and adverse effects of aCGRP use in men and women.

Methods A retrospective observational study was conducted, including men and women who were matched by age and migraine frequency. Clinical characteristics, therapeutic response, functional improvement, and adverse effects were assessed through medical records. Statistical analysis included Student’s t-test and Fisher’s exact test (significance: p < 0.05).

Results A total of 48 patients (24 men and 24 women) were included and matched for age (mean: 41.8 years) and migraine frequency. No significant differences were found regarding migraine type (episodic / chronic) or aura presence. After three months, migraine days decreased by a similar amount in both men and women (50.8% vs. 60.3%; p = 0.394), a trend that was maintained at six and twelve months. Functional improvement, as measured by a reduction in HIT-6 score of at least 5 points, was observed in both sexes, with greater reductions in women at 3 (p = 0.002) and 6 months (p < 0.001). Adverse events were generally mild, with no significant sex differences except for more gastrointestinal symptoms in women at three months (p = 0.048). Overall tolerability was good, with sustained adherence.

Conclusion Despite greater reductions in HIT-6 scores and more initial adverse events in women, the overall efficacy and safety of aCGRP therapies were similar for both sexes. These results help to address the lack of male-specific data and support the applicability of aCGRP therapies regardless of sex.

P648 Sex differences in premonitory symptoms and triggers in migraine: Insights from a tertiary headache clinic

U. Ashraf1, D. Karaca2, S. Tomlinson1

1St Vincent’s Hospital, Neurology, Sydney, Australia; 2King’s College London, Wolfson SPaRC, Camberwell, UK

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P648

Objective To identify sex differences in migraine phenotype between men and women in a tertiary headache clinic.

Methods A cross-sectional, single center study was conducted in consecutive patients attending a tertiary headache clinic between February-November 2024. Patients fulfilling ICHD-3 criteria for migraine were included. Data was collected on age, sex and premonitory symptoms, which were defined as symptoms occurring between 48 h to immediately before headache onset. Data was also collected on triggers, defined as factors that were most of the time followed by migraine symptoms within four hours. Statistical analysis with Fisher’s Exact Test and Mann-Whitney U testing was performed using IBM SPSS (Version 29).

Results A total of 101 patients were included (81 female, 20 male, median age 45 years [IQR 33–56]). Women were not more likely to report high frequency episodic or chronic migraine compared to men (74% vs. 70%, P=0.781). Women reported a greater number of premonitory symptoms than men (6 [IQR 4-9] vs. 4 [IQR 2-7], P=0.005) as well as more triggers (4 [IQR 3-7] vs. 3 [IQR 2-5], P=0.046). Women were more likely than men to report premonitory symptoms of photophobia (83% vs. 55%, P= 0.015), phonophobia (56% vs. 25%, P=0.023), rhinorrhea or nasal congestion (23% vs. 0%, P=0.037) and vertigo (65% vs. 35%, P=0.021). Women were more likely to report heat as a trigger compared to men (53% vs. 25%, P=0.027).

Conclusion Women report more premonitory symptoms and triggers than men and are more like to specifically report premonitory photophobia, phonophobia, nasal autonomic symptoms and vertigo. Women are also more likely to report heat as a trigger. These findings may suggest sexual dimorphism in biological pathways implicated in the pathophysiology of premonitory symptoms and the influence of triggers on these pathways.

P650 Migraine male patients: Profiling a minority using real-world data from the Italian National Migraine Registry (I-GRAINE)

M. Guarinoni1, G. Fiorentini2,3, G. Egeo2, P. Barbanti2,3, P. Torelli1

1University of Parma, Headache Center, Unit of Neurology, Parma, Italy; 2IRCCS San Raffaele, Headache and Pain Unit, Rome, Italy; 3San Raffaele University, Rome, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P650

Objective Migraine is a common primary headache disorder with a marked female predominance (female-to-male ratio 2:1–6:1). Consequently, most sociodemographic and clinical data—and the diagnostic criteria derived from them—are largely female oriented and may not fully capture the male phenotype. This study aimed to characterize male migraineurs, focusing on sociodemographic factors and attack features, using real-world data from the Italian National Migraine Registry (I-GRAINE).

Methods I-GRAINE is an ongoing, multicenter, prospective registry involving 43 publicly funded headache centers. Since April 2021, patients with migraine have been consecutively enrolled. Data are collected through structured, face-to-face interviews conducted by trained neurologists using a dedicated electronic platform. This analysis examined the male subgroup.

Results By 19 September 2025, 2,106 patients had been enrolled (85% female, 15% male), including 319 men. Mean age was 46 years; mean BMI 24.5 kg/m². Current migraine frequency averaged 10.3 days/month versus 6.3 days/month at onset. Mean MIDAS and HIT-6 scores were 47 and 61, respectively.

Conclusion Men with migraine display distinct clinical and lifestyle profiles, underscoring the need for tailored management to improve recognition and treatment in this under-represented population.

O. Dementeva1

1JSC “K+31”, Neurology, Moscow, Russian Federation

Objective Primary headaches in older adults remain under-investigated, particularly regarding the impact of sex, ethnicity, and psychiatric comorbidities. Identifying modifiable factors may improve prevention and management strategies in this age group.

Objective

To analyze the most frequent determinants of primary headache in outpatients aged ≥55 years and to evaluate factors negatively influencing headache chronification.

Methods The study included 49 migraine patients from Russia and Italy aged ≥55 years. P652 Efficacy and safety of nebulization of dexmedetomidine versus saline for treating postdural puncture headache after cesarean section: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2, M. Usman Iqbal1

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P652

Objective This review aims to compare the effectiveness of nebulized dexmedetomidine versus saline for treating postdural puncture headache (PDPH) after cesarean section.

Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov and Google Scholar from inception to September 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing nebulization of dexmedetomidine versus saline for treating PDPH after cesarean section operation. EBP requirements and overall adverse events rates remained comparable between the two groups.

Conclusion Nebulized dexmedetomidine may provide superior analgesic efficacy compared to saline for the management of PDPH following cesarean section, with consistent reductions in pain scores up to 72 h. The intervention did not increase the need for epidural blood patches or the incidence of adverse events, suggesting a favorable safety profile. P653 Beyond pain: Psychological profiles in chronic migraine compared with Fibromyalgia and their comorbidity

S. Bottiroli1,2, M. Cangelosi1, M. Cavicchioli3, M. Mesce3, A. Torelli3, A. Benfante4, A. Romeo4, F. Nimbi5, L. Castelli4, N. Ghiotto2, G. Sances2, R. de Icco1,2, C. Tassorelli1,2, M. di Franco3, C. Iannuccelli3, F. Galli3

1University of Pavia, Brain and Behavioural Sciences, Pavia, Italy; 2IRCCS Mondino Foundation, Pavia, Italy; 3Sapienza University of Rome, Rome, Italy; 4University of Turin, Turin, Italy; 5eCampus Telematic University, Novedrate, Italy

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P653

Objective Chronic migraine (CM) and fibromyalgia (FM) are pain conditions marked by central sensitization and high psychological comorbidity. While they share some clinical features, evidence suggests differences in psychological functioning and symptom burden. Investigating these differences, along with transdiagnostic psychological profiles, may clarify their specificities. The present study aims to compare psychological functioning in CM, FM, and comorbid CM+FM, and to identify transdiagnostic psychological profiles beyond diagnostic categories.

Methods This is a multicenter cross-sectional study including 318 women (97 CM, 130 FM, 91 CM+FM). Participants completed validated self-report measures of depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), psychological distress (SCL-90-R), mental functioning (SF-12), and, defensive functioning (DMRS-SR-30). Conclusion CM shows a more preserved psychological profile than FM, while comorbid CM+FM aligns with the most impaired profiles. These findings support a dimensional, transdiagnostic approach to chronic pain, emphasizing psychological functioning as a key factor for personalized care.

Objective Cluster headache is the most prevalent type of trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC) headache disorder. Cluster headaches affect approximately 0.1% of the population, and they most commonly occur in men around the age of 30. Anti-inflammatory diets can help improve cluster headaches by reducing neuroinflammation. Since the Mediterranean diet is an anti-inflammatory diet, and few studies have examined the role of this type of diet on cluster headaches, this study aimed to investigate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and the occurrence of cluster headaches.

Methods In this cross-sectional study, the case group consisted of 67 cluster patients diagnosed according to ICHD-3 criteria, and the control group comprised 200 healthy individuals with a BMI between 18 and 40 kg/m². P658 SUNCT-like headache secondary to herpes zoster in the ipsilateral ophthalmic nerve distribution: A case report

A. Rajaratnam1, B. Senanayake1

1National Hospital of Sri Lanka, Institute of Neurology, Colombo, Sri Lanka

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P658

Objective Short-lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache attacks with Conjunctival injection and Tearing (SUNCT) is an uncommon trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia. We report a secondary SUNCT-like syndrome following ophthalmic-distribution herpes zoster.

Methods The patient provided informed consent for the case report as per ethical standards.

Results A 52-year-old Sri Lankan male developed painful vesicular eruptions over the right ophthalmic dermatome and was treated with oral acyclovir (800 mg, five times daily). About seven days after vesicle crusting and resolution of herpetic pain, he began experiencing brief episodes of sharp right supraorbital pain radiating to the vertex and temporal region. Each attack lasted 10–15 s, occurred about three times per hour, with a severity of 8/10. His sleep and daily functioning were disrupted. Associated ipsilateral conjunctival injection, tearing, and partial ptosis were reported and were observed during consultation (Fig. 1 A). Healed vesicles and skin allodynia over the right forehead were noted (Fig. 1B). Corneal reflexes and visual acuity were normal. Haemoglobin A1c was elevated at 14.2%, prompting insulin therapy. Brain imaging was unremarkable. Treatment included oral prednisolone (15 mg/day, tapered by 5 mg/week), carbamazepine (100 mg t.d.s., increased to 200 mg t.d.s. from week two), pregabalin (75 mg nocte), and tramadol (50 mg nocte). At two-week follow-up, pain severity reduced to 1/10, and he remained headache-free at one year.

Conclusion This case underscores a SUNCT-like syndrome following ophthalmic zoster, which appears more pharmacoresponsive than primary SUNCT. Immunosuppressive states like diabetes, should be considered underlying zoster reactivation.

P659 Beyond cerebrum and neurosurgery: A systematic review on Chiari Malformation Type I integrating molecular and behavioral methodologies

I. Oezdil1,2, D. Aprile3, C. Beste1,4,5

1TU Dresden, Faculty of Psychology, Dresden, Germany; 2TU Dresden, Faculty of Medicine, Department of Psychotherapy and Psychosomatic Medicine, Dresden, Germany; 3Human Technopole, Milan, Italy; 4TU Dresden, Faculty of Medicine, Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Dresden, Germany; 5TU Dresden, Faculty of Medicine, University Neuropsychology Center, Dresden, Germany

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P659

Objective Chiari malformation type 1 (CM1) radiologically defined as a caudal displacement of cerebellar tonsils exceeding 5 mm through the foramen magnum, represents the most prevalent subtype of Chiari Malformations—a group of developmental disorders characterized by congenital posterior fossa deformities. Given CM1’s predominantly asymptomatic or paucisymptomatic clinical course, epidemiological data primarily reflects symptomatic cases, with prevalence traditionally estimated between 0.1 and 1%. We endeavor to propose a transdisciplinary conceptualization of CM1 that illuminates the cerebellum’s extensive non-motor functions. This review synthesizes evidence from 60+ studies spanning genetics, genomics, neuropsychology, and neuropsychiatry.

Methods Our analysis deconstructs the genetic, familial, and environmental factors through a framework of “CM1 Equifinality” in disease pathogenesis, methodically investigating its significant co-occurrence with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions—particularly autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in both syndromic and isolated cases, where behavioral and genomic tools are consistently validating each other,

Results CM1 frequently presenting alongside functional impairments and problems with self-regulation, as further documented through combined measures of neuropsychology and functional neuroimaging.

Conclusion With this work, we want to emphasize the critical need for psychiatric monitoring, neuropsychological interventions, and psychotraumatological implications in high-risk pediatric populations for CM1 within the general population. We also want to highlight how CM1 represents a unique model of study integrating developmental biology, cognition, and psychiatry through a cerebellar lens. We propose CblOs as a potential tool foreseeing the use of 3D in vitro models to recapitulate the cellular and molecular features of ASD and ADHD in CM1.

P660 COACT study: CGRPmAbs + OnabotulinumtoxinA assessment of chronic migraine treatments study

1Chicago Headache Center and Research Institute, Chicago, IL, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P660

Objective To evaluate the safety and efficacy of combination therapy with the calcitonin gene-related peptide monoclonal antibody (CGRP mAb) fremanezumab and onabotulinumtoxinA in patients with chronic migraine (CM) who were previously treated with a stable dose of onabotulinumtoxinA.

Methods This was a phase 4 prospective, open-label intervention conducted at the Chicago Headache Center and Research Institute. Forty-nine adult patients with CM on stable doses of onabotulinumtoxinA (155 or 195 units) received monthly fremanezumab (225 mg) over a 24-week period. The trial aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of the combined treatment of onabotulinumtoxinA with fremanezumab. Monthly headache days (MHD), monthly migraine days (MMD), and Headache Impact Test (HIT-6) scores were assessed at baseline, week 12, and week 24. Paired t-tests were used to evaluate mean changes from baseline.

Conclusion The addition of fremanezumab to onabotulinumtoxinA resulted in significant reductions in monthly migraine days at 12 weeks and 24 weeks (p <0.001). Significant reductions in HIT-6 scores at 12 weeks and 24 weeks were also seen. These findings support the use of CGRP mAbs and onabotulinumtoxinA for the preventive treatment of chronic migraine.Fig. 1 (abstract P660).

P661 Ubrogepant utilization during prodrome: A case report

B. Torphy1, M. Smith1, S. Koseli1, A. Rakhangi1, S. Cordon1

1Chicago Headache Center and Research Institute, Chicago, IL, USA

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P661

All patient gave their informed consent to publish their details in an open access journal.

Objective To report the successful treatment of migraine episodes with ubrogepant taken during the prodrome phase.

Methods An extensive chart review was conducted to examine a patient’s progress over time with the treatment of migraine attacks with ubrogepant, which was taken during the prodrome phase.

Results The patient reported experiencing neck pain followed by moderate to severe headache. This was identified as her prodrome symptom, and she was advised to take ubrogepant when she experienced neck pain. The patient was able to recognize her prodrome symptom, neck pain, and treat her migraine episodes earlier. Conclusion The success the patient demonstrated with administering ubrogepant at prodrome underscores the importance of the timing of acute treatment for migraine. P662 Comparison of functional responses to CGRP and related peptides in human middle meningeal and superficial temporal arteries

M. Pawlowsky1, D. M. Boucherie1, T. de Vries1, R. Dammers1, A. Vincent1, E. Rivera-Mancilla1, A. H. J. Danser1, A. Maassen van den Brink1

1Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Rotterdam, Netherlands

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P662

Objective The role of extracranial arteries during migraine attacks is unclear. Our aim was to compare the vasodilatory responses of extracranial human superficial temporal arteries (HSTA) and intracranial middle meningeal arteries (HMMA) to CGRP, the amylin analogue pramlintide, and adrenomedullin 2 (AM2), as well as the inhibition induced by the CGRP receptor-binding monoclonal antibody erenumab and the CGRP receptor antagonist olcegepant.

Methods HSTA and HMMA were obtained from patients undergoing neurosurgery (HSTA: n=8, aged 55 ± 15 years, 38% female; HMMA: n=52, aged 54 ± 15 years, 62% female, age and sex not available for 2 donors). After precontraction with 30 mM KCl, concentration-response curves were constructed to CGRP (10 pM - 1 µM), pramlintide (10 pM – 300 nM), and adrenomedullin 2 (10 pM – 300 nM). Concentration-response curves to CGRP were constructed in the presence or absence of 1µM olcegepant or 1µM erenumab.

Results CGRP induced similar, potent vasodilatory responses in HSTA and HMMA (pEC50 8.06 ± 1.10 vs. 8.25 ± 0.46, p=0.65; Emax 63% ± 31% vs. 64% ± 19%, p=0.96). Pramlintide responses were comparable (pEC50 6.33 ± 1.86 vs. 6.40 ± 1.66, p=0.95; Emax 23% ± 12% vs. 18% ± 10%, p=0.48), as were AM2 responses (pEC50 6.56 ± 1.10 vs. 7.03 ± 1.00, p=0.41; Emax 58% ± 23% vs. 54% ± 24%, p=0.74). The blocking potency of olcegepant and erenumab was similar across both arteries (olcegepant: pKB HSTA 8.21 ± 1.36 vs. HMMA 8.52 ± 1.27, p= 0.63; erenumab: pKB HSTA 7.36 ± 0.97 vs. HMMA 7.26 ± 1.02, p= 0.87).

Conclusion The comparable responses of HSTA (innervated by V3) and HMMA (innervated by V1) to CGRP, pramlintide and AM2 do not challenge the potential role of extracranial arteries in the pathophysiology of migraine. Similar CGRP inhibition in both arteries may contribute to the antimigraine effects of CGRP receptor-targeting medications at either location. Finally, these results may also suggest that pain pathways relevant to migraine may overlap with those implicated in temporomandibular disorders.

P664 Comparative efficacy and safety of Levetiracetam versus valproic acid in migraine prophylaxis: A systematic review and meta-analysis

S. Arsalan Wasti1, A. Wasti2, M. Usman Iqbal1

1King Edward Medical University, Lahore, Pakistan; 2Continental Medical College, Lahore, Pakistan

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P664

Objective To systematically compare levetiracetam to valproic acid in the context of migraine prophylaxis.

Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane, Scientific Information Database and Clinicaltrials.gov from inception to September 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing levetiracetam to valproate in migraine prophylaxis. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR) and continuous outcomes as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) in Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4.1.

Results Four trials were included (N = 288, 93.9% female, mean ages 33 to 36 years). Compared to valproate, levetiracetam use was associated with significantly greater reductions in mean headache frequency from baseline (MD -1.07, 95% CI -2.04 to -0.11). However, no significant differences were seen for reductions in mean headache duration, mean headache severity and MIDAS scores. Adverse event rates also remained comparable across the two treatment groups.

Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis suggests that levetiracetam may provide a modest advantage over valproic acid in reducing headache frequency among individuals with migraine. However, the two drugs remained broadly comparable with respect to headache duration, severity, functional disability, and tolerability. However, larger, high-quality trials are needed to further explore the comparative efficacy and safety profiles of levetiracetam and valproic acid, so as to better inform individualized treatment strategies in migraine prophylaxis.Fig. 1 (abstract P664).

P665 The multimodal 7T-MRI study on the mechanism of migraine chronification: Temporal evolution of driving hubs based on dynamic causal network

L. Ma1,2,3,4, R. Wang1,2,3, Z. Dong1,2

1International Headache Center, Beijing, China; 2Chinese PLA General Hospital, Department of Neurology, the First Medical Cente, Beijing, China; 3Medical School of Chinese PLA, Beijing, China; 4PLA Joint Logistic Support Force 983rd Hospital, Department of Neurology, Tianjin, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P665

Objective This study aims to explore the dynamic evolution of brain structure and function in migraine patients as the disease progresses, utilizing multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). It also seeks to identify key neural networks that drive the chronicity of migraines.

Methods Migraine patients, including those with episodic and chronic migraines, along with age- and education-matched healthy controls, were recruited from the Neurology Department’s Headache Center at the PLA General Hospital. Diagnoses were made according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition, by two neurologists. Exclusion criteria included recent medication use (within 3 months) and menstrual period in females. Depression, anxiety, and sleep quality were assessed using the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and PSQI scales, respectively, and headache characteristics were recorded. 7T MRI scans were employed to capture structural and functional brain images, processed via VBM and zfALFF, with adjustments for confounding variables. Multilevel logistic regression was used to identify migraine-related brain regions, construct a disease severity score and a target brain region set. Granger causality testing and cluster analysis were applied to identify key driving networks. Statistical analyses including ADF test and FDR correction ensured robust results.

Results (1) Participant Characteristics The study included 345 participants: 81 healthy controls (HC), 154 with episodic migraines (EM), and 110 with chronic migraines (CM). No significant differences were found in gender, age, or education years among the groups (all P > 0.05); however, age and gender were considered as covariates in further analyses. Compared to the EM group, the CM group had a longer disease duration, significantly higher monthly headache frequency, shorter duration per headache episode, and a higher average medication usage per month, suggesting a higher risk of medication overuse. Psychological and sleep assessments revealed that the CM group scored significantly higher in depression, anxiety, and sleep quality issues compared to both the EM and HC groups (all P < 0.001), indicating more severe psychological and sleep disturbances.

2. Characteristics and Dynamic Evolution of Migraine-Related Brain Regions

2.1Structural and Functional Abnormalities VBM analysis showed significant atrophy in the right thalamic reticular nucleus in both CM (β = -15.294) and EM (β = -8.759) patients (P < 0.001 for both). Asymmetric changes were noted in brainstem nuclei: left locus coeruleus volume increased (CM: β = 4.692; EM: β = 3.313), and right locus coeruleus volume decreased. Significant atrophy was also observed in the right amygdala and accumbens, while CM patients showed increased volume in the prefrontal and cerebellar regions. zfALFF analysis indicates widespread neural activity suppression in EM patients, particularly in the right red nucleus (β = -28.798), bilateral pallidum, and accumbens. CM patients also demonstrated widespread suppression, but with distinct heightened activity in the left substantia nigra pars reticulata (β = 15.797).2.2Brain Region Changes Related to Headache Frequency Sliding window analysis revealed dynamic patterns of brain region characteristics as headache frequency evolved: - Low-Frequency Stage (0-8 days): VBM indicated a negative correlation between volume of left thalamic reticular nucleus and headache severity, with a positive correlation for the left accumbens. zfALFF analysis demonstrated general suppression in the basal ganglia-thalamus system. - High-Frequency Stage (8-14 days): The correlation expanded to wider networks. VBM showed negative correlations with left locus coeruleus and middle frontal gyrus volume, and positive correlations with prefrontal cortex and caudate volume. zfALFF highlighted increased activity in default mode network nodes. - Chronic Stage (15-30 days): Involvement of the sensorimotor and cerebellar systems was evident. P667 Mechanistic study of dopamine and D2 receptors in the medial orbitofrontal cortex involved in migraine

R. Wang1,2,3, Z. Dong1,3

1Chinese PLA General Hospital, Department of Neurology, the First Medical Center, Beijing, China; 2Medical School of Chinese PLA, Beijing, China; 3International Headache Center, Beijing, China

The Journal of Headache and Pain 2026, 27(S1):P667

Objective Chronic Migraine (CM) is a neuropathic pain disorder characterized by recurrent attacks and protracted course, whose pathogenesis is closely associated with brain network dysfunction. The current brain network dysregulation model of migraine reveals that this disorder results from the disruption of dynamic balance between the “top-down” control network (represented by the prefrontal cortex) and the “bottom-up” sensory network (represented by the insula, thalamus, and brainstem). Among them, the functional decline of the prefrontal cortex leads to impaired filtering and inhibition of pain signals, causing hyperactivity and enhanced connectivity in pain-processing regions such as the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and thalamus, which amplifies pain signals and their affective components, potentially participating in the pathophysiological mechanism of migraine. The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), as a vital component of the prefrontal cortex, has gradually attracted attention for its role in chronic migraine. The dynamic changes of the midbrain dopamine (DA) system play a crucial role in pain modulation. Previous studies have shown that alterations in DA release affect pain perception. Our team’s previous clinical study found that patients with chronic migraine complicated by medication overuse exhibited reduced metabolic levels of dopamine transporter (DAT) in the OFC, particularly in the medial OFC (mOFC), suggesting that dynamic changes in DA in the mOFC may be involved in the pathophysiological mechanism of migraine. Our study focuses on the function of dopamine and its receptors in the medial orbitofrontal cortex, aiming to deeply elucidate the specific mechanism of the midbrain dopamine system in the orbitofrontal cortex in pain regulation of chronic migraine, and to provide new theoretical basis and potential targets for targeted therapy of chronic migraine.

Methods A chronic migraine mouse model was established by repeated administration of glyceryl trinitrate (GTN). In vivo fiber photometry was used to monitor the dynamic changes of dopamine in the mOFC. Calcium imaging and immunofluorescence co-staining of c-Fos were used to detect the signal changes of DRD2+ neurons in this brain region; chemogenetic methods were used to activate and inhibit DRD2+ neurons in the mOFC, and immunofluorescence staining was used to identify the types of DRD2+ neurons. Finally, chemogenetic methods were continued to regulate different types of DRD2+ neurons. Behavioral assessments included pain sensitivity (Von-Frey test) and anxiety-like behavior (elevated plus maze test and light-dark box test).

Results Firstly, repeated GTN injection successfully induced migraine-like phenotypes in mice: compared with the normal saline control group, model mice exhibited significantly decreased periorbital and hindpaw withdrawal thresholds (indicating tactile allodynia) and displayed anxiety-like behaviors—including reduced time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze and decreased entries into the light compartment of the light-dark box. Fiber photometry recordings showed a significant increase in dopamine release in the mOFC of model mice. Molecular biological analyses (Western blot and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction [qPCR]) demonstrated that the expression of DRD2 in the mOFC of model mice was significantly upregulated, while the expression of DRD1 showed no significant change. Calcium imaging combined with c-Fos co-staining further revealed that the calcium signal amplitude and c-Fos-positive rate of DRD2⁺ neurons in the mOFC of model mice were significantly lower than those in the control group, suggesting that the function of DRD2⁺ neurons was inhibited in the migraine model. In addition, chemogenetic inhibition of mOFC DRD2⁺ neurons (via hM4Di) significantly alleviated GTN-induced tactile allodynia: both periorbital and hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were increased compared with model mice treated with normal saline, confirming the analgesic effect of inhibiting mOFC DRD2⁺ neurons. Subsequent immunofluorescence co-staining showed that mOFC DRD2⁺ neurons were predominantly excitatory: Camk2a⁺ excitatory neurons accounted for 87.3712±0.90787% of total DRD2⁺ neurons, while GABAergic interneuron accounted for only 10.3226±0.56701%. Finally, subtype-specific chemogenetic manipulation revealed that inhibition of excitatory DRD2⁺ (Camk2a⁺/DRD2⁺) neurons significantly improved both GTN-induced tactile allodynia and anxiety-like behaviors. However, inhibition of inhibitory DRD2⁺ (GABA/DRD2⁺) neurons had no significant effect on migraine-related behaviors.

Conclusion This study clarifies the key role of dopamine and D2 receptors in the mOFC in chronic migraine: in CM model mice, dopamine release in the mOFC is increased, which activates dopamine D2 receptor and inhibits excitatory DRD2+ neurons dominated by Camk2a⁺, thereby improving pain hypersensitivity and anxiety-like behavior. This finding supplements the specific mechanism of the prefrontal control network in the migraine brain network dysregulation model, provides the excitatory DRD2+ neurons in the mOFC as a potential target for targeted therapy of CM, and also lays a foundation for subsequent exploration of the interaction and effect of this pathway with other analgesic systems.Fig. 1 (abstract P667).Fig. 2 (abstract P667).Fig. 3 (abstract P667).Fig. 4 (abstract P667).
